title: LLM Agents for Time-Series: A Survey
abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly being developed for time-series problems, but their design choices vary substantially across task settings. This survey adopts a problem-driven taxonomy that organizes these systems by the time-series problems they address rather than by isolated technical components. We group existing systems into four categories: forecasting and reasoning, augmentation and synthesis, anomaly detection and diagnosis, and decision support. Within each category, we examine how task requirements shape agent architecture, tool use, and memory design. We further summarize representative datasets and environments, and compare reported model performance under shared or closely related settings. Overall, this survey offers a task-oriented guide to designing LLM-based agents for time-series problems and identifies open gaps for future work.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: DynHD: Hallucination Detection for Diffusion Large Language Models via Denoising Dynamics Deviation Learning
abstract: Diffusion large language models (D-LLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to auto-regressive models due to their iterative refinement capabilities. However, hallucinations remain a critical issue that hinders their reliability. To detect hallucination responses from model outputs, token-level uncertainty (e.g., entropy) has been widely used as an effective signal to indicate potential factual errors. Nevertheless, the fixed-length generation paradigm of D-LLMs implies that tokens contribute unevenly to hallucination detection, with only a small subset providing meaningful signals. Moreover, the evolution trend of uncertainty throughout the diffusion process can also provide important signals, highlighting the necessity of modeling its denoising dynamics for hallucination detection. In this paper, we propose DynHD that bridge these gaps from both spatial (token sequence) and temporal (denoising dynamics) perspectives. To address the information density imbalance across tokens, we propose a semantic-aware evidence construction module that extracts hallucination-indicative signals by filtering out non-informative tokens and emphasizing semantically meaningful ones. To model denoising dynamics for hallucination detection, we introduce a reference evidence generator that learns the expected evolution trajectory of uncertainty evidence, along with a deviation-based hallucination detector that makes predictions by measuring the discrepancy between the observed and reference trajectories. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DynHD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while achieving higher efficiency across multiple benchmarks and backbone models.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SAVANT: A Neuro-Symbolic Verification Framework for Adjuvant Design
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can propose vaccine adjuvant designs with plausible mechanistic rationales, but such outputs often lack grounding in established immunological knowledge. We present SAVANT, a neuro-symbolic framework for LLM-based adjuvant design that combines two-stage constrained generation with literature-grounded verification. SAVANT first generates a natural-language design rationale, then renders it into an ontology-constrained domain-specific language (DSL) using logic masks and finite-state control. To reason under fragmented evidence and incomplete first-principles rules, SAVANT verifies generated designs against literature-derived symbolic evidence through minimal sub-theorem proof. In expert-aligned evaluation, SAVANT shows greater stability in stage-level rank alignment than the strongest LLM-judge baselines, while achieving the strongest alignment for immune-effect support and mechanistic reasoning. SAVANT provides graded, interpretable assessments that distinguish supported mechanisms, under-supported hypotheses, and knowledge gaps for hypothesis-driven experimentation. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/banjiuyufen/SAVANT.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ToolSense: A Diagnostic Framework for Auditing Parametric Tool Knowledge in LLMs
abstract: Large language models deployed as agents over large tool catalogs face a critical tool-retrieval bottleneck. As embedding-based retrieval approaches rely on compact encoders that may under-capture specialized tool semantics, parametric tool retrieval addresses this by encoding each tool as a virtual token appended to the LLM vocabulary, fine-tuned in two stages (memorization then retrieval SFT) to use the LLM as a retriever, achieving strong performance on standard ToolBench retrieval benchmarks. Yet these benchmarks use verbose, fully-specified queries, and their evaluation applies constrained decoding that restricts outputs to valid token paths - neither reveals whether the model actually understands its tools. We introduce **ToolSense**, an open-source LLM-powered diagnostic framework that takes any tool catalog as input and automatically generates three benchmarks: a Realistic Retrieval Benchmark (RRB) with queries at three ambiguity tiers, an MCQ probing benchmark, and a QA probing benchmark. Applying ToolSense to ToolBench (\sim47k tools) and evaluating five parametric model training configurations reveals a knowledge-retrieval dissociation: on RRB queries, several configurations collapse by \sim**50-64 percentage points** compared to fully-specified ToolBench benchmarks, falling below embedding-model baseline. Additionally, despite strong retrieval performance, some models score near-random on factual probes, suggesting a knowledge-retrieval dissociation. We open-source the ToolSense framework and the ToolBench diagnostic benchmarks to encourage further research. (see supplementary material)
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: GUI-CC: Benchmarking Contextual Consistency of GUI World Models as Agent Environments
abstract: GUI world models are increasingly evaluated as one-step next-screen predictors, yet their intended use is often as multi-step environments for GUI agents. This mismatch leaves a key requirement under-tested: generated states must remain contextually consistent when they are repeatedly reused for future interaction. We introduce GUI-CC, a benchmark that evaluates contextual consistency of GUI world models as agent environments rather than isolated next-screen predictors. GUI-CC contains two complementary tracks: an offline reference-action track that rolls models along real mobile GUI trajectories, and an online agent-loop track that lets fixed probing agents interact with model-generated UIs. We construct 500 offline trajectory tasks from GUIOdyssey and 200 emulator-verified online tasks across 30 mobile apps. GUI-CC evaluates transition fidelity, transition plausibility, contextual consistency, and task progress. Experiments show that plausible single-step generation does not guarantee reliable environment simulation: current models often produce usable-looking screens while failing to preserve task-relevant context or support executable multi-step rollouts.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Caught in the Story: Narrative Captivity in Multi-turn LLMs Conversation
abstract: People increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for everyday advice, making ethically charged interpersonal problems a practical moral-advisory context. Most prior work has studied this context through single-turn judgments or pressure-laden rebuttals, assumptions that poorly match how guidance is sought in real-world contexts. These assumptions leave unclear whether narration alone, without an explicit opposing position, can shift model judgments during multi-turn moral consultation. Yet real-world moral-conflict conversation often elicits one party’s self-justifying account, which can unfold over multiple turns and create information asymmetry. We introduce narrative captivity, a failure mode in which a model treats an unopposed one-sided account as complete and aligns with the narrator’s interpretation without seeking missing perspectives. To measure this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of 5,078 interpersonal-conflict scenarios spanning six moral dimensions. Across 17 LLMs, narrative captivity is widespread: end-state judgments under multi-turn narration shift by 25 percentage points on average beyond the matched single-turn baseline. Stage-level analysis identifies preference optimization as a major contributor, while four inference-time strategies provide only partial mitigation. We hope our project fosters LLM advisors that preserve independent judgment in real-world consultation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Gradient-Free Test-Time Adaptation for Few-Shot Online Clustering with Large Language Models
abstract: We study few-shot online clustering (FSOC), where an unlabelled stream must be assigned to a dynamically growing cluster inventory using only a few labelled support examples for currently observed classes. We propose a two-component test-time gradient-free framework. First, we adapt Wasserstein Generative Flow Networks (wGFN) as an amortised LLM-based policy for in-distribution assignment and out-of-distribution (OOD) rejection. Unlike prior work that trains separate policies for each evaluation class set, we show that a single policy trained on a few classes generalises to novel support classes at test time without parameter updates and further replace fixed rejection thresholds with a Dirichlet evidence model over candidate class assignments. Second, rejected OOD examples enter an oracle-mediated cluster-formation stage. Under shuffled stream orderings, this stage can create noisy provisional support sets that corrupt later assignments. To address this, we introduce a von Mises–Fisher Dirichlet Process Mixture Model warm start to provide oracle-independent cluster structure over unit-normalised text embeddings before oracle-mediated formation. This improves clustering quality, in some settings by \sim 2\times, even with small LLMs (<1B parameters). To our knowledge, this is the first FSOC framework to couple amortised LLM-based assignment with Bayesian non-parametric warm-starting, enabling growing cluster inventories without data augmentation, novel-class parameter updates or predefined cluster counts.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Target-Local Verifier Choice in Best-of-K Reasoning Selection
abstract: Modern reasoning systems increasingly rely on verifier-guided selection: sample several solution traces, score them with a reward model, and return the top-ranked answer. In multi-generator deployments, this verifier is often reused across generators. We ask whether this reuse assumption is reliable. On a 34-generator math panel with K{=}64 candidates per problem and 7 verifiers, the 7B process reward model (PRM-7B) is the strongest fixed verifier, but a per-target single-verifier oracle gains +1.6 percentage points (pp). We then ask whether this target-local mismatch is actionable. Four label-free candidate-text statistics predict the coarse PRM outcome-verifier regime, and three budgeted responses improve over fixed PRM on the 22-target first-pass panel: a no-label gated router (+1.41 pp), PRM+V4 fusion (+2.35 pp), and a labelled PRM-only verifier-allocation arbiter (PVA-Adapt; +2.26 pp). A same-panel American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) 2026 held-out slice gives +3.88 pp, and a second candidate-bank check keeps the scored and labelled gains positive while weakening the no-label router. We frame the result as a seed- and verifier-family-conditioned deployment diagnostic rather than a universal routing rule; a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) replication also finds no positive transfer from better selected traces.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Syntactic-Guided Semantic Attention Matrix Enhancement for Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction
abstract: Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction (ASTE) is a fine-grained task in Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA), aiming to extract triplets of aspect terms, their corresponding opinion terms, and sentiment orientation. Recent studies have employed semantic and syntactic features to enhance extraction performance. However, as the extraction of both syntactic and semantic information is not task-specific, such information does not target aspect-opinion pairs within sentences, thereby potentially introducing noise unrelated to the task. To address this issue, we propose a Syntactic-Guided Semantic Attention Matrix Enhancement (SG-SAME) framework. First, we use a multi-view masking mechanism and a biaffine-based gating module to derive a task-aligned shared matrix from the existing semantic and syntactic matrices. Second, the shared matrix is injected into the attention score matrix of LLM layers to enhance the model’s representation learning. Finally, we propose a chain-of-thought (CoT) framework with negative candidate injection to steer the model toward autonomous reasoning and error self-rectification. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in ASTE tasks. Code will be available.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: A Man’s World: Measuring Gender Bias in Occupational Status Judgments with Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models can be used in applications that analyze people in professional and social contexts. This raises concerns about whether these models reproduce occupational gender stereotypes. However, it is challenging to evaluate these associations because naturally collected images often combine demographic attributes with clothing, pose, background, and other status-related cues. We introduce a paired-image benchmark to study occupational status judgments in VLMs, containing 5,487 human-validated synthetic images spanning 41 ISCO-08 sub-major occupational groups aggregated into 10 major groups, 7 ethnicity categories, and 5 age groups. Men and women are matched based on occupation, age, ethnicity, and workplace context. We evaluate 5 VLMs using spatial comparisons that avoid direct gender references, explicit gender comparisons, and structured reasoning prompts. We observe persistent male-oriented associations in earnings judgments, even when the prompts avoid direct references to gender. Furthermore, we find that men are more frequently associated with authority, seniority, and earning potential, whereas women are more often associated with warmth. Promotion likelihood exhibits a model-family-dependent pattern: male-oriented associations emerge across Qwen-3-VL models, whereas both Gemma-3 models show the opposite, female-oriented pattern. These findings show that occupational gender stereotypes persist in the evaluated VLMs even under tightly controlled visual conditions. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/NLP-UMUTeam/OccuBiasBench
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CoverPoison: One-to-Many Knowledge Corruption Attacks on Strictly Black-Box RAG Systems
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to knowledge corruption attacks, where adversaries inject malicious texts into external corpora to manipulate generated responses. Existing one-to-many attacks can compromise multiple queries with a small number of injected texts, but they typically require white-box access to the target retriever for gradient-based optimization. In contrast, existing black-box attacks are more practical but usually allow each malicious text to target only one query. In this paper, we study one-to-many knowledge corruption attacks against strictly black-box RAG systems, where the attacker has no access to the target retriever, generator, or corpus contents. We propose CoverPoison, a black-box method that combines competitive similarity clustering, coverage-oriented optimization, and T5-based text refinement. Competitive similarity clustering improves query grouping quality, while the coverage-oriented objective encourages each candidate to cover more queries through query-specific retrieval thresholds. Experiments on three datasets show that CoverPoison substantially improves black-box attack effectiveness. Further analyses across RAG configurations, attack objectives, and defenses validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Attributing and Exploiting Safety Vectors through Global Optimization in Large Language Models
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to mitigate risks, their safety guardrails remain fragile against jailbreak attacks. This reveals limited understanding of components governing safety. Existing methods rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. However, they overlook the cooperative interactions between different components in LLMs, such as attention heads, which jointly contribute to safety mechanisms. We propose Global Optimization for Safety Vector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads through global optimization over all heads simultaneously. We employ two complementary activation repatching strategies: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation. These strategies identify two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors with consistently low overlap, termed Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety purposes. Through systematic analyses, we find that complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total heads are repatched across all models. Building on these insights, we develop a novel inference-time white-box jailbreak attack and a complementary detection-based defense, both grounded in the identified safety vectors. The attack achieves superior performance, while the defense yields strong detection across diverse attack types, providing robust evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed GOSV framework in LLM safety interpretability.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Preference Learning: Response-Preference Disentangled Reinforcement Optimization for Robust Visual Quality Assessment
abstract: Visual Quality Assessment (QA) in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) jointly predicts absolute quality scores and relative perceptual rankings. Existing methods optimize score regression or ranking within a unified formulation, leading to unstable predictions and weak generalization under stochastic generation. We find this instability is amplified by response variability in MLLM reasoning, where stochastic decoding produces inconsistent score distributions and degrades cross-dataset robustness. This indicates QA depends not only on preference alignment, but also on response-level stability. We propose PreResQ-R1, a Response-Preference Disentangled Ranking-and-Scoring Reinforcement Optimization framework. It decouples response stabilization and preference learning, with a dual-branch reward modeling intra-sample consistency and inter-sample score-ranking alignment. For video QA, we introduce temporal-spatial evidence aggregation without dense motion modeling. PreResQ-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming comparable methods by 5.60% on IQA benchmarks and 2.53% on VQA benchmarks.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Making Every Verified Token Count: Adaptive Verification for MoE Speculative Decoding
abstract: Tree-based speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by verifying multiple draft candidates in parallel, but this advantage weakens for sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. As the draft tree grows, different branches activate different experts, expanding the union of activated experts and substantially increasing target-side verification cost. We propose EVICT, a training-free, hyperparameter-free, and lossless adaptive verification method for MoE speculative decoding. EVICT makes every verified token count by truncating the draft tree before target verification and retaining only the cost-effective prefix. It leverages fine-grained drafter signals to estimate candidate benefit, combines them with offline-profiled verification cost, and remains highly compatible with the high-performance graph-based serving framework SGLang. Extensive experiments on diverse MoE backbones and benchmarks show that EVICT achieves up to 2.35\times speedup over autoregressive decoding and an average 1.21\times speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline EAGLE-3, while significantly reducing unnecessary expert activations during verification.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Diagnosis Is Already in the Notes: A Channel-Wise Audit of Diagnostic Shortcuts in Clinical-Text Benchmarks
abstract: Medical AI benchmarks routinely pair a diagnostic image with the same-visit clinical record, delete the recorded diagnosis, and treat what remains as auxiliary context. The recipe is reasonable. It is not. On 5904 ophthalmic visits across eight cohorts, a frozen text probe still recovers the disease label from the diagnosis-redacted record at 0.944 macro-AUROC, against 0.998 on the unredacted record; the most aggressive dictionary scrub closes less than one further percentage point. The diagnosis is already in the notes.It is not in one place. A clinical record is written during the diagnostic process, and its fingerprints persist across channels: narrative text alone reaches 0.978, and a view that erases every value and exposes only which fields were populated still reaches 0.854. We introduce CRAFT (Channel-wise Redaction And Floor Test), a portable audit protocol that renders each record into redacted and channel-isolated views and reports each channel’s label recoverability; rankings reproduce under Qwen3.5-9B. Before clinical-text or image-text fusion gains are read as cross-modal reasoning, the text branch’s channel-level shortcut floors must be reported alongside them. https://github.com/yhc98002-bit/The-Diagnosis-Is-Already-in-the-Notes
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ToSCA: Leveraging Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning on Temporal and Strategic Abstractions of Conversational Agents
abstract: Humans naturally exhibit multiple forms of abstraction in reasoning and interaction, including temporal abstraction across decision timescales and strategic abstraction over communicative intents. Inspired by these complementary abstractions, we propose a two-level hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) framework for conversational agents that bridges the gap between existing token-level and utterance-level RL methods. Built upon a two-level Markov decision process (MDP), our framework conditions token-level response generation on utterance-level actions represented by explicit textual strategies. Based on theoretical analysis and efficiency considerations, we employ DQN to optimize the high-level Q-network and PPO to train the low-level actor-critic. To further alleviate reward sparsity and facilitate convergence, we introduce a dual-granularity reward mechanism that combines the utterance-level satisfaction score with token-level intrinsic self-consistency and a KL-divergence penalty. Experiments on both daily-life and emotional support conversations demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms a wide range of baselines in both strategy determination and response quality. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/AaronJi/ToSCA.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Learnable Termination Safeguard: Token-Level Early Termination for Efficient LLM Safety Monitoring
abstract: Large language models exhibit non-negligible risks of generating policy-violating content, underscoring the need for effective and timely guardrail mechanisms. Existing streaming safety monitoring approaches enable detection during decoding, but still lack a reliable mechanism for deciding when to terminate generation, limiting their ability to act on early risk signals that are often sparse and unstable under partial observability. In response, we propose LTS, a token-level framework that explicitly learns a stopping criterion for preemptive early termination. LTS introduces a risk-aware STOP head for token-level risk assessment and leverages temporally structured supervision with multiscale evidence to model the evolution of safety risks during generation. By casting streaming safety monitoring as a constrained online stopping task and incorporating exponential moving average temporal aggregation, LTS enables reliable translation of emerging risk evidence into stable and timely termination decisions. LTS achieves an F1 score of 95.5% and is able to terminate harmful content at 13% of the generated sequence, substantially outperforming existing methods during early generation. In realistic streaming settings, it achieves around 90% token reduction.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Entity Blackboard: Structured Agent Memory for Long Document Summarization
abstract: Hierarchical merging is commonly used to summarize long documents by splitting the input into chunks, summarizing each chunk independently, and merging the results into a final summary. However, because each chunk is processed independently, entity state changes across chunks are not tracked, leading to coherence and consistency issues in the final summary. We propose EntityBB (Entity Blackboard), an agent memory framework that equips chunk-based LLM summarizers with structured entity memory. During sequential chunk processing, the model records and updates entity states through tool calls, while automatic safeguards and model-driven rejection limit noisy writes. Experiments on three long document summarization benchmarks show that EntityBB consistently improves over a controlled hierarchical merging baseline across ROUGE and BERTScore, while NarrativeFactScore indicates improved source-grounded factuality. Targeted human and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations further indicate fewer entity-level issues and higher judged summary quality.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EntropyPrune: Matrix Entropy Guided Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) incur substantial inference cost due to the processing of hundreds of visual tokens per image. Although token pruning has proven effective for accelerating inference, determining when and where to prune remains largely heuristic. Existing approaches typically rely on static, empirically selected layers, which limit interpretability and transferability across models. In this work, we introduce a matrix-entropy perspective and identify an ”Entropy Collapse Layer”(ECL), where the information content of visual representations exhibits a sharp and consistent drop, which provides a principled criterion for selecting the pruning stage. Building on this observation, we propose EntropyPrune, a novel matrix-entropy-guided token pruning framework that quantifies the information value of individual visual tokens and prunes redundant ones without relying on attention maps. Moreover, to enable efficient computation, we exploit the spectral equivalence of dual Gram matrices, reducing the complexity of entropy computation and yielding up to a 64x theoretical speedup. Extensive experiments on diverse multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that EntropyPrune consistently outperforms established competitive pruning methods in both accuracy and efficiency. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, our method achieves a 57.7% reduction in FLOPs while preserving 98.8% of the original performance. Furthermore, EntropyPrune generalizes effectively to high-resolution and video-based models, highlighting the strong robustness and scalability in practical MLLM acceleration.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Benchmarking Machine Translation on Chinese Social Media Texts
abstract: The prevalence of rapidly evolving slang, neologisms, and highly stylized expressions in informal user-generated text, particularly on Chinese social media, poses significant challenges for Machine Translation (MT) benchmarking. Specifically, we identify two primary obstacles: (1) data scarcity, as high-quality parallel data requires bilingual annotators familiar with platform-specific slang, and stylistic cues; and (2) metric limitations, where traditional evaluators like COMET often fail to capture stylistic fidelity and non-standard expressions. To bridge these gaps, we first introduce CSM-MTBench, an expert-curated benchmark covering five Chinese→foreign language directions and comprising 10,915 total instances, organized into two subsets: **Fun Posts**, featuring context-rich content with frequent slang and neologisms, and **Social Snippets**, focusing on concise, emotion- and style-driven expressions. Next, we propose tailored evaluation approaches for each subset, including slang translation success rate and style-preservation metrics combining embeddings and LLM-asa-judge evaluation. Experiments on over 20 models reveal substantial variation in how current MT systems handle semantic fidelity, slang translation, and stylistic nuances. We further look into model behaviors through prompt sensitivity analysis and qualitative case studies, highlighting the challenges of translating these informal expressions. CSM-MTBench thus serves as a rigorous testbed for advancing MT systems capable of mastering real-world Chinese social media texts.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EDGE: Error Dependency Graph-Guided Multi-Error Attribution in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agent failures often contain multiple related errors rather than a single mistake. Existing attribution methods usually identify a responsible agent, step, or root cause, but do not explicitly model dependency between errors. We introduce EDGE, an error dependency graph-guided framework for multi-error attribution in LLM agent traces. EDGE constructs an error dependency graph from observed error events and validates a reliable causal subset through counterfactual rollout. The inference graph guides a two-stage LLM-as-judge detector for error attribution, and the intervention-validated subgraph provides a more reliable basis for explanation and repair analysis. Experiments on TRAIL and MAST show that EDGE improves category-level multi-error attribution across most evaluated models and settings. Experiments with adapted Who&When-style prompts show that the graph helps across prompting strategies. These results suggest that dependency structure is a useful diagnostic prior for agent failures beyond isolated root-cause prediction.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: FSA-GRPO: Teaching Auditory LLMs to Use Few-Shot Demonstrations
abstract: Few-shot prompting provides an effective way to adapt auditory large language models to low-resource tasks such as children’s speech recognition. However, most auditory large language models are not explicitly trained to perform inference in this demonstration-conditioned format, limiting the extent to which they can benefit from In-Context Learning (ICL). To address this limitation, we introduce Few-Shot Aware GRPO (FSA-GRPO), an RL-based post-training recipe that uses a specially designed reward to encourage the model to leverage few-shot demonstrations, thereby strengthening its few-shot adaptation ability. Notably, training with only 2k high-resource adult ASR utterances improves the model’s general few-shot adaptation ability, yielding gains not only in children’s speech recognition (53.9% relative WER reduction without any in-domain training) but also in multilingual ASR (including low-resource languages), speech translation, and audio understanding. We further study data selection and the weight and similarity cutoffs of the auxiliary reward to identify an effective training recipe. Our experiments show that when in-domain data are unavailable or cannot be used for training, FSA-GRPO is more effective than direct tuning on related out-of-domain data.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Trust Meets Truth: Trust–Truth Separability in LLM-as-Judge
abstract: LLM-as-Judge systems can produce multi-field evaluations, such as trustworthiness, reliability, and factuality. These outputs are often interpreted as independent evidence. We test this assumption for a common pair of judgments: trust scoring and binary truth classification. On correctness-controlled QA, LLM judges align trust scores with truth verdicts more tightly than human behavioral reference, suggesting weaker separations between trust and truth judgment. We then apply stress tests by changing only source cues of identical QA between Human and AI, while holding QA content fixed. Source attribution shifts not only trust scores but also truth verdicts and logit-derived correct-side probabilities. Results show that current LLM-as-Judge protocols should not treat trust scores as independent evidence for truth judgments without testing their separability under trust-relevant perturbations.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Diverse Thinking: Breaking Oppositions in Debates to Foster Synergized Reasoning via Multi-Agent Collaboration
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently face limitations, such as judgment biases and cognitive deadlocks, in complex reasoning due to “Degradation of Thought” in self-reflection. While Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) approaches attempt to address this issue, their inherently adversarial nature suppresses diverse perspectives by overemphasizing antagonism, which results in the loss of partially valid reasoning. In this paper, we propose Multi-Agent Diverse Thinking (MADT), a novel cognitive framework that redefines multi-agent collaboration by shifting from adversarial confrontation toward constructive synergy. To break the oppositional deadlock found in traditional debates, MADT decomposes the thinking process into fine-grained modules: an Affirmative Thinker to preserve rational components, a Critical Thinker to rectify errors, and a Growth-Minded Thinker to provide optimization suggestions. These agents jointly foster a synergistic environment where specialized roles protect valid logic while iteratively refining flaws. Meanwhile, a Leader agent coordinates the collaborations and synthesizes the feedback from multiple thinkers to produce the final result. Extensive experiments on Common Machine Translation and Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic Reasoning tasks show that MADT consistently outperforms Self-Reflection and MAD baselines, validating the superior ability to enhance complex logical and reasoning performance in LLMs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Trust Your Guide Only When Certain: Uncertainty-Aware Sparse Alignment at Inference Time
abstract: A prominent paradigm in inference-time alignment employs lightweight supervisors to steer Large Language Models (LLMs). Through empirical analysis, we identify a structural mismatch in this paradigm: weak supervisors exhibit pervasive high entropy across the vast majority of tokens, yet prevailing dense intervention approaches mandate supervision at every decoding step. This leads to frequent low-confidence interventions that can disrupt valid base-model reasoning and incur substantial utility costs. To resolve this, we propose TUSA (Trust-based Uncertainty Sparse Alignment). Moving away from continuous oversight, TUSA reframes alignment as a dynamic arbitration process, introducing an uncertainty-aware arbiter that authorizes intervention only when two conditions are met: the supervisor is confident and the token is semantically salient. This mechanism effectively filters out uncertainty-driven noise and redundant supervision. Extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show that TUSA consistently improves both safety alignment and general helpfulness. By bypassing approximately 50% of alignment steps, it not only enhances safety preference by up to 15.6%, but also boosts general preference rates by up to 12.0% compared to the dense baseline, demonstrating that selective, high-precision alignment can outperform continuous supervision.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Aligned but Flattened: Analyzing the Trade-off between Cultural Alignment and Diversity in LLMs
abstract: Cultural fine-tuning has become the de facto paradigm for building culture-aware large language models (LLMs), yet existing optimization exclusively for alignment scores provides an incomplete portrait of cultural fidelity by systematically obscuring inherent cultural diversity. This unidimensional evaluation lens prompts a fundamental question: do models genuinely perceive distinct cultural nuances, or do they merely memorize dominant cultural values? To address this, we propose a synergistic evaluation framework that jointly formalizes cultural alignment and diversity. Through extensive benchmarking of six mainstream LLMs on the World Values Survey, this framework uncovers a systematic and critical trade-off: the pursuit of cultural alignment consistently incurs an acute expense of diversity, leading to severe "cultural flattening." Investigating this behavioral shift, we demonstrate that these superficial alignment gains stem from models artificially anchoring to dominant majorities, converging onto a monolithic response pattern that wipes out the heterogeneous distributions inherent to human groups. Crucially, our mechanistic analysis suggests that this diversity collapse is not merely a behavioral anomaly but more likely a structural consequence of the low-rank bias inherent in neural network optimization. Therefore, our findings expose the limitations of current post-training paradigms and call for a shift toward alignment objectives that preserve cross-cultural pluralism.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ClueKV: Self-Guided KV Cache Compression via Adaptive Head Prioritization
abstract: KV cache compression is essential for scaling large language models to long-context inference. However, existing methods excel at explicit retrieval tasks but often degrade on tasks that require multi-step reasoning over dispersed evidence. We present **ClueKV**, a training-free KV cache compression framework that better preserves the reasoning-supportive clues under tight cache budgets. The core design of ClueKV is a self-guided, adaptive headwise token reweighting mechanism. Specifically, ClueKV first uses contrastive probability shifts between the query-conditioned context and a context-free reference to construct an unsupervised clue signal, which highlights context tokens supportive of downstream reasoning under the current input. This signal then serves as self-generated guidance for compression. Based on this signal, ClueKV dynamically identifies, for each input instance, the attention heads that are more aligned with reasoning-relevant context regions, and reweights token importance head by head before KV eviction. Across LongReason, LongBench, and RULER, ClueKV consistently outperforms strong KƒV compression baselines, with the largest gains on complex reasoning tasks. On LongReason, it retains 99.21% of full-KV accuracy at a 50% cache budget, and remains more stable than prior methods as context length increases to 64k tokens. ClueKV also introduces only marginal prefill overhead, making it practical for long-context deployment.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: OptSkills: Learning Generalizable Optimization Skills from Problem Archetypes via Cluster-Based Distillation
abstract: Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically formulate and solve optimization problems from natural language has emerged as an efficient paradigm for automated optimization. However, existing methods still exhibit limited generalization: they are sensitive to superficial narrative variations, reuse experience mainly at the case level, and struggle to adapt to shifted or emerging problem types. We propose OptSkills, an archetype-centric skill learning and reasoning agent system for optimization modeling and solving. To improve robust generalization, our system clusters problems by their underlying archetypes rather than surface narratives. To improve in-distribution generalization, it explores diverse modeling paradigms and solver configurations within each cluster, then distills successful trajectories into reusable workflow-level skills. To improve out-of-distribution generalization, it refines existing skills or expands the skill library using newly obtained trajectories. Our system achieves a state-of-the-art micro-averaged accuracy of 68.27% on datasets encompassing diverse problem types and scenarios. In addition, on MIPLIB-NL, a highly challenging large-scale and high-dimensional benchmark, it achieves 26.91% accuracy, outperforming DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking by 4.53%. After skill learning on Nano-CO, it reaches 72.79% on the OOD NLCO benchmark. Code and skills are available at https://github.com/fujiwaranoM0kou/OptSkills.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MEMMARK: State-Evolution Attribution Watermarking for Agent Long-Term Memory Systems
abstract: Memory-backed agents need provenance that can survive leaked or migrated snapshots, where logs, visible outputs, and trusted metadata may be absent. We propose MEMMARK, a state-evolution attribution watermark that embeds an owner-controlled signal into latent memory-write decisions. At each internal LLM call, MEMMARK samples among admissible candidates using keyed, distribution-preserving selection, and records cryptographic commitments with signed session anchors and reveal evidence. This makes attribution depend on reproducible backend behavior rather than mutable provenance fields. Across A-Mem and Graphiti on LOCOMO, with three LLM backbones, MEMMARK preserves memory utility: Overall F1 retains 99.6 percent of the unwatermarked baseline, while BLEU-1 changes by +0.2 percent. It also provides usable carrier capacity, with 1.16, 1.14, and 1.26 bits of mean entropy for update-target, link-target, and semantic-realization decisions. In the snapshot-only R3 setting, MEMMARK recovers the full 40-bit payload from final snapshots, while wrong-key verification remains near chance. Under nine memory-lifecycle attacks, verification distinguishes tampering, evidence deletion, and partial payload recovery. These results show that robust snapshot-only attribution is feasible for long-term agent memory without surviving traces, trusted metadata, or utility degradation.

title: SurveyGraph: Generating Academic Surveys via Methods-Entity Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Automated survey generation systems increasingly rely on flat retrieval over document collections, limiting their ability to capture the evolutionary structure of research fields. We present SurveyGraph, a framework centered on a Methods-Entity Knowledge Graph (MEKG) that encodes method-level follow-on, competition, and shared-resource relations across papers. The MEKG serves as a unified backbone for core-paper discovery, graph-aware retrieval, hybrid outline generation, and evolutionary narrative synthesis.We evaluate SurveyGraph through a multi-level protocol spanning retrieval benchmarks, semantic-edge validation, citation grounding audits, benchmark-facing collection probes, and same-backend generation-stage diagnostics. In a controlled seven-method equal-budget benchmark, MEKG-anchored fusion achieves the best balance of recall and structural density among all tested methods, demonstrating that typed graph structure provides a complementary signal to simpler retrieval approaches. On the archived graph-native core diagnostic, graph-aware retrieval nearly doubles recall over flat lexical baselines across all eight runs (p = 0.004). A semantic evidence gate with AUC = 0.75 filters noisy edges, and citation-grounding audits over 160 generated sentences confirm 80.6% anchored-or-partial support with evidence-level contrasts validating genuine alignment. Human validation over 108 stratified semantic edges (Cohen’s κ = 0.64 for the binary support decision) confirms 68.5% supported-or-partial after adjudication, with improves relations strongest at 80.6% and extends weakest at 52.8%. A SurveyBench-facing collection probe reaches 0.521 mean reference coverage on four topics under an eight-paper budget; same-backend Qwen diagnostics over a 30-paper/74-relation MEKG further show that removing hybrid outlining lowers artifact organization signals. We report concurrent-system comparisons only as bounded diagnostics rather than same-backend end-to-end claims. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/SurveyGraph.

title: A Survey of LLM Prompt Datasets: Taxonomy, Linguistic Patterns, and Practical Uses
abstract: We compile 129 public LLM prompt datasets with more than 1.22TB and more than 673M instances and organise them into a unified taxonomy. We use seven datasets for detailed analysis and identify lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns that distinguish prompts from general text. We evaluate these features in prompt filtering, source domain routing, and elicited response quality analysis. A 63 dimensional linguistic feature set that can be extracted on a CPU achieves over 91% of the F1 of GPU sentence embeddings and reduces latency per request by nearly half. In cross dataset routing, sentence embeddings reach 0.74 Macro-F1 and a structural feature subset reaches 0.61, compared with the chance level of 0.20. Structural routing features remain negatively associated with elicited response quality after prompt length is controlled on UltraFeedback. The apparent positive association of type to token ratio becomes much smaller under the same control. These findings support prompt processing pipelines that combine efficient structural features with robust semantic routing. Our catalogue, annotations, and code are given at https://github.com/ymzhang-cs/prompt-dataset-analysis.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TimelyRAG: Semantic-Temporal Hybrid Retrieval for Time-Critical Question Answering in Overlapping-Evolving Documents
abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) have advanced open-domain question answering (QA), they remain unreliable when documents evolve through amendments. Existing time-sensitive retrieval methods address only the *disjoint*-evolving environment, where each update is an independent snapshot. However, laws, policies, and regulations often operate in *overlapping*-evolving environments, where amendments override earlier clauses while preserving most content, creating strong semantic overlap across versions. We propose ***TimelyRAG***, a retriever-agnostic framework that incorporates temporal distance into ranking to align queries with version-appropriate documents. We also introduce ***TimelyQABench***, the first benchmark for regulation-heavy domains with overlapping-evolving challenges. Experiments show consistent gains, up to +28.6% in nDCG@10, highlighting the importance of temporal reasoning for reliable QA over evolving documents. All resources are available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/TimelyRAG.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MedRAGChecker: Claim-Level Verification for Biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Biomedical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) produces long-form answers that mix supported, under-evidenced, and contradicted claims, demanding fine-grained verification. We propose MedRAGChecker, a claim-level diagnostic framework that combines textual natural language inference (NLI) with a biomedical knowledge-graph (KG) compatibility signal. Its asymmetric selective-gating rule preserves the textual prediction for most claims and applies KG adjustment only to confident textual entailments assigned low plausibility by the KG back-end. We distill GPT-4.1 claim decompositions and NLI pseudo-labels into compact student models and evaluate three biomedical generators on PubMedQA, MedQuAD, LiveQA, and MedRedQA. The student-ensemble results show that selective BioPortal gating increases macro-averaged faithfulness from 60.8% to 64.4% and reduces the contradiction rate from 19.9% to 15.0%. On 172 annotations of 86 claims whose decisions change after fusion, agreement with human evidence judgments increases from 63.4% to 69.8%. A comparison with DRKG shows that fusion behavior varies substantially with KG coverage, entity linking, score construction, and calibration; the comparison therefore characterizes back-end effects rather than isolating a causal effect of coverage.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Learned Sparse Lexical Representations for Large-scale Authorship Attribution
abstract: Authorship attribution aims to determine whether a query text and a candidate document are written by the same author. %While dense embeddings are effective, recent work suggests that low-dimensional representations limit encoding capacity. We investigate high-dimensional learned sparse representations (LSR) and multi-vector retrieval for authorship attribution. We further propose Sparse ColBERT (SparCol), a late-interaction sparse lexical reranking model. To address the memory cost of vocabulary-size embeddings, we develop fused Triton kernels that can reduce peak memory usage by 5 11 times over the baseline torch implementation. Extensive experiments show that LSR can outperform dense embeddings in both single-genre and cross-genre settings, whereas improves reranking performance over single-vector models only in single-genre settings due to lexical matching bias. In addition to token-based embeddings, we also explore Lexicon-based embeddings that score clusters of tokens, which is competitive with the vocabulary-based LSR with reduced dimensions. We conduct interpretability analysis of LSRs, showing that they allow for a more transparent scoring process.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Latent Dreaming: Let Language Think Yet Latent See in Driving VLA
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving typically express intermediate reasoning entirely in text, which may discard decision-relevant visual information. We propose Latent Dreaming (LatDM), a latent–text reasoning framework that complements textual chain-of-thought with continuous latent states. LatDM uses latent blocks to preserve visually grounded spatial and temporal information, while text handles semantic abstraction and decision communication. A pretrained visual encoder provides latent supervision during training, and the model autonomously interleaves latent and textual reasoning at inference. Experiments on VLADBench, CODA-LM, and NuInstruct show consistent improvements over the underlying VLA backbone, while ablations confirm that the latent channel contributes beyond standard textual fine-tuning.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Continual Graph Memory for Adaptive Recommendation under Intent Drift
abstract: This paper studies adaptive recommendation under intent drift, where feedback from each recommendation outcome can reveal whether the relational evidence used for ranking is useful, missing, or misleading. While Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provide essential semantic structure to handle these shifts, traditional KG-enhanced systems treat the graph as a static retrieval substrate, making it brittle to evolving intents, noisy metadata, and recurring failure patterns. This paper proposes CGM-Rec, a continual graph memory framework for adaptive recommendation. CGM-Rec treats the graph state as a writable memory and maintains two complementary components. Therein, a Semantic Graph Memory is updated conservatively through quality-gated typed operations for storing stable and high-confidence relational knowledge. Meanwhile, an Episodic Lesson Memory acts as a fast reactive memory that learns recent outcomes, failure cases, and corrective hints. During testing, model parameters remain frozen and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. We evaluate CGM-Rec under a frozen-parameter, one-pass reranking protocol, where encoders and prompts remain fixed during testing and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. Experiments across multiple recommendation settings show that CGM-Rec improves over evaluated neural and LLM-based baselines on most metrics. Particularly, under sampled-candidate reranking, CGM-Rec improves HR@1 by up to 29.58% over the strongest LLM baseline on Bundle, and outperforms K-RagRec on metadata-rich ML-100K with HR@5 of 0.5941 versus 0.4746.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Rubric-as-Experts: Case-Specific MQM Rubrics for Translation Error Span Detection
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown potential for reference-free span-level translation quality estimation (QE), yet existing approaches based on Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) typically rely on fixed rubric configurations shared across translation instances. However, translation instances often differ substantially in error complexity, ambiguity, and required evaluation granularity, making static rubric allocation suboptimal for span-level error detection. We find that larger MQM subtype spaces improve error coverage but also introduce more false positives, while different translation instances prefer different rubric granularities, suggesting that evaluation spaces should be allocated dynamically for each case. Therefore, we propose a case-specific dynamic rubric framework that adaptively constructs MQM evaluation spaces for individual translation instances. Unlike methods that generate fully free-form rubrics, our framework remains grounded in the predefined MQM taxonomy while dynamically selecting suitable subtype spaces and evaluation granularity for different cases. Experiments on span-level QE benchmarks from the Conference on Machine Translation (WMT) across multiple model scales demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves F1 and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC).
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SCAMBENCH: A Multi-Dimensional Scam Benchmark through Human-AI Collaborative Data Construction
abstract: Online scams are a growing form of digital harm, yet scam research remains constrained by fragmented datasets and limited annotation depth. We introduce SCAMBENCH, a benchmark of 1,836 authentic scam messages curated from victim-reported incidents across six scam types: employment, investment, imposter, sweepstakes/lottery/prizes, tech support, and advance fee loan scams, along with 1,834 real-world non-scam examples from legitimate sources. SCAMBENCH provides multi-dimensional annotations that capture persuasion strategies from the scammer perspective, red flags from the user perspective, and severity levels reflecting potential harm and urgency. These annotations are produced through a human-AI collaborative pipeline that uses expert-labeled examples to calibrate and validate LLM-assisted annotation at scale. Our analysis shows that these signals vary significantly across scam types, highlighting substantial scam-type heterogeneity. We further use annotated evidence spans to generate cue-removed hard scam examples by rephrasing explicit persuasion and red-flag cues. Evaluating five LLM-based detectors on original and rewritten scams shows that all five detectors perform worse on cue-removed examples, and the performance drop persists on a human-validated subset, suggesting sensitivity to surface-level cues. A qualitative case study identifies five recurring failure patterns. SCAMBENCH provides a resource for scam detection, robustness evaluation, and scam education, publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Shouninger/ScamBench.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Language of Looking: Motion Tokens Reveal Domain-Dependent Local Structure in Gaze Sequences
abstract: Human gaze is the primary high-bandwidth interface through which we parse the semantics of our environment. While often modeled as a sequence, the degree to which gaze exhibits transferable local structure across domains remains underexplored. Using motion tokenization as a diagnostic lens across four diverse datasets, we investigate the transferability of local sequence structure. We demonstrate that while gaze can share a reusable motion-token vocabulary, identical motion tokens are organized into different local transition patterns depending on the dataset and task context. Our results show the limitations of naive data-pooling under low-semantic motion-token representations and provide a framework for evaluating behavioral sequences through information-theoretic diagnostics.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: HGP: An on-device personalized agent memory via hybrid graph storage
abstract: LLM-based agents face challenges in personalized interactive tasks due to heterogeneous, multi-typed, and implicitly constrained long-term traces. Existing memory mechanisms struggle with accurate routing and retrieval, especially on-device where personalization is critical. Most methods use single-vector representations, blurring type distinctions and relational structure. We propose HGP, a hybrid graph memory framework. HGP employs a lightweight self-enhancement classifier for personalized memory routing and constructs episodic, semantic, and procedural memories as graphs. It also extracts working memory as a state trajectory to capture current state and implicit constraints, ensuring reliable decision- making. The classifier reduces large-model calls, enabling on-device deployment, while graph storage enables accurate retrieval and incremental user profile refinement. Experiments on two benchmarks show that on PAL-Set solution selection, HGP achieves an S-score of 35.58, nearly 7 points above the strongest baseline.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Reverse Probing: Supervised Token-level Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models in Clinical Text
abstract: As large language models are increasingly deployed for clinical text, ensuring they can reliably signal their own uncertainty becomes critical. Most existing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods are designed for open-domain generation and cannot localize uncertainty at the token or span level in long clinical text. We propose Reverse Probing, the first uncertainty quantification framework specialized for clinical summarization, which estimates token-level uncertainty directly from pre-existing clinical summaries. Rather than sampling new outputs, Reverse Probing treats the text as a probe into the model’s internal state, extracting uncertainty features from four categories of signals. We evaluate Reverse Probing on two expert-annotated clinical datasets and outperform eight adapted baselines, achieving up to 4\times higher AUPRC while running over 15\times faster than sampling-based methods. Feature analysis reveals that the log-logit difference induced by the source record and the neighborhood context are the most consistent predictors across all models. This study offers interpretable insights into how models internally respond to unsupported clinical content.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Super Paths, Better Reasoning: Multi-Hop Knowledge Graphs Reasoning with LLM via Super-Path Ranking and Constraint Verification
abstract: Knowledge graph reasoning (KGR) composes multi-hop facts over KGs to support complex knowledge-intensive tasks, providing reliable external factual support for large language models (LLMs) and helping mitigate hallucinations. However, building compact, faithful, and high-quality contexts from large-scale KGs remains challenging. We observe a non-monotonic relationship between retrieval scale and reasoning quality: insufficient retrieval misses critical paths, while excessive retrieval introduces redundant and noisy paths that burden LLMs reasoning. Motivated by this observation, we propose super-path ranking and constraint verification (SPaRC), an efficient framework that constructs, ranks, and verifies super-paths before LLMs reasoning. SPaRC compresses redundant paths into super-paths, ranks them with contrastive learning, verifies top-ranked paths under query semantic constraints, and provides the verified context to the LLMs for answer reasoning. Experiments on WebQSP and CWQ show that SPaRC achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving Hit@1 by up to 12.0 points and F1 by up to 5.9 points on CWQ. On challenging settings covering deeper hop reasoning, multiple topic entities, and multi-answer questions, SPaRC further improves F1 on two benchmarks by up to 17.6% and 42.1%, 26.7% and 5.9%, and 10.4% and 79.4%, respectively, while reducing reasoning tokens by 29.7% and retrieval time by 25%.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Not All Acoustic Frames Contribute Equally: Frame-Selective Acoustic Conditioning for Dysarthric ASR Correction
abstract: Not all acoustic frames are equally useful for correcting dysarthric ASR errors. In dysarthric speech, acoustic deviations are unevenly distributed across frames, but LLM-based generative error correction systems often inject acoustic features uniformly, under-emphasizing deviant frames and over-correcting reliable ones. We propose a frame-selective acoustic conditioning method driven by a Frame Deviation Score (FDS) and VGate. FDS is a control-referenced per-frame deviation score computed over Whisper encoder frames, and VGate uses standardized per-frame FDS to reweight acoustic value vectors. Across ten personalized TORGO settings, we compare VGate with Plain, an acoustic-adapter baseline without the VGate gating module, and show that VGate is conditional rather than universally beneficial. Three findings support conditional use. (1) Plain residual headroom (the gap between Plain and Oracle@5 WER) and utterance-mean FDS-DIV characterize high-benefit cases, with gains concentrated in ref-preserved and overgeneration cases and the largest improvements driven by insertion control. (2) A development-calibrated FDS-DIV router lowers pooled WER from 19.55% to 18.29% while routing only 20.72% of utterances. (3) Cross-corpus COPAS results and blinded listening further support this conditional-use strategy. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/doraemon500/FSAC.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Explication of Refusal: Jailbreaking LLMs by Exploiting Refusal Explanations
abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) face a dilemma between helpfulness and harmlessness, where LLMs are expected to refuse harmful requests while remaining helpful by explaining their decisions. In this work, we observe a phenomenon caused by this dilemma. When asked to explain a refusal triggered by a harmful query, LLMs disclose exploitable elements in their refusal explanations. These elements allow attackers to induce the generation of harmful content. We formalize this vulnerability as Induced Refusal Explication (IRE). To identify and exploit IRE, we propose Explication of Refusal (EoR), a black-box and multi-turn jailbreak method with a dual-agent framework. EoR induces and analyzes refusal explanations from victim models and then generates follow-up queries to jailbreak them. We evaluate EoR across nine victim models. EoR achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of **37.05** within five turns. When we apply EoR to the queries that PAIR fails to jailbreak, EoR reaches an average ASR of **66.0** across the nine victim models, which demonstrates that exploiting refusal explanations is complementary to existing automated jailbreak methods. We release our data and code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoR-6234.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Attention Escapes: Diagnosing and Mitigating Hallucination in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations by grounding generation in retrieved evidence, yet failures persist when models underutilize the retrieved context. While prior work attributes this to conflicts between external context and internal parametric knowledge encoded in Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs), our empirical analyses reveal that FFN-derived signals are unstable and insufficient for reliable diagnosis across diverse contexts. We therefore propose the Attention Escape Score (AES), a training-free diagnostic framework that provides a mechanistic lens on RAG hallucinations via dynamic attention routing failures. We models the failures as weakened Semantic Anchoring, increased Contextual Distraction, and heightened Generation Inertia, moving beyond static component-level analyses. Extensive experiments show that AES significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with robust cross-model generalization. Furthermore, we introduce Pruning Escape Routes (PER), a lightweight inference-time intervention that suppresses hallucinations by attenuating identified escape pathways, achieving improved faithfulness with negligible degradation to complex reasoning and general capabilities.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SMRC: Aligning Large Language Models with Student Reasoning for Mathematical Error Correction
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often make reasoning errors when solving mathematical problems, and how to automatically detect and correct these errors has become an important research direction. However, existing approaches mainly focus on self-correction within the model, which falls short of the “teacher-style” correction required in educational settings, i.e., systematically guiding and revising a student’s problem-solving process. To address this gap, we propose SMRC (Student Mathematical Reasoning Correction), a novel method that aligns LLMs with student reasoning. Specifically, SMRC formulates student reasoning as a multi-step sequential decision problem and introduces Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to explore optimal correction paths. To reduce the cost of the annotating process-level rewards, we leverage breadth-first search (BFS) guided by LLMs and final-answer evaluation to generate reward signals, which are then distributed across intermediate reasoning steps via a back-propagation mechanism, enabling fine-grained process supervision. Additionally, we construct a benchmark for high school mathematics, MSEB (Multi-Solution Error Benchmark), consisting of 158 instances that include problem statements, student solutions, and correct reasoning steps. We further propose a dual evaluation protocol centered on solution accuracy and correct-step retention, offering a comprehensive measure of educational applicability. Experiments demonstrate that SMRC significantly outperforms existing methods on two public datasets (ProcessBench and MR-GSM8K) and our MSEB in terms of effectiveness and overall performance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Knowledge Is Not Free: Cost-Aware Evidence Selection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) typically assumes that external knowledge is free, but many high-quality sources are paywalled, licensed, restricted, or otherwise costly to access. We introduce cost-aware RAG, a setting where retrieved evidence is assigned access-cost tiers and systems must answer under an explicit evidence-access budget. We instantiate this setting by augmenting MS MARCO v2.1 with access-friction tiers and evaluate budgeted evidence selection across general-domain and domain-specific QA benchmarks. Our results show that static selection is brittle: no fixed selector uniformly dominates, and larger budgets do not reliably improve answer quality, even when costly evidence is domain-matched. We then study agentic cost-aware RAG, where an LLM decides when to retrieve, which tier to access, and when to stop. Agents show strong promise as adaptive evidence-acquisition controllers, but their behavior remains highly model- and task-dependent. These findings suggest that cost-aware evidence acquisition is a central challenge for the next generation of RAG systems. All code and data are available at https://github.com/Mignonmy/Cost-Aware.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Routing Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Intra-Adapter Subspace Contention in MoE+LoRA Fine-Tuning
abstract: Multi-domain fine-tuning often combines MoE routing with LoRA, assuming that token-level routing separates domain-specific updates. We test this assumption in MoE+LoRA using Python code paired with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning. Although these domains show near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, indicating that routing separation alone may not prevent negative transfer. To localize the failure, we introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity, which measure expert sharing and update compatibility, respectively. These diagnostics indicate that interference arises mostly from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. We address this issue with SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. We evaluate SpawnLoRA on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings and find that it effectively reduces negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA. These results demonstrate that structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: 0xClaw: Autonomous Open-ended Agents with Phase-aware Budget Allocation and Temporal Pressure
abstract: Large language model agents handle structured coding tasks well, but open-ended projects are harder. A hackathon gives an agent an open goal, a hard deadline and several artifacts to deliver. The agent has to decide how to split its budget across phases and when to stop widening scope. Most agents do neither. 0xClaw is a multi-agent framework that splits a hackathon run into seven phases. Each phase hands a typed artifact to the next. The Budget Router is a small fine-tuned Qwen3.5-2B model. It reads the workspace state and predicts a per-phase control token for token budget, time, reasoning effort and repair rounds. The Deadline Framer turns each token, together with the cumulative execution log, into a plain deadline instruction given to the agent at the start of each phase. Our study covers 20 hackathon tasks, 10 baselines and more than 200 agent runs. 0xClaw matches Claude Code at the best pass@1 (1.00) and exceeds ARIS (0.95), the two strongest baselines. Against Claude Code, it achieves comparable quality and pass@1 while using 59% fewer tokens. The trade-off is wall-clock time, about 2.5 times that of ARIS.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: On the Representation Bias of Disabilities in Generative Text-to-Image Models
abstract: Emerging text-to-image (T2I) models perpetuate biases, creating stereotypical portrayals of disability. This study investigates whether an agent-based, human-in-loop, AI workflow, that iteratively refines user-provided queries, can produce fairer representations of disability compared to standard models like Stable Diffusion, DALL·E-3, and MidJourney. Sixteen raters (eight with disabilities and eight without) evaluated images generated from models, prompted with textual inputs that targeted professional, medical, or social contexts. In an initial survey, raters were asked if an image depicted a disability, the type of disability if present, and if the setting aligned with the given text prompt to the model. Qualitative comments were collected. A post-survey asked raters to choose which image of a pair (standard vs. agent-based workflow) more accurately represented disability. Results revealed that standard models disproportionately produced images featuring physical disabilities or wheelchairs (p < 0.001), consistent with broader dataset biases. In contrast, the agent-based model’s images were deemed more representative in approximately two-thirds of comparisons (p < 0.0001), especially among raters with disabilities. Qualitative analyses underscored the need for nuanced, contextually rich portrayals.These findings suggest disability bias and that targeted debiasing can help mitigate stereotypes in generative AI, fostering more equitable outputs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Time Travel Engine: Ordered Temporal Geometry Enables Era-Level Historical Steering in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models compress centuries of discourse into fixed parameters, yet how they organize historical variation and whether this organization shapes generation remain unclear. We introduce the Time Travel Engine (TTE), a framework that compares geometric accounts of era-conditioned residual states and tests their behavioral accessibility under fixed prompts. Across six decoder language models in Chinese and English, broad eras repeatedly form ordered trajectories, although their exact spacing varies across model–language settings. Steering along these trajectories shifts both historical register and access to period-compatible knowledge, while adjacent anchors support local interpolation. Epistemic effects partly survive style removal, linking temporal steering to knowledge access beyond surface register. Across Chinese and English, partially alignable trajectories reveal corresponding chronological relations whose geometric realization remains language-specific. Together, ordered temporal geometry offers a testable account of how static language models organize diachronic variation, linking internal structure to historical register and access to period-compatible knowledge. Code and datasets: https://github.com/LilTiger/Time-Travel-Engine.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CycleIE: Robust Document Information Extraction through Iterative Verification and Refinement
abstract: In document AI, reliable analytics require converting long, noisy (often multi-document) corpora into heterogeneous structured data—e.g., tables for numerical fields, graphs for relations, and trees for hierarchies. Yet, one-pass LLM extraction often yields incomplete or inconsistent structures because it lacks explicit verification and opportunities to revise earlier choices. We present CycleIE, an iterative information extraction (IE) framework that closes the loop between reasoning and acting by coupling ReAct with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). CycleIE employs a multi-agent workflow to iteratively retrieve, structure, extract, and refine content under verification guidance. By treating extraction as a feedback-driven search process, CycleIE systematically corrects omissions and inconsistencies that defeat one-pass methods, while remaining orthogonal to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Experiments on challenging document-based QA benchmarks demonstrate that CycleIE delivers >10% relative improvements over strong baselines, particularly in lengthy or multi-document contexts.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Coordinate Structure Alignment of Patent Claims by LLMs
abstract: This paper proposes an LLM-based method for cross-lingual alignment of coordinate structures in Japanese–English and Chinese–English patent claims. The approach has two components. First, we construct task-specific alignment datasets by translating Penn Treebank-3 English sentences into Japanese and Chinese and projecting coordinate-structure annotations using syntactic parse trees, word alignments, and the GHKM algorithm. Second, we formulate alignment as a TANL-based text generation task in which LLMs generate the target sentence with the corresponding span tagged. Although the training data are derived from a general-domain corpus, evaluation is conducted on manually annotated real patent claims. Across four translation directions, the proposed approach consistently outperforms SpanAlign, an encoder-based alignment baseline built on SQuAD-style cross-lingual span prediction and ILP-based alignment. Controlled analyses show that the TANL formulation improves performance independently of supervised fine-tuning and that automatically generated demonstrations achieve performance close to manually constructed examples in the tested 3-shot setting. Supervised fine-tuning with the automatically constructed datasets further improves open-weight LLMs, with the best fine-tuned model in each direction achieving an F1 score above 0.8.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Embedding-space Posterior Calibration for Zero-shot Vision-Language Models
abstract: Zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP demonstrate strong open-vocabulary recognition capabilities, yet their prediction confidences are often poorly calibrated. Existing calibration methods often estimate prediction stability by applying multiple augmentations in input space, introducing substantial computational overhead and limiting practical deployment. To this end, this paper proposes an embedding-space posterior calibration approach for zero-shot VLMs, which shifts the sampling process from the input space to the embedding space.
