title: Doc2Weight: In-Weights Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Parameter Injection
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically incorporates external knowledge by appending retrieved documents to the input prompt. While effective for knowledge-intensive tasks, this in-context formulation increases memory use and serving cost as the retrieved context grows. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Doc2Weight, an in-weights RAG framework that injects retrieved information into model parameters rather than the textual context. Doc2Weight converts retrieved documents into parameter-efficient low-rank updates and fuses them in weight space according to their relevance to the query. This enables retrieval augmentation with a query-only prompt, decoupling retrieval depth from prompt length while allowing multiple retrieved passages to influence generation within a single forward pass. We evaluate Doc2Weight on instruction-tuned language models of different scales, including LLaMA-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and LLaMA-3-8B, across major QA benchmarks. Experiments show that Doc2Weight achieves the best average F1 among standard in-context RAG and prior in-weights RAG baselines across backbones and prompting settings, while matching the throughput of in-context RAG once document signatures are cached. Our code is publicly available.

title: From Memory to Behavior: A Behavior-Aware Role-Playing Framework for Social Media Influencers
abstract: Large language models have shown strong potential as role-playing agents for real individuals, yet faithful impersonating remains challenging. Existing in-context learning-based methods fail to capture how individuals react under different situations. In addition, LLM-based evaluation is difficult for obscure individuals. To address these challenges, we propose Situation–Internal state–Behavior Persona method to incorporate situation-dependent behavioral strategies. We further design an evaluation protocol that provides LLM evaluators with references about the impersonated individual. We evaluate our approach on a newly constructed dataset for the task of generating replies on social media. Experimental results show that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art ICL-based baselines, while our evaluation protocol achieves moderate correlation with human judgment. Besides, experiments on fictional-character benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method is applicable beyond the social media setting. These findings suggest that incorporating behavioral information broadly improves the fidelity of role-playing for real individuals on social media or fictional characters

title: When Evidence Conflicts: Reliability-aware Meta-review Generation
abstract: Generating coherent meta-reviews from multiple peer reviews is challenging when reviewer evidence conflicts and varies in reliability. Existing approaches typically formulate meta-review generation as a multi-document summarization task and aggregate reviewer feedback uniformly, making it difficult to determine which opinions should be prioritized under disagreement. In this paper, we study meta-review generation through reliability-aware evidence aggregation. Our framework first extracts aspect-level opinions from peer reviews and identifies conflicting evidence within each aspect. It then estimates opinion-level support and review-level quality to measure evidence reliability. Based on these signals, the framework assigns reliability-aware weights to reviewer feedback, enabling the generator to prioritize better-supported arguments while preserving diverse perspectives. Experiments demonstrate that our method consistently improves meta-review generation over strong baselines on both automatic and human evaluations, with clear gains in conflict recognition and resolution under high-conflict review scenarios. The code and implementation details are publicly available at https://github.com/Wangxz729/reliability-aware-meta-review.

title: More Evidence Is Not Always More Support: Controlled Diagnostics for Evidence Aggregation in Fact Verification
abstract: Final-context accuracy in multi-passage fact verification can hide whether an added passage contributes a new verdict-relevant fact or merely repeats evidence already present. We introduce a controlled same-prefix diagnostic derived from HoVer supporting-fact annotations to measure marginal evidence contribution. For each claim, a shared prefix covers one fact’s evidence while leaving another required fact absent; the next passage either repeats the covered fact or supplies the missing fact. The diagnostic contains 1,180 same-prefix pairs and an exact-repetition ladder testing whether repeated copies of one evidence sentence can change a verifier’s label. Supervised verifiers with similar clean F1 scores, from 0.6324 to 0.6528, differ sharply in eight-repeat flip rate, from 8.5% to 30.3%. Conservative pooling and natural-language-inference (NLI) scoring reduce duplicate sensitivity but give near-zero missing-fact gain, while gain-oriented systems improve gain but remain repetition-sensitive. Latent-Gated Evidence Dynamics (LGED), a compact stateful reference model, shows that low duplicate sensitivity and positive missing-fact gain can coexist. Surface controls and decision-level analyses support this diagnostic interpretation. Redundancy and reader tests extend the duplicate-sensitivity finding beyond HoVer, while prompted open-weight LLMs reveal a gap between role recognition and verdict updating.

title: PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit mode collapse, where their output distribution concentrates on familiar semantic modes. When diversity disappears, repeated sampling becomes semantic repetition rather than discovery, making rare but stronger solutions unlikely to surface and leaving self-evolution and continual learning difficult to sustain. Most remedies intervene only at inference time, shaping samples without making diversity a model capability. We propose PRISM, a training-time framework that internalizes diversity within the model. PRISM combines (i) submodular curation that pairs each prompt with diverse-yet-correct multi-teacher solutions, and (ii) stochastic embedding modulation, which turns special-token perturbations into implicit signals for sampling distinct outputs. A theoretical analysis establishes the stability of this mechanism. On WritingPrompts and BookMIA, PRISM moves the quality-diversity frontier outward, achieving the best generation quality in all model-benchmark settings while maintaining the strongest or near-strongest semantic diversity across two open-weight model families. It also improves sampling efficiency on math and code benchmarks. Beyond inference, PRISM yields a stronger initialization for reinforcement learning, sustaining diverse rollouts and mitigating the diversity collapse commonly observed during RL fine-tuning.

title: DarterSD: Dynamic Token-Weighted Distillation for High-Efficient Speculative Decoding
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive LLM generation with a lightweight draft model, yet existing distillation methods treat all historical tokens equally despite their divergent contributions to next-token prediction. We discover that attention in draft models is extremely concentrated: the top-3 historical tokens capture 80% of attention weight, while over 90% of tokens contribute negligibly. This uniform training paradigm forces the draft model to learn from noisy, low-importance tokens, diluting the learning signal from informative positions and limiting the alignment between draft and target distributions. To address this, we propose DarterSD, a dynamic token-weighted distillation framework for efficient speculative decoding. DarterSD employs a learnable sigmoid gate in self-attention to compute per-token importance scores, and designs a multi-objective distillation loss comprising distribution alignment, logit matching, and gate regularization to focus training on high-informative tokens. We further introduce a lightweight Boolean-mask denoising strategy at inference to suppress contextual noise, without modifying the target model’s verification pipeline. Experiments show DarterSD delivers a lossless speedup up to 5.52x , outperforming EAGLE3 (4.67x), and boosts the average accepted token length by 12.9%.

title: AgentSwing: Adaptive Parallel Context Management Routing for Long-Horizon Web Agents
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents for long-horizon information-seeking, managing finite context capacity has become a critical bottleneck. Existing context management methods typically commit to a single fixed strategy throughout the entire trajectory. Such static designs may work well in some states, but they cannot adapt as the usefulness and reliability of the accumulated context evolve during long-horizon search. To formalize this challenge, we introduce a probabilistic framework that characterizes long-horizon success through two complementary dimensions: search efficiency and terminal precision. Building on this perspective, we propose AgentSwing, a state-aware adaptive parallel context management routing framework. At each trigger point, AgentSwing expands multiple context-managed branches in parallel and uses lookahead routing to select the most promising continuation. Experiments across diverse benchmarks and agent backbones show that AgentSwing consistently outperforms strong static context management methods, often matching or exceeding their performance with substantially fewer interaction turns while also improving the ultimate performance ceiling of long-horizon web agents. Beyond the empirical gains, the proposed probabilistic framework provides a principled lens for analyzing and designing future context management strategies for long-horizon agents.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: NS-Copilot: An LLM-Driven Agent System for Autonomous Neuroscience Analysis
abstract: AI is rapidly advancing neuroscience, yet many laboratories fail to fully unleash its potential due to significant interdisciplinary barriers. While pre-trained neural models for physiological data are progressing quickly, their heterogeneous architectures and modality-specific constraints hinder systematic integration, selection, and evaluation. Despite recent advances in large language model (LLM)-based agent systems for intelligent scientific applications, existing approaches often still lack the domain expertise required to effectively select and coordinate diverse neuroscience pre-trained models and handle unique data types in this domain. We present NS-Copilot, an LLM-driven multi-agent system for neuroscience analysis that autonomously supports end-to-end workflows for diverse professional tasks. It unifies domain-specific pre-trained models and supports key neuroscience modalities, including EEG and extracellular spike data, through a natural-language interface. Given raw data and a task description, NS-Copilot orchestrates agents with specialized roles for planning, adaptive control, code generation, and result synthesis, enabling analysis without dataset-specific heuristics. We evaluate NS-Copilot on neuroscience benchmarks spanning Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and working memory spike decoding. Across 8 trials per task, the system consistently outperforms strong baselines on the primary metric, demonstrating the ability of NS-Copilot for effective and scalable neuroscience analysis.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: You Won’t Believe This Click: Content Rewriting for Agentic Choice
abstract: Language models are increasingly used as agents to help humans decide what information is surfaced. This usage incentivizes content creators to optimize content in ways that appeal not only to humans, but also to agents that mediate access to them. In this paper, we study selection shifts induced by rewriting in agentic decision-making. Given a set of competing content snippets, we rewrite only one snippet while leaving the rest unchanged, and then measure how it impacts the agent’s choice. We operationalize this setup with AgentBait an advisor-rewriter framework in which the advisor learns to propose rewriting strategies and the rewriter revises the snippet. While a rewriter with a fixed prompt improves target snippet selection from 17.1% to 34.8%, our AgentBait raises its selection to 98.5%. We further show that the advisor trained with AgentBait effectively transfers to setups with different agents, languages, and snippets in other domains (e.g., scientific papers). However, higher target selection can reflect unsupported rewrites rather than better content. Adding a reward for support from the original snippet redirects the advisor toward more supported rewriting strategies, revealing a trade-off between factuality and target selection. Together, our results show that once agents mediate access to information, content can be rewritten to be chosen by the agent, even when selection and usefulness diverge.

title: MANGO: Manga Active Narrative Grounding Optimization
abstract: Manga visual question answering requires models to answer questions over panel-based visual narratives, where relevant evidence is distributed across ordered panels, embedded text, recurring characters, and implicit event transitions. This structure makes passive page encoding insufficient, as the model must identify which panels to inspect, what clues to retain, and when the accumulated evidence is sufficient for answering. We propose MANGO (Manga Active Narrative Grounding Optimization), an unsupervised framework for active manga visual question answering. MANGO introduces Active Narrative Sketching (ANS), which iteratively selects panels, extracts concise grounded clues, and decides when to stop, forming a compact question-directed evidence sketch before answer generation. To optimize this behavior without human-annotated answers or rationale paths, MANGO samples multiple ANS rollouts and applies group-relative training with two rewards: answer preference from listwise self-ranking and path consistency from stable ordered panel trajectories. The combined reward is optimized with group-relative policy training, encouraging the model to improve both final answers and the panel-level evidence paths that support them. Experiments on standard manga understanding benchmarks show that MANGO achieves state-of-the-art performance across different settings.

title: TSA-RAG: Structure-Preserving Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Tiered Document Graph
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) effectively mitigates hallucinations and knowledge obsolescence in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, prevailing RAG systems typically retrieve evidence from discrete chunks or through decoupled structures, making it difficult to jointly preserve cross-document navigability and within-document coherence on complex tasks. To address this challenge, we propose TSA-RAG (Tiered-Structure-Aware RAG), a unified framework that recasts retrieval as structure-preserving navigation over a Tiered Document Graph (TDG). The TDG offers a joint retrieval space that explicitly couples relational topology with hierarchical skeletons, enabling seamless traversal across granularities. Building on this representation, TSA-RAG navigates evidence through a progressive Expand-Route-Retrieve paradigm, which expands query-focused subgraphs under path-consistency constraints, routes the query to structural entry points within relevant documents, and retrieves subtree-structured evidence preserving discourse continuity. Extensive experiments on seven QA datasets demonstrate that TSA-RAG consistently outperforms strong baselines while yielding more compact retrieval contexts. Quantitative analyses further confirm the scalability and robustness of our framework. Code is available at https://github.com/ZKYQUQ/TSA-RAG.

title: OneVision: An End-to-End Generative Framework for Multi-view E-commerce Vision Search
abstract: Traditional vision search follows the multi-stage cascading architecture (MCA) paradigm to balance efficiency and conversion, yet optimization objectives collide across stages, making it difficult to achieve Pareto optimality. Meanwhile, pronounced multi-view discrepancies of the same item undermine retrieval accuracy, as embedding-similarity methods fail to bridge large appearance variations. In this paper, we propose OneVision, an end-to-end generative framework that addresses both challenges. OneVision introduces VRQ, a vision-aligned residual quantization method that assigns consistent shallow-level codes to visually similar images of the same item while preserving fine-grained differences at deeper levels. It further employs a multi-stage training pipeline to retrieve all relevant items across views for a query image and incorporates user-specific signals for personalized preference modeling. In offline evaluations, OneVision performs on par with online MCA. Dynamic pruning further reduces its inference latency by 18% over the unpruned variant. In A/B tests, it achieves significant improvements: +3.61% item CTR, +2.43% CVR, and +5.89% order volume. The code will be publicly available.

title: ShotFinder: Imagination-Driven Open-Domain Video Shot Retrieval via Web Search
abstract: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have made rapid progress in information retrieval, yet existing research has mainly focused on text or static multimodal settings. Open-domain video shot retrieval, which involves richer temporal structure and more complex semantics, still lacks systematic benchmarks and analysis. To fill this gap, we introduce ShotFinder, a benchmark that formalizes editing requirements as keyframe-oriented shot descriptions and introduces five types of controllable single-factor constraints: Temporal order, Color, Visual style, Audio, and Resolution. We curate 1,210 high-quality samples from YouTube across 20 thematic categories, using large models for generation with human verification. Based on the benchmark, we propose ShotFinder, a text-driven three-stage retrieval and localization pipeline: (1) query expansion via video imagination, (2) candidate video retrieval with a search engine, and (3) description-guided shot localization. Experiments on multiple closed-source and open-source models reveal a significant gap to human performance, with clear imbalance across constraints: temporal localization is relatively tractable, while color and visual style remain major challenges. These results reveal that open-domain video shot retrieval is still a critical capability that multimodal large models have yet to overcome.

title: P-Space: Puncturing the Null-Space to Resolve Cognitive Dissonance in Continual Knowledge Editing
abstract: Existing continual knowledge editing methods suffer from cognitive dissonance: after an edit, the model answers the edit prompt correctly but reverts to the old fact under complex equivalent queries. This means old and new facts coexist rather than the old being replaced. The root cause of cognitive dissonance is that existing methods fit the new fact on the target prompt without overwriting the old one. In constrained methods, static null-space projectors lock outdated representations into the protected subspace, forcing updates into orthogonal directions. To resolve cognitive dissonance, we propose P-Space (Puncturing the Null-Space to Resolve Cognitive Dissonance in Continual Knowledge Editing), which at each edit step (1) punctures the protected covariance to unprotect the outdated representation, (2) overwrites the old mapping in closed form along its original direction under the punctured projector, and (3) anchors the new fact into the covariance with adaptive scaling so that future edits preserve it. Experiments on two datasets show that P-Space outperforms existing methods while preserving general capabilities.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CEE: An Inference-Time Jailbreak Defense for Embodied Intelligence via Subspace Concept Rotation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for task understanding and action planning in embodied intelligence (EI) systems, but their adoption substantially increases vulnerability to jailbreak attacks. While recent work explores inference-time defenses, existing methods rely on \textbf{static} interventions on intermediate representations, which often degrade generation quality and impair adherence to task instructions, reducing system usability in EI settings. We propose a \textbf{dynamic} defense framework. For each EI inference request, we dynamically construct a task-specific safety-semantic subspace, project its hidden state to the most relevant direction, and apply SLERP rotation for adaptive safety control. At comparable defense success rates, our method preserves generation quality, improves usability, reduces tuning cost, and strengthens robustness in EI scenarios.

title: SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization
abstract: Agent skills, which consist of reusable strategies that guide agent reasoning and action, have shown strong potential for improving model capability at inference time. However, current skill construction methods treat the problem as one-shot extraction, overlooking a fundamental tension: a skill tailored to the specific task fails to transfer, while the abstracted skill often provides insufficient guidance. We attribute this fragility to the absence of explicit mechanisms for skill specification and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce SkillComposer, a framework that decomposes skill construction into three learnable operations: create, improve, and merge. Trained via systematic rejection sampling recipe, SkillComposer enables language models to self-evolve skills at inference time and supports three deployment modes: offline for building generalized libraries, online for task-specific refinement, and hybrid for combining both. Comprehensive experiments on -Bench, LiveCodeBench v6, and AppWorld show that SkillComposer consistently outperforms baselines. Our SkillComposer-4B improves a 27B executor by up to +4.5 on agent tasks and +3.4 on code tasks, while generalizing across domains and task types unseen during training. Analysis reveals that merge and improve address orthogonal quality dimensions and that skill composition is a transferable meta-ability, providing a practical recipe for skill-augmented inference.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Search-Time Contamination in Deep Research Agents: Measuring Performance Inflation in Public Benchmark Evaluation
abstract: Public benchmarks enable fair and reproducible evaluation of LLM reasoning, but they become fragile for deep research agents that actively search the web during inference. Such agents may retrieve public benchmark metadata, question context, or even ground-truth answers via web search. This gives rise to Search-Time Contamination (STC), where external retrieval bypasses intended reasoning and inflates measured performance. We systematically study STC in deep research agent evaluation. We define three contamination types with increasing severity, namely Benchmark Metadata Leakage, Question-Context Leakage, and Explicit Answer Leakage, and develop detection algorithms to identify them and quantify their impact on agent performance. Evaluating modern deep research agents on seven public benchmarks, we find that STC is widespread and can inflate performance by up to 4%. Our findings show that existing evaluations may overestimate true reasoning ability. We therefore advocate contamination-aware practices, including isolated sandboxes, transparent search trajectories, and controlled benchmark access.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Can Large Reasoning Models Save Thinking? Mechanistic Analysis of Behavioral Divergence in Reasoning
abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable success on complex tasks, yet their tendency to "overthink” leads to inefficiencies. Although "save-thinking” prompts are intended to mitigate this issue, we find that LRMs still frequently enter the "Still-thinking” mode instead of the expected "No-thinking” mode, especially when facing difficult queries. First, we examine the LRM’s confidence when terminating thinking process, finding that high perplexity signals internal uncertainty and precedes the thinking process. Second, we analyze the divergence in internal attention distributions across different LRMs. Third, we investigate where the LRM allocates its attention within the prompt, identifying a critical "re-reading” pattern. Based on these analyses, we propose an attention intervention method to regulate this behavior. While this intervention successfully suppresses thinking, we find it causes a drop in accuracy, confirming that the thinking process is functional. Our work provides a mechanistic explanation for this behavior, highlighting the trade-off between instruction following and reasoning correctness, and offers insights for developing more controllable LRMs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MedMT-Bench: Can LLMs Memorize and Understand Long Multi-Turn Conversations in Medical Scenarios?
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various specialist domains and have been integrated into high-stakes areas such as medicine. However, as existing medical-related benchmarks rarely stress-test the long-context memory, interference robustness, and safety defense required in practice. To bridge this gap, we introduce MedMT-Bench, a challenging medical multi-turn instruction following benchmark that simulates the entire diagnosis and treatment process. We construct the benchmark via scene-by-scene data synthesis refined by manual expert editing, yielding 400 test cases that are highly consistent with real-world application scenarios. Each test case has an average of 22 rounds (maximum of 52 rounds), covering 5 types of difficult instruction following issues. For evaluation, we propose an LLM-as-judge protocol with instance-level rubrics and atomic test points, validated against expert annotations with a human-LLM agreement of 91.94%. We test 17 frontier models, all of which underperform on MedMT-Bench, with the best model reaching 66.75%. MedMT-Bench can be an essential tool for driving future research towards safer and more reliable medical AI. The benchmark is available in https://github.com/hiyyc/MedMT-Bench.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Seeing Is Not Believing—A Benchmark for Search-Grounded Video Misinformation Detection
abstract: Video misinformation increasingly operates at the semantic and evidential level: authentic footage may be selectively edited, temporally reordered, spliced across sources, or augmented with AI-generated content to construct false narratives. Such evidence-dependent manipulations cannot be reliably verified from the input video alone, because the missing, reordered, replaced, or recontextualized evidence lies outside the video itself. We introduce EVID-Bench, a benchmark for search-grounded video misinformation detection, where a system must search the open web for related videos and identify what information is false through cross-video comparison. EVID-Bench comprises 222 videos spanning 9 manipulation types across 3 categories: AI generation, single-source editing, and multi-source editing. All samples are verified to be undetectable by frontier models through visual inspection alone. We evaluate nine frontier multimodal models using a retrieval-augmented verification baseline. The best system achieves only 61.43% point-level accuracy and 43.24% video-level accuracy, with AI-generated manipulations remaining especially difficult. Error analysis reveals recurring challenges: models fixate on irrelevant anchors, misattribute synthetic content to editorial splicing, and terminate search prematurely before fully explaining the manipulation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Attributing Structured-Output Gains in Function Calling: Interface Alignment versus Procedural Transfer
abstract: Function-calling benchmarks assess whether language models can select appropriate tools and supply the required arguments. Because their scores also depend on expressing calls in an evaluator-specific format, gains from prompt-prepended skills may reflect interface compliance rather than transferable task-solving procedures. We introduce a four-layer gain-attribution protocol for prompt-prepended skill injection, combining canonicalized rescoring, format-only controls, repaired/balanced induction, and portability checks. Applied to the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) and scoped with API-Bank, MATH-500, and MultiHop-RAG, the protocol shows that several apparent gains are better attributed to interface alignment than to procedural transfer: format-only prompts match or exceed full skills in key BFCL cells, repaired/balanced induction removes the largest sub-frontier gains, and API-Bank target-native gains are matched within 0.5 percentage points (pp) by length-matched generic procedural prompts. These findings treat format compliance as a useful engineering capability while clarifying what a structured-output score certifies. We release BFCL-CANONICAL and recommend canonicalized metrics, balanced induction, and format-only baselines for function-calling skill-gain attribution. Code is available at https://github.com/wanyichen06/skill-injection-attribution.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Attention-Aware Remasking: A Training-Free Approach for Enhancing Visual Fidelity in Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Multimodal diffusion Large Language Models (dMLLMs) emerge as a compelling alternative to traditional autoregressive paradigms. But they still suffer from hallucinations driven by an inherent language bias. Through an analysis of the dMLLM inference dynamics, we observe that visual tokens frequently receive disproportionately low attention scores. We identify that the conventional low-confidence remasking strategy redundantly leverages logit-based probabilities during the token selection process, thereby exacerbating this language bias. To address this vulnerability, we propose Attention-Aware Remasking, a training-free, plug-and-play strategy that incorporates newly defined visual confidence scores to select the final output tokens, effectively promoting visual grounding. To enhance the logical integrity and inference efficiency of dLLMs, we further propose clue-based answering and echo-filling. Evaluations on representative Visual-Language Natural Language Explanation (VL-NLE) tasks, including VQA-X and e-SNLI-VE, demonstrate that our method achieves the highest BERTScore on both VQA-X and e-SNLI-VE, and the best answer accuracy on VQA-X among the compared methods. Our study reveals that the widely adopted logit-based remasking is not necessarily the optimal approach, highlighting promising new avenues for visually grounded inference in dMLLMs. Our code is available at: https://github.com/yechancha/Attention-aware-Remasking.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Agentic Reward Modeling for Medical Reasoning
abstract: Large language models have achieved strong performance on medical reasoning benchmarks, yet their deployment in clinical settings demands rigorous verification to ensure factual accuracy. While reward models offer a scalable approach for reasoning trace verification, existing methods face two limitations: they produce only scalar reward values without explicit justification, and they rely on single-pass retrieval that precludes adaptive knowledge access as verification unfolds. We introduce Med-TIV, an agentic framework that addresses these limitations by training medical reward models to iteratively query external medical evidence during evaluation. Our approach combines tool-augmented verification with an iterative reinforcement learning paradigm that requires only trace-level supervision, alongside an adaptive curriculum mechanism that dynamically adjusts training data distribution. Across four medical reasoning benchmarks, Med-TIV achieves substantial gains over existing methods, improving MedQA accuracy by 23.5% and MedXpertQA by 32.0% relative to the base generator. Crucially, Med-TIV demonstrates an 8\times reduction in sampling budget compared to prior reward model baselines. These findings establish that agentic medical reward modeling offers a principled path toward more reliable medical reasoning systems.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Less Is More: An Empirical Study of Prompt-Pattern Composition
abstract: Prompting is the primary interface through which users interact with large language models. Although individual prompting strategies have been extensively studied, it remains unclear whether combining multiple strategies can yield additive benefits. We present a systematic empirical study of prompt pattern composition across multiple LLMs and composition mechanisms, evaluating 18 prompt pattern categories over 7 benchmarks spanning 6 task types. Among the three models for which we exhaustively evaluate all 306 ordered pairs of functional prompt patterns, only 6.86%, 10.46%, and 4.25% of compositions outperform their stronger constituent prompt, respectively. We further find that prompt accumulation provides only limited early-stage gains, while local additive predictions increasingly overestimate actual performance as compositions grow longer. Moreover, selection-based mechanisms generally provide a more favorable performance profile than direct prompt accumulation. Overall, our results reveal a scoped less-is-more tendency in the prompt-composition settings studied here: effective use of multiple prompt strategies depends more on selecting suitable strategies than on simply accumulating additional instructions.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: GRAD: GRADient Rectification based on Authentic Data for Low-Resource Neural Machine Translation with Back Translation
abstract: Synthetic data augmentation, especially back-translation with Large Language Models (LLMs), has become a standard strategy for low-resource Neural Machine Translation (NMT). However, jointly training on synthetic and authentic data may suffer from conflicts. We propose GRADient Rectification based on Authentic Data (GRAD), an asymmetric gradient-level framework that treats authentic parallel data as an Authentic Anchor, and rectifies conflicting synthetic updates through orthogonal projection while preserving non-conflicting components. Furthermore, we leverage gradients of multiple authentic batch for comparison and use the most similar one for gradient rectification to alleviate information loss with the synthetic data. Experiments on six low-resource pairs across three LLM families (Qwen, Gemma, Llama) and different scales (4B/8B) show that GRAD consistently outperforms supervised fine-tuning, back-translation, and multi-stage baselines. Notably, on the lowest-resource En-Kk pair, GRAD achieves the highest COMET (83.65) among all evaluated systems. Further analysis shows that synthetic-induced gradient conflicts are localized, and parameter-wise rectification substantially outperforms global-wise rectification.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: OASIS: An Open-vocabulary Benchmark for Aspect-Opinion-Sentiment Extraction with Implicit-aspect Specificity
abstract: In e-commerce product review mining, Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) aims to extract fine-grained opinions toward specific aspects in reviews. Existing ABSA benchmarks have expanded from aspect-level sentiment classification to opinion-aware tuple extraction. However, they still provide limited support for evaluating implicit aspects with fine-grained specificity. In particular, implicit aspects are often omitted, collapsed into placeholders, or mapped to predefined categories, which can obscure what reviewers actually evaluate. We introduce OASIS, a review-level Open-vocabulary benchmark for Aspect-Opinion-Sentiment (AOS) extraction with Implicit-aspect Specificity. OASIS contains 6,775 Amazon reviews across eight product domains and 21,054 annotated tuples, where implicit aspects are directly represented as contextually inferred noun phrases rather than closed-set labels. This design yields an implicit-aspect-heavy evaluation setting, with 70.10% of tuples involving implicit aspects. We evaluate a range of open-source and proprietary LLMs under fine-tuned and few-shot settings, showing that full AOS extraction remains challenging even for strong models. We further show that open-vocabulary aspect phrases in OASIS can provide task-useful information. Our benchmark and experimental code is available at: https://github.com/DILAB-HYU/OASIS.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: A Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents via Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning
abstract: As AI research increasingly moves beyond systems optimized for static tasks, a central challenge is building agents that learn continuously through experience-driven lifelong learning (ELL). In this paper, we introduce StuLife, a synthetic benchmark designed to evaluate selected operational capabilities relevant to ELL. Particularly, StuLife simulates a student’s college journey, from enrollment to academic and personal development, across three core phases and ten detailed sub-scenarios. StuLife is designed around four key design principles: From Isolated Tasks to Stateful Interaction, From Passive to Proactive, From Context to Memory, and From Imitation to Learning. In this dynamic environment, agents must acquire and distill practical skills and maintain persistent memory to make decisions based on evolving state variables (e.g., resource availability and time), and are also expected to initiate actions without external prompting. To this end, StuLife provides an evaluation protocol with dedicated metrics (e.g., StuGPA) for these capabilities. Our evaluation reveals that even the highest-StuGPA model, GPT-5, scores only 17.9/100, highlighting large gaps in long-term retention and proactive task initiation. Beyond evaluating LLMs on StuLife, we also explore the role of context engineering in improving agent performance on lifelong learning tasks.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: InsightChain: Optimized Chain-of-Insight Analytics for LLM-driven Data Visualization
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for automated data visualization, yet existing approaches often frame visualization generation as a single-step mapping from user query to figure or code, overlooking the iterative analytical reasoning process of expert analysts. We present InsightChain, a four-step visualization prompting pipeline (Explore-Focus-Test-Present) that emulates expert analytical workflows for complex data visualization, together with VG-COPRO, a novel automatic prompt optimization (APO) algorithm for jointly optimizing pipeline performance. To further bridge the evaluation gap for complex data visualization, we introduce the Insight Progression Metric (IPM), a rubric combining four text-based dimensions with a vision-based dimension. Experiments on public datasets demonstrate that InsightChain consistently outperforms competing prompting baselines. We further show that VG-COPRO is more effective than existing APO methods at optimizing chain-based visualization prompting strategies.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ClinicalReTrial: Clinical Trial Redesign with Self-Evolving Agents
abstract: Clinical trials constitute a critical yet exceptionally challenging and costly stage of drug development (2.6B per drug), where protocols are encoded as complex natural language documents, motivating the use of AI systems beyond manual analysis. Existing AI methods accurately predict trial failure, but do not provide actionable remedies. To fill this gap, this paper proposes ClinicalReTrial, a multi-agent system that formulates clinical trial optimization as an iterative redesign problem on textual protocols. Our method integrates failure diagnosis, safety-aware modifications, and candidate evaluation in a closed-loop, reward-driven optimization framework. Serving the outcome prediction model as a simulation environment, ClinicalReTrial enables low-cost evaluation and dense reward signals for continuous self-improvement. We further propose a hierarchical memory that captures iteration-level feedback within trials and distills transferable redesign patterns across trials. Empirically, ClinicalReTrial turns 56.7\% of failed protocols into predicted successes under the simulation environment, with a mean success probability gain of 7.4\% at negligible cost (0.156 per trial). Extensive retrospective case studies further show that ClinicalReTrial recovers clinically meaningful modification patterns that align with real-world expert-driven protocol changes.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: GSSPO: Group Sentence-Specified Sequence Policy Optimization for LLM Personality Alignment
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities, yet achieving nuanced personality alignment for simulating human conversation remains challenging. This difficulty stems from two bottlenecks: the scarcity of scalable, privacy-respecting training data and the limited ability of conventional reinforcement learning (RL) rewards to capture subtle personality-relevant signals. In this work, we introduce a unified framework to address these issues. First, we propose the Personality Alignment Choice Forge (PACF), an automatic pipeline that transforms existing conversational datasets into structured, multiple-choice benchmarks, constraining the model’s action space and enabling scalable evaluation grounded in observed human choices. Second, we present Group Sentence-Specified Sequence Policy Optimization (GSSPO), an RL algorithm designed to address the coarse credit assignment problem in methods that apply a uniform reward across all tokens. By integrating stable sequence-level updates with differentiated, rubric-guided token-level feedback, GSSPO assigns reward signals to more localized spans of the response. This targeted approach mitigates optimization instabilities caused by undifferentiated reward signals, leading to more effective training in our experiments. On the Qwen3 model family, GSSPO achieves the best personality-alignment accuracy on every benchmark and scale in the SFT+RL regime, and leads the other RL methods on five of six in the SFT-Free regime. These results suggest a scalable route toward training LLMs that better match measured personality-alignment preferences. Our core code is available at https://github.com/HKUST-FintechLab/GSSPO
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Towards Effective Experiential Learning: Dual Guidance for Utilization and Internalization
abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a promising paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL-based training remains only a rough approximation to human learning, where humans leverage external experience to guide exploration and gradually internalize problem-solving strategies into stable knowledge. Motivated by this gap, we ask: how can LLMs better utilize and internalize experience during RLVR training? To answer this question, we propose Dual Guidance Optimization (DGO), which treats experience as a bridge between external guidance and internal policy learning. Rather than using experience only as an inference-time aid or trajectories only as optimization signals, DGO couples them in a closed loop: experience guides exploration, improved trajectories renew the experience bank, and guided trajectories are rewritten as self-contained traces for policy distillation. This enables the model to better utilize external experience while yielding consistent gains under experience-free inference. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that DGO consistently outperforms baselines under both experience-free and experience-guided inference, suggesting that coupling utilization and internalization leads to effective reasoning.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Ask Only When Needed: Proactive Retrieval from Memory and Skills for Experience-Driven Lifelong Agents
abstract: Online lifelong learning agents must decide not only how to act but also when to consult prior experience to continually improve on long-horizon tasks. Existing methods typically retrieve memories passively, such as at task initialization or after each step, and therefore miss knowledge gaps that arise during interaction. We propose ProactAgent, an experience-driven lifelong learning framework for proactive retrieval over a structured Experience Base. ProactAgent continually improves through ExpOnEvo, which jointly updates policies and refines memory, organizing past interactions into factual, episodic, and skill repositories. It further introduces ProactRL, which treats retrieval as an explicit policy action and learns when and what to retrieve. By comparing paired continuations from identical interaction prefixes with and without retrieval, ProactRL provides step-level process rewards that encourage retrieval only when it improves task outcomes or efficiency. Experiments on SciWorld, AlfWorld, and StuLife show that ProactAgent consistently outperforms all baselines, achieving up to 32% relative improvement in success rate and over 33% reduction in interaction rounds.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Citation-Closure Retrieval and Per-Rule Attribution for Real-World Regulatory Compliance Question Answering
abstract: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) for regulatory compliance demands rigorous traceability via comprehensive citations across multi-tiered authority structures. Unlike traditional multi-hop or legal QA, this task requires structured procedural lookups and evidence-set closure rather than entity resolution or case-law reasoning. Existing RAG systems struggle here due to flattened citation edges, fragmented retrieval expansions, and fragile post-hoc attribution. We formalize Regulatory Compliance QA with RegOps-Bench, a novel benchmark featuring an Operational Knowledge Graph derived from complex national R&D regulations. To address these bottlenecks, we propose RefWalk, a unified framework driven by a shared topic anchor. RefWalk traverses cross-document citations, fuses multi-view candidates via max-based aggregation, and enforces per-rule attribution to explicitly map claims to sources. We establish a strong baseline with substantial improvements in retrieval recall and citation accuracy. Finally, a contrastive evaluation on a U.S. health compliance dataset (HIPAA) reveals that existing systems exhibit saturation on flat-structure rules, underscoring the need for RegOps-Bench. Our code is available at https://github.com/yeongjoonJu/RefWalk.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: OVIBench: Benchmarking Online Video Question Answering under Interruption
abstract: Recent vision language models (VLMs) have achieved strong progress in video understanding. However, most existing video QA research and benchmarks still follow an offline, single-round paradigm, overlooking realistic interactions where users may interrupt the model during answer generation. To address this gap, we study online video QA under interruptions. We formulate the Online Video Question Answering under Interruption task and introduce OVIBench, the first standardized benchmark for this setting. OVIBench categorizes interruptions into three types: Cancellation, False Trigger, Correction and supports both open-ended and multiple-choice evaluations. To enable large-scale and reproducible testing, we develop an offline simulation protocol that reproduces interruption during generation under a unified temporal setup, together with a multi-dimensional metric suite for assessing interruption understanding and response generation. Experiments reveal clear weaknesses of mainstream VLMs in this setting, especially in reliably following user correction requests. Finally, we construct a train set OVI-Train for interruption-aware fine-tuning, which yields significant gains on OVIBench and validates the effectiveness of our benchmark and data design. OVIBench, OVI-Train, and the evaluation code will be released.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Disentangling In-Language Alignment and Cross-Lingual Safety Borrowing in Low-Resource Languages
abstract: We study two modes of low-resource language safety: in-language alignment, where models refuse harmful instructions in the target language, and cross-lingual safety borrowing, where they rely on a better-aligned proximate high-resource language, including via response-language fallback. We evaluate 11 commercial APIs on English, Mandarin, Cantonese, Tibetan, and Russian, plus 3 Tibetan-specialized open-source models, using native-speaker-verified datasets. Results reveal two patterns: Tibetan, for which response-language fallback provides limited aggregate protection in our setting, shows a safety cliff with ASR of 12.69–60.96%, far above English; Cantonese, which shares script and vocabulary with Mandarin, keeps aggregate ASR in single digits, but Cantonese-reply ASR exceeds aggregate ASR for all 11 models (sign test, p < 0.001), exposing in-language safety gaps concealed by aggregate metrics. We release Cantonese-AdvBench and Tibetan-AdvBench.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MemFail: Stress-Testing Failure Modes of LLM Memory Systems
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory systems to remain consistent across long-horizon interactions, but little empirical work has been done to understand the specific failure modes and design choices that these systems present. Existing benchmarks report aggregate question-answering accuracy and treat memory systems as black boxes, making it impossible to attribute an incorrect answer to a particular failure mode of the system. We introduce MemFail, a diagnostic benchmark that isolates the failure modes of modern LLM memory systems. We begin by formalizing memory systems as the composition of three canonical operations—summarization, storage, and retrieval—and identify the potential failure modes induced by each. Based on these hypothesized failure modes, we construct five datasets spanning four tasks, each adversarially designed to test a specific operation of a memory system. Using these datasets, we evaluate four state-of-the-art memory systems on MemFail and demonstrate how MemFail can be used to empirically understand the tradeoffs induced by differences in memory system architectures.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PATS: Process-Level Adaptive Thinking Mode Switching
abstract: Current large-language models (LLMs) typically adopt a fixed reasoning strategy, either simple or complex, regardless of reasoning complexity. This neglect of variation in task and reasoning process complexity leads to an imbalance between performance and efficiency. Existing methods attempt to implement training-free fast-slow thinking system switching to handle problems of varying difficulty, but are limited by coarse-grained solution-level strategy adjustments. To address this issue, we propose a novel reasoning paradigm: Process-Level Adaptive Thinking Mode Switching (PATS), which enables LLMs to dynamically adjust their thinking mode based on the difficulty of each reasoning step, optimizing the balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Our approach integrates Process Reward Models (PRMs) with Beam Search, incorporating progressive mode switching and bad-step penalty mechanisms based on thresholds derived from a data-driven methodology. Experiments on diverse mathematical and non-mathematical benchmarks across various model families and scales, with PRMs of varying quality demonstrate that our methodology achieves high accuracy while maintaining moderate token usage. This study emphasizes the significance of process-level, difficulty-aware thinking mode adaptation, offering insights into efficient inference for LLMs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Age of Curiosity Meets the Age of AI: Benchmarking Child Safety in Large Language Models
abstract: Children increasingly have access to Large Language Models (LLMs), which may expose them to responses that are developmentally inappropriate or require age-sensitive safety, guidance, and boundaries. Existing LLM safety evaluations largely focus on general harmful-content avoidance and do not explicitly target child-facing safety. We introduce KIDBench, a benchmark for evaluating child-facing LLM safety for ages 7-11 using a LLM-as-a-Judge rubric grounded in developmental-psychology. KIDBench contains realistic child queries across ten categories, with single-turn prompts and multi-turn child-actor simulations. We compare no-cues prompts with no child context, implicit-cues prompts that suggest a child speaker, and explicit age instructions. Implicit-cues improve scores by 8.6-46.8% over no-cue, while explicit age provides an additional 9.9-30.4% improvement over implicit-cues. Cross-lingual and cultural evaluations show uneven safety behavior across languages and country contexts. Multi-turn simulations show peak quality drops of up to 0.959 points on the 1-5 scale. We also introduce KIDGuardLlama, a child-safety evaluator, and KIDLlama, a child-safe response model. Code, data, and evaluation resources are available at https://github.com/MichiganNLP/kidbench.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Reflection: Affirmation as a Promising Behavioral Marker Associated with Quality in Text-Based Counseling
abstract: While AI-assisted text-based counseling is gaining attention, it remains empirically unclear which counselor behaviors are associated with higher dialogue quality. Existing research often focuses heavily on Reflection, borrowing frameworks from Motivational Interviewing. To address this gap, we conduct a multi-layered analysis using KokoroChat, a large-scale Japanese text counseling dataset conducted by professional counselors and trainees, newly annotated with counselor strategy tags and client distress levels. Our results show that, under the quality indicators used in this study, Affirmation is more consistently associated with session quality than Reflection among the analyzed strategies. Cross-dataset transfer experiments further suggest that this quality signal can be observed to some extent on ESConv, an English dataset with non-expert supporters. These findings provide empirical implications for counselor training and emotional support system design. We release the additional KokoroChat annotations and experimental source code at https://github.com/UEC-InabaLab/BeyondReflection
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Auditing and Mitigating Privacy Leakage in Cloud-Edge Collaborative Decoding
abstract: Applications such as personalized assistance and proprietary document analysis require large language models (LLMs) to generate outputs from private data. Yet powerful LLMs typically cannot be deployed on the resource-constrained devices where private data resides, and uploading private data to cloud-hosted LLMs exposes sensitive information. Recent work addresses this tension with a cloud-edge collaborative decoding paradigm, where private data are kept on the edge with a small language model (SLM) producing next-token distributions, which are fused with predictions from a cloud LLM operating solely on public data. In this paper, we systematically analyze the privacy risks of such a paradigm with a novel evaluation framework using constructed QA datasets, which show that such collaboration can expose substantial private-context information. To address such privacy leakage, we propose CoVeil, a defense mechanism which dynamically optimizes transmitted signals to suppress leakage during decoding time while preserving the collaborative quality. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that CoVeil consistently improves the privacy-utility trade-off over existing baselines by reducing data leakage by up to 87.2%, with minimal accuracy loss.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RoutePO: Personalized Routing Policy Optimization for LLM-based Multi-Channel Recall
abstract: LLM-based rerankers in recommender systems are inherently constrained by limited context windows: they can only reorder a small retrieved candidate set, so any relevant item missed by upstream retrieval cannot be recovered at ranking time. To mitigate this dependency, we propose RoutePO, which repositions the LLM from an item ranker to a recall strategy router for multi-channel recall. Conditioned on a user’s profile/context (interaction history and optional demographics), the LLM outputs personalized fusion weights over heterogeneous retrieval experts, enabling dynamic candidate aggregation without exposing long candidate lists from the entire item pool to the prompt. We train the router via a synergistic two-stage alignment process: Coarse Routing Alignment (SFT) warm-starts the policy with a quality-aware oracle prior over retrieval experts, and Fine-grained Metric Optimization (RL) directly optimizes recall-stage ranking metrics (e.g., NDCG) by sampling simplex-valued routing weights and rewarding fused-list quality. To support continuous exploration over the simplex under GRPO-style optimization, we introduce SofT-GRPO based on Gumbel–Softmax reparameterization with nucleus restriction and KL regularization. Finally, we instantiate fusion with both weighted score merging and a weight-aware interleaving strategy (Snake Fusion) that preserves within-channel rankings. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate consistent gains over strong individual recallers and multi-channel fusion baselines, including up to 15.88% relative improvement in NDCG@50 on Food. Our implementation is available on https://github.com/zhengzaiyi/RoutePO.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PrefTool: Lightweight Preference-Aware Retrieval for Personalized Tool Selection
abstract: Personalized tool selection for LLM-based agents aims to identify tools that align with both user intent and individual preferences, particularly in redundant API ecosystems where multiple tools offer similar functionality but differ in non-functional attributes. Existing generative approaches typically depend on fine-tuning large language models to infer user preferences, leading to substantial computational overhead and deployment costs. Despite these expensive training requirements, they still struggle to reliably distinguish functionally equivalent tools and often fail to capture users’ implicit non-functional preferences. To this end, we propose PrefTool, a lightweight yet effective preference-aware retrieval framework for personalized tool selection. PrefTool avoids costly generative preference modeling by employing a dual-encoder retrieval architecture that maps user context and tools into a shared representation space. Through structured tool representations, type-aware history modeling, and hard negative sampling, it efficiently captures users’ non-functional preferences while maintaining strong selection accuracy. Experiments on a personalized tool selection benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of PrefTool.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Mitigating Exploration Bias in RL for Multi-Instruction Following
abstract: RL has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing the instruction following capabilities of LLMs. While existing training recipes achieve substantial gains, we find that they suffer from **exploration bias towards easy instructions** when the training data has multiple instructions in a prompt. This bias is caused by two main reasons: 1) **the policy model’s initial ability to satisfy hard instructions is too low** to trigger successful exploration during RL training, so the optimization is biased to easy instructions and 2) canonical RL training recipes typically employ a cumulative reward (the number of instructions fulfilled), **treating all the instructions equally**; the policy model is biased to fulfill the easy instructions to get the same amount of rewards. To address these, we first propose two metrics to measure the exploration bias of instruction following and then introduce a two-stage framework to alleviate it: 1) Behavioral Bootstrapping: a lightweight rejection sampling fine-tuning before RL to activate hard instructions and 2) Scarcity-Aware Rewards: a new RL reward function that assigns rewards to instructions based on their empirical scarcity. Experiments show that the proposed metrics are highly correlated with model performance and our methods unleash the potential of RL training: our best models outperform the baselines by a significant margin across three verifiable instruction following benchmarks.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SCAFFOLD: Self-Improving Web Agents via Recursive Parametric Skill Abstraction
abstract: Web agents need to navigate visually rich, long-horizon interfaces that change across sites, yet most previous agents still learn each task in isolation and discard the procedural knowledge they accumulate. Recent skill-augmented frameworks take an important first step, but they treat the skill library as a flat or two-tier prompt-side cache and offer no principled mechanism for compressing redundancy or composing skills recursively. We introduce Scaffold, a self-improving framework for visual web agents that (i) induces parametric, executable skills from successful trajectories under a multi-instance abstraction constraint, (ii) maintains a recursively composed hierarchy in which higher-level skills invoke lower-level ones, (iii) compacts the library via a minimum-description-length (MDL) criterion and behavioral equivalence checking, and (iv) periodically distills skill-augmented trajectories back into model weights to internalize the abstractions. Across WebArena, VisualWebArena, and a held-out split of Online-Mind2Web, Scaffold improves success rate by 11.1–17.2 absolute points over the strongest skill-augmented baseline and shows monotonic gains across five self-improvement iterations without library collapse. We release the code and documents in the Github [repository](https://github.com/BokwaiHo/SCAFFOLD).
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: How Order-Sensitive Are LLMs? OrderProbe for Deterministic Structural Reconstruction
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at semantic understanding, yet their ability to reconstruct internal structure from scrambled inputs remains underexplored. Sentence-level restoration is difficult to evaluate automatically because scrambled sentences often admit multiple valid reorderings. We introduce OrderProbe, a deterministic benchmark for structural reconstruction using fixed four-character expressions in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, which have a unique canonical order and thus support exact-match scoring. We further propose a diagnostic framework that evaluates models beyond recovery accuracy, including Semantic Accuracy, Logical Validity, Structural Consistency, Robustness, and Information Density. Experiments on twelve widely used LLMs show that structural reconstruction remains difficult even for frontier systems: zero-shot recovery frequently falls below 35%. We also observe a consistent gap between meaning-oriented generation and exact structural reconstruction, suggesting that structural robustness is not an automatic byproduct of semantic competence.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EIBench: A Simulator-Based Benchmark and Turn-Credit RL for Emotion Management
abstract: Emotional intelligence (EI) in large language models (LLMs) is often evaluated through static understanding tasks or single-response dialogue generation. However, emotion management is interactive. A good response should improve the user’s emotional and relational state over several turns. We introduce EIBench, a simulator-based benchmark for interactive emotion management. EIBench contains 2,222 scenarios, with 2,009 for training and 213 for held-out testing. The scenarios are organized by a 2×2 taxonomy covering Support, Defense, Repair, and Charm. We evaluate 15 open- and closed-source LLMs. Current models perform well on support and rapport-building scenes, but struggle with boundary maintenance under user pressure. To improve the EI ability of LLMs, we propose Centered Turn-Credit GRPO (CTC-GRPO), a GRPO extension that reuses the simulator’s per-turn state updates as dense turn-level feedback while preserving the final outcome reward. CTC-GRPO improves Qwen3-8B from -22.4 to +22.4 on EIBench and also improves on out-of-distribution evaluations including SAGE (+12.4) and EQBench3 (+20.9%). Our results show that simulator-tracked user states can support both evaluation and training for multi-turn emotion management.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CoRe-MoE: Compact Reusable MoE for Continual Multimodal Instruction Tuning
abstract: Continual multimodal instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to acquire new task abilities sequentially while preserving previously learned knowledge. LoRA-MoE provides a promising solution by introducing expert-based capacity, but repeatedly learning and maintaining full LoRA experts leads to substantial parameter overhead. This raises a natural question: is full expert expansion necessary for every new task? To answer it, we analyze the SVD of task-specific LoRA updates and observe substantial overlap in their input- and output-side LoRA direction subspaces, with task-specific adaptation largely captured by lightweight coordinates over these subspaces. Motivated by this observation, we propose CoRe-MoE, a Compact Reusable MoE framework for parameter-efficient continual multimodal instruction tuning. CoRe-MoE extracts reusable input- and output-side direction bases from an initial expert bank, and for subsequent tasks trains only compact coordinate experts together with task-specific low-rank routers. Experiments on two representative MLLMs show that CoRe-MoE improves final average performance over the strongest competing baseline by up to 5.90 points, while using less than 1% of the trainable parameters required by sequential LoRA for later tasks.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Modality Fault Lines: Structural Corruptions Reveal Fragile Omni-Modal Reasoning
abstract: Omni-modal large language models are increasingly evaluated on clean text–vision–audio inputs, where every channel is present, synchronized, and readily interpretable. Such scores are often taken as evidence of robust cross-modal fusion, but clean evaluation cannot tell whether success depends on stable cross-modal structure or on cues sufficient only in intact inputs. To address this gap, we define a modality fault line: a boundary at which model behavior becomes unstable when a modality remains present and human-interpretable, but its internal evidence structure is perturbed. We introduce SCEval (Structure-Corruption Evaluation) a diagnostic evaluation protocol that keeps the question, answer space, and modality channels fixed while applying controlled structural corruptions to text, vision, and audio individually and jointly. Built from 273 human-verified tri-modal examples from Social-IQ, OmniBench, and VALOR, SCEval evaluates 15 proprietary and open-source omni-modal systems. The results show that structural corruption lowers clean accuracy, text–vision damage forms the most stable shared fault line, and multi-modal degradation is non-additive rather than a simple function of the number of corrupted modalities. Clean omni-modal accuracy therefore does not establish that a model will remain reliable when cross-modal evidence becomes structurally unreliable.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Diagnosing Order Dependence in Vision-Language Task-Progress Judgment with Equal-State Supervision
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly applied to embodied task settings, yet it remains unclear whether their task-progress judgments are grounded in physical state comparison or in input-order shortcuts. We study a diagnostic two-frame setting: given two robot manipulation states and a task goal, the model must decide which state is closer to completion, or whether the two states are effectively equal. We observe a strong Forward-Backward Performance Gap: models often answer correctly in the natural forward order, but fail when the same two physical states are shown with their image slots swapped. This reversal is not intended to mimic the dominant deployment order of robot execution; rather, it is a counterfactual diagnostic for testing whether the selected physical state remains consistent under input-slot inversion. To reduce this order dependence, we introduce Equal-State supervision as a zero-point calibration signal, training models to output equal when no task-relevant progress difference is present instead of defaulting to a directional answer. From real manipulation videos, we construct the Embodied Causal-Temporal Reasoning (ECTR) dataset and propose Tri-Stage Weighted Alignment (TSWA), a staged fine-tuning procedure that strengthens spatial description, task-conditioned comparison, and answer calibration in sequence. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, TSWA reduces GAP from 60.50% to 5.14% and raises overall accuracy from 44.66% to 80.19%. This comes with a small decrease in forward accuracy, but large gains in backward accuracy, equal-state recognition, and pairwise consistency, suggesting that TSWA replaces order-dependent correctness with more calibrated state comparison.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RegioZH: Unveiling Comprehension Disparities across Regional Chinese Varieties in LLMs
abstract: Current evaluations often treat Chinese varieties as monolithic, obscuring failures for regional users. We introduce RegioZH, a 2,607-item multiple-choice benchmark for regional lexical reasoning across Mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Malaysia. Built by region-specific annotators and expert-validated, it targets localized idioms, slang, code-mixing, politeness conventions, and sociocultural expressions. Zero-shot results on eleven LLMs show large disparities, including a 29.4-point average accuracy gap between Taiwan and Singapore. Persona and structured chain-of-thought prompts for five models yield selective gains, suggesting that some errors stem from retrieval or framing rather than only missing knowledge. Representation, attention, calibration, and surface-feature analyses show a dissociation between marker attention and semantic grounding, overconfident forced-choice errors, and localized lexical density as a consistent difficulty predictor. Qualitative analysis finds terminology misunderstandings, sociocultural inference gaps, and cross-regional semantic divergence. RegioZH demonstrates that apparent Chinese proficiency can mask uneven understanding across regional varieties, motivating intra-language robustness evaluation alongside multilingual generalization.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Cascade: Hierarchical Recoverability Control for Large Language Model Unlearning
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or copyrighted knowledge while preserving general utility. Existing methods often leave residual knowledge in intermediate representations, which can still be recovered. To address this, we propose Cascade, a hierarchical recoverability control framework that minimizes the internal identifiability of target knowledge. Cascade combines three complementary controls: path-level routing to suppress privacy-associated activation routes, representation-level compression to reduce geometric separability, and decoding-level intervention to limit residual recovery. Experiments on TOFU, MUSE-News, and WMDP, including robustness tests with query reformulation and extraction-style prompts, show that Cascade effectively reduces recoverability while maintaining stable model utility.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PeLA: Prompt-Enhanced Logit Adaptation for Personality-Trait Steering in LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in long-running user-facing applications where responses may need to maintain a consistent interaction style. Prompting is easy to reuse but often weak, while fine-tuning and representation interventions can be stronger but are typically model-specific. We present PeLA, Prompt-Enhanced Logit Adaptation, a parameter-efficient framework for Big Five personality-trait steering. PeLA keeps the base LLM frozen, uses a personality prompt to specify the desired trait direction, and applies a learned logit adapter during decoding. The adapter contributes a base-relative residual controlled by a token-position gate, refining the prompt-conditioned distribution only when intervention is useful. Because the control module operates in output-token space, it can be reused across models with identical tokenizer vocabularies and token-id order. On open-ended PersonalityBench questions, PeLA improves macro-average target-direction scores over a strong Personality Prompt baseline on Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, while cross-size experiments demonstrate tokenizer-compatible transfer within both the Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 families after validation-based scale calibration. PeLA narrows the gap to model-specific steering while preserving a frozen base model.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Evidence Absence Is Not Evidence Insufficiency: Diagnosing NEI Construction Artifacts in Fact Verification
abstract: Evidence absence is not evidence insufficiency, but fact verification benchmarks can make them observationally similar. The Not Enough Information (NEI) label is often operationalized through constructed evidence conditions, and that choice silently determines what a verifier learns. We introduce NEI-CAP, a construction-aware diagnostic protocol for insufficient-evidence evaluation. Each NEI example carries the construction family that produced it; NEI-CAP audits shortcut cues, validates hard cases through human adjudication, and tests whether competence transfers across constructions. We instantiate the protocol on SciFact, with FEVER and HoVer as bounded external controls. Across these settings, NEI competence does not transfer reliably: encoder verifiers and an instruction-tuned decoder trained on shortcut-prone constructions fail to recognize semantically related insufficient evidence, and mixed-construction training narrows but does not close the gap. Fixed-claim diagnostics further show that the evidence condition shifts confidence in the reference Support/Refute label, not only NEI recall, so an aggregate NEI score can hide which problem a model has actually solved. We therefore recommend reporting the construction family alongside the score, and distill the results into a checklist for benchmarks that carry an insufficient-evidence label.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CoEffi: Enhance Efficient Code Generation via Dynamic Collaborative Decoding
abstract: Code LLMs exhibit remarkable capabilities in automated code generation, but the generated code often suffers from low computational efficiency. Existing solutions have two limitations: (1) direct fine-tuning lacks transferability across model scales; (2) The efficiency optimization method for iterative generation-evaluation loops incurs high overhead. We propose CoEffi, which adopts inference-side intervention that directly operates on the decoding process without modifying base model parameters, enabling real-time efficiency improvement across different model scales while avoiding iterative reevaluation. CoEffi uses a small efficiency expert model for proposal and the base model to evaluate its acceptability, additionally introducing a region-aware dynamic acceptance threshold mechanism that maintains a sliding window to record historical acceptance rates and adjusts the dynamic threshold accordingly. We extensively evaluate CoEffi on four mainstream code LLM families and three efficiency benchmarks. Compared with vanilla instruction-tuned models, CoEffi improves average Beyond@1 by 9.12%–38.62% across the evaluated model families. It also improves Pass@1 on Mercury and ENAMEL, while EffiBench exhibits model-dependent correctness gains and regressions. A family specific trained expert can be reused across compatible base model scales within the same model family.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: A Cross-lingual Comparison of Human and Classification Model Entrainment Behavior in Code-switched Speech Settings
abstract: Conversational entrainment is well-studied in monolingual and written contexts, but remains underexplored in spoken code-switching (CSW). We present a cross-lingual analysis of entrainment in Mandarin-English, Hindi-English, and Spanish-English dialogue, replicating and extending an established Spanish-English framework (Bhattacharya et al., 2024) to two new language pairs, and show that, while lexical entrainment generalizes across language pairs, entrainment over acoustic-prosodic and CSW style aspects exhibits context-specific variation.
