We build on these findings by asking whether classification models capture these human behavioral patterns. Using feature importance and ablation analyses, we find that classical and Transformer-based classifiers detect entrainment reasonably well but consistently prioritize features other than those most salient to human entraining behavior. Our approach introduces a human-grounded framework for evaluating model decision-making in multilingual stylistic contexts, and suggests challenges for developing conversational agents capable of producing naturalistic code-switched speech.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: KV Cache Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: KV cache quantization is well studied for autoregressive language models, where cached prefix states are exact under causal attention and quantization is mainly a cache reconstruction problem. Diffusion language models (dLLMs) break this assumption. Fast dLLM inference reuses KV states across denoising steps, but bidirectional token representations can change as masked tokens are revealed, so the reused cache may already differ from full recomputation before quantization is applied. We study KV cache quantization under this cache-reuse error. We adapt KIVI and KVQuant to Fast-dLLM-style prefix and dual cache reuse, and introduce TraceKV and KProtect. TraceKV reconstructs feasible dLLM reveal trajectories from prompt-answer pairs, providing calibration states that match iterative masked decoding. KProtect uses these trajectories to choose per-layer K-cache entries that remain in high precision according to output- and attention-level behavior metrics, while applying standard low-bit value quantization. Across LLaDA and Dream evaluations on GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH, and MBPP, KProtect achieves the highest average score among quantized methods across the reported 4-bit and 2-bit prefix/dual cache settings.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Improving Information Extraction with Learned Queries
abstract: When information extraction fails, a natural instinct is to improve the model doing it: for example, by scaling it up or refining its reasoning. In this paper, we show that another part of the pipeline matters at least as much: the queries used to elicit this information. Across four clinical benchmarks and five LLMs, improving the question design alone raises performance by 18.6 F1-score points, i.e. more than using larger extraction models. To make such question design learnable, we introduce List of Questions (LoQ), which generates document-specific question sets, and FeedQ, a feedback-driven optimization method that iteratively refines questions against extraction outcomes. The resulting optimized questions can be used to train lightweight generators: with fine-tuning, 4B-parameter models match or outperform expert-derived baselines and substantially exceed the performance of much larger untuned models. We release a dataset of 12,820 optimized questions to support a broader shift in information extraction research toward treating question design as a first-class problem.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Single Gold Labels: Human Variability and Conceptualisation in Chinese Classifier Use
abstract: Chinese classifier prediction is often evaluated as a single-label classification problem, assuming one gold classifier for each context. We argue that this assumption overlooks the inherent variability and conceptual nature of classifier use. We propose a controlled experimental framework for studying Chinese classifiers in humans and vision-language models across three tasks: Classifier Choice, Head Noun Completion, and Referring Expression Generation. Based on a human behavioural dataset, we evaluate models against human response distributions rather than single gold labels. Our results show that classifier use is shaped by noun specificity, animacy, and task setting, and that models differ from humans not only in classifier choice but also in classifier-mediated conceptualisation. Although explicitly encoding the behavioural patterns learned from the human experiments into prompts improves model alignment with human behaviour, especially for smaller models, its effect is uneven across tasks: it helps models better match dominant human preferences, but does not enable them to reproduce the full distribution of human variability or fully close the gap in natural generation settings.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: From Topical Relevance to Answerability: Entailment Distillation for Conversational Retrieval
abstract: Existing conversational retrievers commonly treat topical relevance as a proxy for answerability. However, a passage that closely matches the dialogue context is not necessarily the one that supports the correct answer. We identify this mismatch as a systematic answerability gap. To address this issue, we propose CLEAR, a framework that shifts conversational retrieval from topical relevance to answerability. The core of CLEAR is entailment distillation, which transfers answer-passage entailment supervision into a cross-encoder reranker so that the reranker discriminates answer-supporting passages from topical distractors at inference time, without requiring answers. CLEAR is complemented by a passage-centric abductive recall module that brings low-similarity yet answerable passages into the candidate pool by inferring answerable queries from passages with an LLM. Across TopiOCQA, QReCC, and out-of-domain TREC CAsT datasets, CLEAR consistently improves top-ranked precision over strong query-rewriting and dense-retrieval baselines, with the largest gains observed in conversations involving heavier topical noise. Moreover, applying our reranker on top of an LLM-driven query rewriter yields further gains.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: DualEval: Joint Model-Item Calibration for Unified LLM Evaluation
abstract: Current LLM evaluation relies on two complementary but often disconnected signals: static benchmarks with objective correctness labels and arena-style preference data that better reflect open-ended user interactions. We introduce DualEval, a latent model-item calibration framework that represents models and evaluation items in a shared space, jointly estimating model ability together with item difficulty and sharpness. We apply DualEval across four domains: coding, math, miscellaneous domain-knowledge tasks, and generic everyday user queries. Our evaluation uses 18 frontier LLMs, static benchmark labels, and reward-model scores validated against held-out human preferences for open-ended model responses. Empirically, our framework produces reliable and balanced model rankings, and its learned item-level profiles support downstream applications such as benchmark compression for sample-efficient evaluation and anomaly detection for contamination or outlier analysis. Overall, DualEval unifies static and arena-style evaluation through joint model-item calibration, producing model rankings and item-level diagnostics that support more sample-efficient, interpretable, and auditable evaluation pipelines.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PaperGraph-Bench: Graph-Guided Benchmark Construction and Multi-Turn Evaluation for Scientific Paper Reading
abstract: Scientific-paper reading requires models to recover a paper’s core argument, connect claims to textual and multimodal evidence, and avoid unsupported inferences across dialogue turns. We introduce PaperGraph-Bench, a graph-guided benchmark that turns each paper into a paper-specific evaluation state graph with macro stages, evidence-grounded knowledge components (KCs), verified reasoning edges, multimodal assets, rubrics, and trajectory state. The graph drives macro coverage questions, challenge questions, reasoning threads, and bounded repair turns, while the evaluator tracks KC coverage, challenge failures, hallucination events, and repair outcomes. Experiments on a human-audited prototype with ten models show that coverage, robustness, hallucination type, and repair behavior reveal distinct paper-reading abilities. Our code and current dataset are available at https://github.com/furao0011/PaperGraphBench.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Know When to Reflect: Entropy-Guided Adaptive Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning
abstract: Self-correction has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing LLM reasoning, yet recent studies reveal a troubling phenomenon: without external oracle feedback, iterative reflection often degrades rather than improves performance. Our analysis uncovers that toxic reflection, where correct answers deteriorate into incorrect ones, occurs at rates comparable to effective corrections. We identify the root cause as the shortsightedness of existing methods: models focus only on the previous output while neglecting the global reasoning state, rendering them unable to quantify uncertainty. To address this, we propose two complementary reflection signals — Reflecting Entropy for snapshot disagreement among reasoning trajectories and Belief Shift for inter-round belief revision — paired with a two-stage hierarchical controller that schedules reflection adaptively. We instantiate these ideas as REGAR (Reflecting Entropy-Guided Adaptive Reflection), a framework that maintains a pool of candidate reasoning trajectories and applies a single, uniform reflection primitive when correction is needed. Experiments on mathematical and commonsense reasoning demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines while reducing computational overhead, highlighting both effectiveness and efficiency.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Take Only What You Need: Rank Minimization as an Implicit Forgetting Regularizer in Continual Learning
abstract: The central tension in continual learning (CL) is the trade-off between plasticity (acquiring new knowledge) and stability (retaining prior knowledge). We study how a pre-trained backbone can be continually updated to absorb new knowledge while preserving existing capabilities, via capacity control: regulating the effective rank of each parameter update, a per-step quantity directly controllable inside a LoRA update. A controlled probe of LoRA rank and placement across modules and tasks reveals a consistent trade-off, with a moderate-rank sweet spot that varies by placement and task, leaving no universally optimal fixed rank; a formal bound shows forgetting grows with rank. Building on these findings, we propose Continual Dynamic Rank-Selective LoRA (CoDyRA), which jointly trains each LoRA update with rank minimization via sparsity-promoting regularization on per-component importance weights. The supervised objective drives plasticity; rank minimization regularizes forgetting. We show that rank minimization serves as an implicit forgetting regularizer in the CL regime, protecting general capability and prior-task knowledge simultaneously by controlling forgetting against the current model state. Across MTIL, X-TAIL, and TRACE (CLIP, LLaMA, Gemma), CoDyRA outperforms prior CL methods on new knowledge learning and forgetting, achieving a strong plasticity–stability balance. Project page: https://artificer-ai-lab.github.io/CoDyRA.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Illusion of \textit{What If}: Evaluating the Breakdown of Counterfactual Reasoning in LLMs
abstract: Counterfactual reasoning requires models to reason beyond the observed world and explain how altered conditions propagate through downstream consequences. Existing benchmarks largely target bounded settings with fixed variables or single gold outcomes, overlooking open-domain scenarios requiring causal-process evaluation. To this end, we present \textbf{WhatIfBench}, a diagnostic benchmark for open-domain, open-form, long-horizon counterfactual causal reasoning, containing 220 what-if questions across STEM, HSS, and Hybrid scenarios. To evaluate free-form responses, we further propose \textbf{PRISM}, which first converts each natural-language explanation into a Response-Derived Semantic Causal Graph of events, states, and mechanisms. On top of this graph, PRISM then jointly applies a Process Metric assessing graph-level causal validity and a Rubric Metric assessing answer-level explanatory adequacy. Evaluating six frontier LLMs with this framework, we find that WhatIfBench remains far from saturated: even the strongest model reaches only a 64.62% final score. Further analysis reveals persistent causal gaps, premise drift, and topology fragmentation, suggesting that fluent counterfactual narratives often mask fragile causal processes. The benchmark, code, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zju-gt/WhatIfBench.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: IterInject: Indirect Prompt Injection Against LLM Agents via Feedback-Guided Iterative Optimization
abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed for complex tasks requiring planning, tool use, and interaction with external services. Their reliance on untrusted external content exposes them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), in which adversarial instructions embedded in retrieved data hijack agent behavior. Existing attacks rely on static payloads that cannot adapt to agent-specific defenses; even recent adaptive methods lack structured feedback to guide optimization. We introduce IterInject, a feedback-guided iterative framework that closes the loop between injection, diagnosis, and refinement: a rule-based diagnoser produces structured outcome labels with behavioral descriptions, and an LLM-based optimizer refines payloads conditioned on the full optimization history. A synthesis step generates new disguise seeds from failure patterns, enabling the strategy space to self-evolve. On AgentDojo and InjectAgent, IterInject substantially outperforms static baselines and existing adaptive methods across four victim models. Extension experiments on Claude Code, a production-grade coding agent with layered defenses, show that optimized payloads achieve full success on 5 of 9 targets; even those that resist full exploitation exhibit measurable improvement from iterative refinement. We further present a mechanistic analysis of IPI, identifying an attention-mediated threshold mechanism in mid-to-late layers; three causal interventions validate this finding and point to concrete defense directions.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Typology-Aware Dual-Track: Detecting Hybrid AI Text Across Languages
abstract: Existing generalist detectors, such as mDeBERTa based classifiers, struggle with fine-grained AI-text detection in multilingual settings, particularly when hybrid authorship and morphologically rich languages obscure machine-generated artifacts. We propose a typology-aware Smart Routing Late Fusion Framework for 4-class detection: Human-Written (HW), Machine-Generated (MG), Machine-Humanized (MH), and Human-Polished (HM). The framework consists of two complementary tracks. Branch A targets agglutinative languages, including Korean, Turkish, and Hungarian, using error focused hard-negative refinement and Dependency Distance Minimization(DDM) / Uniform Information Density(UID) based pairwise calibration to recover weak generative signals hidden by dense morphology. Branch B applies RADAR-inspired invariant learning to capture machine-originated artifacts that persist after adversarial rewriting in languages with clearer segmentation cues. Experiments across eight languages show that typology-aware routing improves detection in agglutinative languages while maintaining strong multilingual performance. Our results highlight the importance of modeling both linguistic typology and hybrid authorship for robust multilingual AI-text detection.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: LLM Pedagogical Behavior in AI Tutoring Interactions
abstract: Students increasingly use LLMs as tutors for coursework and problem solving. Little is known about the level of assistance LLMs provide when students use them as tutors in authentic learning interactions. This matters because tutoring responses can differ substantially in how directly they help students complete a task. We operationalize this dimension as scaffolding level and develop a five-level scale, validated against human annotations, that characterizes responses according to the degree of direct assistance they provide. We apply the scale to 14,637 LLM responses from 203 students in a university AI course, where the model received no pedagogical instruction beyond a generic helpful-assistant system prompt. Responses are overwhelmingly concentrated at high levels of assistance, with more than 95% classified as either Explaining or Solving. Scaffolding level is systematically associated with students’ subsequent conversational behavior, but provides little additional predictive information about performance on three subsequent exams beyond prior achievement and dialogue behavior. These findings provide an empirical baseline for LLM assistance in tutoring interactions and a measurement framework for evaluating how alternative tutoring designs change that assistance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Style-Ruler: Inference-Only Stylized Translation via Unsupervised Extraction and Agentic Collaboration
abstract: While Large Language Models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in general machine translation, they frequently struggle to adhere to complex stylistic nuances and lexical constraints strictly and often revert to a neutral style. The scarcity of style-specific parallel data hinders existing solutions, whereas standard prompting lacks rigorous verification mechanisms. To bridge this gap, we propose Style-Ruler, an inference-only agentic framework that operationalizes style via unsupervised extraction and neuro-symbolic verification. Style-Ruler orchestrates three specialized agents: (1) a Style-Reverse Analyst (SRA) that mines quantifiable linguistic constraints from monolingual reference texts via unsupervised extraction; (2) a Constraint-Adaptive Translator (CAT) that employs a Style-Chain-of-Thought mechanism to plan stylistic adherence before generation explicitly; and (3) a Sandbox-Augmented Auditor (SAA) that provides heterogeneous feedback through deterministic code execution. These components form a closed-loop refinement mechanism where symbolic logic guides neural generation. Extensive experiments on the GuoFeng Webnovel dataset and WMT24++ benchmark demonstrate the superiority of our approach. Style-Ruler achieves a CSR of 82.4% on stylized translation, surpassing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting by over 50%, while improving BLEU scores by +1.0 on En\toZh.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Diagnosing Subword Boundary Conflicts in Diffusion Language Models through Sentence Simplification
abstract: Sentence simplification is a source-grounded rewriting task in which outputs often keep parts of the source while editing adjacent spans. Diffusion language models (DLMs) are well suited to this setting because masked denoising can fill rewritten spans using bidirectional context. However, parallel filling can create subword-boundary errors when incompatible subword fragments are committed together. We define these errors as Subword Boundary Conflicts (SBCs): malformed output words, such as Australianways, formed from incompatible fragments at subword boundaries. To measure them, we introduce a surface-form taxonomy and a detection pipeline based on candidate extraction, LLM-as-a-Judge filtering, and human verification. We evaluate Dream and LLaDA variants on ASSET and MED-EASi, with autoregressive and task-specific simplification baselines. We find that SBCs occur across DLMs but vary by model. Under standard unmasking, LLaDA variants remain at or below 2.80%, whereas Dream-7B-Instruct reaches 6.32% on ASSET and 9.03% on MED-EASi. Beyond model choice, decoding parallelism is a key driver. In the Dream unmasking setting at 128 denoising steps, increasing parallelism from 1 to 4 raises SBC rates from near zero to 25.63% on ASSET and 34.67% on MED-EASi. Further analyses show that SBCs occur under light-to-moderate edits, are not limited to rare words, and can often be repaired by local masked span regeneration. These findings establish SBCs as a word-form reliability target for robust diffusion-based text generation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RouteVerify: A Diagnostic Study of Tool-Augmented Chest X-ray Agents
abstract: Tool-augmented medical agents promise clinical control and interpretability, yet their specialized outputs are often invoked broadly and compressed into text. It remains unclear whether failures arise from this textual interface or low-fidelity upstream tools. We study this question through RouteVerify, a transparent diagnostic sandbox combining a lightweight linear router, compact evidence cards, and verifier-gated multimodal reinspection. On matched and held-out ChestAgentBench splits, RouteVerify improves answer accuracy by about seven points over naive always-call-tools execution while roughly halving token use. However, it remains about two points below a direct VLM-only baseline and uses nearly twice the tokens. Oracle probes clarify the bottleneck: replacing predicted evidence with benchmark-side gold explanations raises the same downstream text reasoner above 95 percent accuracy, or above 91 percent after removing explicit answer cues. Thus, text cards can express sufficient evidence on this benchmark; the dominant practical limitation is upstream tool quality. An external JSRT/SCR audit supports this diagnosis, revealing limited nodule-classification discrimination and structure-dependent segmentation quality. The remaining raw-versus-sanitized oracle gap also indicates sensitivity to human-authored cues. We present RouteVerify as an empirical boundary study of where current tool-augmented medical agents fail.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ARIA: Affect-Responsive Interaction Alignment for Emotional Support Policies via Implicit Multimodal Affective Feedback
abstract: Effective emotional-support dialogue requires more than fluent empathy: responses must adapt to the support seeker’s evolving state. Existing emotional-support systems are largely optimized at the response level and may therefore learn the form of supportive counseling without reliably adapting to client-side change. We introduce ARIA, Affect-Responsive Interaction Alignment, a client-centered alignment framework that constructs DPO preference pairs from the support seeker’s subsequent multimodal affective trajectories observed in human interactions. ARIA distills audio- and visual-derived valence trajectories into text-based predictors and uses cross-modal consensus and uncertainty-aware filtering to identify high-confidence preferences associated with delayed client-side valence improvement. Experiments show that ARIA improves process-oriented measures of client progress beyond surface compliance and produces support that is more timely and calibrated to the seeker’s evolving openness. Behavioral analyses further show a phase-sensitive shift from restrained pre-open support toward more active support after openness emerges. Human and counseling-expert evaluations provide evidence that ARIA’s responses are more timely, targeted, and supportive of the client’s own process.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Learning Solvability Boundaries in LLMs: Improving Reasoning, Detecting Unsolvability, and Calibrating Refusal
abstract: Reasoning alignment usually assumes each query has a determinate answer, rewarding models for reaching it and penalizing or ignoring failures. This assumption breaks on flawed queries with missing information or contradictory constraints, causing models to hallucinate invalid answers or over-refuse difficult valid tasks. We study this failure mode as solvability boundary learning: separating input-side answerability defects from model-side inability on well-posed tasks. To address this, we introduce UnsolvableQA, a verifier-backed multi-domain benchmark built with deterministic checks and audited math verification, and UnsolvableRL, an alignment framework that decouples reasoning, unsolvability detection, and capability-calibrated refusal. UnsolvableRL yields over 85% unsolvability detection on Qwen3-4B while improving solvable accuracy from 43.4% to 69.4%, with a +35.4-point solvable-accuracy gain on Llama3-8B. Diagnostic tuning further distinguishes missing-information defects from constraint conflicts and transfers to interactive clarification, improving Detail Recovery from 47.8% to 60.7% for Llama3-8B. Ablations reveal Capability Collapse: refusal penalties degrade detection without unsolvable data, but act as a rigor regularizer when such data are included.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Decoupled Analysis-Judging: An Automated Creativity Evaluator Using LLMs in Complex Multi-step Creativity Tasks
abstract: Automated evaluation of creativity tasks remains challenging for LLM-as-a-Judge, as LLM is susceptible to biases such as verbosity bias and leniency bias. Such limitations are particularly evident in Contextually-Grounded and Procedurally-Structured Tasks (CGPST), a complex multi-step creativity task where inter-step dependencies, highly subjectivity, and wide scoring ranges lead to more unstable and biased judgments. Existing approaches either rely on task-specific training or directly apply LLM-as-a-Judge, both of which struggle to ensure reliable evaluation under such complexity. To bridge these gaps, we propose **CreaEval**, an automated **crea**tivity **eval**uator for CGPST that decouples typical LLM-as-a-Judge into analysis and judging. Correspondingly, CreaEval involves two critical phases: **Memory-augmented Analysis**, a SoT-LLM converts multi-step responses into structured evaluation evidence, incorporating cross-step memory; and **Evidence-based Judging**, a Judge-LLM uses the extracted evidence for judging without accessing raw responses. Comprehensive experiments on CGPST show that CreaEval achieves an average human-LLM agreement of 0.64 (QWK) on CGPST, improving over the second-best baseline (supervised training) by 0.17. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CreaEval-0058/.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: IA-RAG: Interval-Algebra–Driven Temporal Reasoning for Dynamic Knowledge Retrieval
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has shown strong effectiveness in grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) with external knowledge. However, existing RAG and Graph RAG frameworks largely treat knowledge as static or associate time with coarse-grained timestamps or metadata, failing to capture rich temporal structures such as duration, overlap, and containment. We propose IA-RAG, a hierarchical temporal RAG framework that models knowledge as time intervals and performs retrieval under formal temporal constraints. IA-RAG represents facts as Interval Event Units (IEUs) and organizes them into a hierarchical Thematic Forest, where temporal dependencies are governed by Allen’s Interval Algebra. To handle incomplete or uncertain temporal boundaries, IA-RAG further introduces a Sub-graph Time Tightening mechanism that refines fuzzy intervals through logical constraints within connected event subgraphs. In addition, IA-RAG supports implicit temporal semantic retrieval through interval-algebra-guided traversal. Experiments on multiple temporal question answering benchmarks, including TimeQA, TempReason, and ComplexTR, demonstrate that IA-RAG achieves strong temporal retrieval and reasoning performance, particularly on complex compositional temporal reasoning tasks. Our code is released at https://github.com/xiaoAugenstern/IA-RAG.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CHisAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Event Taxonomy Construction in Ancient Chinese Cultural Systems
abstract: Due to the long temporal span and highly diverse expressions in historical documents, large language models (LLMs) still struggle with historical and cultural reasoning in Chinese history. Although taxonomic structures can effectively organize historical knowledge and facilitate knowledge-rich applications, existing historical taxonomies remain limited due to the high cost of manual construction. To address this limitation, we propose CHisAgent, a multi-agent LLM framework for automated historical taxonomy induction in ancient Chinese history. CHisAgent explicitly decomposes taxonomy construction into three role-specialized stages: a bottom-up Inducer that derives an initial hierarchy from raw historical corpora, a top-down Expander that introduces missing intermediate concepts using LLM world knowledge, and an evidence-guided Enricher that integrates external structured historical resources to ensure faithfulness. Extensive reference-free and reference-based evaluations show that the collaboration among these agents improves taxonomy coverage and hierarchical completeness, while further analysis suggests that the induced taxonomy facilitates cross-cultural alignment of historical concepts. Code and experimental data are available at  https://github.com/tangxuemei1995/CHisAgent.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Grounding Structure in Language: Enriching Symbolic Representations for Molecular Reasoning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promise for scientific applications but struggle when domain knowledge is encoded in complex structures. Chemistry exemplifies this challenge: molecular structures encode rich relational data that dictates chemical meaning, yet standard formats like SMILES obscure this through arbitrary linearization. In this work, we systematically characterize which structural information lost during linearization most severely hampers LLM reasoning, decomposing the problem into IUPAC-grounded dimensions: substituent positions (locants), attachment points (anchoring), and modification constraints (valency). Our diagnostic reveals non-uniform failures across dimensions, with locant identification being especially challenging. We directly address the failures by grounding the linearized representations in structural context with each component targeting its corresponding diagnostic dimension. General-purpose LLMs with explicit grounding can outperform chemistry-specialized models on structure-aware molecule manipulation, suggesting structural context can compensate for domain-specific training. Moreover, we investigate a training-free inductive protocol that nearly doubles the accuracy of weaker models. These results point toward explicit structural grounding as a principled path to more reliable molecular reasoning across model scales.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: A Four-Stage Decomposition of Word-Problem Solving and Mechanistic Fragility in LLM Math Reasoning
abstract: Large language models solve grade-school math word problems with high accuracy, yet a single irrelevant clause inserted into the problem can collapse it. We reconcile these observations with a mechanistic account. We show that the model’s internal computation decomposes into a four-stage sequential pipeline, Schema Abstraction, Operation Planning, Operand Binding, and Computation, each stage producing a distinct intermediate representation in an identifiable band of layers. Using the same scaffold to diagnose distractor-induced failure, we localize the corruption to a single stage, Operation Planning, implemented by a set of attention heads whose causal role we validate bidirectionally. In short, we provide a mechanistic interpretation of math word problem reasoning in LLMs, and their failure when distracted.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ReimburseBench: Benchmarking LMMs as Full-Workflow Auditors for Financial Internal Control
abstract: Expense reimbursement internal control is a high-stakes corporate finance task that combines multimodal, visually rich evidence (e.g., receipts and approval forms), firm-specific policy text, and multi-step compliance reasoning. No existing benchmark evaluates large multimodal models (LMMs) in this domain. We introduce ReimburseBench, the first benchmark targeting full-workflow multimodal audit reasoning in corporate internal control. It comprises 151 expert-constructed reimbursement workflows, each packaging an application, receipts and supporting documents, and a firm-specific policy, evaluated by a process-level rubric grounded in twelve auditing logic points. Benchmarking nine frontier and locally deployable systems, we find the strongest attains only 72.5%, and no model exceeds 47.7% on hard workflows. Beyond this aggregate score, risk-aware, process-level evaluation surfaces three structural findings: (i) a persistent gap between binary admissibility judgment and precise quantitative computation; (ii) a systematic lenient bias in monetary predictions that poses deployment risk; and (iii) a performance pattern consistent with compositional-generalization difficulties under realistic workflow load. We provide ReimburseBench as a testbed for advancing LMMs toward trustworthy financial systems. Data and code: https://github.com/ikerzhan/ReimburseBench.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PersonaTree: Structured Lifecycle Memory for Person Understanding in LLM Agents
abstract: Persistent LLM agents require memory representations that make the formation of person understanding explicit across long term interaction. Existing agent memory methods emphasize information retention and retrieval, yet give limited account of how accumulated interaction evidence is abstracted into person understanding. We view this process as schema formation, where situated evidence is abstracted into reusable patterns and stable person level claims. We introduce PersonaTree, a structured lifecycle memory framework that realizes this view as a three level persona tree with explicit support paths from evidence to claims. PersonaTree maintains the tree through conservative writing, confidence guided consolidation, and query conditioned path retrieval, returning only the evidence depth required by each query. Across six person understanding and persistent memory benchmarks with three answer backbones, PersonaTree ranks first in 12 of 18 compact scores and reaches the top two in 16 settings. Ablations show that hierarchy improves abstract person understanding on KnowMe, while support path retrieval improves RealPref alignment under a comparable context budget.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?
abstract: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: From AI Scientists to AI Scientific Communities: A Survey of Collective AutoResearch
abstract: Scientific research is not merely a sequence of tasks to be automated, but a knowledge-production process in which claims must remain verifiable, criticizable, revisable, and accountable. Yet most AutoResearch systems remain single scaffolds that collapse generation, execution, interpretation, and review into one loop. This survey diagnoses three resulting epistemic limits of such architectures: collapsed skepticism, where a single scaffold produces not only errors but also the narratives that allow them to survive; unverified translation from discovery to application, where proposal generation outpaces independent verification; and invisible evidence trails, where final manuscripts hide the failed attempts and post-hoc decisions that produced them. To overcome these structural fragilities, we propose a shift from autonomous AI scientists to AI research communities, where specialized agents, shared memory, inspectable artifacts, and governance checkpoints distribute epistemic labor. We synthesize AutoResearch as a transition from metric-driven search loops to AI-scientist workflows, domain-mediated discovery, research infrastructure, and accountable human–AI co-evolution. Across these layers, we argue for a fundamental shift from productivity-centered evaluation to verifiability-centered evaluation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TurnFlow: Benchmarking User-State Reasoning in Multi-Turn LLM Agents via Scene-Guided User Simulation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed through conversational interfaces, yet strong single-turn performance does not imply reliability in multi-turn setting. Multi-turn assistance requires a model to maintain an evolving representation of user requirements and to reason over that representation before complying with later requests. Failures can therefore be subtle: models may fail to recognize a changed constraint or hidden conflict, or recognize it without enforcing it in the final response. Existing benchmarks primarily test fully specified prompts, long-context recall, or controlled domain environments, leaving open-domain requirement reconciliation undermeasured. We introduce TurnFlow, an interactive benchmark for evaluating whether models preserve, revise, and act on user requirements across turns. TurnFlow combines adaptive user simulation with verifiable judging, allowing conversations to unfold naturally while keeping hidden requirements and pass/fail criteria controlled. In our main evaluation, twelve current LLMs achieve only 27.5%–51.0% aggregate pass rate on 490 scenarios. The failures show that current LLMs can remain fluent and cooperative while losing the global state of the conversation, exposing a gap between conversational helpfulness and robust requirement reconciliation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ProtSynGen: Knowledge Graph-Guided Open-Ended Data Synthesis for Protein LLMs
abstract: The performance of large language models (LLMs) depends critically on the quality of their instruction-tuning data. For protein LLMs, existing instruction-tuning datasets are typically derived from structured protein annotations through template-based or label-guided generation. Although these datasets capture important biological facts, their construction paradigms often lead to two limitations: instruction homogenization and reasoning superficiality. The former refers to questions concentrating around repetitive forms and narrow topics; the latter to answers relying on shallow annotation lookup rather than evidence-rich biological reasoning. To address these limitations, we propose ProtSynGen, a knowledge graph-guided open-ended data synthesis framework for protein LLMs. ProtSynGen integrates structured protein databases with unstructured scientific literature into a protein-centric knowledge graph, and uses hierarchical graph sampling to guide LLMs in generating open-ended QAs across atomic, aggregated, and complex reasoning scenarios. Experiments show that ProtSynGen produces instruction-tuning data with broader topic coverage, richer reasoning depth, and stronger quality metrics than existing protein LLM instruction datasets. Models trained on ProtSynGen data further achieve superior performance on open-ended protein QA benchmarks, consistently outperforming baseline methods across atomic, aggregated, and complex reasoning scenarios.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: BanglaMemeX: Advancing Cultural Metaphoric Image Interpretation in Bangla with a Multimodal Explainable Dataset
abstract: Vision Language Models have achieved strong performance on multimodal benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about culturally grounded and metaphor-rich content remains insufficiently studied. Internet memes present a challenging setting where meaning emerges from implicit interactions between image, overlaid text, sarcasm, and shared socio-cultural knowledge rather than literal visual recognition. This challenge is amplified in low-resource languages such as Bangla, where code-mixing, stylized scripts, and culturally specific symbolism introduce substantial distribution shift. In this work, we introduce **BanglaMemeX**, a culturally grounded multimodal benchmark comprising 3,000 Bangla memes annotated with multi-dimensional labels (humor, sarcasm, offensiveness, motivational intent, and overall sentiment) and human-written explanations that explicitly describe textual and visual metaphors. We systematically evaluate modern VLMs on both classification and explanation generation, revealing that current models struggle to interpret implicit cultural cues despite reasonable surface-level accuracy. Our results highlight the need for culturally-aware multimodal systems capable of grounded reasoning under linguistic and cultural distribution shift.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SignFLIP: A Unified Model for Sign Language Translation and Generation via Stage-wise Alignment at Scale
abstract: Sign language translation and generation share the goal of bidirectional alignment between text and sign representations. However, existing approaches either treat them as isolated tasks or are only verified on limited datasets, limiting effective modeling between modalities. In this paper, we propose SignFLIP, a unified LLM-centered framework for translation and generation. To enable bidirectional mapping between text and sign, SignFLIP adopts a symmetric architecture together with a stage-wise training strategy built on large-scale data. The shared sign–text representation is progressively refined: pre-alignment facilitates subsequent SLT, while the SLT-adapted representation further benefits SLG. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SignFLIP shows competitive performance compared with task-specific models on both translation and generation tasks, as well as strong transferability to sign language recognition.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Title It Right: Faithful and Attractive Paper Title Generation via Pareto Dominance Alignment
abstract: Generating academic paper titles requires balancing two key goals: faithfulness to the content and attractiveness to readers. Existing methods often treat title generation as a simple summarization task, producing accurate but unengaging titles. While multi-objective Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) offers a potential solution, our empirical analysis shows that combining conflicting objectives into a single reward is associated with substantial gradient interference during training. To address this problem, drawing inspiration from Pareto dominance in multi-objective optimization, we propose Multi-Objective Dominance Alignment (MODA), a data-centric training strategy tailored for academic title generation. MODA retains preference pairs with strict Pareto dominance, thereby reducing exposure to supervision with opposing reward directions. We implement MODA using dual reward models to independently score both dimensions. Across our experiments, this filtering strategy improves the observed balance between faithfulness and attractiveness, outperforms Human Author baselines, and approaches the performance of frontier models despite using an 8B backbone. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/realyoume/title_it_right.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RecoverAgent: Intent-Preserving Recovery from Indirect Prompt Injection in Tool-using LLM Agents
abstract: Tool-using LLM agents execute multi-step tasks by iteratively reasoning and interacting with external tools. However, they are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in tool outputs can divert benign user intents into unsafe actions or unintended goals. Existing defenses mainly prioritize reducing unsafe behaviors, while paying limited attention to preserving the original user intent. As a result, safety improvements may come at the cost of interrupting execution or distorting benign task goals. This reveals a key gap in current LLM-agent defenses: the trade-off between safety and intent preservation remains largely underexplored. We propose RecoverAgent, an intent-preserving recovery framework that enables agents to continue execution after detecting unsafe intermediate responses. Instead of terminating the task, RecoverAgent rewrites unsafe responses into safe and executable alternatives while maintaining alignment with the original user intent. Experiments on R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, and BadAgent demonstrate that RecoverAgent reduces attack success and harmful behaviors while substantially improving trajectory completion and intent fidelity compared to other defenses under IPI.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Reinforcing Step-level Reasoning for Effective Self-Correction in LLMs
abstract: Achieving effective self-correction, where models verify and correct their own mistakes, remains a fundamental challenge for large language models (LLMs). In this work, we propose Self-Fix Step-DPO (SFS-DPO), a reinforcement learning based, two-stage framework for step-level self-verification and self-correction. The first stage strengthens step-level reasoning via step-level preference optimization, while the second stage explicitly trains models to self-verify and self-correct. We further introduce a teacher-assisted variant, SFS-DPO-R, which incorporates explanatory rationales for error verification to provide stronger corrective signals. Comprehensive in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations across multiple LLMs demonstrate that SFS-DPO and SFS-DPO-R consistently outperform prior step-level training baselines. Our analysis further reveals improvements in self-correction frequency and effectiveness, highlighting the importance of strengthening step-level reasoning for robust performance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: OPD-Evolver: Cultivating Holistic Agent Evolver via On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Memory has become a standard substrate for self-evolving agents, yet retaining experience is not the same as learning how to evolve through it. Existing memory agents can store trajectories, retrieve reflections, or accumulate skills, but often lack the holistic competence to select useful experience, act on it, write reusable knowledge, and maintain a growing repository. We introduce OPD-Evolver, a slow-fast co-evolution framework that cultivates such an agent evolver through on-policy self-distillation. In the fast loop, OPD-Evolver interacts with a four-level memory hierarchy to read, use, write, and maintain experience for rapid test-time evolution. In the slow loop, outcome-calibrated memory attribution and privileged hindsight distill these four abilities into the deployable policy. Across multi-domain benchmarks, OPD-Evolver surpasses memory systems such as ReasoningBank by up to 11.5 points, and training-based methods such as Complementary RL by ~6.45 on average. Further analysis shows that OPD-Evolver internalizes high-value experience and memory management, enabling OPD-Evolver-9B to challenge giant counterparts such as Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and Step-3.5-Flash, pointing beyond memory-augmented agents toward genuinely qualified agent evolvers.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Clarify User Expertise: Towards Proactive Conversational Agents Tailoring Responses to User Proficiency
abstract: In the context of information seeking, conversational agents are undergoing an evolution from reactive tools to proactive, personalized assistants. A critical aspect of this evolution is the ability to tailor strategic interactions to a user’s unique needs and expectations. Unlike existing studies that focus on proactively clarifying query ambiguities, we center on clarifying the user’s expertise in order to tailor responses for better user comprehension. We find that existing agents struggle to determine user expertise from queries alone, a limitation that prevents them from dynamically adapting their responses. To address this gap, we introduce PASSING to empower the agent to proactively clarify a user’s expertise through targeted inquiries. This is achieved by our What-to-ask and How-to-ask strategies, induced by LLM self-play. Our extensive experiments also show our superiority. We believe that PASSING represents a crucial step towards creating more human-centric conversational agents.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Progress-SQL: Improving Reinforcement Learning for Text-to-SQL via Progressive Rewards
abstract: Reinforcement learning has recently shown promise in improving large language models for Text-to-SQL generation, yet existing methods typically optimize one-shot rewards defined over a single SQL state. Such rewards provide limited guidance for iterative SQL correction and are insufficient to capture the improvement of multi-turn SQL refinement. In this paper, we propose Progress-SQL, a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework with progressive rewards for Text-to-SQL. Our approach introduces an Oracle-guided Diagnostic Tree (ODT), which abstracts SQL queries into clause-level structural profiles and produces diagnostic feedback for next-turn refinement. To provide dense and robust reward signals, we combine ODT-based structural alignment with lexical alignment and define a progressive reward that measures the improvement from the initial SQL to the final SQL. We further incorporate a progression latency reward that favors earlier correctness and an execution status reward that encourages recovery from the invalid SQL. Experiments on BIRD, Spider, and Spider robustness variants demonstrate that our method consistently improves Text-to-SQL performance across both primary and robustness evaluations.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Dual-Group Exploration: Reinforcement Learning for Video Understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has significantly enhanced reasoning in Large Language Models. However, applying state-of-the-art RL methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to video-based Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains sub-optimal. We identify two key exploration bottlenecks: (1) Advantage Vanishing: generating multiple responses from invariant video contexts leads to near-uniform rewards, neutralizing learning signals after in-group standardization; (2) Visual Overfitting: standard RL lacks mechanisms to regularize sensitivity to visual perturbations under single-epoch training, causing policies to overfit to sparse temporal cues. To address these, we propose Dual-Group Exploration, a framework revitalizing learning signals at both input and output levels. At the input level, a Dual-Group Sampling strategy breaks visual determinism via complementary temporal sequences. At the output level, an Entropy-rated ELO Advantage captures inter-group quality variances. Concurrently, a Cross-Visual Counterfactual Weight establishes a Visual Consistency Region, safely driving exploration by enforcing reasoning consistency across varied views. Achieving state-of-the-art performance across six video reasoning benchmarks, our method demonstrates that consistency-guided exploration is beneficial for video understanding.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TRONTOR: To RoPE or Not to RoPE for Long-Context Modeling
abstract: While Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is widely used in large language models, its inductive biases can impair long-context reasoning and lead to attention sinks. In this work, we propose TRONTOR, a method that effectively combines RoPE and No Positional Encoding (NoPE) through a simple fine-tuning phase, bypassing the need for expensive pretraining modifications. Our preliminary experiments demonstrate that mixing RoPE and NoPE at the attention-head level can enhance long-context capabilities, while static selection strategies fail to capture the varying complexity of inputs. Based on this observation, TRONTOR employs a lightweight context-aware routing method that dynamically switches each attention head between RoPE and NoPE at every token step. This router-only configuration provides an efficient operating point, yielding long-context performance gains with minimal inference overhead. For further gains, we extend TRONTOR to TRONTOR-Agg, which applies simple unweighted averaging over multiple RoPE bases within RoPE-active heads while avoiding learnable intra-head routing. Evaluated on the RULER benchmark using Llama-3.2 (1B and 3B) and Qwen3 (1.7B and 4B), TRONTOR improves long-context performance by mitigating attention sinks and dynamically reallocating attention toward relevant mid-context tokens.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Demystifying Entropy Conflict: Why Reasoning Compression Stalls in Large Reasoning Models
abstract: Large reasoning models achieve strong problem-solving performance, but often generate excessively long chain-of-thought outputs, which substantially increase inference cost and limit practical deployment. Existing reasoning compression methods reduce length only partially and often suffer from unstable optimization or accuracy degradation. We trace this limitation to an underlying trajectory-level objective conflict: when the compression objective and the accuracy objective are optimized jointly, compression favors short-and-correct trajectories while accuracy optimization continues to preserve long-but-correct ones that remain useful on hard problems. This conflict creates opposing gradients on the same behaviors and can trap training in a local trade-off where further compression harms accuracy while accuracy recovery reintroduces verbose reasoning. At the model-decision level, we refer to the resulting failure mode as entropy conflict: the policy fails to fully collapse onto concise trajectories because accuracy-oriented updates keep restoring broader support over long-correct reasoning paths. To address this issue, we propose an entropy-guided training framework. Instead of forcing a mixed objective to follow an unstable path toward the final efficient-output set, we first contract the policy to a short-output set and then expand from this compact regime to recover accuracy and robustness. Experiments on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our method achieves performance comparable to the original model using only about 25% of its reasoning tokens.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Write Policy Determines Source Retention in External FIFO Memory: A Delayed-Copy Diagnostic
abstract: External hidden-state memories can extend Transformers beyond local attention windows, but the write policy deciding which states enter finite memory is often treated as an implementation detail. We study this factor with a controlled delayed-copy diagnostic using a windowed Transformer augmented with an external FIFO hidden-state memory. Under forced masking, query-to-source attention is blocked, removing this shortcut and making source retention directly testable. We define a capacity boundary as the minimum memory size needed to reach a fixed copy-accuracy threshold. We find that write policy changes this boundary predictably under constrained FIFO memory: an idealized source-only policy, which assumes that relevant states are identifiable at write time, yields an approximately delay-invariant boundary near the source length, whereas an unfiltered prefix-all policy induces a delay-dependent boundary that grows with written non-source content. Intermediate partial-prefix write policies produce intermediate boundaries, while source-pinned controls and memory diagnostics show that prefix-all degradation is dominated by FIFO eviction of source states rather than retrieval interference from retained non-source states alone. A symbolic key–value retrieval diagnostic shows the same qualitative trend. Within this controlled setting, our results highlight write policy as a central variable in evaluating finite FIFO external-memory Transformers.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Does Generating More Help? Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling
abstract: Synthetic data can be scaled along two routes: Source Expansion (SE), which enlarges the source by adding seed materials or generators, and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), which holds the source fixed and scales the generation budget. Existing scaling studies typically expand the source as the data grows, conflating SE with FSS and leaving FSS underexplored. We isolate FSS within a standard rejection sampling (RS) pipeline and derive a scaling form for it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. Empirically, fit on low budgets, the form predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher–student pair. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets, but adding seed questions outperforms spending the same budget on more responses at large budgets. Within FSS, neither synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol consistently outperforms plain RS across matched budgets. FSS is thus a bounded scaling axis and a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. We will release our code and data to facilitate further research.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Efficient Language-to-Vision Feature Injection for Referring Single-Object Tracking
abstract: Referring single-object tracking enables language-grounded target initialization and subsequent tracking by jointly leveraging semantic cues and visual templates. The core difficulty is to use language differently across stages: it is indispensable for grounding but can induce semantic drift during tracking when overemphasized. Meanwhile, current methods often require costly vision-language alignment training. We present LVTrack, a pure transformer framework that introduces a mode-conditioned Gated Feature Injector to adaptively regulate textual guidance and alleviate semantic drift. Together with targeted adaptations, it directly harnesses a frozen vision-language pretrained model, greatly reducing training cost and preserving strong language understanding. To further improve temporal localization, LVTrack integrates hybrid relative-absolute positional encodings with a lightweight memory mechanism and optimizes autoregressive box prediction using a Gaussian-smoothed KL loss. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that LVTrack achieves strong performance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CreaMem: A Scene-Aware Memory Architecture for Personalized Agents
abstract: Long-term memory is a core capability for personalized LLM agents. To support it, existing memory systems organize information using various criteria such as topic segments or summary hierarchies. However, we identify two major limitations in these designs. First, they lack scene awareness: memories from unrelated life scenes share the same retrieval space, which inflates the search space and introduces cross-scene interference. Second, they encode each memory from a single perspective, making it difficult to retrieve complementary views of the same event. In this paper, we propose the CreaMem architecture, which enables scene-aware memory organization by partitioning memory into several Life Scene Memories to reduce cross-scene interference at retrieval. Within each memory, entries are dual-coded from both episodic and trait-based perspectives. To go beyond the single perspective and achieve cross-memory synergy, we further devise a per-memory balanced sampling strategy at retrieval time. Extensive experiments on two long-term memory benchmarks show that CreaMem improves QA accuracy across all evaluation metrics, with particularly large gains on multi-hop reasoning performance, validating scene-aware partitioning and cross-memory synergy.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ToolDF: Tool-Integrated Reasoning for Mixed-Authenticity Audio Deepfake Detection
abstract: Audio deepfake detection is commonly formulated as clip-level binary classification of single-domain audio. However, real-world manipulated audio can exhibit mixed authenticity, where genuine and manipulated cues coexist across temporal transitions, overlapping sources, or both. This setting requires not only detecting manipulated audio but also localizing the components that provide evidence for the decision. We propose ToolDF, a tool-integrated reasoning framework for mixed-authenticity audio deepfake detection. ToolDF employs an audio large language model as an orchestrator trained with supervised tool-use trajectories. It adaptively analyzes the audio scene, selectively performs source separation, routes components to domain-specific experts, and aggregates their evidence into an interpretable verdict. We further introduce a mixed-authenticity ADD benchmark covering temporal transitions, acoustic overlaps, and hybrid mixtures. Experimental results show that ToolDF achieves the best overall performance on composite-type detection, achieving macro-F1 gains of 3.72 and 14.39 points over the strongest monolithic baseline and a fixed pipeline, respectively, while providing interpretable evidence localized to temporal regions and acoustic sources. Our source code and dataset are publicly available online at https://github.com/rlataewoo/tooldf.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CE-GAD: Curriculum-Efficient On-Policy Adversarial Distillation of Large Language Models
abstract: Generative adversarial distillation (GAD) provides on-policy feedback for black-box distillation by training a discriminator that ranks teacher and student responses to the same prompt. While effective, GAD is also costly: every step pays for a discriminator update, an actor update over the full response, and the indirect cost of recovering whenever the discriminator and the actor progress at incompatible rates. We argue that the right way to make GAD efficient is not to make individual updates cheaper but to decide **when each update is worth its cost**. We introduce **curriculum-efficient GAD (CE-GAD)**, an adaptive recipe that monitors a small set of training signals and uses them to:- (i) skip discriminator updates that would not change the reward, - (ii) constrain actor updates and prune per-token gradients to the subset that actually carries signal, and - (iii) rescale rewards and normalize advantages to preserve within-batch contrast under saturation.Evaluations across four models from two open-source families (Qwen2.5 at 3B/7B/14B and Llama-3.2-3B) demonstrate that CE-GAD matches or surpasses vanilla GAD on quality while winning on 12 out of 16 individual benchmark configurations. Specifically, on Qwen2.5-7B, CE-GAD improves the average score by up to **+3%** relative compared to the base model, while reducing per-step wall-clock time by up to **8x** relative to vanilla GAD.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Logic Tree: Topology-Aware Backtracking for DeepResearch Agents
abstract: Autonomous large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong potential for open-ended information-seeking tasks. However, existing agent frameworks primarily rely on sequential execution, making them vulnerable to error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning. Recent plan-and-execute approaches partially alleviate this issue, but their fixed planning strategies still struggle to recover from intermediate failures. We propose Logic Tree, a non-linear agentic reasoning framework formulated as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Instead of following a fixed plan with sequential execution, Logic Tree models complex task solving as a dynamically evolving and recoverable graph search process. The framework decomposes queries into parallel execution branches and incorporates a two-level self-correction mechanism. Local backtracking performs targeted rollback to repair failed reasoning states, while global replanning revises high-level execution strategies and preserves verified intermediate conclusions through a knowledge sanitation process. Experiments on BrowseComp, GAIA, and XBench show that Logic Tree consistently outperforms both sequential and plan-and-execute baselines. Further ablation studies demonstrate that combining DAG-based parallel execution with dynamic error recovery substantially improves robustness in long-horizon research tasks.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: KnowMT-Bench: Benchmarking Knowledge-Intensive Long-Form Question Answering in Multi-Turn Dialogues
abstract: Multi-Turn Long-Form Question Answering (MT-LFQA) is a key application paradigm of Large Language Models (LLMs) in knowledge-intensive domains. However, existing benchmarks are limited to single-turn dialogue, while multi-turn dialogue benchmarks typically assess other orthogonal capabilities rather than knowledge-intensive factuality. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce **KnowMT-Bench**, a new benchmark designed to systematically evaluate MT-LFQA for LLMs across knowledge-intensive fields, including medicine, finance, and law. To faithfully assess the model’s real-world performance, KnowMT-Bench employs a dynamic evaluation setting where models generate their own multi-turn dialogue histories given logically progressive question sequences. Our experiments on a diverse suite of LLMs show a clear degradation in both factual capability and information delivery efficiency in multi-turn dialogue. We further probe the underlying causes and investigate mitigation strategies spanning domain-specific finetuning, active context denoising, and RAG. The results show domain-dependent gains from finetuning, while active context denoising and RAG more consistently mitigate these issues, with RAG notably reversing this performance degradation. These findings underscore the importance of our benchmark for evaluating LLMs’ conversational factual capabilities in real-world applications.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SCIT: Testing Causal Cache Carriers in Latent Chain-of-Thought Models
abstract: Latent chain-of-thought models move intermediate reasoning into continuous states, obscuring which internal object causally carries a computation. We introduce SCIT, the Suffix Cache Interchange Test, which patches exact source–recipient counterfactuals and crosses cache-segment sufficiency with K/V splits, hidden-state and semantic-source controls, decoded validation, and matched corruption. In GPT-2 arithmetic, counterfactual transfer concentrates in value-cache suffix trajectories rather than hidden states, keys, answer slots, or single-token triggers. Full sufficiency-and-necessity closure holds only for the main CODI-GPT2 checkpoint; the Sim-CoT-style reproduction supports sufficiency and decoded transfer but not necessity. Across broader competent cells, arithmetic-like GPT-2/1B tasks retain latent-tail value/KV transfer, whereas 8B and repaired non-arithmetic tasks shift to prompt-prefix or full-cache K/V; ungated cells receive no call. SCIT thus provides a cache-level diagnostic, a checkpoint-specific arithmetic mechanism, and a competence-gated carrier map—not a universal latent-tail claim. Code: https://github.com/YIDING4869/scit-emnlp-2026
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CoT-Lock: Embedding Logic Fingerprints into the Chain-of-Thought of Large Reasoning Models
abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are valuable intellectual property due to their substantial training and alignment costs, creating a need for reliable ownership verification under black-box access, where a verifier can only query a suspect model and inspect its returned output. Existing trigger–response fingerprints are easy to test but are often weakly coupled with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning and can be fragile under paraphrasing or post-hoc model modifications. We propose CoT-Lock, a reasoning-mediated fingerprinting framework that casts ownership verification as a structured conflict-resolution task. CoT-Lock constructs verification queries in which a default semantic constraint is superseded only by a higher-priority meta-override rule, training the model to resolve fingerprint activation through priority-based arbitration. Our primary ownership test is output-only on confidential held-out probes; when reasoning traces are visible, trace-level verification further checks the expected arbitration process. Experiments on representative reasoning architectures show that CoT-Lock achieves stable black-box verification while preserving reasoning ability with minimal performance degradation, low false positives, and improved robustness against paraphrasing, fine-tuning, pruning, and quantization. Our code is available at https://github.com/acang425/CoT-Lock.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Redundancy: Information-Conserving Semantic Packaging for Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) achieve strong multimodal understanding but suffer from high inference costs due to redundant vision tokens. Existing hard-pruning methods discard low-scoring tokens directly, inevitably sacrificing fine-grained visual context. We propose SPack, a training-free token compression method that reframes pruning as information-energy redistribution rather than deletion. Instead of discarding pruned tokens, SPack transfers their semantic mass to retained tokens, enforcing a global principle we term Information Energy Conservation (IEC): the total information contained in redundant tokens is strictly conserved and fully transferred as information gain to the retained components. To realize this conservation, we introduce Optimal Transport (OT) theory, which treats removed energy as mass density and retained tokens as receiver slots. Solving the optimal transport plan under the Wasserstein distance yields a minimum-cost mapping that precisely transfers geometric structure and higher-order moments according to semantic affinity. Concretely, we estimate token importance via relation attention, semantic affinity, and value-space energy, then adaptively route pruned tokens to multiple retained tokens using OT, producing hyper-dense tokens that preserve both local semantics and global context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPack consistently achieves a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared to state-of-the-art methods. The code will be released upon acceptance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Lexical Coupling in GUI Element Grounding: Sentence Embeddings Track Labels across Mobile and Web
abstract: GUI grounding evaluations often treat high instruction–element embedding similarity as evidence of semantic grounding. Across three mobile and web benchmarks (AndroidControl, MoTIF, Mind2Web), we show this interpretation is frequently confounded by visible-label recovery: no off-the-shelf encoder significantly exceeds a BM25 lexical baseline at top-1, and encoder hit@1 is predictable from lexical rank, candidate-pool size, and label type at AUC 0.85–0.88. On AndroidControl, oracle fusion could lift R@1 by +12.8 pp, but standard reciprocal-rank fusion of the same signals instead degrades it by 1.4 pp. One epoch of in-domain contrastive fine-tuning of a small 22M encoder then beats every lexical and zero-shot baseline by +13.6 pp, localising the failure to off-the-shelf encoders rather than dense retrieval. These results suggest that, on its own, embedding similarity is not sufficient evidence of semantic GUI grounding beyond visible-label recovery; it should be reported against lexical controls and label-type stratification.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CAPO-SLT: Confidence-Aware Policy Optimization for Stable Sign Language Translation Generation
abstract: Recent sign language translation methods have advanced visual-language alignment, yet autoregressive generation remains vulnerable to unstable policy updates under ambiguous visual evidence. Such instability may cause locally plausible continuations to accumulate into sentence-level semantic deviations, especially when reinforcement learning is used with noisy reward and advantage estimates. Existing PPO-style policy optimization applies confidence-agnostic clipping bounds to all generated tokens, which limits its ability to distinguish between over-amplified confident predictions and low-probability tokens that may still carry useful corrective signals. To address this issue, we propose CAPO-SLT, a reinforcement learning based framework for stable sign language translation generation. CAPO introduces a confidence-aware policy optimization strategy that adapts the upper clipping bound according to old-policy token probability. It applies more conservative updates to high-confidence predictions while preserving update capacity for low-probability positive-advantage tokens. In addition, CAPO caps negative-advantage updates to improve robustness under noisy supervision. This design provides a simple drop-in replacement for standard clipping and stabilizes generation-stage optimization without changing the underlying visual encoder or reward function. Experiments on Chinese and American sign language benchmarks show consistent improvements over pose-based baselines under the same input setting, suggesting that CAPO-SLT provides an effective optimization strategy for stable sign language translation generation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EntangleCodec: A Unified Discrete Audio Tokenizer via Semantic-Acoustic Entanglement
abstract: Audio tokenizers serve as the discrete interface between continuous audio and Audio Language Models (ALMs), but existing tokenizers often struggle to support both understanding and generation. Reconstruction-oriented codecs preserve acoustic fidelity but lack rich semantics, while semantic-aware tokenizers typically rely on separate semantic and acoustic streams, introducing redundancy or misalignment.We propose EntangleCodec, a unified discrete audio tokenizer that learns caption-aligned semantic-acoustic representations before quantization. By aligning audio with rich captions rather than ASR transcripts, EntangleCodec captures linguistic content, speaker identity, emotion, prosody, and acoustic scenes within a compact token stream. A flow-matching diffusion decoder further enables high-quality reconstruction across speech, music, and general audio.EntangleCodec achieves reconstruction quality competitive with specialized codecs, outperforms all codec-based baselines on audio understanding by up to +7.4% on MMAR, and supports both TTS and TTA generation in a unified framework. Furthermore, EntangleCodec-based audio language models demonstrate strong scaling behavior: even at 0.6B parameters, the model surpasses specialized continuous-representation LLMs with over 13B parameters across three benchmarks using 22x fewer parameters; scaling to 8B further establishes new state-of-the-art results on MMAR, highlighting that representation quality is as critical as model scale in audio language modeling. Code and model weights are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EntangleCodec-BA01.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SCHEDBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Constraint Faithfulness in Natural-Language Combinatorial Scheduling
abstract: This paper introduces **SCHEDBench**, a natural-language benchmark for evaluating **combinatorial scheduling** constraint faithfulness under surface-form variation. Grounded in canonical scheduling instances and solver-derived feasibility and optimality, SCHEDBench assesses whether large language models (**LLMs**) generate schedules with the same constraint-feasible behavior across varied natural-language (NL) surface forms. SCHEDBench spans 1,132 instances across job-shop scheduling problems (JSP), single and multi-mode resource-constrained project scheduling problems (RCPSP), nurse rostering/scheduling, and curriculum timetabling problems of varying difficulty.
