Instances are templated into natural language problems using domain-specific templates, themed entities, lexical-syntactic template rephrasing, and constraint-level surface-form variation—with reference solutions verified for feasibility and objective optimality. Across thirteen frontier and open-weight LLMs, we find that models are not reliably invariant to semantically equivalent renderings of the same scheduling problem. Surface-form variation reduces feasibility and induces above-noise shifts in per-instance hard-constraint violations on matched instances. Among the tested isolated axes, constraint reordering yields the clearest above-noise sensitivity.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Implicit Hierarchical Modeling for Cross-System Legal Case Retrieval
abstract: Legal Case Retrieval (LCR) identifies relevant precedent cases to support legal reasoning and sentencing. A core challenge for cross-system LCR is the structural divergence between legal systems: civil-law systems provide explicit statutory hierarchies but lack inter-case citations, while common-law systems offer rich citation networks but lack uniform codified semantic hierarchies. Existing methods exploit only one side of this divide, remaining system-specific. We propose DSLaw, which unifies both systems by implicitly modeling hierarchical semantics through residual quantization and using the resulting discrete representations as semantic anchors for cross-case graph reasoning. By progressively decomposing legal semantics from coarse concepts to fine-grained distinctions, DSLaw constructs implicit connections even without explicit citations. Experiments on COLIEE2025 (common law) and ELAM (civil law) show DSLaw consistently outperforms strong baselines, while joint training further validates cross-system generalization. The implementation is provided at https://github.com/KDEGroup/DSLaw.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MCTL: Meta-Cognitive Tool-Learning Framework for Multimodal Fake News Detection
abstract: Multimodal fake news proliferates on social media, yet its verification is hindered by context sparsity and analytical heterogeneity: deceptive posts often hinge on implicit social background, while distinct misinformation patterns demand different verification strategies. Existing methods rely on either representation-driven classifiers or LLM-based retrieval-augmented and tool-using pipelines, which act as opaque black boxes or follow rigid, predefined tool chains, failing to adapt reasoning to diverse news and yielding weakly grounded, uninterpretable decisions. To this end, we propose MCTL, a Meta-Cognitive Tool-Learning Framework that reformulates detection from static classification into in-context cognitive orchestration with dynamically planned tool-based reasoning. Specifically, MCTL retrieves cross-modal contextual evidence as external memory to compensate for context sparsity, performs meta-cognitive planning to construct a sample-specific Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) reasoning blueprint, routes specialized tools along the DAG, and fuses conflicting judgments via consensus-aware arbitration, enabling context-grounded, sample-adaptive, and traceable verification. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MCTL consistently outperforms recent state-of-the-art agentic and RAG baselines, confirming its effectiveness and reliability.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Um, Actually: Timely and Calibrated Fact-Checking with DIVER
abstract: Fact verification pipelines are often unrealistic: they assume full-input access, operate on isolated atomic claims, and overlook the central question of when a system should act under partial evidence. We introduce DIVER (Deliberative and Iterative fact VERification), an LLM-based framework for calibrated incremental fact-checking. DIVER incrementally extracts verifiable atomic claims from progressively revealed input, retrieves and refines evidence through iterative web search, and triggers a correction as soon as a claim is reliably refuted; if no such trigger occurs, it performs a passage-level revision over the full input to recover missed errors. Across standard fact-checking benchmarks, DIVER outperforms strong LLM-based verification pipelines, with especially large gains on retrieval-intensive settings. We further introduce UmActually, a real-world benchmark built from the Internet game Um, Actually, to evaluate not only whether a system finds an error, but whether it does so at the right time. On UmActually, DIVER reports the strongest end-to-end results while typically buzzing close to the earliest valid decision point, supporting its effectiveness for calibrated incremental fact-checking.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Neural Procedural Memory: Empowering LLM Agents with Implicit Activation Steering
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel as static solvers, transforming them into autonomous agents remains challenging. This transition requires continuous environmental interaction, yet current agents lack the necessary persistent procedural memory. Existing approaches predominantly employ Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to inject explicit textual guidelines into model contexts. However, relying solely on symbolic instructions can introduce a text-action disconnect, frequently failing to activate the internal representations necessary for correct task execution. To address this, the paper introduces Neural Procedural Memory (NPM), a training-free framework that represents agent memory through implicit activation steering rather than explicit instructions. By distilling procedural skills from historical contrastive experiences into steering vectors in the activation space, NPM directly activates the task-relevant neural mechanisms to guide task execution. Evaluations across four agent benchmarks show that NPM performs comparably to baselines using explicit textual instructions. Furthermore, the results show that combining implicit steering with explicit workflows provides complementary advantages, leading to more robust task execution. Representational analyses indicate that these steering vectors encode consistent task logic, forming organized structures within the activation space. These findings suggest that implicit activation steering provides a promising approach for managing agent memory.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: In-Context Neurofeedback: Can LLMs Control Their Internal Representations through Privileged Access?
abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) can control their own internal representations matters for both machine metacognition and AI safety. A recent study applied neurofeedback to LLMs and claimed that they can control their internal representations. However, the reported control may rely on superficial mechanisms rather than genuine internal access because the control targets in that study are not privileged, meaning that a third party can infer them from the prompt. We redesign the neurofeedback paradigm for LLMs so that the control target satisfies the privileged access requirement, which is closer to neurofeedback experiments in human cognitive neuroscience. Under this stricter setting, the models do not demonstrate reliable control over privileged internal representations, suggesting that previously reported control cannot exclude the possibility that it relies on superficial mechanisms. Our results indicate that rigorous assessments of metacognition in LLMs require evaluation methods that demand privileged access.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Scenario-based Probing and Steering Cultural Values in Large Language Models
abstract: Evaluation of cultural value alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) typically relies on direct prompting with survey-style questions, which often elicit neutral or safety-aligned responses and fail to capture the model’s underlying cultural orientation. To overcome these challenges, we propose a framework for probing and steering latent cultural representations in LLMs along the two Inglehart–Welzel axes of the World Values Survey (WVS). By translating social value questions into scenario-based dilemmas, we extract token-level probabilities to measure implicit values and apply activation steering, optionally combined with country-conditioned prompting, to shift model behavior without retraining. Across three 4B-open-weight LLMs, four countries and three social domains, we find substantial variation in steerability. Importantly, we identify latent entanglement, where interventions along one Inglehart–Welzel axis induce a shift along the other. This entanglement is consistent with correlations present in human WVS data and persists across our experimental settings. Our work identifies empirical constraints on cultural alignment in LLMs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EffectMem: Effectiveness-Driven Memory Reuse for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have stimulated increasing interest in LLM-based agents for long-horizon interactive decision-making. As a lightweight alternative to parameter-level optimization, many studies enhance LLM agents through retrievable experience memory. However, existing retrieval strategies primarily optimize for the relevance of historical memories, leaving the applicability conditions and verifiable execution effects of retrieved trajectories insufficiently captured. To mitigate this executability gap between relevance-driven retrieval and executable reuse, we propose Effectiveness-Driven Memory (EffectMem), a framework that reframes trajectory memory as executable guidance whose applicability and effects are checked during interaction. During memory construction, EffectMem structures successful trajectories into positive executable contracts and localizable failures into negative experience guards. At inference, EffectMem retrieves candidate contracts, verifies their applicability to the current state, executes aligned chunks under guard constraints, and invokes discrepancy-guided correction when observed effects deviate from expected postconditions. Experiments on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop demonstrate that EffectMem outperforms competitive baselines and improves the effectiveness of memory-augmented LLM agents.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: AdaSpec: Adaptive Routing by Ranking for Speculative Agents
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents execute sequences of reasoning, tool-use, and environment-interaction steps, making end-to-end latency a central deployment bottleneck. Speculative agents reduce this latency by leveraging a faster draft agent to propose the action trajectory while a stronger target agent verifies each action to ensure lossless action trajectories. Recent systems adapt how many future actions a preselected draft agent proposes before verification, but leave the drafter itself unchanged across tasks and episodes. Our experiments show that the best drafter varies across tasks and trajectory prefixes, revealing substantial latency headroom from adaptive drafter selection. This motivates the question: which draft agent should speculate for a given task and target agent to achieve low end-to-end latency? We propose AdaSpec, an adaptive routing framework for speculative agents with an objective distinct from standard model routing: selecting the drafter that minimizes realized speculative-execution latency for a target agent, rather than selecting the model that produces the final answer. AdaSpec profiles a pool of candidate draft-agent configurations for each target agent and trains a lightweight, latency-supervised router to rank them by measured speculative latency. The router supports both query-level routing and episode-level rerouting before each draft-and-check segment, while the target agent remains responsible for verifying actions. AdaSpec improves fixed-drafter baselines across multiple datasets and target-agent settings.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: From Correctness to Utility: Gain-Based Prefix Evaluation for LLM Reasoning
abstract: Reasoning prefixes shape the future trajectory of LLM problem solving, yet existing process reward models usually evaluate them through local step correctness. We argue that correctness is a useful but indirect proxy for the effect we ultimately care about: whether a prefix increases the probability of successful completion. We define this effect as prefix gain, the solve-rate improvement induced by conditioning lightweight student model group on a prefix, and use it to train a Prefix Utility Model (PUM) with a simple pairwise ranking objective. PUM learns outcome-grounded prefix utility and can score both complete trajectories and partial reasoning prefixes. Across Best-of-N selection, beam search, and reinforcement learning on mathematical reasoning, PUM provides a strong prefix-level supervision signal, especially when candidate pools are large, search budgets increase, or rule-based rewards are sparse.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MERTA: Multi-Expert Retrieval for Token Allocation in Video Large Language Models
abstract: Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) excel in video understanding but suffer from significant computational overheads due to extensive visual tokens. Existing mainstream solutions including visual token compression and query-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Video RAG), face notable limitations: the former typically pursues task-agnostic compression of global video semantics, lacking query awareness, while the latter fails to optimize visual token construction and relies on costly, rigid annotation data. To address these challenges, we propose MERTA (Multi-Expert Retrieval for Token Allocation), a plug-and-play framework that integrates selective multi-expert collaborative retrieval with query-aware token allocation. MERTA selectively leverages lightweight experts to capture multimodal semantics, adaptively identifying key frames by measuring the relevance among queries, visual content, and auxiliary annotations. It then dynamically allocates the visual token budget, assigning higher budgets to key frames while keeping the total visual token budget constant. MERTA integrates seamlessly without requiring architectural modifications, demonstrating superior efficiency and performance over existing methods across multiple video understanding benchmarks.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: A Unified Framework to Elicit Structured Feedback for Interpretable Multi-Trait Essay Scoring
abstract: Multi-trait Automated Essay Scoring (AES) requires rubric-grounded reasoning across interdependent traits, rather than isolated score prediction. Existing feedback-enhanced methods often decouple feedback from scoring or assess traits independently, weakening score–feedback consistency and rubric alignment. We propose HiFTS, a unified autoregressive framework that generates hierarchical CoT feedback before predicting trait-level and holistic scores. HiFTS distills rubric-grounded hierarchical CoT feedback from a teacher LLM and trains student models to jointly generate feedback and scores. HiFTS further applies Group Relative Policy Optimization with a composite reward balancing score agreement, calibration, feedback quality, and structural validity. At inference, a lightweight global prior provides holistic guidance to reduce drift during long-form reasoning. We also introduce CFMS-34, a Chinese multi-trait AES dataset with 951 essays annotated with holistic scores and 34 rubric-based traits. Experiments on CFMS-34 and ASAP++ show that HiFTS achieves strong holistic and trait-level scoring while producing coherent, rubric-aligned feedback.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: GAGPO: Generalized Advantage Grouped Policy Optimization
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for post-training large language model (LLM) agents. However, credit assignment in multi-turn environments remains a challenge. Agents typically receive sparse, trajectory-level rewards only at the end of an episode, making it difficult to identify which specific intermediate actions led to success or failure. Consequently, effectively propagating delayed outcomes back to individual steps without relying on costly auxiliary value models remains an open problem. In this paper, we propose Generalized Advantage Grouped Policy Optimization (GAGPO), a critic-free RL method that enables precise, step-aligned temporal credit assignment. GAGPO constructs a non-parametric grouped value proxy from sampled rollouts to compute TD/GAE-style temporal advantages, recursively propagating outcome supervision backward through time. Coupled with group-wise advantage normalization and an action-level importance ratio, GAGPO extracts stable and localized optimization signals directly from multi-turn trajectories. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that GAGPO outperforms strong RL baselines. Further analyses reveal faster early-stage learning, improved interaction efficiency, and smoother optimization dynamics, offering a simple yet highly effective framework for multi-turn agentic RL.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Estimating Uncertainty from Reasoning: A Large-Scale Study of Multi- and Crosslingual MCQA Performance in LLMs
abstract: Uncertainty estimation (UE) enables LLM-powered systems to recognize when to abstain, yet existing research has predominantly focused on English. We present the first large-scale evaluation of UE methods across 22 languages, spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource settings. Using two human-curated Q A datasets, we compare open and closed box UE methods (nine in total) across different model sizes and architectures while eliciting long-form reasoning, avoiding LLM-as-a-judge and embedding-based scoring, which can introduce evaluation noise. We report three main actionable findings. First, we find that prompting models to reason in English while keeping questions in low-resource languages substantially improves UE performance, suggesting that comprehension of low-resource languages is largely intact, and that the reliability bottleneck lies in generation rather than understanding. Second, prompting models to reason in English closes the UE performance gap between low and high-resource languages, demonstrating that generation language matters more than the question language. Third, the choice of UE method should depend on model scale: at smaller scales, open-box probability-based methods outperform alternatives; at larger scales, closed-box self-verbalized uncertainty becomes superior. Finally, we provide an analysis of threshold selection for selective prediction, offering guidance on calibrating abstention in multilingual settings. We publish our code to support further research in multilingual UE. Our code available in Anonymous Github[https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Cross-and-Multilingual-Uncertainty-Estimation-7976/].
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: DisCon4Gen: A Semantic Alignment Framework Through Discriminative Conditioning for Generation
abstract: Generative language models (GLMs) excel at text generation and instruction following, while discriminative language models (DLMs) provide strong semantic representations for understanding tasks. Under the manifold hypothesis, natural language semantics can be regarded as lying on a shared latent semantic manifold, while DLMs and GLMs learn different representations of this manifold in their respective latent spaces. However, due to differences in training objectives and modeling strategies, these representation spaces are not naturally aligned, preventing discriminative representations from being directly utilized by GLMs through simple concatenation or linear transformation. To address this issue, a semantic alignment framework through discriminative conditioning for generation (DisCon4Gen) is proposed. From a manifold-based perspective, DisCon4Gen transforms DLM semantics into continuous conditions for GLMs. It further incorporates both global semantic signals and fine-grained discriminative cues to guide generation, enabling GLMs to better exploit external discriminative semantics. Experiments on five downstream datasets show that DisCon4Gen improves over strong supervised fine-tuning baselines and achieves competitive performance across both semantic understanding and generative reasoning tasks.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: On the Learnability of Antidistillation Reasoning Traces
abstract: Unauthorized distillation turns reasoning traces into a conduit for transferring proprietary models’ reasoning behavior to smaller students. Antidistillation Sampling (ADS) perturbs decoding to preserve task utility for legitimate users while obstructing student imitation. Our token-level Metropolis–Hastings diagnosis reveals that current ADS-style defenses leave the trace’s intrinsic learnability largely intact: most tokens still follow the original teacher, while a few teacher-uncertain positions induce extreme loss and dominate optimization. ADS hides learnable reasoning behind a sparse high-loss tail instead of eliminating it. We therefore reformulate reasoning distillation as offline reinforcement learning from imperfect demonstrations, with credit assignment that reinforces high-quality reasoning behavior while suppressing disruptive segments. Across two teachers, six students, and six datasets, the resulting learner extracts reasoning from current anti-distillation traces, outperforming vanilla maximum-likelihood training and eight supervised fine-tuning baselines by up to 21%. We then turn the same principle into an adaptive defense that directly targets high-value reasoning behaviors, exploiting the perceptual gap between humans and models to preserve readability while disrupting model-visible Unicode sequences. This strategy sharply degrades both classical distillation and the adaptive learner, and scales to protect GPT-5.5 traces. These results suggest that robust anti-distillation should optimize for low intrinsic learnability, not merely high token-level surprise.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ElementCheck: Complexity-Aware Long-Form Text Factuality Evaluation via Sentence Elements
abstract: Existing long-form factuality evaluation relies on the decompose-retrieve-verify pipeline. However, the pipeline suffers from noise from claim decomposition and fixed verification granularity, resulting in unreliable results. We propose ElementCheck, a complexity-aware framework that verifies long-form outputs via sentence elements. Instead of uniformly decomposing sentences into atomic sub-claims, ElementCheck extracts entity pairs that are explicitly linked through verifiable connections in the original sentence as elements, and organizes these into an element graph. The graph topology provides a structural signal for estimating sentence complexity, enabling direct verification for simple sentences and targeted element-level refinement and verification for complex ones. To support fine-grained evaluation, we construct a new benchmark FastFact-Sent by mapping isolated claims from FastFact-Bench back to their source sentences. Experiments on FastFact-Sent and two domain-specific benchmarks show ElementCheck consistently improves factuality verification across five backbone models while maintaining a favorable accuracy-cost trade-off. Further analyses demonstrate that complexity-aware verification reduces unnecessary re-verification and maintains stability across different backbones. The code is available at Here.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: STQA: A Benchmark for Stock-Focused Tabular Question Answering over Historical and Forecasted Data
abstract: Stock market analysis inherently requires composite reasoning over historical records and future projections, yet existing benchmarks remain fragmented across isolated tasks. We introduce STQA (Stock-focused Tabular Question Answering), an end-to-end benchmark designed to systematically evaluate natural-language question answering over historical data, numerical forecasts, and forecast-based reasoning. Built on a large-scale financial dataset, STQA covers 4,451 stocks and contains 30,500 question–answer pairs derived from expert-crafted templates, accompanied by fine-grained intent and slot annotations. To operationalize this benchmark, we present SQFRS (Stock Query–Forecast–Reasoning System), an agent-based unified framework that orchestrates SQL retrieval and time-series forecasting tools. Experiments demonstrate that while current large language models perform well on historical queries, forecast-based reasoning poses a substantial challenge, revealing critical bottlenecks in tool coordination and reasoning under uncertainty.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Confidence: Test-Time Scaling for Multi-Turn Search Agents via Retrieval Grounding
abstract: Confidence-based voting aggregates parallel LLM rollouts by weighting each with internal signals such as token log probabilities, and has been actively studied for single-turn reasoning. However, modern LLMs increasingly act as multi-turn search agents that retrieve and condition on external documents. In this paper, we show that confidence-based voting transfers poorly to this multi-turn setting, and identify the underlying failure reason as copy inflation: when retrieved documents are appended to an agent’s context, tokens copied from those documents receive systematically inflated log probabilities. This flattens confidence scores within each question and weakens the resulting weighted vote. To address this issue, we propose Retrieval-Grounded Voting (RGV), which scores each rollout by the lexical overlap between its final answer and the documents it retrieved. By computing the signal outside the contaminated context, RGV sidesteps both token log probabilities and additional LLM calls. Across four search-agent benchmarks and five LLMs, RGV consistently outperforms confidence-based voting, with gains of up to +5.4% accuracy and +35% on minority-correct questions, where the correct answer appears in only 1-2 of 8 rollouts.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Hallucination as Exploit: Evidence-Carrying Multimodal Agents
abstract: Multimodal agents increasingly choose tool calls from screenshots, documents, and webpages, where a false perceptual claim can turn hallucination from an answer-quality error into an authorization failure. We formalize this failure as hallucination-to-action conversion (H2AC) and propose evidence-carrying multimodal agents (ECA), in which model text may propose actions but cannot authorize them: constrained DOM/OCR/AX verifiers issue typed certificates for action-critical predicates, and a deterministic gate executes only what the certificates support. Across verifier red-teaming, 7,488 replayed authorization traces, and end-to-end and live-browser evaluations, ECA executes no unsafe action, while GPT-5.4 judge baselines admit 79–99% of unsafe actions under the same threat model; benign actions are occasionally deferred to user confirmation (6.4% on live pages) but never hard-blocked. The guarantee is conditional, extending exactly as far as the verifiers, schemas, and gate implementation that form ECA’s trusted base.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Personalizing How Recommendation Agents Reason: Self-Evolving Per-User Skills for Recommendation Agents
abstract: LLM-based recommendation agents personalize what they know through evolving per-user semantic memory, yet how they perform reasoning relies on a universal, static system prompt shared across all users. When a recommendation fails, the agent only updates its memory, but never examines or revises the reasoning that leads to the failure. To close this gap, we propose SAGER (Self-Evolving Agent for Personalized Recommendation), the first framework to equip each user with a dedicated, continuously evolving policy skill. SAGER incorporates three tailored mechanisms for recommendation scenarios: (i) a two-representation skill architecture constrained by a Cognitive Injection Boundary, decoupling a rich evolution substrate from a minimal inference-time injection; (ii) a contrastive differential chain-of-thought engine that diagnoses ranking errors against unchosen near-misses under a refine-not-replace principle; and (iii) skill-augmented listwise reasoning that mitigates the Score-Tie Bottleneck, enabling the slim skill to serve as an active tie-breaker. Evaluated on four public benchmarks, SAGER achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Furthermore, plugging its policy skill layer into three structurally distinct host agents delivers consistent 9%–12% gains on the H@1 metric. These results indicate that policy skill evolution provides architecture-agnostic improvements that are largely complementary to memory accumulation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Debate Messages Help or Hurt: Diagnosing Communication in Self-Distillation
abstract: Multi-agent debate is widely used to enhance reasoning in language models, yet the exchanged messages are rarely analyzed. We study these messages in a Debate+SFT self-distillation loop by tracking their round-level evolution, intervening on peer messages with T-CIC at inference time, and comparing against matched Solo controls. Across three 5-seed discovery tasks–MATH, GSM-Hard, and 2WikiMultiHopQA–we observe weak refinement on MATH (+0.9pp for Debate versus +9.0pp for Solo), harmful homogenization on GSM-Hard (-11.3pp, with messages 27.5% longer and more self-similar), and mild inflation on 2WikiMHQA (-0.5pp with moderate length growth). A 2-seed T-CIC check on round-4 adapters shows different forms of message dependence: MATH collapses when peer messages are removed, shuffled, or replaced (-16 to -23pp), GSM-Hard is selectively sensitive to mismatched context, and 2WikiMHQA is mostly stable except under cross-problem shuffling. Debate messages should therefore be measured and stress-tested before they are trusted as a training signal.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SAMAC: Collaborating with Multi-Disciplinary Team for Adaptive Medical Decision-Making
abstract: Multi-agent large language model systems offer a promising paradigm for multidisciplinary medical decision support by integrating heterogeneous expert perspectives. However, existing frameworks often rely on loosely structured interactions, where disagreement is insufficiently diagnosed and discussion may collapse into superficial consensus or parallel opinion aggregation. We propose Structured Adaptive Multi-disciplinary Collaboration (SAMAC), a structured and strategy-aware multi-agent framework for adaptive MDT-style medical reasoning. SAMAC introduces Structured Deliberation to detect opinion disagreement and majority not confident, along with a Consensus Purification mechanism that transforms disagreement into constructive and collaborative refinement. When disagreement arises, SAMAC adaptively selects between Self-refinement and Counter-questioning to enable evidence-grounded negotiation. Experiments on three medical datasets—RADCURE, HANCOCK, and OSCCPI—show that SAMAC consistently improves overall performance and collaborative gains over existing multi-agent baselines. In particular, SAMAC improves the Average Score by 4.29 points on the RADCURE dataset and achieves higher Relative Self-Correction Scores (RSS), indicating more effective resolution of disagreement and stable collective decisions. These results highlight the importance of controlled and diverse interaction dynamics in multi-agent medical reasoning. Code will be released upon publication.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: DualResearch: Entropy-Gated Dual-Graph Retrieval for Answer Reconstruction in Deep Research Agents
abstract: Deep Research Agents (DR-Agents) extend LLMs with multi-step retrieval, tool use, and intermediate computation to solve complex problems. However, their execution logs often contain redundant context, noisy evidence, and brittle dependencies among intermediate decisions. As a result, final answers can be sensitive to irrelevant or weakly verified information. We propose DualResearch, a log-based post-processing framework for answer reconstruction. Given a query and a completed DR-Agent log, DualResearch normalizes the log into event records and constructs two evidence graphs: a breadth semantic graph for declarative evidence and a depth causal graph for procedural provenance. It then retrieves breadth nodes and depth paths, assigns higher weights to retrieval channels with more concentrated retained candidate distributions, and jointly considers relevance and cross-view agreement to select evidence for reconstruction; the concentration measure reflects retrieval confidence rather than factual correctness. Experiments on HLE, GAIA, and GPQA show consistent accuracy improvements over underlying DR-Agents and controlled log-reuse baselines.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ESPO: Error-Structured Prompt Optimization via Diagnose, Diversify, and Stabilize
abstract: Evolutionary prompt optimizers such as GEPA suffer from prompt bloat: each iteration appends rules and caveats, producing prompts that are 2–3× longer yet no more accurate. We trace this to three deficiencies - incomplete error observation, limited search diversity, and unreliable selection - and propose ESPO (Error-Structured Prompt Optimization), which decomposes prompt optimization into three phases: Diagnose clusters all training errors into structural patterns in one round; Propose generates candidates via four complementary strategies with independent biases; Select applies bootstrap stability selection. On seven public NLP benchmarks - Tweet, MMLU, GSM8K, HotpotQA, ScoNe, HoVer, and PUPA - ESPO wins 6/7 datasets with +3.76% average accuracy over the state-of-the-art (74.67% vs. 70.91% for GEPA), while producing prompts 47% shorter (1,004 vs. 1,878 chars) and faster at inference. Cross-model experiments across four additional student models (Gemma 3 12B, Mistral 14B, Qwen3 32B, Claude Haiku 4.5) show ESPO yields the best average accuracy on every model tested, with the largest gap on Qwen3 GSM8K (15.00% → 91.40%). A generalization bound (Appendix) grounds each phase in a corresponding term of the test-time gap, and the ablation confirms a key prediction: adding diversity without bootstrap selection actually hurts performance (-1.20%).
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: VIBE: Video Instruction-aligned Background music gEneration
abstract: Current video-to-music (V2M) models lack semantic control and fail to penalize instruction violations, largely due to their reliance on reconstruction objectives and the representational bottleneck of static cross-modal conditioning in Diffusion Autoregressive (DAR) architectures. To resolve this, we introduce VIBE, a novel text-and-video-to-music (T+V2M) generation model that leverages: (1) Conditioning Connection, a depth-wise cross-layer conditioning mechanism that dynamically bridges the planning and diffusion refinement heads and (2) a comprehensive reward modeling taxonomy, optimizing for both hard, verifiable constraints (e.g., tempo, key) and soft, subjective qualities (e.g., musicality, multimodal alignment) with a structured 5-stage training curriculum. Upon evaluation using audio-visual alignment, instruction following, and audio quality metrics, along with a subjective human evaluation study, we observe that VIBE demonstrates enhanced controllability and instruction adherence while performing comparably to most evaluated baselines on generation fidelity and multimodal alignment.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Out-of-Distribution Checkpoint Selection Has a Resolution Problem: Auditing Sparse Exact Match with Token Likelihood
abstract: Exact match (EM) can make checkpoint selection ambiguous when a small labeled out of distribution (OOD) validation set leaves several checkpoints tied at zero or at the maximum. Without an explicit tie rule, the reported metric does not identify which checkpoint produced the final test score. We study this validation resolution problem in semantic parsing and morphological reinflection. Our protocol reports the reference budget, token likelihood choice under teacher forcing, and latest tied candidate, while using EM for a unique nonzero maximum. Across 600 draws from 30 runs, 8 references leave every early checkpoint at zero in 48% of draws and the maximum tied in 57%. Within tied draws, mean full split regret falls from 0.063 under random selection to 0.050 with token likelihood. The latest tied candidate performs better on average for mostly monotone trajectories, but token likelihood independently orders candidates that hard EM cannot distinguish. These results support reporting both orderings when small labeled OOD validation sets guide checkpoint selection.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Can LLMs Compress Wireless Signals? Physics-Informed Prompting for Training-Free Signal Compression
abstract: Wireless signals are a unique form of time-series data that encode rich physical characteristics of the propagation environment. As large volumes of signals are continuously generated in wireless sensing systems, efficient compression is essential for scalable transmission under limited system resources. However, wireless signals exhibit strong variability across environments and time, making it difficult to design universal compression schemes that generalize across domains while preserving the physical fidelity required for accurate reconstruction and sensing. Meanwhile, recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning and adaptation capabilities across diverse modalities and domains. This raises an intriguing question: can LLMs compress wireless signals in a training-free manner while preserving physical fidelity? To the best of our knowledge, this problem remains unexplored. To answer this question, we propose a physics-informed prompting framework for training-free wireless signal compression. The framework incorporates environmental context and scenario-specific knowledge as physical priors in the prompt. We further introduce a dictionary module with self-learned patterns to stabilize inference and a key prompt module to align the semantics between the LLMs used for compression and reconstruction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves high-fidelity reconstruction under cross-domain settings, highlighting the promise of physics-informed prompting as a new paradigm for processing and compressing low-level physical signals.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Node-to-Neighborhood Semantic Consistency: Text-Topology Alignment for TAGs Anomaly Detection
abstract: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) is vital for applications such as fraud detection and academic integrity verification. Existing approaches generally fall into two paradigms. GNN-based methods capture structural patterns but struggle to capture fine-grained textual semantics. Methods integrating LLMs with graphs improve semantic understanding yet fail to fully comprehend topological relationships among neighbors. Moreover, both paradigms overlook the correspondence between textual semantics and graph topological relationships, limiting their ability to identify nodes whose semantics are inconsistent with their neighborhoods. In this paper, we formalize TAG anomaly detection as a node-to-neighborhood semantic consistency problem, where anomalies may arise from either textual semantic mismatch or topological deviation between a node and its neighbors. We propose N2NSC (Node-to-Neighborhood Semantic Consistency), a framework that captures the correspondence between graph topology and textual semantics through two complementary fusion paths. The two pathways work synergistically, enabling the LLM to jointly use textual and structural neighborhood information for anomaly detection. Extensive experiments across eight benchmark datasets, with additional validation on two real-world fraud datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of N2NSC.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MedReaMM: Evaluating Large Multimodal Models on Expert-Level Clinical Diagnostic Synthesis
abstract: The application of Large Language Models (LLMs) to diagnostic decision-making has garnered growing interest. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on textual reasoning or isolated visual question-answering (VQA) tasks, lacking holistic integration of clinical narratives and medical imaging, and thus failing to assess the multimodal diagnostic synthesis capability central to expert clinical judgment. To bridge this gap, we introduce **MedReaMM**, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate models’ ability to synthesize heterogeneous clinical evidence consisting of detailed patient histories alongside multiple medical images into accurate differential diagnoses under a complete-information paradigm. Constructed from case reports sourced from top-tier medical journals and curated clinical case databases, MedReaMM comprises 625 expert-validated cases with an average of 2.79 medical images per case and a total of 1,042 standardized diagnoses annotated with ICD-11 codes. These cases predominantly represent rare, atypical, or multi-system presentations that demand expert-level evidence integration beyond routine pattern recognition. We evaluate 23 Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) and find that most achieve diagnostic accuracy scores below 50%, underscoring a substantial gap in multimodal diagnostic synthesis capability. Further analysis reveals that medical knowledge proficiency, medical image understanding, and evidence integration are all highly correlated with diagnostic performance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CoCoA: Context-Conditional Cultural Alignment for Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often favor Western-associated entities across cultural contexts. Conventional debiasing methods aim for uniform neutrality, but cultural bias mitigation demands context-conditional behavior, preferring culturally appropriate entities when cultural cues are present and remaining neutral when they are absent. We propose CoCoA (Context-Conditional Cultural Alignment), a framework that learns this behavior through dual-context training on the same entity pairs under contexts with and without cultural cues. CoCoA combines a contrastive alignment objective with calibration and drift regularization, optimized through goal-aware gradient reconciliation. We evaluate CoCoA on CAMeL and Camellia, two entity-centric cultural bias benchmarks, across ten language settings and four LLMs. CoCoA reduces the Cultural Bias Score from 43 to 24 on average while maintaining near-neutral preferences at 50.2, with minimal impact on general performance across five standard benchmarks. These findings highlight that effective cultural alignment requires context-conditional modeling rather than uniform debiasing, and establish a new direction for mitigating entity-centric cultural bias in LLMs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Think Before You Score: Pedagogical Chain-of-Thought Annotation and Reinforcement Learning for Low-Resource Multilingual Essay Evaluation
abstract: Automated Essay Scoring (AES) in low-resource, non-English educational settings faces a compounded challenge: existing corpora record only a final holistic score, discarding the rich intermediate reasoning that human examiners rely on. We argue this annotation gap may contribute to Rubric Drift—the observed tendency of LLMs to apply scoring norms misaligned with the target curriculum, potentially reflecting Anglocentric defaults. To address this, we introduce MPEAB-2430, a multilingual AES benchmark spanning Malay, Hindi, and Arabic curricula, annotated with Pedagogical Chain-of-Thought (P-CoT) trajectories that capture sub-dimensional analyses, explicit error attribution, and curriculum-conformant feedback, derived entirely from independent, language-specific expert practice. Leveraging this rich but modest-scale supervision, we propose RL-CRAF++, a sample-efficient pipeline combining CoT-SFT with Constrained GRPO. Crucially, our RL formulation relies entirely on human-annotation-derived rewards, completely bypassing the potential biases of external LLM judges. Evaluated independently per language, a 4B parameter RL-CRAF++ model consistently surpasses zero-shot frontier models (including GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V3.2) on in-domain test sets. Ablation analysis reveals that P-CoT supervision accounts for approximately 78.1% of the alignment gain over standard SFT, providing strong evidence that, in this culturally situated evaluation setting, process-level structural supervision contributes substantially more than RL-stage calibration alone. Our code is available at https://github.com/TW-NLP/MPEAB
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Distilling LLM Reasoning into an Interpretable Policy Tree for Human-AI Collaboration
abstract: Constructing efficient and reliable policies to assist humans is indispensable for human-AI collaboration. Existing methods mainly follow two lines of work. The majority of prior work relies on multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to learn black-box policies, which limits interpretability and raises safety concerns. Recent methods query large language models (LLMs) at each decision step, causing slow responses and high inference costs. We propose Co-\pi-tree, a closed-loop method that learns an executable policy tree consisting of a partner-behavior prediction tree and an agent-action selection tree. Co-\pi-tree constructs a policy through distilling LLM reasoning into policy tree code. It then evaluates the policy through partner interaction, obtains feedback, and uses natural language summaries of interaction feedback to improve problematic branches. Experiments in Overcooked-AI show that Co-π-tree improves average reward by 6.4% over the strongest LLM baseline, while reducing the number of LLM queries by 77.7% and test-time latency by 97.1%. Project page: https://beiwenzhang.github.io/Co-pi-tree/.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: IndicDetect: Evaluating Cross-Lingual LLM-Generated Text Detection for Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil
abstract: The rapid proliferation of LLMs has further heightened the necessity to develop dependable AI-generated text detection, especially beyond English. Nevertheless, current benchmarks pay little attention to Indic languages and test detectors in idealized settings that do not represent the real world. We present a generalized benchmark for AI-generated text detection in Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil, which we name IndicDetect is a benchmark designed to assess the robustness of detectors under realistic distribution shifts. IndicDetect comprises highly curated human-written texts matched with LLM-generated counterparts across various domains and generators, and systematically evaluates detectors in the presence of domain shift, generator shift, and adversarial perturbation. Using a single and repeatable evaluation scheme, we evaluate a wide range of statistical and neural detectors. We find substantial robustness failures: supervised neural detectors perform well in-distribution, but most training-free methods fail catastrophically on unseen generators and adversarial attacks, with larger failures observed for Telugu and Tamil than for Hindi. These results highlight that the primary weakness of existing detectors in Indic settings lies in their robustness, not peak accuracy. IndicDetect provides standard data splits, an evaluation protocol, and baselines to establish a robust, language-aware foundation for AI-generated text detection in Indic scripts.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Distilling Multimodal Evolution with Adaptive Anchors for Cloud-Edge Collaborative MLLMs
abstract: Cloud-edge collaboration provides a practical paradigm for deploying MLLMs on resource-constrained devices, where compact edge-side models are improved with supervision from stronger cloud-side models. However, existing cloud-edge distillation methods mainly rely on pseudo labels or static feature alignment, overlooking how the teacher progressively transforms multimodal inputs into answers. In this paper, we propose A^2-MED, Adaptive Anchor-Guided Multimodal Evolution Distillation for cloud-edge MLLMs. Our key idea is to organize the teacher’s layer-wise multimodal evolution into functional stages through adaptive teacher-side anchoring, and transfer the resulting stage-wise evolution as process-level supervision. Specifically, we adaptively identify functional anchors from the teacher according to layer-wise indicators of cross-modal binding, semantic integration, and answer prediction, and then project these anchors to the student to establish corresponding functional stages. Under these teacher-defined stages, we align teacher-student anchor states and distill inter-stage multimodal evolution relations, enabling the student to learn how the teacher progressively transforms multimodal inputs into answers. Experiments on A-OKVQA and VizWiz show that our method consistently improves over representative cloud-edge and distillation baselines, with further analyses validating the effectiveness of adaptive anchors and evolution distillation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Doc-CoB: Enhancing Document Understanding with Visual Chain-of-Boxes Reasoning
abstract: Document understanding aims to perform question answering and information extraction over document images, where the visual content is highly information-dense and most queries rely on only a few relevant layout regions. However, existing methods either adopt a one-pass strategy that implicitly assumes all layouts are equally important, or focus excessively on small regions at the cost of losing critical layout information. To address these limitations, we introduce Doc-CoB (Chain-of-Boxes), a simple-yet-effective framework that integrates coarse-to-fine layout-aware visual reasoning into multimodal large language models. Instead of directly zooming into small regions, Doc-CoB progressively focuses on query-relevant layouts while preserving global document information. Specifically, it first selects key layout boxes and then focuses on them for further understanding with visual prompting. To support this paradigm, we introduce two reasoning tasks for box recognition and box reasoning, with an automatic pipeline that constructs 249k training samples with intermediate visual supervision. Experiments on seven benchmarks with four popular models show that Doc-CoB significantly improves performance, demonstrating its effectiveness and wide applicability. The code and the data are available at https://github.com/Doc-CoB/Doc-CoB.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: FORGE: Fine-grained multimodal evaluation for manufacturing quality assurance
abstract: The manufacturing sector is increasingly adopting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to move from low-level perception toward higher-level reasoning and decision support, yet current evaluations rarely reflect the fine-grained precision that real-world manufacturing demands. Progress is further hindered by data scarcity and a lack of fine-grained domain semantics in existing datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce FORGE, a benchmark for three core quality-assurance tasks of discrete manufacturing: workpiece verification, structural surface inspection, and assembly verification. We first construct a high-quality multimodal dataset spanning real-world 2D images and 3D point clouds, annotated with fine-grained domain semantics such as standardized model numbers. We then evaluate 18 state-of-the-art MLLMs on these three tasks, revealing significant performance gaps. Counter to conventional understanding, our bottleneck analysis on five representative models indicates that visual grounding is not the primary limiting factor. Instead, insufficient domain-specific knowledge is the key bottleneck. Beyond evaluation, we show that our structured annotations can serve as an actionable training resource: supervised fine-tuning of a compact 3B-parameter model on our data yields up to 90.8% relative improvement in accuracy on held-out manufacturing scenarios, providing preliminary evidence for a practical pathway toward domain-adapted manufacturing MLLMs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Skill-as-Pseudocode: Refactoring Skill Libraries to Pseudocode for LLM Agents
abstract: Markdown skill libraries for LLM agents ship as free-form prose, forcing the agent to re-derive both the input schema and the concrete invocation syntax on every retrieval. This produces a "confused → re-retrieve → still confused" loop: the agent issues a partially-correct action, receives uninformative feedback, and re-retrieves the same prose. We propose Skill-as-Pseudocode (SaP), an automatic conversion of markdown skill libraries into typed pseudocode with deterministic quality control. From each cluster of similar procedural passages, SaP extracts a typed contract and filters it through a four-check deterministic verifier (coverage, binding, replacement, risk). Promoted contracts are inlined into a rewritten skill skeleton alongside restored action templates, giving the agent two complementary signals: a typed signature for what a skill does and a concrete template for how to invoke it. On the ALFWorld unseen split (134 games, gpt-4o-mini, three seeds), SaP wins 82/402 paired games versus 47/402 for the Graph-of-Skills (GoS) baseline (pooled McNemar p = 8.2 × 10⁻⁵), at −22.8 ± 6.4% input tokens and −14.5 ± 4.1% LLM calls per game. A bundle-component ablation attributes the gain to the pairing of typed contracts with concrete action templates: the contract alone falls below the prose baseline.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: AEGIS-D: Multi-Agent Debate for High-Precision Verification of Hard Competition Mathematics
abstract: Fluent but subtly wrong mathematical solutions can contaminate training, evaluation, and reward-labeling data. We present AEGIS-D (Assessment- and Evidence-Gated Inspection System via Debate), a precision-first multi-agent pipeline for blind verification of competition-level mathematics. Five same-model, role-prompted agents exchange structured arguments, while an assessment gate accepts a candidate only when at least three report positive confirming evidence rather than mere non-refutation. On 195 hard-to-verify variants from 58 IMO/USAMO/Putnam-level problems, a single judge achieves 55.1% precision; AEGIS-D achieves 92.5% precision and 63.8% recall, reducing false positives from 24.7 to 3.0 per run (8.2-fold). A repeated two-by-two factorial associates role prompting with the largest observed false-positive reduction and finds a smaller conditional benefit from gating. Paired round and threshold analyses expose the cost-precision trade-off, and single-run transfers to Omni-MATH and OlymMATH provide preliminary evidence beyond the constructed stress test.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: STARS: Skill Triage via Activation Risk Scoring for LLM Agents
abstract: The risk of an agent skill call depends not on the skill alone but on the invocation context: the same file-reading skill is benign when listing logs, yet dangerous when tainted content steers the agent toward secret exfiltration. We formalize invocation-time auditing: intercept a proposed skill call before execution and score its risk from the user request, the candidate skill, and the runtime context. STARS implements this as a three-stage pipeline that fuses a static capability prior with a request-conditioned invocation scorer. The primary configuration, STARS-LLM, uses an LLM judge; STARS-Rules is a deterministic, API-free alternative. On SIA-Bench, a 3,000-record synthetic benchmark with a 180-record human check at Fleiss κ = 0.709, request-conditioned scoring improves high-risk retrieval on held-out indirect prompt injection, where static metadata cannot see the attack. On a frozen 500/100 scoring subset, STARS-LLM raises rules-only HR-AUPRC from 0.297 to 0.728 in-distribution and from 0.504 to 0.757 on held-out IPI. That gain is in ranking: under frozen thresholds, held-out classification accuracy does not improve. SIA-Bench is a ranking stress test, not an estimate of real-world prevalence.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CoopAgent: Training Multi-Agent Cooperation from Single-Agent Execution Trajectories
abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated strong potential for solving complex tasks, yet reliable collaboration remains challenging. While most training-based methods rely on multi-agent trajectories, we investigate whether cooperative behaviors can be strengthened using only single-agent execution data. We propose CoopAgent, a training framework that learns solely from single-agent execution trajectories and transfers to multi-agent deployment. To bridge the gap between single-agent training and multi-agent environments, we introduce PADPO (Perturbation-Aligned DPO), which aligns action preferences between original observations and task-related perturbations that mimic changes caused by other agents. We train CoopAgent on single-agent execution trajectories collected in Minecraft and evaluate it on VillagerBench. The results demonstrate its potential to enhance collaboration on VillagerBench while preserving strong single-agent execution ability. We further assess CoopAgent on out-of-domain benchmarks, showing improvements in several multi-agent settings and performance comparable to the multi-agent training method AT-GRPO on the coding benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/hlpzz/CoopAgent.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Evaluating LLM Agents Beyond Local Edit Validity
abstract: Evaluations of sequential large language model (LLM) agents often report local action validity or final success. Delayed constructive tasks additionally require recoverability, meaning each accepted edit must leave the partial artifact completable within the remaining budget. We introduce a measurement protocol across Word Ladder, an alloy composition proxy, and the fitness landscape of the B1 domain of protein G (GB1). We call an episode surface clean when every action is well formed and locally admissible. Across six models, Word Ladder exposes interface failure with 36.1% local validity. Alloy and GB1 episodes are often surface clean, yet only 16.0% and 6.8% of them succeed. Exact enumeration of 625 GB1 variants over budgets from zero to six decomposes failure. Among surface clean episodes, 51.4% cross a recoverability boundary, while 14.1% of the remaining episodes succeed. Bounded composition audits and intervention checks connect bottlenecks to repair classes. These results establish recoverability as a decomposable and auditable evaluation axis that informs interventions for sequential agents.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PersonaEdit: Representative Sample Selection for Personalized Model Editing
abstract: Personalization has attracted growing interest in LLM applications, yet existing retrieval-based approaches depend heavily on retrieval quality and degrade in long-term interactions. Model editing, which directly modifies internal model parameters to incorporate new knowledge, has demonstrated effective knowledge modification capabilities in factual knowledge editing tasks and may provide a potential solution for personalization. However, scaling model editing to personalization is non-trivial. Editing large amounts of user data increases computational cost and causes interference among edits, motivating the need for effective sample selection. To address this issue, we propose, PersonaEdit, a hidden representation clustering strategy that selects representative editing samples through proportional stratified sampling. Experiments show that model editing is effective for personalization, and that our selection strategy preserves most of the performance while substantially reducing the number of required editing samples. Beyond standalone editing, we find that combining model editing with retrieval-based prompt augmentation further improves personalization, as edited knowledge and retrieved context provide complementary information. These results demonstrate the potential of model editing as an efficient and scalable approach for LLM personalization.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: AMU-GEC: A Polish Native Speaker Grammatical Error Correction Benchmark
abstract: For many languages, grammatical error correction (GEC) remains underexplored due to the lack of dedicated datasets and evaluation benchmarks. Moreover, many existing GEC datasets are based on texts written by second-language learners, which narrows the research focus to specific error types. To address these gaps, we introduce a new Polish GEC benchmark, AMU-GEC, built from texts written by native Polish speakers and manually annotated by expert linguists. The benchmark is released as a machine learning challenge, without revealing the expected labels, to prevent contamination. To set baselines, we evaluate recent multilingual and Polish LLMs, finding that smaller models may perform better when trained on monolingual (Polish) data. We also conduct a human analysis of the best performing model to gain more insights about the model behavior when it is different from human annotations. The analysis shows that most of the changes suggested by the model do not introduce errors into the texts; instead, they typically either slightly improve text fluency or represent valid alternative corrections.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Struggle Between Continuation and Refusal: A Mechanistic Analysis of the Continuation-Triggered Jailbreak in LLMs
abstract: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), the safety of LLMs has become a critical concern. Despite significant efforts in safety alignment, current LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks. However, the root causes of such vulnerabilities are still poorly understood, necessitating a rigorous investigation into jailbreak mechanisms across both academic and industrial communities. In this work, we focus on a continuation-triggered jailbreak phenomenon, whereby simply relocating a continuation-triggered instruction suffix can substantially increase jailbreak success rates. To uncover the intrinsic mechanisms of this phenomenon, we conduct a comprehensive mechanistic interpretability analysis at the level of attention heads. Through causal interventions and activation scaling, we show that this jailbreak behavior primarily arises from an inherent competition between the model’s intrinsic continuation drive and the safety defenses acquired through alignment training. Furthermore, we perform a detailed behavioral analysis of the identified safety-critical attention heads, revealing notable differences in the behaviors of safety heads across different model architectures. Grounded in these mechanistic findings, we propose Head Competition Steering (HCS), a mechanistically grounded inference-time strategy that explicitly leverages the competition between safety heads and continuation heads to suppress harmful generation, and further distill its behavioral signal into a student model via knowledge distillation, achieving inference-time safety improvements without additional computational overhead.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation
abstract: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role-driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, VAB-Challenge) via dual-role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM’s generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross-role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role-dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation-directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation-analysis-mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/VALCON.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MemGovern: Enhancing Code Agents through Learning from Governed Human Experiences
abstract: While autonomous software engineering (SWE) agents are reshaping programming paradigms, they currently suffer from a “closed-world” limitation: they attempt to fix bugs from scratch or solely using information from the current repository, ignoring the immense historical human experience available on platforms like GitHub. Accessing this open-world experience is hindered by the unstructured and fragmented nature of real-world issue-tracking data. In this paper, we introduce MemGovern, a framework designed to govern and transform raw GitHub data into actionable experiential memory for agents. MemGovern employs experience governance to convert human experience into agent-friendly experience cards and introduces an agentic experience search strategy that enables logic-driven retrieval of human expertise. By producing 135K governed experience cards, MemGovern achieves a significant performance boost, improving resolution rates on the SWE-bench benchmark by 4.65%. As a plug-in approach, MemGovern provides a solution for agent-friendly memory infrastructure.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TokenPilot: Cache-Efficient Context Management for LLM Agents
abstract: As LLM agents are deployed in long-horizon sessions, context accumulation drives up inference costs. Existing approaches utilize text pruning or dynamic memory eviction to minimize token footprints; however, their unconstrained sequence mutations alter layouts, introducing prefix mismatches and cache invalidation. This reveals a critical trade-off between text sparsity and prompt cache continuity. To address this, we present **TokenPilot**, a dual-granularity context management framework. Globally, *Ingestion-Aware Compaction* acts as a framework harness to stabilize prompt prefixes and eliminate open-world environmental noise at the ingestion gate. Locally, *Lifecycle-Aware Eviction* monitors the ongoing residual utility of context segments, enforcing a conservative batch-turn schedule to offload content segments only when task relevance expires. Experiments on ‘PinchBench‘ and ‘Claw-Eval‘ under both isolated and continuous modes demonstrate that TokenPilot reduces costs by **61%** and **56%** in isolated mode, and **61%** and **87%** in continuous mode, while maintaining competitive performance compared to prior systems.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Romanized Arabic Across Dialects: Views, Usage Patterns, and Linguistic Variation
abstract: Arabizi refers to Arabic written in Latin script. Although previous studies have shown that the prevalence and usage of Arabizi vary by factors such as region and age group, most NLP research on Arabic texts treats it as a temporary phenomenon resulting from limited technological support for the Arabic script. In this work, we engage with Arabic speakers to collect insights on their perceptions and usage of Arabizi. We further examine writing norms among speakers of different dialects, focusing on Algerian, Egyptian, Lebanese, Moroccan, and Tunisian Arabic. To this end, we release two resources. First, we perform a character-level alignment of Arabic words to study inter- and intra-dialectal variation across these five dialects, based on words transliterated by the surveyed participants (VARabiziLex), finding systematic intradialectal regularity and inter-dialectal variation. Second, to study Arabic speakers’ ability to identify this stylistic variation at the sentence-level, we build VARabiziCues, a manually curated parallel corpus of sentences written in Arabic script alongside multiple Arabizi transliterations, collected from speakers of the same five dialects. Our study presents the largest human-centered, cross-dialectal study of Arabizi’s perceptions and practices to date.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: HeTGB: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Heterophilic Text-Attributed Graphs
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have demon- strated success in modeling relational data pri- marily under the assumption of homophily. However, many real-world graphs exhibit het- erophily, where linked nodes belong to dif- ferent categories or possess diverse attributes, such as webpages, Wikipedia articles, social networks, and e-commerce platforms. Addi- tionally, nodes in many domains are associated with textual descriptions, forming heterophilic text-attributed graphs (TAGs). Despite their sig- nificance, heterophilic TAGs remain underex- plored due to the lack of dedicated benchmarks that jointly capture heterophilic structures and rich textual attributes. To address this gap, we introduce the Heterophilic Text-attributed Graph Benchmark (HeTGB), a novel bench- mark comprising five real-world heterophilic graph datasets from diverse domains, with nodes enriched by extensive textual descrip- tions. HeTGB enables systematic evaluation of GNNs, pre-trained language models (PLMs) and co-training methods on the node classifi- cation task. Through extensive benchmarking experiments, we showcase the utility of text attributes in heterophilic graphs, analyze the challenges posed by heterophilic TAGs and the limitations of existing models, and provide in- sights into the interplay between graph struc- tures and textual attributes.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Alignment by Stereotyping: How LLMs Sacrifice Individual Distinctiveness for Cultural Adaptation
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed for personalized interaction, and demographic conditioning via user profiles is a widely adopted strategy for cultural adaptation. We ask whether this approach genuinely serves individual users or achieves accuracy by erasing individual distinctiveness. Studying seven models including frontier GPT-5.1 on the World Values Survey, we find that demographic profiles improve value alignment accuracy for most models, but at a systematic cost to individuality. That is, models pull responses toward demographic group centroids rather than preserving individual differences, a behavioral pattern we term alignment by stereotyping. Permutation tests (10,000 permutations, six demographic attributes, seven models) certify that top-performing models compress individuals far above the human baseline; within-family scaling amplifies this tradeoff while degrading intrinsic cultural understanding. Using a synthetic dialogue dataset validated on real human-chatbot conversations from PRISM (Kirk et al., 2024), we further show that distributing demographic signals across conversational turns partially suppresses prototype retrieval compared to compact demographic labels, a finding validated on real conversations via PRISM but requiring replication at larger scale.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EM²Mem: Event-Centric Multimodal Memory for Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal memory offers a scalable interface for long-video question answering, but existing methods often retrieve captions, frames, transcripts, summaries, or graph facts as isolated fragments. Although searchable, such fragments are not generation-ready: language models must reconstruct cross-modal and temporal alignments at inference time, when context is limited and attribution is difficult. We propose EM^2Mem, an event-centric multimodal memory framework that binds heterogeneous evidence to event anchors during memory construction. Each event-indexed memory cell aligns multimodal records, temporal context, graph-linked relations, semantic facts, and provenance, enabling compact evidence readout over grounded multimodal events rather than modality-specific fragments. Across three long-video QA benchmarks, EM^2Mem improves average accuracy over the strongest memory baseline by 2.0, 2.4, and 3.7 points, improves strict event-level Top-5 evidence recall by 7.0 points, and reduces per-query latency by 4.67\times and total inference tokens by 63.66%.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: AIMER: Calibration-Free Task-Agnostic MoE Expert Pruning
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models increase parameter capacity without proportional per-token computation, yet deployment still requires storing the full expert pool, making expert pruning important for reducing memory and serving overhead. Existing task-agnostic expert-pruning methods are typically calibration-dependent: they estimate expert importance from routing or activation statistics on a calibration set, making pruning decisions sensitive to calibration-data variation while introducing substantial preprocessing cost. We propose AIMER (Absolute mean over root mean square IMportance for Expert Ranking), a simple calibration-free criterion that identifies more distinct experts by capturing the concentration pattern of expert weights, making it well suited for task-agnostic expert pruning. Across 7B to 47B MoE language models with distinct architectures and 16 diverse benchmarks, AIMER consistently delivers stronger capability balance across diverse tasks than existing calibration-free methods. Surprisingly, AIMER also achieves better balance than strong calibration-based expert-pruning baselines calibrated on the widely used task-agnostic C4 corpus, while requiring only 0.22–2.06 seconds to score all experts.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EMemBench: Interactive Benchmarking of Episodic Memory for VLM Agents
abstract: We introduce EMemBench, a programmatic benchmark generator for evaluating long-term episodic memory of agents through interactive games. Rather than using a fixed set of questions, EMemBench generates questions from environment-grounded trajectories, covering both text-only and visual game environments. Each template computes verifiable ground truth from underlying game signals, with controlled answerability and balanced coverage over memory skills: single/multi-hop recall, induction, temporal, spatial, logical, and adversarial. We evaluate memory agents with strong LMs/VLMs as backbones, using in-context prompting as baselines. Across 15 text games and multiple visual seeds, results are far from saturated: induction and spatial reasoning are persistent bottlenecks, especially in visual settings. Persistent memory yields clear gains for open backbones on text games, but improvements are less consistent for VLM agents, suggesting that visually grounded episodic memory remains an open challenge. A human study further contextualizes the difficulty and interpretability of EMemBench.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: LiST: Local-Simplex Test-Time LoRA Fusion
abstract: Task-specific LoRA adapters offer a modular way to specialize large language and vision-language models. However, existing adapter composition methods are mostly static and cannot adapt to individual test inputs. To address these issues, we propose LiST, a label-free test-time LoRA fusion framework that converts an existing LoRA bank into a target-conditioned local simplex and searches sample-specific fusion weights at inference time. LiST builds joint task representations from LoRA parameter anchors and prompt-level behavior vectors, retrieves neighboring adapters as a local search space, and performs branch-preserving fusion without updating the backbone or adapters. Candidate weights are selected by a prompt-level energy with prior, geometric, and stochastic-consistency constraints, and are deployed only when they pass a safe acceptance rule. Otherwise, LiST falls back to a target-conditioned prior. Experiments on multimodal and language benchmarks show that LiST outperforms static LoRA merging and conventional test-time adaptation baselines, while preserving task-specific adapter utility and improving robustness on unseen tasks.
