Our results reveal substantial gaps between semantic answer quality and dialectal fidelity, highlighting the limitations of existing evaluation metrics for dialectal Arabic generation. EDRAC provides a realistic and challenging MRC benchmark for future research on dialectal Arabic NLP.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RoleArena: Autonomous Plot Progression for Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Role-Playing
abstract: Improving the plot progression ability of role-playing language agents (RPLAs) plays a critical role in enhancing user experience and dialogue immersion. However, research on plot progression in role-playing language agents is still limited. Existing datasets often contain too few dialogue turns and lack large-scale sentences with clear deterministic plot turns, which restricts further model development and evaluation. To bridge this gap, we propose RoleArena, an innovative multi-agent role-playing environment. By introducing a critic agent and combining discrete plot lines with environment-agent-based dynamic judgments, the system generates long multi-turn dialogues with key markers for plot progression. Based on RoleArena, we construct the PlotStream dataset, which contains 39.3k characters and 170k dialogues, with annotations for key plot progression sentences. In addition, based on PlotStream, we further develop PlotRole-7B and PlotRole-72B, RPLAs built upon the Qwen2.5 model and specialized in plot progression capabilities. Extensive experiments show that RoleArena and PlotRole improve dialogue generation with plot progression and strengthen the ability of plot progression.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: DARTS: Diversity-Aware Reasoning Tree Search for Test-Time Scaling
abstract: Test-time tree search improves the reasoning capability of large language models under fixed inference budgets. However, existing solution-level MCTS often suffers from local homogenization: once a promising solution pattern is found, subsequent search tends to refine nearby variants rather than explore distinct reasoning paths. This wastes computation on redundant candidates and limits solution-space coverage. To address this problem, we propose Diversity-Aware Reasoning Tree Search (DARTS), a Bayesian tree-search framework that treats reasoning-path diversity as an explicit search objective. DARTS separates expansion into local refinement and orthogonal regeneration, and updates action posteriors using a joint reward over task quality and reasoning-path diversity. On LiveCodeBench and CodeContests, DARTS achieves the best exploration performance and produces more diverse correct solutions. With half the budget, it matches or exceeds the strongest tree-search baseline in four of six settings. On molecular optimization tasks, DARTS improves both optimization quality and structural diversity, suggesting cross-domain transfer.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Procedural Blind Spots in Agent Evaluation: A Survey, Coverage Analysis, and New Missions for NLP
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in multi-step, multi-turn settings that combine user interaction, tool use, state changes, and communication. Most agent evaluation still emphasizes task completion, while procedure-aware checks remain fragmented. We conduct a systematic survey and introduce \mathcal{F}^*, a systematic organizing map that maps scattered procedural checks into a shared audit space spanning integrity relations and quality dimensions. Applying this framework to recent agent-evaluation work reveals three procedural blind spots: most work remains outcome-focused or procedurally under-specified, procedure-aware checks mostly remain local spot-checks, and communication grounding lags action compliance. To close these gaps, we propose four new Natural Language Processing (NLP) missions around communication grounding, constraint semantics, reasoning faithfulness, and procedural equity. This survey provides a  comprehensive overview of procedure-aware agent evaluation, offering a common vocabulary and coverage map that clarify what current benchmarks can certify and provide clear guidelines for future research.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Arabic Sentence Segmentation Across Genres and Punctuation Conditions
abstract: Sentence segmentation in Arabic is challenging due to ambiguous and inconsistent punctuation, with many texts lacking reliable sentence boundary markers. Existing approaches rely heavily on punctuation cues and are typically evaluated on well-formed text, limiting their robustness in realistic Arabic settings. To address this, we introduce AraSEG, a genre-diverse sentence segmentation corpus spanning eight genres and a wide range of punctuation and document structure conditions. Using AraSEG, we evaluate LLMs, lightweight encoder models, and dependency parser-based models under increasingly challenging segmentation settings. Our experiments show that lightweight encoders, and even dependency parser-based models, outperform LLMs under the hardest conditions. We further investigate the effects of training data size and genre diversity, finding that performance eventually saturates and cross-genre generalization remains challenging. We also demonstrate that accurate sentence segmentation substantially improves downstream dependency parsing. We make our code, data, and models publicly available.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: AutoBackdoor: Automating Backdoor Attacks via LLM Agents
abstract: Backdoor attacks are an important safety risk for large language models (LLMs), yet existing studies often rely on manually crafted triggers and fixed poisoning pipelines. This limits the diversity of attack behaviors and makes it difficult to systematically evaluate defense robustness. We introduce AutoBackdoor, an agent-driven framework for scalable LLM backdoor red-teaming. Given a target scenario, AutoBackdoor automatically generates triggers, constructs poisoned samples, refines them through self-feedback, and produces backdoored models through fine-tuning. We evaluate the framework across four realistic scenarios: Bias Recommendation, Hallucination Injection, Error Code Generation, and Peer Review Manipulation. Experiments on LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and GPT-4o show that AutoBackdoor can achieve over 90% attack success with only a small number of poisoned samples. We further find that existing defenses provide limited protection against these agent-generated attacks. These results suggest that automated red-teaming can serve as a useful tool for stress-testing LLM backdoor defenses and understanding emerging risks from agent-driven model customization pipelines. Our code is available at https://github.com/bboylyg/AutoBackdoor.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Prompted Values and Deployed Policies: A Truth–Propriety Diagnostic in Language Models
abstract: Prompting a language model to endorse a value does not by itself establish how that value is deployed when responses require tradeoffs. We study this gap in truth–propriety dilemmas, where direct truth-telling can conflict with tact, face-saving, deference, or role-sensitive restraint. We introduce Truth–Propriety Alignment (TPA), a 600-prompt diagnostic benchmark over 100 scenario groups, and conduct a single-model diagnostic evaluation of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under deterministic decoding. The model remains predominantly truth-oriented, but trigger-assigned scenario groups differ sharply in how residual responses are distributed. Because value triggers are fixed within scenario groups, we interpret this pattern as trigger-associated residual composition rather than a causal trigger effect. A small semantic audit shows that compatible residuals are mixed: they include substantive reframings but also tonal and lexical tracking. Finally, a hidden-state probe is nearly matched by an exact-prompt BoW baseline, and deleting the explicit value-trigger sentence does not reduce BoW performance, indicating that behavioral-label predictability is distributed across the prompt surface. We therefore frame TPA as a diagnostic audit of prompt intent, observed behavior, scenario/trigger priors, annotation boundaries, and probe evidence, rather than as evidence for prompt-independent value representations.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Reward-Free Signals Are Not Directions: A Gradient-Level Diagnostic for Test-Time Reasoning Optimization
abstract: First-order test-time optimization (TTO) updates continuous variables such as logits or latent states for a single input. Successful methods usually rely on external reward models or verifiers to supply a semantic gradient. We ask whether reward-free signals from model distributions or prompted self-verification can supply comparable update directions for reasoning tasks. In logit-space TTO, we compare each reward-free gradient with an operational reward-model reference direction, instantiated as the reward-model gradient on the same logits. Across Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, confidence gradients remain nearly orthogonal to the reference, entropy-slope gradients have vanishing scale near greedy rollouts, and terminal answer certainty is sparse and reference-sensitive. Prompted-verifier gradients are more reference-dependent: in a tokenizer-matched Llama diagnostic, four variants attain moderate RM-relative alignment and measurable local RM-score gains. Nevertheless, in end-to-end TTO on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the selected reward-free signals produce no wrong-to-correct flips on MATH-500, AIME-2024, AIME-2025, or GSM8K, while a separate reward-model-guided TTO reproduction provides an external positive control with measurable gains.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Scope3Trace: Evidence-Based Identification and Extraction of Scope 3 GHG Emissions from Sustainability Reports
abstract: Scope 3 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions account for the majority of corporate carbon footprints, yet remain difficult to analyze at scale due to sparse disclosures, heterogeneous report document formats, and limited evidence traceability. Existing approaches typically rely on large language models to extract emissions information from ESG reports, but often lack explicit evidence grounding or depend on costly manual annotation and verification to ensure extraction reliability. To address these challenges, we propose **Scope3Trace**, an evidence-grounded information extraction framework designed to extract interpretable and traceable Scope 3 emissions information from real-world ESG and sustainability reports. The framework integrates a document information extraction pipeline that performs PDF collection and OCR parsing, LLM-assisted page localization and table reconstruction, and hybrid rule–LLM extraction of organization- and building-level emissions disclosures with evidence-grounded verification. Building upon this framework, we further contribute a dual-level, evidence-grounded, multimodal dataset comprising organization-level Scope 3 disclosures extracted from heterogeneous sustainability reports. **Scope3Trace** enables reliable extraction and transparent integration of heterogeneous sustainability disclosures, achieving high accuracy in extracting Scope 1–3 totals and category-level disclosures from sustainability reports. The code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/Scope3Trace.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: STRETCH the Boundaries: A Unified Self-Taught Framework for Progressive LLM Evolution
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often suffer from capability stagnation in self-improvement training due to fixed difficulty levels. To address this issue, we propose STRETCH (Self-Taught Reasoning Evolution via Targeted CHallenge) inspired by cognitive scaffolding theory. STRETCH introduces a dynamic Stretch Zone mechanism that continuously aligns question difficulty with the model’s solving capability. Within a single parameter space, the model alternates between a Scaffolder that generates adaptive challenges and a Learner that solves them through reinforcement learning. This dual-loop co-evolution process stabilize training and promote progressive reasoning growth. Experiments on both negotiation and operation research benchmarks demonstrate that STRETCH consistently outperforms strong prompting and domain-specific baselines. Further analysis shows that dynamic difficulty alignment is critical for sustained capability improvement and synchronized reasoning evolution.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: A Unified Framework for Low-Resource Sawndip–Chinese Bidirectional Translation and Bilingual Dialogue Modeling
abstract: The decline of proficient practitioners poses an existential threat to numerous ancient writing systems, risking the loss of the cultural heritage they encode. Among these systems is Sawndip, a logographic script whose computational preservation faces severe challenges due to the scarcity of standardized corpora. In this paper, we present the first systematic framework for low-resource Sawndip-Chinese translation and bilingual conversational modeling. We introduce a newly curated dataset comprising sentence-level Sawndip-Chinese parallel data and character-level lexical definitions. Building upon this foundation, we propose a knowledge-enhanced supervised fine-tuning paradigm that incorporates lexical knowledge during training. To address the additional challenges of Chinese-to-Sawndip generation, we further develop a manually curated template-based substructure substitution strategy for synthesizing reverse-direction data. Bilingual conversational data is then constructed through a dimension-conditioned dialogue generation and multi-candidate back-translation pipeline, enabling controllable and diverse dialogue synthesis. Experimental results show that our final unified model effectively supports both Sawndip-Chinese translation and bilingual conversational abilities. Ultimately, this work provides a foundational reference for the digital preservation of Sawndip, offering broader insights into the computational documentation of globally-endangered languages.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: BenchCompass: From Scores to Signals for Training and Harness Decisions in Payment-Domain LLMs
abstract: Payment operations are a critical financial infrastructure, but the value of large language models in this domain remains unclear because payment rules change quickly, evidence is fragmented, and decisions depend on transaction state, participant role, region, and payment rail. Existing benchmarks do not isolate whether failures come from missing payment-rule knowledge, poor use of supplied evidence, or brittleness under imperfect harness inputs. We introduce BenchCompass, a payment-domain benchmark whose construction pipeline builds scenario-grounded tasks from typed evidence packs, applies LLM-based quality checks, creates task-input attack variants, and reserves final item admission for domain experts. The release contains an expert-reviewed Pro benchmark covering payment knowledge, context-grounded scenario reasoning, and Attacked Open robustness, plus a lower-assurance Normal pool for inspection and future curation. Across 16 model variants, BenchCompass shows qualitatively different failure modes: missing parametric payment knowledge, incomplete reasoning over supplied rules, and failure to reject plausible but invalid workflows. The benchmark remains unsaturated: the best frontier model reaches 89.6% on Open Context-Grounded Reasoning and 81.7% under attacked inputs, while a representative 32B open-weight model reaches 69.8% and 42.6%. The benchmark, data, and code are publicly available at https://github.com/ant-intl/BenchCompass.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: F^2DR: A Fine-Grained Full-Pipeline Reward Framework for DeepSearch Workflows
abstract: With the widespread industrial deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), DeepSearch has emerged as the dominant paradigm for resolving complex user queries. It implements an iterative closed-loop workflow consisting of planning and reflection, information retrieval, and answer generation. However, existing reward models (RMs) are largely designed for static single-turn tasks, failing to capture the full-pipeline complexity of DeepSearch workflows. To address this limitation, we propose F^2DR, a fine-grained full-pipeline reward framework. F^2DR evaluates DeepSearch workflows across three dimensions: Content, Trajectory, and Answer, enabling comprehensive process-level assessment. We further construct DeepSearch RM-Bench, a dedicated benchmark for evaluating RMs in DeepSearch scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that F^2DR achieves significantly higher evaluation consistency than existing baselines, while DeepSearch RM-Bench exhibits strong discriminative capability across existing open-source RMs. We will publicly release the complete DeepSearch RM-Bench dataset.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Teacher-Guided Policy Optimization for On-Policy Reasoning Distillation under Large Policy Divergence
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for reasoning-oriented post-training of large language models (LLMs), especially when combined with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). Existing OPD methods rely on reverse KL (RKL)-based teacher supervision over trajectories sampled from the student policy. However, we identify a critical limitation: under large teacher–student policy divergence, RL-driven exploration often produces trajectories that the teacher assigns low probability, resulting in uninformative negative feedback. To address this, we propose Teacher-Guided Policy Optimization (TGPO). Unlike existing OPD methods that evaluate student-sampled actions using the teacher, TGPO directly guides next-token generation using the teacher’s predicted distribution on student-generated contexts, yielding an on-policy forward-KL objective. Combined with RLVR, this guidance steers exploration toward improved continuations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks show that TGPO outperforms existing RKL-based OPD methods and remains robust across different teacher models. Furthermore, we find that teacher top-1 predictions suffice for effective guidance, without requiring the full teacher distribution.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Script Choice in LLMs: Evidence for Late-Layer Commitment
abstract: In this paper, we investigate how script knowledge is distributed across the layers of LLMs using two complementary interpretability methods: logistic regression probing and logit-lens analysis. Our probing experiments reveal a clear asymmetry: both the input script and the instructed output script are encoded in the earliest layers of the network, while, in contrast, commitment to the actual output script emerges only in the final layers, with the model’s intermediate representations defaulting to Latin throughout most of the layers. This two-stage process is confirmed by logit-lens analyses, which show that script commitment consistently occurs at the very last layers of the LLMs. Together with the weaker script-following performance observed in smaller models, these results form a converging body of evidence linking script commitment to model depth, with broader implications for the design of sufficiently deep, inclusive multilingual architectures.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: IPA-Verified Singable Lyrics Translation with LLM Agents
abstract: Translating song lyrics while preserving singability requires satisfying musical constraints, including syllable counts, rhyme schemes, and syllable patterns, that standard machine translation ignores. We present a framework that exposes IPA-based phonetic analysis as a suite of composable Agent Skills, each defined by a natural-language description plus deterministic verification scripts that the orchestrating LLM invokes on demand. The agent extracts constraints from source lyrics, then translates through a multi-phase process, calling skills to verify syllable counts and rhyme and iteratively refine syllable-count mismatches. We formalize the three musical constraints, describe the IPA skill suite and agent architecture, and propose three evaluation metrics: Syllable Error Rate (SER), Syllable Count Relative Error (SCRE), and Adjusted Rand Index (ARI). Experiments across three frontier orchestrators, with component ablations, confirm that tool-verified translation dramatically improves constraint satisfaction and preserves rhyme structure substantially better than a supervised baseline, while requiring no task-specific training and no parallel corpora, and transferring to Spanish and Japanese targets with only a small language-specific syllabification adapter.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Argument Quality Assessment with Large Language Models: A Pairwise Bradley-Terry Approach
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in tasks related to reasoning and judgment. However, assessing the quality of arguments requires a rigorous evaluation. We investigate the extent to which LLMs can effectively perform this task. We tested 12 open-weight LLMs of different sizes and families under zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought to approximate human pairwise comparisons of argument quality across three dimensions—logical, rhetorical, and dialectic—and used these comparisons in a Bradley-Terry model to infer latent strength scores and derive a ranking of arguments. Our insights show that LLMs have promising but moderate correlation with human judgment, with Llama-70B obtaining the strongest alignment, reaching moderate Cohen’s κ = 0.493 and moderate correlations with Bradley-Terry scores derived from these annotations (Kendall, Pearson, and Spearman: 0.327-0.477). Other LLMs exhibit weak, moderate, or high alignment with Llama-70B while achieving comparable results against human judgment, suggesting partial but complementary understanding of underlying quality dimensions despite differences in model size and family. Moreover, LLM predictions are stable across trial runs, with fewer than 7.75% of cases yielding different labels. Remaining variability is handled via majority voting and few-shot prompting for large-size models.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Diagnosing and Selecting Synthetic Motion Tasks for Video RLVR
abstract: Synthetic video data with verifiable rewards offers a scalable source of supervision for temporal motion understanding in video-language models, yet it remains unclear which synthetic tasks transfer reliably to real-video benchmarks.We investigate this question through a diagnostic framework that treats each synthetic task as a controlled intervention.Starting from a shared Qwen3-VL-2B checkpoint with frozen vision encoder, we independently train nine programmatic motion tasks with RLVR and evaluate each resulting model across six temporal-motion dimensions, such as direction, rotation, and velocity, yielding an interference matrix of cross-dimensional transfer. The matrix reveals substantial variation in transfer that surface-level label alignment fails to explain: a frame-to-frame velocity task yields a large gain on its target dimension, whereas a nominally aligned trajectory-shape task degrades the dimension it is intended to improve. We find that transfer is better explained by computational alignment, namely whether the training task induces the local, order-sensitive temporal computation that the downstream capability requires.Counterfactual tasks that share semantic targets but differ in computational demands support this account, and the patterns hold on InternVL3-2B. We further introduce a training-free answer-invariance test under frame shuffling that flags shortcut-prone tasks prior to RLVR training. Using the interference matrix to filter tasks yields a task mixture that consistently outperforms uniform mixing on TOMATO, with positive transfer trends on MVBench, TempCompass, and TemporalBench.Our framework thus reframes synthetic video generation as an empirically grounded task-selection problem.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Alignment: Value Diversity as a Collective Property in Multicultural Agent Systems
abstract: Multicultural multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed in globally diverse settings, where different agents are grounded in different cultural backgrounds. Existing cultural evaluation focuses on value alignment: how closely a single agent matches a target culture. Yet alignment is a per-agent property and cannot reveal whether a system, taken as a whole, preserves the cultural plurality it is meant to represent. We propose value diversity as a system-level evaluation axis for multicultural agent systems, defined through the dissimilarity between culturally conditioned agents’ responses on a shared value survey. Using the World Values Survey, we evaluate 19 cultures and 18 backbone models across a wide range of system configurations. We find that diversity is largely uncorrelated with alignment, indicating that the two capture complementary system properties, and that current multicultural agent systems fall substantially below human societies in value diversity. Mixed-backbone systems narrow this gap but do not close it, and the gap persists across culture compositions and agent scales. Social interaction further erodes diversity by driving agents toward consensus, and a participatory budgeting case study shows that this homogenization narrows the breadth of collective decision-making. Together, our results establish value diversity as a distinct evaluation axis for multicultural multi-agent systems and reveal a persistent homogenization tendency in current LLM-based societies. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/MultiAgent-Diversity.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Syn-Omni: Structured Specialization and Progressive Collaboration for Omnimodal Embeddings
abstract: Omnimodal embeddings naturally involve both shared representations and modality-specific features across heterogeneous inputs. However, existing omnimodal embedding methods often rely on a single shared parameter space over mixed-modality data, limiting structural separation between universal and modality-specific representations. To address this, we propose Syn-Omni, a unified framework for structured omnimodal adaptation with modality specialization and controlled cross-modal collaboration. Specifically, we introduce Orthogonal Modality-Expert LoRA (OME-LoRA), which decomposes adaptation into a shared LoRA path for universal semantics and modality-expert LoRA paths for modality-aware specialization. Furthermore, Progressive Synergy Routing (PSR) enables experts to first establish modality-specific priors, then gradually interact with other modality-experts for cross-modal synergy. Evaluated across 81 diverse tasks spanning image, video, audio, and audiovisual modalities, Syn-Omni consistently outperforms omnimodal baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured specialization and cross-modal progressive collaboration.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ReFrame: Evidence-Guided Test-Time Safety Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) extend model capabilities beyond text, they also make safety alignment increasingly challenging. Multimodal safety alignment methods must address cross-modal jailbreaks, safety-awareness failures, and over-sensitive refusals. However, existing methods often rely on retraining or internal-state inspection, limiting their applicability to deployed closed-source MLLMs and motivating test-time safety alignment. We analyze this setting and identify two key obstacles, utility dominance and reasoning inertia, which cause models to overlook latent risks or follow malicious reasoning trajectories. Guided by these insights, we propose **ReFrame**, a training-free multimodal input reframing framework where two agents share a lightweight locally deployed MLLM: the evidence-generation agent constructs complementary risk and utility evidence, and the rewrite-and-routing agent converts it into a safe proxy prompt and image-routing decision before calling the downstream MLLM, without modifying it or accessing its internal information. Experiments across multiple MLLMs and benchmarks show that ReFrame improves jailbreak defense, safety awareness, and oversensitivity reduction while preserving multimodal utility.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SMAH-CTI: A Unified Sentence-Level Benchmark for Multi-Task Cyber Threat Intelligence Extraction
abstract: Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) reports describe adversary behavior and attack infrastructure in natural language but remain largely unstructured and difficult to process at scale. Existing CTI benchmarks are limited in realism or scope, often relying on synthetic or knowledge-base-derived data, coarse document-level annotations, or isolated subtasks. We introduce SMAH-CTI, a human-annotated benchmark derived from 100 public CTI reports from five threat intelligence providers. It contains 12,304 validated sentence-level instances annotated for (i) relevance classification, (ii) CTI-specific named entity recognition (NER), and (iii) multi-label MITRE ATT CK tactic, technique, and sub-technique mapping, together with grounded procedure descriptions. By unifying these tasks over evidence grounded in real CTI reports, SMAH-CTI provides a reproducible benchmark for evaluating structured CTI extraction and transforming unstructured reports into machine-interpretable intelligence.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Evaluating Large Language Models on Urdu Idioms
abstract: Idioms remain a persistent challenge in natural language processing due to their figurative and culturally grounded meanings, which distinguish them from literal expressions. Although recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have improved idiom handling across several languages, limited attention has been given to low-resource languages such as Urdu. In this work, we present a comprehensive benchmark for Urdu–English idiomatic translation, consisting of a manually verified dataset of 4,000 aligned idiom–sentence pairs in both Perso-Arabic (native Urdu script) and Romanized Urdu. We evaluate multiple tasks, including translation, paraphrasing, idiom span detection, and back-translation, using diverse prompting strategies such as cultural prompting, idiomatic prompting, and few-shot learning. Our findings show that frontier LLMs consistently outperform traditional neural machine translation systems across all evaluation settings, particularly in preserving figurative and metaphorical meaning. While models demonstrate relatively stable performance on native Urdu script, the absence of standardized orthography in Romanized Urdu introduces substantial challenges for consistency and idiom span detection. This work establishes a high-quality benchmark for cross-script idiomatic evaluation in Urdu and underscores the importance of prompt engineering in preserving figurative language meaning across languages.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Can LLM Annotators Match Human Consistency? Benchmarking Human Agreement and Optimizing Multi-Agent with Contrastive Knowledge
abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{ANT-A Benchmark}, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss’ \kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose \textbf{ANT-OR}, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@\ge2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss’ \kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: GRAM: Empowering Agent with Actively Managed Graph-Structured Memory via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents face a fundamental bottleneck called context flooding in multi-turn information retrieval: as evidence accumulates across interaction turns, their context windows become saturated with redundant, conflicting, and outdated facts. Existing research either compresses interaction history into rolling summaries, sacrificing relational precision, or relies on retrieval-augmented pipelines that lack mechanisms for resolving knowledge conflicts and maintaining a globally consistent belief state. In this work, we introduce GRAM, a reinforcement learning framework designed to train an agent to actively manage and utilize a dynamic graph-structured memory. Rather than passively accumulating retrieved text, the agent learns to incrementally construct and revise a coherent knowledge graph that serves as its persistent belief state, resolving contradictions and preserving logical relationships in memory. Furthermore, We employ Group Relative Policy Optimization to train small language models (under 4B) to master these complex memory-governance behaviors. Experimental results across multiple mainstream question-answering benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of the GRAM framework over existing agentic memory baselines and conventional RAG systems.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Audit Quality Fails to Predict Downstream Utility: Synthetic-Data Selection for Low-Resource Classification
abstract: Quality-aware synthetic-data selection assumes that examples rated highly by an LLM judge will help downstream learning. We test this assumption in a controlled replay across two low-resource African-language classification tasks, four languages, and seven selectors. Six selectors retain 64 examples per task-language cell. CoSDA-V2 yields the highest judged label correctness (0.904 versus 0.767 for naive) and the lowest measured shortcut score, but AlpaGasus leads CoSDA-V2 on downstream Macro-F1 in both the main replay (0.202 versus 0.163) and the three-seed refit (0.193 versus 0.157).Adding the audit’s strict gate to AlpaGasus reduces Macro-F1 by 0.029, driven by one cell where only 31 of 64 candidates survive. Because the gate changes pool composition and training-set size, this comparison measures their joint effect. LESS also falls below naive when unconstrained top-k collapses label balance, but recovers with quotas. At this budget, retention constraints account for more of the observed differences than a consistent ranking advantage. In this replay, audit scores do not reliably predict downstream utility. We therefore recommend reporting both metrics for the same retained sets.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Attention-Aligned Reasoning for Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to generate a long reasoning chain when solving complex tasks. However, as the reasoning chain extends, critical intermediate steps and the original prompt will be buried in the context, receiving insufficient attention and leading to errors. In this work, we present ATAR, a novel reasoning method that leverages the inherent reasoning structure to steer LLM attention. Our experiments show that ATAR outperforms SOTA methods across six benchmarks, achieving up to 15.39% absolute improvement. Furthermore, with ATAR, “non-reasoning” models achieve comparable or even better performance compared to reasoning models of the same size in most benchmarks. Finally, our ablation studies show that the attention alignment component contributes significantly, and that these improvements are persist under different attention-steering backends.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Attribute-Based Diagnosis of LLM Alignment with Hate Speech Annotations
abstract: Hate speech annotation is costly, subjective, and prone to annotator disagreement, making large-scale dataset construction challenging. We systematically analyze how well large language models (LLMs) align with human judgments across ten theoretically grounded subjective attributes, such as dehumanization, violence, and sentiment, evaluating both small and large variants of Llama 3.1 and Qwen 2.5. Our analysis reveals a consistent split across all models: behaviorally explicit dimensions (insult, humiliate, attack-defend) correlate strongly with human annotations, while evaluative dimensions (respect, sentiment, hate speech) are systematically inverted. Demographic persona conditioning reduces model confidence without improving alignment. Building on these insights, we propose combining attribute-level LLM predictions via a confidence-weighted Ridge regression to reconstruct continuous hate speech scores from the Measuring Hate Speech corpus, achieving R^2 of up to 0.71 and outperforming direct prompting baselines, demonstrating that structured attribute decomposition recovers a richer and more human-aligned signal than end-to-end label prediction alone.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Decoding Self-Knowledge from Latent Reasoning Models for Selective Prediction and Adaptive Routing
abstract: Latent reasoning models compress chain-of-thought into hidden states, but whether these representations retain usable self-knowledge about correctness remains unclear. We study two compression-based paradigms, Latent-SFT and CoLaR, and find a sharp distinction between problem-level and trajectory-level self-knowledge. A lightweight attention probe predicts which problems the model will solve (AUC 0.805/0.853) and transfers across datasets and compression ratios, yet cannot reliably rank rollouts of the same problem; distribution-matched retraining does not recover this signal. This distinction maps directly to downstream use: selective prediction improves accuracy by 20–25pp at 50% coverage, and adaptive routing outperforms either solver while reducing token cost, whereas latent best-of-N yields negligible gains despite available oracle headroom. The problem-level signal also persists on a 7B math checkpoint but vanishes on StrategyQA. These results identify an algorithm–paradigm boundary for exploiting self-knowledge in latent reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/Arthas777/latent-probe.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Paraphrases: Generalization Across Task Formats in Parametric Knowledge Editing
abstract: Knowledge editing aims to update specific facts in language models to ensure reliable and up-to-date behavior. A key challenge is whether edited knowledge generalizes beyond the format in which the edit is applied, yet existing evaluations primarily assess generalization using paraphrases. In this work, we identify a critical blind spot: generalization across heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice and verification-based question answering. We show that paraphrase-based evaluations overestimate robustness, as models that perform well on paraphrases exhibit substantial performance drops across task formats. While model predictions are consistent across formats prior to editing, editing introduces format-dependent inconsistencies. We further observe that heterogeneous task formats exhibit distinct decision landscapes, where single-format objectives lead to format-specific local optima with divergent edit directions, resulting in misaligned outputs across formats. To address this issue, we demonstrate that aligning edit directions across task formats improves cross-format generalization and consistency. These findings highlight the need to move beyond paraphrase-based evaluation and to develop editing methods that maintain consistent factual behavior across diverse task formulations.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RankSteer: Can Pointwise LLM Rankers Be Calibrated at the Representation Level?
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are strong zero-shot pointwise rankers, but lag behind pairwise and listwise methods. Beyond missing comparative signals, we identify a calibration gap: ranking-relevant information encoded in hidden states is not fully captured by the scalar output head. We propose RankSteer, a post-hoc activation-steering framework that calibrates ranking via projection-based interventions along multiple directions at inference time: decision, evidence, and, optionally, role. This is achieved without updating model weights or introducing cross-document comparisons. We instantiate RankSteer on two structurally distinct pointwise variants and observe improvements over their respective baselines on most TREC DL and BEIR datasets across three backbones. This suggests that the calibration gap is a general property of pointwise rankers. Our additional geometric analysis shows that steering improves ranking by concentrating each query’s document representations along an existing ranking geometry, offering new insight into how LLMs internally represent and calibrate relevance judgments.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PRISM: Calibrated Prior-Risk Integration for Safe and Useful Test-Time Alignment
abstract: This paper investigates the problem of safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) during the testing phase, particularly under jailbreaking attacks. Previous methods typically rely on identifying malicious request intentions or adjusting the LLM’s decoding strategy to inject safe behavior. However, this often leads to over-rejection, limiting their practical application. To address this, we propose an innovative framework called Prior-Risk Integration for Safe Mixture decoding (PRISM). Specifically, PRISM first uses a lightweight semantic risk evaluator to calculate the prior probability of harmfulness at the prompt level, and then continuously tracks the cumulative risk signal provided by a safety evaluator during the generation process. By comprehensively considering these two types of risks, PRISM adaptively mixes the base model’s probability distribution with a safety preference distribution, triggering a rejection response only when both the prompt prior probability and the generation risk are sufficiently high. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of PRISM in resisting jailbreaking attacks and its practicality. Across five jailbreaking attack methods and three neutral datasets, PRISM demonstrates superior performance compared to other baseline methods.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SAGE: An Extensible Benchmark for Service Agent Graph-guided Evaluation
abstract: LLMs are transforming customer service, yet evaluating service agents across diverse business scenarios remains costly and fragmented, as each new domain requires building a dedicated benchmark from scratch. Existing benchmarks rely on static, scenario-specific scripts with two fundamental limitations: ***Scenario Silos***, where each domain demands costly independent annotation with no shared evaluation structure, and ***Dialogue Dynamics Gap***, where fixed scripts fail to capture the full range of real user behaviors. We propose **SAGE** (**S**ervice **A**gent **G**raph-guided **E**valuation), to our knowledge the first scenario-extensible benchmark to jointly assess logical SOP compliance and conversational quality, abstracting any SOP as a directed graph and bridging Scenario Silos through a lightweight two-step extension mechanism. SAGE further enables dynamic multi-turn simulation via adversarial user agents to overcome the Dynamics Gap. Across six industrial scenarios representative of real-world customer service deployment, we evaluate 27 mainstream LLMs spanning both closed-source systems and open-source families, offering a fine-grained capability map to guide real-world model selection. Our experiments further reveal two systematic failure patterns shared across all tested models: while models generally succeed at recognizing user intent, they frequently struggle to follow complex business logic and execute the correct subsequent action; and they sustain a warm and empathetic conversational tone even when their underlying procedural reasoning has already failed. **Code and resources are available at: https://github.com/lingshi6565/SAGE-Bench.**
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Context-anchored Asymmetric Conformal Prediction for Uncertainty-aware Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs
abstract: This paper studies the problem of uncertainty-aware reasoning over knowledge graphs (KGs), which aims to incorporate uncertainty quantification into unseen knowledge predictions over KGs. Previous works typically incorporate uncertainty measurement tools such as conformal predictions into graph representation learning. Despite the progress, the performance of these approaches remains limited since they usually neglect both structural information in KGs and intrinsic asymmetry between over-estimation and under-estimation. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Context-anchored Asymmetric Conformal Prediction for uncertainty-aware REasoning over KGs (CARE). The core of our CARE is to identify the context of each query using anchors, which guide the construction of triple-specific asymmetry prediction intervals. In particular, we first take the subset of the calibration set as a reference pool. For each triple query, we summarize the KG structural statistics into a vector, which guides the identification of its anchor samples from the pool. The confidence residuals between query and anchors are utilized to quantify over-estimation and under-estimation, producing contextual nonconformity scores. Finally, we utilize the unselected calibration dataset to determine cutoff levels for constructing asymmetric prediction intervals. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of CARE. The code can be found at https://github.com/fanboyang/CARE.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: AdaptiveGuard: Treating Constraints as Falsifiable Hypotheses for LLM Agents in Dynamic Interactive Environments
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive reasoning capabilities in agents for complex interactive environments. However, these agents frequently propose actions that violate physical or procedural constraints. Recent neuro-symbolic guards mitigate such errors by compiling explicit admissibility rules from oracle demonstrations, yet treat them as fixed laws—a closed-world assumption that breaks down under sparse demonstrations or environment shift, leaving either missing rules that fail to block unsafe actions or stale rules that wrongly reject valid alternatives. To address this, we introduce **AdaptiveGuard** ([code](https://github.com/lpxwork666111/AdaptiveGuard)), an Adaptive framework that Guards LLM agents by treating constraints as *falsifiable hypotheses*. Each rule is represented by a Beta-distributed validity belief mapped to *tentative*, *confirmed*, and *deprecated* tiers; uncertain rule blockers are then challenged through a zero-extra-call falsification gate; and these rule beliefs are continuously updated via contrastive feedback attribution from environment evidence. Benchmark experiments on ScienceWorld and VirtualHome show aggregate gains over strong static constraint guards, especially in novel scenarios. Complementary post-hoc diagnostics under sparse supervision and controlled shift show improved adaptation, while observed failed-trial runs remain below the configured budget cap and the conservative-bias proxy declines over the measured horizon.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Preserving Memory Function in Hybrid Language Models: A Survey of State, Evidence, Access, and Granularity
abstract: Hybrid language models combine Transformer attention with recurrent, state-space, or online-updated components to lower long-context serving cost while preserving memory fidelity. Existing surveys mostly organize this space by architecture family, chronology, or efficiency technique, leaving workload-specific memory functions underspecified. We propose State-Evidence-Access (SEA) for this constraint: bounded State may lose distinctions needed by future queries not fixed in advance. Architectures therefore allocate active State, addressable Evidence, and a per-step Access budget to jointly support reusable structure, query-conditioned recovery, and effective use. This view helps explain why attention ratios or average perplexity can be misleading: a hybrid can save memory while losing the retrieval, state-update, or access function needed by the task. We survey hybrids by allocation locus—from key-value (K-V) and head-level mechanisms through layer, block, external-memory, and system-cache policies—and characterize their *function-granularity mismatch* risks. For workloads such as long-document QA, SEA attributes failure to missing evidence, unstable state updates, access bottlenecks, or poor integration.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ExecRubrics: Executable Tool-Augmented Rubrics for Verifiable, Efficient and Explainable Evaluation
abstract: Rubrics aim to make language-model evaluation transparent by decomposing response quality into interpretable criteria. However, natural-language rubrics are often ambiguous, require LLM judges, and typically assume criteria aggregated through linear weighted sums, limiting their ability to capture dependencies, alternatives, penalties, and override conditions. We propose ExecRubrics, a framework for representing rubrics as compact executable programs. ExecRubrics encodes evaluation logic as verifiable Python scoring functions, giving natural-language rubric intent an operational semantics: a fixed decision procedure that can be inspected, executed, and edited. On three long-form response benchmarks – HealthBench, HelpSteer, and ArgQuality – we show that ExecRubrics can recover substantial preference signal without an LLM judge at evaluation time. On ArgQuality and HelpSteer, the strongest executable variants are within 1.1 and 4 percentage points, respectively, of the direct GPT-5.5 agentic baseline. Executable rubrics are also considerably faster, achieving a 192× average speedup. We show that incorporating external logic and resources from text processing libraries such as NLTK and spaCy can further improve preference accuracy. Our results suggest a novel way of approaching automated evaluation, by offering a faster, more explainable, and less ambiguous alternative to black-box rubric evals, particularly in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and banking where precision and auditability are critical.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Endogenous Observations in Agent Self-Evolution: A Survey
abstract: As training regimes centered on human-curated data encounter rising costs and an increasingly binding scaling ceiling, a core question in agent learning shifts from enlarging exogenous datasets to enabling agents to **self-evolve** under limited exogenous supervision. Prior surveys on self-evolution and self-improvement typically organize the literature by evolutionary stages or system architectures. While effective for summarizing implementation pipelines, these perspectives do not offer a unified explanation of what an agent actually observes during self-improvement, nor why such signals can serve as sufficient and reliable supervision. To address this gap, we introduce **endogenous observations**, defined as learning signals that arise from an agent’s own generation, evaluation, and interaction processes rather than exogenous labels. We systematize existing approaches into three categories—model-internal, peer-induced, and scenario-grounded observations—according to how these signals are produced, and we summarize the characteristic properties and typical application settings of each category. Finally, we discuss key challenges in reliability, scalability, and long-horizon stability, and outline open directions toward robust and sustainable self-evolving agents.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Rethinking Fairness in LLM-Based Recommender Systems: A Survey
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping recommender systems by enabling more semantic, generative, and interactive recommendation pipelines. However, this shift also introduces new fairness challenges, as biases may arise from pretrained knowledge, prompts, generated explanations, decoding strategies, and feedback loops. This survey provides a systematic review of fairness in LLM based recommender systems, organizing existing studies through a two-dimensional view of bias mechanisms and fairness targets, together with a structured overview of the evaluation landscape and mitigation strategies. We further connect fairness with broader trustworthy concerns, including explainability, privacy, robustness, and controllability. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first survey specifically focused on fairness in LLM-based recommender systems, aiming to provide a structured foundation for future research on comprehensive and reliable fairness evaluation in LLM-based recommender systems.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Enhancing Pun Meme Understanding with Visual Semantic Cues
abstract: Internet memes have become important carriers of online expression, and pun memes, as a typical multimodal category, pose significant challenges to machine understanding due to their reliance on textual ambiguity and cross-modal interaction with visual content. Existing multimodal models for pun meme understanding suffer from classification bias, weak sentiment perception, and performance gaps compared to human comprehension, mainly due to neglecting fine-grained correlation cues for semantic reasoning. To address this, we propose a fusion framework enhanced by multi-source auxiliary cues, including visual salient perception, textual deep semantics, and abnormal pun linguistic features, which are embedded into the multimodal reasoning pipeline. Experiments show that our framework stably optimizes vision-language models, improving accuracy in pun meme detection and implicit sentiment fine-grained analysis.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SubtleMemory: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Relational Memory Discrimination in Long-Horizon AI Agents
abstract: Persistent AI assistants, such as OpenClaw, accumulate large collections of related memories over long-term interactions. As these memories grow, they may reinforce one another, diverge across contexts, or directly conflict, making correct assistance depend on memory relations rather than isolated recall. Existing long-term memory benchmarks do not systematically probe how agents preserve and utilize such relations during downstream tasks. To address this gap, we introduce SubtleMemory, a benchmark for fine-grained relational memory discrimination in long-running AI agents. SubtleMemory constructs relation-controlled latent semantic artifacts whose variants instantiate complementary, nuanced, or contradictory relations, and embeds them into realistic user-agent histories, requiring agents to recover distributed relational structures during later queries and instructions.The benchmark contains 1,522 evaluation instances over 10 long histories, grounded in 1,090 relation-controlled memory-variant sets and spanning user-related and non-user-related queries. Evaluating six standalone memory systems, two Claw-style agents with native memory modules, and three Claw-style agents with plugin memory modules, we find that current systems remain weak on fine-grained relational memory discrimination. We further introduce diagnostic protocols that reveal distinct capability profiles across memory preservation, retrieval, and downstream reasoning stages.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Endpoint Gains: A Weight-Delta Audit of Medical Specialization
abstract: Specialist language models are usually understood through endpoint gains: the generalist scores lower, the specialist scores higher, and the difference is treated as evidence of specialization. This leaves the released update itself largely unexamined. We propose a paired weight-delta path audit and apply it to two public, aligned generalist-to-medical-specialist checkpoint pairs: Gemma-3-4B-IT → MedGemma-4B-IT and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct → HuatuoGPT-o1-7B. In both pairs, the full decoder-side update strongly reconstructs measured medical benchmark movement (0.974 and 1.183 endpoint-normalized retention), making each decoder delta an appropriate substrate for the audit. Yet the movement is not cleanly localized. MLP is the strongest broad component family in both pairs, but mixed off-domain movements, 10-seed matched controls, and endpoint-anchored rollbacks prevent a unique coarse-family explanation. The audit therefore separates update-level reconstruction from component-level explanation. Its claims concern text-only multiple-choice benchmark movement, not clinical validation, repair, or circuit-level mechanism.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RelayS2S: Dual-Path Speculative Generation for Real-Time Dialogue
abstract: Real-time spoken dialogue systems face a fundamental tension between latency and response quality. End-to-end speech-to-speech (S2S) models respond immediately and naturally handle turn-taking, backchanneling, and interruption, but produce semantically weaker outputs. Cascaded pipelines (ASR ➔ LLM) deliver stronger responses at the cost of latency that grows with model size. We present RelayS2S, a hybrid architecture that runs two paths in parallel upon turn detection. The fast path—a duplex S2S model—speculatively drafts a short response prefix that is streamed immediately to TTS for low-latency response onset, while continuing to monitor live audio events. The slow path—a cascaded ASR ➔ LLM pipeline—generates a higher-quality continuation conditioned on the committed prefix, producing an uninterrupted utterance. A lightweight learned verifier gates the handoff, committing the prefix when appropriate or falling back gracefully to the cascaded pipeline. With GPT-4.1 as the back-end, RelayS2S substantially reduces response latency while preserving nearly all of the cascaded pipeline’s textual quality. On synthetic voice dialogues, it achieves a P90 first-chunk latency of 81 ms, excluding TTS and network latency, compared with 1,006 ms for the cascaded baseline. On real voice dialogues, RelayS2S reduces average first-chunk latency by 479 ms while retaining 99% of the cascaded pipeline’s textual quality. These benefits become larger as the slow-path model scales. Because the prefix handoff requires no architectural modification to either component, RelayS2S serves as a lightweight, drop-in addition to existing cascaded pipelines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/mailong25/relays2s.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EDIT: Evidence-Diagnosed Intervention Training for Rule-Faithful LLM Grading
abstract: Reliable rubric grading requires more than accurate score prediction. Each judgement must be grounded in the mark scheme and evidence from the student answer. Existing credit-assignment and intervention methods, primarily designed for self-contained reasoning tasks such as mathematics reasoning, struggle in this setting because they do not identify where grading reasoning goes wrong or how the model’s belief about the final mark changes during reasoning. We propose Evidence-Diagnosed Intervention Training (EDIT), a two-phase framework for training more rubric-faithful LLM graders. First, EDIT-SFT locates problematic reasoning steps using internal model signals: posterior belief over the final mark and input-grounding scores. It then revises only these local steps with help from a rubric checklist. Second, EDIT-RL calibrates the grader with belief-guided reward shaping, penalising large harmful belief drifts while still allowing helpful exploration. Experiments on two real-world, multi-subject grading benchmarks demonstrate that EDIT consistently outperforms strong supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain splits, with ablation studies confirming that internal-state diagnostics drive these gains. Under deterministic rubric-edit interventions, EDIT-SFT is the most rule-responsive of all evaluated systems, and EDIT-RL largely retains this responsiveness while improving accuracy.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Action-Level Credit Assignment for Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning
abstract: Complex question answering over large document collections requires models to identify missing information, issue sub-queries, and iteratively gather evidence before producing an answer. Reinforcement learning offers a natural framework for training such behaviour, but standard GRPO-style training provides only a sparse final-answer reward and assigns the same advantage to every token in a rollout. We introduce PACE-GRPO (Potential-based Action Credit Estimation GRPO), a variant of GRPO that combines potential-based reward shaping with action-level credit assignment. PACE-GRPO computes a state potential from inexpensive retrieval-derived signals, including retrieval utility, coverage, and passage diversity, and uses potential differences to provide step-level feedback. Unlike prior intermediate-reward methods, it requires no gold evidence annotations, teacher traces, reward model, or additional forward passes. Across six multi-hop QA benchmarks, PACE-GRPO learns a tool-use policy that selectively invokes the more expensive retrieval operation only when it is beneficial. This adaptive tool use yields consistent improvements over standard GRPO and strong search-augmented baselines. Our code and data are in https://github.com/lauhaide/pace.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: LLaVA-RadZ: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Effectively Tackle Zero-shot Radiology Recognition?
abstract: Recently, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong visual understanding and reasoning abilities across vision-language tasks. However, conventional Visual Question Answering (VQA) pipelines do not fully exploit the visual features and medical knowledge captured by MLLMs, leading to limited performance in zero-shot medical disease recognition. To address this issue, we propose LLaVA-RadZ, a simple yet effective framework for zero-shot radiology recognition. LLaVA-RadZ introduces Decoding-Side Feature Alignment Training (DFAT), which leverages decoder-side representations with modality-specific tokens for image-text alignment, and a Domain Knowledge Anchoring Module (DKAM), which incorporates disease-aware semantic anchors to mitigate the category semantic gap. Extensive experiments show that LLaVA-RadZ substantially improves the zero-shot disease recognition ability of MLLMs and achieves competitive performance compared with well-established CLIP-based radiology recognition methods.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SEA-LION-Embedding: Open and Reproducible Text Embeddings for Southeast Asia
abstract: Text embeddings are fundamental to many downstream applications, making robustness important for real-world NLP. However, most recent state-of-the-art embedding models are not reproducible because they rely on closed or undisclosed training data, and they remain insufficiently robust for Southeast Asian languages. We present SEA-LION-Embedding, a fully open and reproducible text-embedding pipeline for Southeast Asian languages trained only on publicly available data, and use it to study three core factors of robust embedding design: data composition, training objective, and base encoder initialization. SEA-LION-Embedding achieves state-of-the-art results on SEA-BED while enabling systematic and reproducible analysis of robust text embeddings for the region.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Latent-Space Intervention for Cross-Lingual Factual Consistency: Consistency Improvements without Accuracy Drops
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often answer the same factual question differently across languages. We study whether cross-lingual latent-space intervention can reduce this inconsistency. We train layer-specific autoencoders on parallel multilingual representations and apply inference-time corrections to factual QA prompts. We find that latent intervention improves geometric alignment between languages, and that this improvement translates into consistent gains in cross-lingual consistency with English across both open-ended and multiple-choice QA formats, without degrading factual accuracy. In open-ended QA, Spearman’s rank correlation between English and non-English languages improves substantially, with gains of 0.16 for English-Arabic and 0.20 for English-Russian pairs. In multiple-choice QA, answer agreement with English improves consistently across both KLAR and mParaRel. Ablations show that AE reconstruction drives these gains, whereas PCA-based and mean-shift subspace projections contribute only marginally to the observed improvements in consistency.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: BIRDS: Characterizing and Understanding Biodiversity Impact of Large Language Model Serving
abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving creates environmental impacts beyond carbon and water, including ecosystem damage through biodiversity-related pathways. We present BIRDS, a framework for Biodiversity Impact of Request-Driven LLM Serving. BIRDS defines request-level functional units, quantifies operational and embodied biodiversity impact, and introduces Quality-Normalized Biodiversity Impact (QNBI) to jointly analyze ecological impact and response quality. Across diverse workloads, models, GPUs, and regions, BIRDS reveals that reveals that biodiversity impact accumulates at scale and exposes quality-aware serving tradeoffs. The code is available at https://github.com/TianyaoShi/BIRDS.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Sycophancy Suppression Can Impair Rational Updating: Anti-Sycophancy Should Preserve the Ability to Update
abstract: Large language models often exhibit sycophancy, revising their answers to align with users when users push back. Such answer flips, however, can arise from different causes. One possibility is that the model simply aligns with the user’s feedback in order to satisfy them. Another is that the feedback genuinely contains useful evidence, prompting the model to update its answer in a rational way. We distinguish them as *Unsupported-Yielding* and *Rational-Updating*. Prior work focuses primarily on suppressing *Unsupported-Yielding*, while overlooking its effect on *Rational-Updating*. We address this gap with a two-turn evaluation framework that measures the two behaviors separately. Across representative training-time and inference-time interventions, we find that anti-sycophancy methods often encounter a trade-off in which reducing *Unsupported-Yielding* can sacrifice *Rational-Updating*, and vice versa, even when the two objectives are optimized jointly. Mechanistic analysis suggests that the two behaviors share an internal substrate: the MLP neurons and attention heads driving them overlap substantially, and their associated steering directions are positively aligned. We further conduct a preliminary orthogonalized steering exploration, which yields modest, backbone-dependent selectivity gains. Overall, our results suggest that anti-sycophancy should be treated not as a simple suppression problem, but as a selectivity problem, where effective interventions should preserve *Rational-Updating* while reducing *Unsupported-Yielding*.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: OpenIDC: Reconstructing the Evidence Chain for Lightweight Image Difference Captioning
abstract: Image Difference Captioning (IDC) has produced many task-specific models, but their gains are often entangled with isolated implementations, data processing, training protocols, and evaluation settings. As a result, the field accumulates method-level scores more easily than reusable structural evidence. This paper proposes OpenIDC, a flexible and extensible codebase that reconstructs a unified evidence chain for lightweight task-specific IDC. OpenIDC standardizes data pipelines, model interfaces, training strategies, and evaluation protocols, enabling 8 representative method families with 9 executable variants across 3 benchmarks to be reproduced, compared, decomposed, and diagnosed under consistent conditions. Beyond reproduction, OpenIDC advances IDC from final-score comparison to normalized design-space diagnosis. Based on this diagnosis, we introduce SIDFormer, a compact Spatially-guided Invariant-Difference Transformer that serves as a structural answer to lightweight IDC by organizing spatial anchoring, pseudo-change suppression, and reliable difference evidence through functional fusion. Experiments show improved reproducibility and comparability, together with competitive SIDFormer performance across the evaluated benchmarks. Code, reproduced methods, and models will be released.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Evolutionary Trajectory of Medical Multi-Agent Systems: A Survey
abstract: Breakthroughs in large language models are accelerating the evolution of medical artificial intelligence from standalone models to multi-agent systems. To organize this landscape, we propose a hierarchical taxonomy spanning Level 0 to Level 5. Given that foundational Level 0 to Level 2 architectures face cognitive and collaborative bottlenecks in complex clinical workflows, this survey focuses primarily on the architectural paradigm shift between Level 3 and Level 4. Specifically, we examine how systems transition from static Level 3 collaboration based on predefined roles to Level 4 self-evolving architectures that iteratively refine internal strategies through interactive feedback. Concurrently, we explore governance frameworks required to ensure system safety and trustworthiness under stringent clinical standards. Finally, we highlight that the capacity to dynamically generate agents and reconstruct collaborative topologies based on real-world scenarios will be essential for surpassing current capability limits. Building on this concept, we envision a Level 5 medical AI landscape defined by evolutionary agent swarms. To help researchers continuously track this field, our updated GitHub repository (https://github.com/Tiany1Yu/Medical_Multi_Agent_Systems_Survey_Papers) is publicly available.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MEMORA: Embodied Action Memory from Egocentric Videos for Reasoning and Planning
abstract: Embodied agents must reason and act from experience accumulated before future questions or goals are known, yet existing memory systems often treat such experience as flat text, retrieved clips, or static graphs. We introduce MEMORA, an embodied memory framework that forms persistent participant-specific world memory from continuous egocentric video. MEMORA instantiates a formation–consolidation lifecycle: online memory editing maintains typed stores for spatial context, object identity and state, and temporal action evidence, while offline consolidation abstracts repeated experience into reusable routines, habits, and preferences. We evaluate MEMORA with MEMORA-Bench, a 45-hour egocentric-video suite for retrospective memory faithfulness and prospective memory-grounded planning. Across four open-weight answer models, MEMORA improves over no-memory, flat-text, and graph-structured memory baselines under matched perception and retrieval. The gains are largest on out-of-distribution planning, where MEMORA improves robot-grounded planning score by up to , showing that formed memory can compose new goals from remembered procedures, objects, and preferences. A physical-robot demonstration further suggests that memory formed from human egocentric video can guide participant-grounded action without in-domain robot data.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: GRACE: Gradient-guided Coreset Selection for LLM Unlearning
abstract: Machine Unlearning methods for Large Language Models typically assume pre-specified forget and retain sets. In realistic settings, however, requests may provide only a few examples of undesired behaviour, requiring forget and retain sets to be inferred from heterogeneous corpora. We study this data-selection problem and propose GRACE, a gradient-guided coreset selection method that constructs both forget and retain sets for LLM unlearning. GRACE first computes a forget direction from seed examples that elicit the undesired behaviour, then selects a compact forget coreset whose gradients approximate this direction using non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit. To preserve model utility, it selects retain examples after projecting out the forget direction and applying clustered orthogonal matching pursuit in the remaining gradient space. Across two target domains, two model families, and four unlearning algorithms, GRACE improves model utility while maintaining comparable forget quality, with particularly consistent gains over prior gradient-based selection methods.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SocialMaze: A Benchmark for Evaluating and Enhancing Social Reasoning in Large Language Models in Complex Social Environments
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially grounded applications, where success requires interpreting context, inferring others’ mental states, and reasoning about unreliable information. Yet existing benchmarks rarely evaluate these demands jointly in complex, evolving settings. We introduce SocialMaze, a benchmark that organizes six tasks across social deduction games, daily-life interactions, and digital community platforms along three descriptive design axes: deep reasoning, dynamic interaction, and information uncertainty. These axes characterize intended sources of task difficulty rather than latent, factor-analytic dimensions of model capability. Automated checks and human validation support data quality. Evaluations of twelve proprietary and open-weight LLMs show substantial variation in the use of evolving interaction histories; stronger chain-of-thought reasoners perform better on tasks requiring deeper inference, while uncertainty consistently degrades performance. Reasoning workflows help weaker short-chain-of-thought backbones but saturate on stronger reasoners. Finally, targeted fine-tuning on curated reasoning traces substantially improves structured social-reasoning tasks, whereas transfer to language-aggregation tasks remains statistically inconclusive. The project homepage is available at https://xzx34.github.io/socialmaze/.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SAGE: Answer-Conditioned Uncertainty Targets for Verbal Confidence Alignment
abstract: Large language models increasingly express uncertainty through verbalized confidence, yet these expressions often fail to reflect the model’s sampled behavior. We study verbal confidence alignment as a distributional calibration problem, where the confidence target for a prompt is estimated from repeated model outputs rather than from a single response. However, group rollouts alone are insufficient, since the resulting target must provide a useful training signal. We propose Semantic-Answer Guided Entropy (SAGE), a group-level uncertainty target that constructs an answer-conditioned uncertainty geometry over sampled responses. SAGE preserves categorical, numeric, and symbolic answer distinctions while maintaining a smooth and scale-preserving calibration signal. We further introduce Group-Uncertainty Preference Optimization (GUPO), an uncertainty-channel training framework that supervises verbal confidence expressions rather than the full response. Experiments across factual, mathematical, and multiple-choice reasoning tasks show improved confidence ranking, lower calibration error, and reduced overconfidence.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Don’t Box Me In: Dynamic Cultural Adaptation and Cognitive Tracking for Social Understanding
