With EMQ supervision, the updated 4B model produces competitive results on temporally anchored oncology staging, reaching 64.8% answer accuracy and 59.6% rationale accuracy on SEER-Bench. Diagnostic analyses suggest that EMQ exposes denser clinical contrast signals while preserving discriminative representations with smaller movement from the base model. These results show that medical knowledge updating depends not only on the update algorithm, but also on how knowledge is structured as supervision.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Perception Is the Bottleneck for Large Audio Reasoning Models
abstract: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has revolutionized text-based LLMs, its application to the audio modality reveals a counter-intuitive thinking paradox: forcing models to “think” via prompting or post-training often degrades performance compared to direct answering. In this work, we investigate the bottleneck of audio reasoning and reveal a critical insight: the primary constraint is not the model’s logical deduction capability, but its inability to accurately perceive acoustic details. We demonstrate that keeping perceptual cues effectively activates the LALM’s internal reasoning potential. Building on this finding, we propose Audio-ReaPer, a post-training framework and corresponding model designed to unlock Reasoning potential by explicitly fortifying Perception. Our approach reforms the post-training paradigm through three key strategies: (1) utilizing agentic data generation pipeline to synthesize perception-enhanced data for SFT; (2) curating perception-focused data for RLVR; and (3) introducing a novel perceptual density reward during RL to stabilize the learning process and balance observation with deduction. Extensive experiments show that Audio-ReaPer establishes a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks such as MMAU, MMAU-Pro, and MMAR. Notably, our 7B model outperforms previous open-source models by significant margins and surpasses proprietary models like GPT-4o Audio and Gemini 2.5 Flash. The model and code will be open-source to facilitate further research for audio reasoning.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Towards Better Legal Reasoning LLMs: Signal Balancing and Reward Scheduling
abstract: In the legal domain, LLMs can improve reliability and interpretability by generating explicit reasoning traces. However, training LLMs to produce high-quality reasoning traces remains challenging. Existing supervised fine-tuning methods struggle when reasoning traces are significantly longer than final answers, as the learning signal for the answer becomes diluted. Meanwhile, reinforcement learning methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization also have several limitations, including costly reward design, performance plateaus, and reward hacking. We therefore propose a two-stage training framework. In Stage I, JurisCoT-SFT employs a length-normalized dual objective to balance learning signals between reasoning traces and final answers. In Stage II, Lifecycle-Aware Backtrackable Policy Optimization dynamically evaluates and retires auxiliary reward signals based on their impact on final evaluation objectives, enabling efficient reward utilization. Our framework substantially improves legal reasoning performance on relevant tasks selected from multiple legal benchmarks, including ChJGBench, LawBench, and LegalBench. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements in both reasoning trace quality and final answer accuracy, while our models remain competitive with larger models.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Harmless Yet Harmful: Neutral Prompting Attacks for Stealthy Hallucination Steering in Agent Skills
abstract: LLM-powered coding agents increasingly participate in software development workflows by generating code, selecting dependencies, and producing package installation commands. This creates a new software supply chain risk: when an agent hallucinates a non-existent package, an attacker may register the hallucinated name and later compromise users who install it. Existing package hallucination attacks and defenses primarily focus on naturally occurring hallucinations, targeted dependency steering, or post-hoc package validation. In this paper, we introduce *Neutral Prompting Attack* (NPA), a stealthy attack paradigm in which semantically benign instructions, such as encouraging imagination and exhaustiveness, increase package hallucination propensity without containing explicit malicious intent. Unlike targeted dependency steering, NPA does not specify an attacker-chosen package. Instead, it shifts the model’s dependency generation behavior toward more speculative package names. We evaluate NPA across multiple coding-oriented LLMs and package hallucination benchmarks. Our results show that NPA increases both *Hallucination ASR* and *Pip Install ASR*, changes the distribution of hallucinated package names, and evades existing static-analysis, LLM-based, and agent-based Skill defenses. These findings reveal that harmless-looking prompts can covertly manipulate hallucination behavior and create downstream software supply chain risks.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: LLMs Can Predict Failure Risk, But Struggle to Predict Which Collaboration Protocol Pays Off: Cost-Aware Protocol Routing Across Reasoning Tasks
abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems can improve reasoning by spending more computation, but deployment requires deciding when extra collaboration is worth its cost. We isolate this decision by running every problem under four protocols while holding the solver fixed within each setting: direct solving (Baseline), iterative self-correction (Single), planner–executor–reviewer collaboration (PER), and multi-agent deliberation (Broadcast). The primary benchmark comprises 4,181 competition-level math problems; paired robustness checks cover four benchmarks spanning competition math, biology, and broader science with two solver families. Across fixed policies, trained routers, and frozen LLM routers, conservative policies under-escalate, whereas higher-solve frozen routers often over-escalate. A post-answer, pre-collaboration gpt-oss-120b probe ranks Baseline failures with 0.8847 AUROC (4,151 parseable cases; 95% CI [0.8732, 0.8955]). The same score remains informative for predicting whether any collaboration helps (0.7683 AUPRC), but is much weaker for identifying PER- or Broadcast-specific value (0.1674 and 0.1041 AUPRC). Separately, the pre-answer self-confidence gate reaches 78.0% solve at 45K tokens, compared with 73.8% at 71.3K for a frozen gpt-oss-120b router and 92.4% for a retrospective fixed-order oracle. Across 10 paired model–condition settings, the oracle adds 23.2–58.3 points of retrospective coverage over Baseline, but protocol profiles vary by task. In the six settings with held-out router evaluations, oracle gaps remain 18.5–28.9 points. Confidence can therefore support initial escalation, while protocol-specific cost-aware routing remains unresolved.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: LISAA: A Framework for Large Language Model Information Security Awareness Assessment
abstract: LLM-based assistants have become ubiquitous, yet information security awareness (ISA) remains an underexplored aspect of LLM safety. ISA encompasses not only security knowledge, but also the attitudes and behaviors required to recognize implicit security risks and avoid prioritizing user satisfaction over secure guidance. We introduce LISAA, a framework for evaluating LLM ISA under realistic end-user interactions. The framework includes a dataset of 100 realistic scenarios spanning all criteria of an ISA taxonomy, each with a tension between implicit security implications and user satisfaction. We further introduce methods for systematically refining realistic ISA scenarios from authentic user queries and for selecting reliable LLM judges without requiring large annotated datasets. Robustness analyses show that LISAA rankings remain stable under scenario resampling and stochastic generation, while construct-validity experiments demonstrate sensitivity to changes in security behavior. Applying LISAA to leading LLMs reveals that many widely deployed models still exhibit medium-to-low ISA levels, and that strong performance on traditional cybersecurity knowledge benchmarks does not necessarily translate to high ISA. In addition, the framework enables comparative analyses across model families, revealing consistent trends such as higher ISA in newer and larger variants, although meaningful gaps persist even among recent models. We release the dataset, evaluation pipeline, source code, and an online tool for evaluating new models using the LISAA framework.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Chain-of-Thought Hurts When the Answer Speaks for Itself
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision has become a default assumption in fine-tuning large language models for reasoning tasks, with the intuition being that exposing models to intermediate reasoning steps leads to deeper learning than training on answers alone. We challenge this assumption. We introduce answer backtrackability, a measurable quantity capturing the degree to which a question can be reconstructed from its answer, and argue it is a key determinant of whether CoT supervision helps or hurts during fine-tuning. To test this, we construct two novel benchmarks derived from automata theory (NFA and DFA), where answers are transition tables from which the question is largely recoverable, and fine-tune three LLMs using LoRA on CoT and No-CoT versions of five datasets: GSM8K, MathInstruct, MATH, and our two formal-language benchmarks. On mathematical datasets, CoT consistently outperforms No-CoT. Within MathInstruct, Program-of-Thought (PoT) problems, where executable code answers are high-backtrackability, favour No-CoT, while CoT-format problems favour CoT. On our benchmarks, the pattern reverses: No-CoT outperforms CoT across all models and difficulty tiers. When the answer encodes sufficient structure to reconstruct the reasoning process, intermediate supervision adds noise rather than signal.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ThaiPaliBench: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Thai-Script Pali Understanding
abstract: The application of large language models (LLMs) to Pali written in the Thai script remains limited in accuracy due to its low-resource setting, complex grammar, and the absence of standardized evaluation benchmarks. In this paper, we introduce ThaiPaliBench, a comprehensive benchmark dataset designed to systematically evaluate LLM proficiency in Thai-script Pali. Our proposed dataset is an LLM-assisted benchmark derived from the Royal Pali Examination corpus and spans Parian Tham levels 1-9. ThaiPaliBench, comprises multiple-choice and sentence-pair tasks that evaluate grammatical knowledge, reading comprehension, natural language inference, and translation understanding. To verify the effectiveness of our benchmark, we evaluate over 10 model variants across 3 commercial and open-source LLM families, including ChatGPT, Claude, Kimi, Grok, Typhoon, GPT-OSS-120B, ThaiLLM, and SEA-LION. Our experiments show that even the best-performing model, Kimi K2.5 (1T), achieves only 68.3% overall accuracy, with performance dropping substantially on grammatical reasoning and semantic inference tasks. These results highlight the unique challenges posed by Thai-script Pali and confirm that ThaiPaliBench serves as a reliable, linguistically grounded benchmark for evaluating LLM proficiency in this low-resource language. Our proposed dataset is publicly available at: https://github.com/ainrg-llm-dev/ThaiPaliBench
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Structured Strategy Injection for Data Analysis Agents
abstract: Data analysis agents often produce shallow or non-auditable summaries because they lack the explicit reasoning frameworks and validation habits used by domain experts, especially when evidence must be gathered across heterogeneous data sources. We propose structured strategy injection, which injects compact methodology specifications with explicit checkpoints into an agent’s controller context, turning expert workflows into executable plans and enabling compliance-based transparency. To make such methodology-driven planning executable and auditable in heterogeneous settings, we introduce Data2MCP, a router-based orchestration infrastructure that standardizes SQL databases, knowledge graphs, vector stores, and tables as MCP-compatible tools and routes queries dynamically for multi-source retrieval and join-like reasoning. We compare Data2MCP against a RAG baseline and DA-Agent across multi-source retrieval, DAComp, and BIRD MiniDev. In multi-source retrieval, Data2MCP outperforms DA-Agent, and strategy injection benefits both architectures. On DAComp, strategy injection improves DA-Agent from 50.84 to 57.17 (+6.33). The code is available at https://github.com/turambar928/Data2MCP.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Visual-Prior Conflicts
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) must often arbitrate between visual evidence and world-knowledge priors when an image conflicts with commonsense expectations. Existing work has demonstrated that activation steering vectors can bias model outputs toward either source of information, but it remains unclear whether this arbitration mechanism generalizes across languages. To investigate this, we construct a multilingual extension of the Visual CounterFact color split and derive activation steering directions that contrast image-grounded answers with prior-based answers. Across 12 languages, we find that English-derived and shared multilingual steering directions consistently shift model outputs on non-English prompts, suggesting that visual-prior arbitration has a substantial cross-lingual component. At the same time, we find that performance gains on common knowledge questions can come at the cost of image-grounded accuracy, a trade-off that is particularly pronounced for lower-resource languages. Code and data are available at https://github.com/elffiona/cross-lingual-visual-prior-steering.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: STAIF: A Stage-wise Optimization for Complex Instruction Following
abstract: Following complex instructions with multiple explicit constraints remains a fundamental challenge for large language models (LLMs). Existing alignment methods, such as DPO, optimize holistic reward signals that often under-emphasize strict satisfaction of individual constraints, particularly under out-of-distribution or multi-constraint settings. In this paper, we propose STAIF, a stage-wise optimization framework that decouples the alignment of subjective (soft) constraints from the optimization of objectively verifiable (hard) constraints. Stage 1 applies preference optimization with multiple negative samples to sharpen the sensitivity to soft constraints, while Stage 2 applies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to enforce strict compliance with hard constraints. To support this method, we construct STAINSTRUCT, a high-quality bilingual (English, Chinese) dataset of approximately 31,000 complex multi-constraint instructions. Extensive analyses validate the design of STAIF and show state-of-the-art performance on representative benchmarks against strong baselines, as well as genuine generalization.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RUBAS: Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning for Agent Safety
abstract: The evolution of LLMs into tool-enabled agents creates a new class of safety challenges associated with real-world execution rather than simple text generation. Existing alignment methods often rely on coarse refusal signals or static supervision, making it difficult to balance safety with useful tool execution across diverse agentic risks. We introduce RUBAS, a rubric-based reinforcement learning framework for agent safety. RUBAS decomposes agent behavior into four dimensions: tool-use safety, argument safety, response safety, and helpfulness. These structured rubrics provide fine-grained and interpretable rewards over complete agent trajectories, enabling reinforcement learning to optimize safe tool use while preserving task completion. Extensive experiments across multiple agent safety benchmarks and models show that RUBAS improves safety over standard alignment baselines, reduces tool-grounded hallucinations, and maintains competitive utility. Our results suggest that multi-dimensional rubric rewards provide an effective training signal for aligning LLM agents in safety-critical tool-use settings.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models
abstract: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SOURCECLASH, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models shows that the answer-preference difference typically reaches its maximum shortly after generation begins. Residual replacement moves the model toward valid answers, while attention decomposition attributes most of the repair to value vectors. Intervention at the identified value pathway also improves final answer validity. These results characterize how partly conflicting retrieval changes skill-guided generation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ParaCalib: Semantically Calibrated Paralinguistic Modeling for Depression Detection
abstract: Vocal behavior provides important signals for speech-based depression detection, but its interpretation often depends on what is being said and how it functions in context. However, existing methods typically treat acoustic cues as context-independent markers, making it difficult to distinguish vocal form from its context-dependent communicative function. We propose ParaCalib, a framework that semantically calibrates paralinguistic behavior by interpreting vocal patterns relative to utterance-level semantic context and inferred communicative function and representing them in a comparable state space. Concretely, ParaCalib uses an Audio-Language Model (ALM) to generate contextualized vocal descriptions and an LLM-based Paralinguistic State Extractor (PSE) to map these descriptions into a structured Semantically Calibrated Paralinguistic (SC-Para) representation. ParaCalib achieves the highest mean Macro-F1 among the evaluated methods, reaching 71.9% on DAIC-WOZ and 90.5% on MODMA. Our controlled analysis provides direct evidence of semantic calibration at the PSE stage: under a fixed caption-level acoustic description, varying the accompanying semantic context changes the inferred depression-related paralinguistic evidence. Our exploratory analysis further identifies recurring configurations of paralinguistic states associated with depression labels rather than a single uniformly dominant state.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: GIFT: Reconciling Post-Training Objectives via Variational Finite-Temperature Gibbs Initialization
abstract: The prevailing post-training paradigm for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)—Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL)—suffers from an intrinsic optimization mismatch: the rigid likelihood maximization in SFT induces distributional collapse, thereby exhausting the exploration space necessary for subsequent RL. Motivated by the Gibbs optimum of KL-regularized RL, we derive a token-level variational surrogate that makes the SFT target structurally compatible with the subsequent RL stage, and propose Gibbs Initialization with Finite Temperature (GIFT). Standard SFT emerges as a degenerate zero-temperature limit of this surrogate, while a finite temperature preserves structural diversity. Our experiments demonstrate that GIFT outperforms standard SFT and surpasses competitive baselines when utilized for RL initialization. Our code is available at https://github.com/zzy1127/GIFT.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Bridging Lexical Divergence: LLM-Assisted, Cost-Efficient, Zero-shot Scientific Entity Linking
abstract: Scientific domain entity linking (EL) differs from general domain EL because mentions and entity names often lack lexical overlap. Another challenge is that specialized terminology is used in the scientific domain, which is rarely encountered in models pretrained on general domains. Therefore, models trained on general domains transfer poorly to scientific domains. To address this, in-domain fine-tuning is the natural remedy. However, many scientific domains lack expert-annotated data, motivating the need for a zero-human-annotation approach. Existing zero-shot methods heavily rely on LLMs to generate aliases across entire mention corpora, which incurs substantial computational cost, and those methods provide no mechanism to filter out noise from LLMs. To address these challenges, we propose Sci-ZSEL, a framework that selectively generates entity aliases with an LLM to control computational cost, and applies an ontology-aware filter to remove aliases that semantically drift toward ontology neighbors. Then, filtered aliases are used to construct pseudo-labeled mention-entity pairs for fine-tuning. To enable evaluation of EL under low lexical overlap, we also release a new animal science EL benchmark linked to three livestock trait ontologies, where mentions and entities exhibit substantially lower lexical overlap than in existing benchmarks. Across five benchmarks, Sci-ZSEL outperforms the non-fine-tuned baseline, is most useful on nonoverlapping mentions, and combining it with curated synonyms gives the best performance in most settings.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ARMOR-PRM: Adversarially Robust Process Reward Models via Counterfactual Margins and Invariance Regularization
abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are vulnerable to reward hacking: policies exploit surface cues such as confident phrasing or structured formatting in place of logical correctness, which yields an inverted-U collapse under optimization pressure. We propose ARMOR-PRM, which augments standard PRM training with three regularizers: a counterfactual margin loss, an adversarial invariance loss with low-score anchoring, and a gradient penalty on the reward head. On ProcessBench (three splits; "math" excluded due to training data overlap), ARMOR-PRM improves Detection Rate by 14.9 percentage points and AUROC by 4.1 percentage points over Vanilla PRM, and is the only variant whose Best-of-N reranking accuracy improves monotonically through N=128. A domain-shift diagnostic further shows that objective-level robustness and data coverage are distinct but complementary axes: ARMOR-PRM responds best to iterative hard-negative retraining, suggesting a practical two-stage deployment path.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Toppling the Hierarchy in Byte-level Language Modeling
abstract: This work examines recent byte-level models and their failure to perfectly manipulate characters. State-of-the-art byte-level models use a hierarchical structure, starting at the byte level, downsampling to the word level, and then upsampling back to bytes. While this improves training and inference efficiency, we find that the hierarchical design itself limits character-level understanding, with pure byte-level models consistently outperforming hierarchical variants on character manipulation tasks. Ablating transformer layers into attention and feed-forward components further reveals that byte-level attention is the primary mechanism driving this behavior. Together, our results provide an explanation for the character-level failures of hierarchical byte models and establish a clear trade-off between computational efficiency and fine-grained character understanding.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Users Don’t Ask: Benchmarking Context-Driven Memory Retrieval in Conversational Agents
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as long-horizon conversational agents, motivating growing interest in memory systems. However, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate memory through QA-style probing rather than in-situ conversational usage. We introduce LOCOMO-CONV, a conversational memory benchmark derived from LoCoMo with four query styles: dialog, implicit, counterfactual, and composed. Across four representative memory systems, we evaluate both retrieval recall and end-to-end response quality. Our experiments show that conversational framing exposes substantial retrieval gaps overlooked by QA benchmarks, especially on implicit and composed queries, which multi-facet query rewriting narrows for raw-turn but not abstractive memory. We further find that strong retrieval does not fully translate into response quality, and that implicit queries exhibit silent grounding, where memory improves contextual grounding without explicitly surfacing the gold fact. These results point to reasoning-based memory elaboration as a promising direction, and we release auxiliary supportive_memory annotations capturing conversationally useful context beyond the original gold evidence.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Guided Permutation Scoring (GPS) : Option-Order Permutation for Multiple-Choice Question Answering
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are sensitive to the order in which answer choices are presented in Multiple-Choice Question Answering. The same question can yield a different prediction when its options are shuffled. Although exhaustive majority voting over all permutations can mitigate this bias, its factorial cost makes it impractical at inference time. We propose GPS (Guided Permutation Scoring), a two-stage inference-time pipeline that selects option orderings more likely to produce correct predictions from a frozen LLM. A sensitivity classifier first identifies which questions are genuinely vulnerable to positional interference; robust questions are answered directly, while sensitive ones are forwarded to a trained permutation scorer that identifies a more position-stable option ordering, promoting better predictions. Unlike prior approaches that either enumerate all permutations uniformly, or require modifying the LLM’s parameters, GPS is the first method to actively select permutations so that the base model can consistently give better answers. GPS steadily improves Accuracy, and Macro F1 across all evaluated model-dataset combinations, with remarkable reductions in positional bias metrics.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Reflecting What Matters: Same-Surgery References for Postoperative Clinical Note Generation
abstract: Generating the first postoperative outpatient note requires selecting which information from heterogeneous clinical records should be reflected in the final note, rather than merely summarizing all inputs. We evaluate this task on an original 170-case set of de-identified clinical cases collected at Seoul National University Hospital (SNUH), involving two surgical divisions and five physicians. We then extend the evaluation to 1,329 cases across 10 surgery groups within the same institution to examine whether the main trends persist at a larger scale. We introduce physician- and surgery-specific same-surgery references: structured reflection maps that capture how information is selected and rewritten in prior same-surgery cases. Experiments show that these references become most effective when carried into the merge stage, suggesting that the main bottleneck is deciding what to reflect across records. We further show that cross-patient references can induce unsupported transfer from prior cases. To analyze this trade-off, we use a human-validated two-source FactScore that checks each generated fact against both the source records and the physician-written note. A lightweight grounding constraint reduces hallucination while maintaining or improving alignment with physician-written notes across divisions and LLMs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Do MLLMs Really Understand Space? A Mathematical Spatial Reasoning Evaluation
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on perception-oriented tasks, yet their ability to perform mathematical spatial reasoning, defined as the capacity to parse and manipulate two- and three-dimensional relations, remains unclear. While humans easily master textbook-style spatial problems, current MLLMs exhibit substantially higher error rates, exposing a fundamental weakness in spatial comprehension. To investigate this gap, we present MathSpatial, the first large-scale and systematic dataset resource dedicated to mathematical spatial reasoning in MLLMs. MathSpatial provides two complementary subsets: MathSpatial-Bench (2,000 problems) for evaluating spatial reasoning isolated from perceptual noise, and MathSpatial-Corpus (8,000 problems) equipped with structured reasoning traces for training. Benchmarking 20+ MLLMs reveals a severe deficit: non-reasoning models largely languish below 60% accuracy, and even the strongest reasoning models fall ~16 percentage points behind human performance (96.3%). Crucially, we demonstrate that fine-tuning on MathSpatial-Corpus yields consistent performance gains across model families. MathSpatial provides a vital resource for diagnosing and advancing spatial reasoning in MLLMs. The dataset and related resources are available at https://github.com/shuolucs/MathSpatial.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Agent Tools Orchestration Leaks More: Dataset, Benchmark, and Mitigation
abstract: LLM agents can combine individually non-revealing tool returns and disclose a sensitive conclusion, creating Tools Orchestration Privacy Risk (TOP-R). We formalize TOP-R through three conditions: conclusion sensitivity, single-source non-inferability, and compositional inferability. We introduce Library-Grounded Reverse-Inference Seed Expansion (LRSE), a four-library reverse-construction pipeline, and use it to build TOP-Bench, a 1,000-instance benchmark evaluated under a controlled two-stage tool-use protocol. Across six LLM agents, average task completion, leakage, and H-score are 98.0 percent, 88.6 percent, and 20.4. With native reasoning enabled, four models average 81.4 percent final-response leakage and 82.4 percent reasoning-trace leakage. With reasoning disabled, three prompt-only safeguards improve H-score by an average of about 3.4 points on TOP-Bench. We further propose TOP-Align, an SFT+DPO method for learning safer task-completion boundaries. On a separate post-training evaluation set, TOP-Align improves H-score by 16.2 points over the base model, versus a 5.0-point average gain from prompt-only mitigation on the same set. These results show that TOP-R requires defenses beyond prompting alone. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/1Ponder/TOP-R.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CausalPrism: Component-Level Evaluation of Intervention-Based Causal Reasoning in Large Language Models
abstract: Evaluating causal reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is complicated by benchmarks that conflate distinct reasoning operations into aggregate scores. We propose CausalPrism, an evaluation framework grounded in structural causal model semantics and cognitive models of causal inference, which decomposes intervention-based causal reasoning into three functional primitives—Causal Prior, Forward State Tracing, and Belief Updating—plus a consistency primitive, Agency Sensitivity. Primitives are instantiated in directed acyclic graphs and evaluated across three narrative domains of varying semantic richness. Across 14 open-source and frontier LLMs, Belief Updating is the dominant bottleneck: the best model reaches only 0.613 accuracy, while GPT-5.2 and GPT-5-mini score 0.531 and 0.517 despite near-ceiling performance on Causal Prior and Forward State Tracing. Prior exhibits systematic domain sensitivity and over-rejection. Agency framing effects are family-dependent for weaker models. We argue against treating causal reasoning as a unitary capability and motivate targeted evaluation and training along multiple primitive axes.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: GAMS: Geospatial Knowledge Enhanced Agentic Framework for Urban Human Mobility Behavior Simulation
abstract: Recently, researchers have explored leveraging the commonsense knowledge and reasoning capabilities of large language models to accelerate human mobility simulation. However, these methods suffer from several critical shortcomings, including inadequate modeling of urban spaces, poor integration with individual mobility patterns, and weak alignment with collective mobility distributions. To address these limitations, we propose Geospatial Knowledge Enhanced Agentic framework for Mobility Simulation (GAMS), an agentic framework that leverages the language based geospatial foundation model to simulate human mobility in urban space. GAMS comprises three core modules: MobExtractor, which extracts template-based mobility profiles and synthesizes new ones during simulation; GeoGenerator, which generates trajectory points considering collective mobility knowledge and urban geospatial knowledge; and TrajEnhancer, which captures individual mobility regularities from real-world trajectories and refines to generate style-aligned synthetic trajectories. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that GAMS achieves superior performance over various state-of-the-art methods, with more than a 17% improvement by capturing diverse mobility regularities. Our codes and datasets are open-sourced via https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CAMS-1992/.
