title: Learning to Predict Future-Aligned Research Proposals with Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist ideation in research, but evaluating the quality of LLM-generated research proposals remains difficult: novelty and soundness are hard to measure automatically, and large-scale human evaluation is costly. We propose a verifiable alternative by reframing proposal generation as a time-sliced scientific forecasting problem. Given a research question and inspiring papers available before a cutoff time, the model generates a structured proposal and is evaluated by whether it anticipates research directions that appear in papers published after the time. We operationalize this objective with the Future Alignment Score (FAS), computed via retrieval and LLM-based semantic scoring against a held-out future corpus. To train models, we build a time-consistent dataset of 21,835 paper occurrences across 3,642 instances from targets and their pre-cutoff citations, and synthesize reasoning traces that teach gap identification and inspiration borrowing. Across Llama-3.1 and Qwen2.5 models, future-aligned tuning improves future alignment over unaligned baselines (up to +10.6% overall FAS), and domain-expert human evaluation corroborates improved proposal quality. Finally, we demonstrate practical impact by implementing two model-generated proposals with a code agent, obtaining 4.17% accuracy gain on MATH from a new prompting strategy and consistent improvements for a novel model-merging method.

title: Quantifying and Mitigating Default Behaviors in Text-to-Image Models
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models consistently collapse to stereotypical attribute values when prompts leave concepts underspecified, a phenomenon we term default behaviors. We conduct a large-scale empirical study using , an LLM-driven measurement approach that quantifies diversity at the level of individual concept attributes. We find pervasive default behaviors across all evaluated T2I models, with stronger models tending to exhibit less diversity. We trace these defaults to reporting bias in training captions: when captions omit common attributes, the accompanying images are dominated by a narrow set of values, and model outputs closely mirror this skew. We confirm this link causally with controlled fine-tuning interventions. As a proof of concept, we show that making sampled attribute values explicit broadens outputs, with some loss of faithfulness to secondary prompt details. Together, our results recast low diversity not as an inherent limitation of T2I models, but as a measurable and steerable consequence of what their training captions leave unsaid. Code and data available at: https://royira.github.io/GRADE.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SPUR-XMC: Context-Adaptive Spurious Correlation Mitigation for Extreme Multi-Label Classification of Biomedical Literature
abstract: Extreme multi-label text classification (XMTC) of biomedical literature aims to classify articles into a set of pre-defined labels from a large and highly skewed label distribution space. While recent pretrained language model (PLM)-based XMTC approaches have made substantial advances, they still struggle to generalize to tail labels representing concepts of high biomedical significance (e.g., rare diseases). A key factor contributing to poor tail-label performance is the presence of spurious correlations, where models inadvertently learn non-informative feature-label associations. To address this issue, we propose a novel context-adaptive spurious correlation mitigation technique, SPUR-XMC, which selectively attenuates spurious influences according to the context of the input article. A unique advantage of the proposed framework is that it does not modify existing PLM architectures for XMTC and instead operates as an add-on enhancement module. Extensive experiments across benchmark biomedical literature datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: HarmMetric Eval: Benchmarking Metrics and Judges for LLM Harmfulness Assessment
abstract: Automatic harmfulness metrics and LLM-based judges are central to LLM safety assessment, yet differences in evaluation criteria, methodologies, and output formats may yield inconsistent judgments for the same model response. The lack of systematic research on these evaluators undermines the credibility and consistency of LLM safety assessments. To bridge this gap, we introduce HarmMetric Eval, a benchmark for both overall and fine-grained assessment of harmfulness evaluators. We construct a dataset of representative harmful prompts paired with diverse harmful responses and non-harmful counterparts across multiple categories. We propose a flexible scoring mechanism that rewards metrics for correctly ranking harmful responses above non-harmful ones, making it applicable to nearly all metrics and judges with varying output formats and scoring scales. Using HarmMetric Eval, we find that conventional reference-based metrics such as ROUGE and METEOR can outperform existing LLM-based judges in fine-grained harmfulness evaluation, challenging prevailing assumptions about LLM superiority. Fine-grained analysis reveals that LLM judges tend to overestimate irrelevant and useless responses. Furthermore, we build a new harmfulness judge by incorporating fine-grained criteria into its prompt template and leveraging reference-based metrics to fine-tune its base LLM. The resulting judge demonstrates leading performance on HarmMetric Eval and two external human-labeled datasets.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: A Survey on Rubric-guided Reinforcement Learning for Language Models
abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has become the dominant paradigm for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, traditional RLHF relies on scalar reward signals that lack interpretability and fail to capture the multifaceted nature of response quality. Rubric-guided reinforcement learning addresses these limitations by introducing structured, interpretable evaluation criteria, or rubrics, as the backbone of reward design, feedback generation, and policy optimization. In this survey, we introduce a Bayesian framework that defines constitutions as prior distributions P(\mathcal{R}) over evaluation criteria and rubrics as conditional instantiations \mathcal{R}_x \sim P(\mathcal{R}|x). Under this unified view, we present a taxonomy of rubric-guided RL along the prior-posterior axis, covering constitutional AI, instance-specific rubrics, process-level supervision, self-evolving rubrics, and their agentic and multimodal extensions. Furthermore, as rubrics are natural-language artifacts, we present a linguistic analysis of how granularity trade-offs, semantic drift, and linguistic reward hacking impact alignment reliability, identifying key open problems for future research.

title: Revising Context, Shifting Simulated Stance: Auditing LLM-Based Stance Simulation in Online Discussions
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate social media users and infer how individuals may respond to online discussions. However, it remains unclear whether these simulations reflect precise user-specific beliefs or whether they are highly sensitive to semantically independent changes in conversational contexts. In this work, we study counterfactual context revision as a framework for auditing LLM-based stance simulation. Given an original online conversation, we first infer a target user’s stance toward a specific topic. We then apply controlled revision strategies to the conversational context and simulate the user’s stance again under the revised context. We compare text-only revision strategies with a multimodal one that incorporates meme-based context and evaluate two main effectiveness metrics, i.e., average directional stance shift and stance transition rate. The results reveal effective and robust stance transitions in both text-only and multimodal strategies across different polarization-preference mechanisms. Our study contributes an evaluation framework for understanding the context sensitivity of LLM-based stance simulation (https://github.com/STARResearchLab/StanceShift). More broadly, it highlights both the promise and risk of using LLMs as proxies for social media users in social simulation.

title: MedCPEnv: A Reproducible Cost-Aware Simulated Hospital for Benchmarking and Training Medical LLM Agents
abstract: Real-world clinical competence demands more than answering medical knowledge questions—it requires proactively gathering incomplete patient information, selecting appropriate examinations, and formulating safe, cost-conscious treatment plans through multi-turn interaction. Existing medical LLM benchmarks rely predominantly on static QA formats, failing to assess interactive information acquisition, tool use, or cost–quality tradeoffs. We propose MedCPEnv, a reproducible, cost-aware simulated hospital environment for evaluating and training medical LLM agents. Built from MIMIC-IV-NOTE discharge notes, MedCPEnv comprises 48,803 curated cases, a 1,000-case benchmark, and a 371,550-entry medical QA knowledge base, exposing four deterministic action types (ASK, EXAM, KNOWLEDGE, FINAL) to eliminate high-variance LLM role-playing artifacts. Evaluating eight frontier models, GPT-5.4 achieves the highest composite score (3.69/5) and diagnostic accuracy (60.3%), yet treatment accuracy remains only 19.4%, identifying treatment plan generation as the primary bottleneck. Substantial inter-model variation in the cost–quality tradeoff further demonstrates that clinical correctness alone is insufficient to characterize agent behavior. GRPO-based Agentic RL on Qwen3-4B shows that medical quality rewards consistently improve tool-use strategies, raising the composite score from 2.97 to 3.14 and diagnostic accuracy from 26.0% to 31.2%, establishing MedCPEnv as both a rigorous evaluation benchmark and a reproducible training environment for medical agent research.

title: Post-Training Shifts Confidence: A Three-Stage Analysis of How SFT, RL, and OPD Shape CoT Calibration
abstract: Large language models have made strong reasoning gains through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation, yet these post-training methods are usually evaluated only by final-answer accuracy. We study how they reshape confidence during reasoning. We introduce a three-stage calibration framework that evaluates confidence before, during, and after chain-of-thought generation, corresponding to difficulty estimation, early termination, and answer aggregation. Through a controlled comparison on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, we find that OPD provides the most useful pre-reasoning confidence, SFT gives the strongest online signal for early stopping, and RL produces the most reliable trace-level signal for aggregation. We further show that confidence reliability is position-dependent: RL confidence becomes informative after a path-commitment phase, while OPD confidence is useful early but can become inversely calibrated later. Based on this observation, we propose PosConf, a position-aware confidence strategy that uses confidence only from reliable relative-position intervals. PosConf improves RL answer aggregation by 6.1 points over majority voting and consistently improves OPD early stopping under tight token budgets, with gains up to 4.3 points by avoiding its later inverse-calibration region, showing that confidence in reasoning models should be used both stage-wise and position-awarely. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Post-Training-Calibration.

title: CultureVLM: Characterizing and Improving Cultural Understanding of Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced human-AI interaction but struggle with cultural understanding, often misinterpreting symbols, gestures, and artifacts due to biases in predominantly Western-centric training data. In this paper, we construct CultureVerse, a large-scale multimodal benchmark covering 19,682 cultural concepts, 188 countries/regions, 15 cultural topics, and 3 question types, with the aim of characterizing and improving VLMs’ multicultural understanding capabilities. Then, we propose CultureVLM, a series of VLMs fine-tuned on our dataset to achieve significant performance improvement in cultural understanding. Our evaluation of 16 models reveals significant disparities, with a stronger performance in Western concepts and weaker results in African and Asian contexts. Fine-tuning on our CultureVerse training set enhances cultural perception, demonstrating cross-cultural, cross-continent, and cross-dataset generalization without sacrificing performance on models’ general VLM benchmarks. We further present insights on cultural generalization and forgetting. We hope that this work could lay the foundation for more equitable and culturally aware multimodal AI systems.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Taming the Thinker: Conditional Entropy Shaping for Adaptive LLM Reasoning
abstract: Entropy-based deep reasoning has emerged as a promising direction for improving the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), but existing methods often either increase response length indiscriminately or shorten responses at the cost of accuracy. To better balance this trade-off, we introduce Conditional Entropy Shaping (CES), a framework that dynamically controls token-level response entropy, enabling LLMs to produce concise solutions on simple problems while encouraging deeper exploration on hard ones. Built on DAPO, CES uses token-level entropy as an uncertainty signal and applies a conditional bidirectional policy: it penalizes high-entropy "forking point" tokens on correct reasoning paths to improve conciseness, and rewards them on incorrect paths to encourage exploration and error correction. We implement CES on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and evaluate it on 12 mathematical benchmarks. CES consistently improves average accuracy while reducing response length relative to DAPO, and supplementary experiments show similar trends on a smaller 1.5B backbone and on out-of-domain benchmarks.

title: Thought-Aware KV Cache Compaction for Reasoning via Adaptive Attention Matching
abstract: Reasoning language models generate lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) sequences whose key-value (KV) cache grows linearly and becomes a memory bottleneck during decoding. Existing compaction methods treat reasoning trajectories as flat token sequences and apply uniform compression, ignoring the hierarchical structure of CoT reasoning where different steps vary drastically in importance. We propose Thought-Aware Attention Matching (TAM), which exploits this structure through three mechanisms: (i)thought segmentation that decomposes the trajectory into reasoning blocks, (ii)adaptive budget allocation that assigns compression budget based on each segment’s importance and size, and (iii)pivotal token protection that preserves high-attention reasoning anchors. We prove that the allocation rule is optimal under a convex error model and that cumulative error under sequential compaction remains bounded. Experiments on AIME 2024 and MATH-500 with Qwen3-4B show that TAM improves accuracy over uniform compaction at the same memory footprint, with periodic compaction bounding peak memory to 3.1–3.2,GB (a 65% reduction) while maintaining competitive accuracy.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Revisiting Task Vectors: A Structural Analysis of Their Limits
abstract: To mitigate high inference costs for in-context learning, prior works have proposed activation-space task vectors that encapsulate demonstration contexts into static representations. However, performance occasionally degrades across tasks, leaving it unclear whether this stems from sub-optimal extraction heuristics or fundamental limitations. We resolve this by decomposing Transformer self-attention to establish a theoretical best-case approximation: the Minimal-Gap Approximation. By isolating structural constraints from heuristic flaws, the Minimal-Gap Approximation reveals that task vectors are fundamentally bottlenecked by attention and length gaps. Specifically, because task vectors lock contextual information to fixed attention maps and positional alignments, they structurally fail under dynamic routing, length mismatches, and multi-token generation. We further show that these findings consistently hold across training-free extract-and-inject task vector methods, model architectures, and model scales.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Does Reasoning Preserve Alignment? On the Trustworthiness of Large Reasoning Models
abstract: Instruction-tuned LLMs are increasingly converted into reasoning models through post-training to improve multi-step task performance. This conversion is usually optimized for reasoning accuracy, without explicitly preserving the instruction-tuned model’s alignment behavior, such as safe refusal, bias avoidance, and privacy protection. We ask: does this conversion preserve alignment? We study this question through a trustworthiness audit and find that it is not behavior-preserving by default. For a systematic analysis, we compare reasoning models produced via supervised fine-tuning, RL-based post-training, and distillation against matched instruction-tuned baselines across six trustworthiness dimensions: safety, toxicity, stereotyping and bias, machine ethics, privacy, and out-of-distribution robustness. We observe that reasoning models often improve on mathematical reasoning benchmarks but exhibit alignment regressions, including increased toxicity, amplified stereotyping, miscalibrated refusal, and contextual privacy leakage. These regressions are consistent with behavioral drift from the instruction-tuned baseline, measured by KL divergence. Our results show that reasoning-model releases should report trustworthiness metrics alongside capability gains.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: From Narrative to Auditable Forecasts: A Structured Scaffold for Agentic Forecasting
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for live forecasting, where they retrieve up-to-date information and produce estimates for unresolved future events. However, current agentic forecasting often relies on implicit narrative aggregation: agents collect evidence, discuss it in prose, and often assign a probability without an explicit update path from evidence to forecast. This limits both forecasting accuracy and auditability. We propose AuditForecast, an agentic scaffold for structured probabilistic forecasting. AuditForecast first anchors the forecast with a suitable quantitative baseline model, uses model-guided data retrieval to derive a base probability, and then applies situational factor updates outside the model’s scope through mechanical aggregation in odds space. This turns forecasting from a prose-based judgment into a structured process with explicit intermediate objects. Across multiple live forecasting benchmarks, AuditForecast improves forecasting accuracy and calibration relative to strong agentic baselines, surpasses market-implied references in several settings, and outperforms substantially more expensive deep-research agents while remaining Pareto-dominant in the cost–accuracy tradeoff. Beyond performance gains, AuditForecast produces an auditable forecasting report that makes forecast construction explicit and supports systematic post hoc analysis.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RAMP: Regime-Aware Merge-Prune Token Compression for ASR-Oriented Audio-Language Models
abstract: ASR-oriented audio-language models (ALMs) encode speech into long audio token sequences for LLM decoding, substantially increasing the inference cost of transcription. This motivates token compression methods that reduce audio token sequence length while preserving the acoustic evidence needed for transcription. However, existing compression methods often inherit vision-language criteria that are poorly matched to temporally ordered audio representations, or require attention-map access outside the standard FlashAttention path. Through a multi-axis geometric analysis, we show that ALM audio representations exhibit two distinct representation regimes: a locally redundant encoder regime and a dispersed post-projector regime. Motivated by this geometric shift, we propose **RAMP** (**R**egime-**A**ware **M**erge-**P**rune), a training-free method for FlashAttention-compatible audio token compression that applies bipartite L_2 merging in the encoder and centroid-distance-guided pruning after the projector. Across seven ASR benchmarks and two primary ALMs, RAMP achieves the lowest average WER multiplier among the evaluated training-free compression baselines at every evaluated retention ratio. At the most aggressive setting (r=0.4) on Audio-Flamingo-3, RAMP attains a 2.36\times average WER multiplier, compared with 4.26\times for the best non-RAMP baseline, while reducing time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 24.8% over Vanilla.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RADAR: Accelerate Large Language Model Inference with RL-Based Dynamic Draft Trees
abstract: Inference with modern Large Language Models (LLMs) is expensive and slow, and speculative sampling has emerged as an effective solution to this problem. However, the number of calls to the draft model for generating candidate tokens in speculative sampling is a preset hyperparameter, lacking flexibility. To generate and utilize the candidate tokens more effectively, we propose RADAR, a novel speculative sampling method with RL-based dynamic draft trees. RADAR formulates the draft tree generation process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and employs offline reinforcement learning to train a prediction model, which enables real-time decisions on calls to the draft model, reducing redundant computations and further accelerating inference. Evaluations across three LLMs and four tasks show that RADAR achieves a speedup of 3.17x-4.82x over the auto-regressive decoding baseline.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: DeepResearch RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Deep Research Report
abstract: Empowered by Large Language Models (LLMs), deep research systems integrate online information into research reports through multi-step web searching and information synthesis. Evaluating these reports presents a significant challenge due to their long context, high information density, and domain specificity, necessitating the use of AI evaluation as a substitute for prohibitively expensive human assessment. However, few studies have examined the effectiveness of existing reward models or LLMs in understanding and evaluating such research reports. To bridge this gap, we introduce DeepResearch RewardBench, the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating reward modeling for research reports. We collect diverse report candidates from multiple agents or tool-augmented LLMs. These candidates are scored using query-specific rubrics and judged LLMs, and we ensure data quality and difficulty through a combination of multi-round filtering and human verification. Our benchmark comprises preference datasets formatted as pairs, triplets, and quadruplets to test ranking capabilities across varying levels of difficulty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that while current reward models handle general coherence effectively, their performance significantly degrades when evaluating research reports. In contrast, generative LLMs acting as judges demonstrate comprehensive superiority in this domain, with comparative evaluation proving more effective than direct scoring methods. We anticipate that this benchmark will serve as a vital testbed for the evaluation and advancement of research agents.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Not All Tokens See Equally: Perception-Grounded Policy Optimization for Large Vision-Language Models
abstract: While Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has advanced reasoning in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), prevailing frameworks suffer from a foundational methodological flaw: by distributing identical advantages across all generated tokens, these methods inherently dilute the learning signals essential for optimizing the critical, visually-grounded steps of multimodal reasoning. To bridge this gap, we formulate Token Visual Dependency, quantifying the causal information gain of visual inputs via the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between visual-conditioned and text-only predictive distributions. Revealing that this dependency is highly sparse and semantically pivotal, we introduce Perception-Grounded Policy Optimization (PGPO), which is a novel fine-grained credit assignment framework that dynamically reshapes advantages at the token level. Through a threshold-gated, mass-conserving mechanism, PGPO actively amplifies learning signals for visually-dependent tokens while suppressing gradient noise from linguistic priors. Extensive experiments based on the Qwen2.5-VL series across seven challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that PGPO boosts models by 18.7% on average. Both theoretical and empirical analyses confirm that PGPO effectively reduces gradient variance, prevents training collapse, and acts as a potent regularizer for robust, perception-grounded multimodal reasoning.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Social Caption: Evaluating Social Understanding in Multimodal Models
abstract: Social understanding abilities are crucial for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to interpret human social interactions. We introduce Social Caption, a framework grounded in interaction theory to evaluate social understanding abilities of MLLMs along three dimensions: Social Inference (SI), the ability to make accurate inferences about interactions; Holistic Social Analysis (HSA), the ability to generate comprehensive descriptions of interactions; Directed Social Analysis (DSA), the ability to generate relevant information from interactions. We analyze factors influencing model performance in social understanding, such as scale, architectural design, and spoken context. Experiments with MLLM judges demonstrate a path towards scaling automated evaluation of multimodal social understanding.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ZipRL: Adaptive Multi-Turn Context Compression with Hindsight Response Replay
abstract: Adaptive context compression is vital for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to complex, multi-turn agent tasks. However, rule-based compression methods may discard task-critical nuances, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches usually struggle to balance information retention and token efficiency under the sparse rewards inherent to long-horizon workflows. To bridge this gap, we propose ZipRL, a novel adaptive compression framework tailored for Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). ZipRL features a multi-granularity compression mechanism for active, non-uniform information reduction, coupled with Hindsight Response Replay (HRR)—a technique designed to densify training signals during RLVR optimization. Theoretically, we prove ZipRL’s superior task-relevant utility over uniform methods. Concretely, ZipRL utilizes coarse-to-fine prompts for macro-compression and incorporates HRR into GRPO via generalized advantage reshaping. Multiple models of varying versions and parameter scales validate the effectiveness of our approach. Benchmarks on five agent tasks show ZipRL outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by 27.9% and 34.7% across Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B models, while maintaining exceptional token efficiency and robustness under extreme 256-turn extrapolation stress tests. Our code is available at https://github.com/huzhexin/ZipRL.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ProofFrontier: Turning Verified Proofs into Boundary-hard Tasks for Formal Theorem Proving
abstract: Formal theorem proving provides executable verification signals from proof assistants, making it a key domain for improving the reliable reasoning ability of large language models through reinforcement learning (RL). However, RL-based prover training is increasingly bottlenecked by the scarcity of high-quality hard tasks: many existing Lean instances are either already solvable by current provers or too uninformative to drive further improvement. We propose ProofFrontier, a proof-structure-guided method for generating statement-preserving boundary-hard training tasks from verified Lean proofs. Instead of synthesizing open-ended problems that may be ill-posed or unverifiable, ProofFrontier starts from existing theorems with Lean-certified proofs, preserving task completeness and formal verifiability. It selectively withholds proof-structural guidance around important local nodes, encouraging the prover to rediscover nontrivial intermediate reasoning while keeping the original theorem statement unchanged. We further introduce capability-aware filtering to retain tasks that are solvable in principle but not easily solved by the base prover, yielding hard yet rewardable RL data. Training with GRPO on ProofFrontier-generated tasks consistently improves DeepSeek-Prover-V2 and Goedel-Prover-V2 on miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench. Notably, these gains are achieved using only hundreds of synthesized tasks, showing that complete boundary-hard tasks can be more data-efficient than simply scaling weak or already-solved proof data for theorem-proving RL.

title: You Frame It: How Conceptual Representations Shape LLM Detection and Reasoning about Antisemitism
abstract: LLMs enable the integration of external conceptual resources at inference time, creating new opportunities for detecting ideologically and historically complex phenomena such as antisemitism. We investigate how different forms of conceptual grounding affect antisemitism detection and explanation behavior across four state-of-the-art LLMs. Using two expert-annotated datasets, we compare definitional, fine-grained taxonomic, example-augmented, and large-context representations of antisemitism. We find that fine-grained taxonomic representations substantially improve recall, while simultaneously reducing precision. Surprisingly, supplying substantially larger conceptual resources yields no additional quantitative benefit. Post-Holocaust antisemitism poses the most persistent challenge across models and configurations. Analysis of explanations further reveals systematic limitations including overproduction of conceptual references, reliance on lexical cues, overconfidence, and difficulties with subtle or justificatory forms of antisemitism. Our findings highlight both the potential and the remaining limitations of conceptually grounded LLMs for antisemitism detection and reasoning.

title: Learning When to Think: Utility-Guided Adaptive Reasoning for Efficient Text Retrieval
abstract: Reasoning-conditioned embeddings can improve retrieval by progressively refining semantic constraints. However, additional reasoning may introduce over-generalized or semantically noisy abstractions that weaken retrieval specificity. Existing methods largely supervise reasoning through final retrieval outcomes, providing limited guidance over the refinement process itself. We propose AURA, a framework that directly supervises intermediate reasoning states according to how well they separate relevant documents from hard distractors. AURA further trains a lightweight utility estimator over prefix-conditioned embeddings to adapt reasoning depth at inference time. On the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark, AURA-4B achieves 34.7 average nDCG@10 while using 2.8 reasoning steps and 96 generated tokens per query. Under matched deployment conditions, adaptive stopping reduces latency from 4.6 to 0.76 seconds relative to full-trajectory reasoning. Results on MS MARCO further suggest that this specialization need not substantially degrade conventional in-domain retrieval.

title: MMRad-22K: A Structured Multimodal Evidence Dataset for Chest X-ray Report Generation
abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) reporting follows a region-based clinical workflow in which radiologists inspect anatomical regions and integrate localized findings into a final report. However, existing resources for CXR report generation provide these supervision signals in fragmented forms. We introduce MMRad-22K, a dataset that organizes regional textual observations, anatomical grounding coordinates, localized image evidence, and report targets into structured multimodal evidence units for CXR report generation. To motivate this formulation, we first compare different evidence formats for report generation and find that structured multimodal evidence is generally more useful than text-only or bounding box-based evidence. We then adapt a unified LVLM backbone using MMRad-22K and show that adaptation with multimodal evidence outperforms both textual-evidence adaptation and end-to-end adaptation on language and clinically oriented metrics. Under the same evaluation protocol, the adapted model also reaches a performance level comparable to several open-source LVLM references. Together, these results support MMRad-22K as a practical structured multimodal resource for training and evaluating CXR report generation aligned with clinical reading workflows. The code is available at https://github.com/qiuzyc/MMRad.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: LSH-RL: Long-Short Horizon Reinforcement Learning for Persona-Level Role-Playing Agents
abstract: Role-playing agents (RPAs) must sustain persona fidelity, natural interaction, and scene progression across multi-turn trajectories. However, supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and coarse episode-level RL can over-reinforce safe stylized responses that appear in-character but are repetitive, low-information, or weakly grounded in the evolving scene. We propose LSH-RL, a Long-Short Horizon Reinforcement Learning framework for persona-level RPAs. LSH-RL trains a shared policy through dynamic multi-role self-play, combining short-horizon utterance/action rewards with long-horizon character-trajectory rewards. A gated trajectory-to-turn reward fusion mechanism prevents locally degenerate turns from receiving undeserved long-horizon credit, while a dialogue-action curriculum supports staged optimization. Experiments on PersonaArena and CharacterBox show that LSH-RL improves over SFT and DPO in both dialogue-only and full interaction settings. Further analyses show reduced repetition and stronger human preferences, suggesting a path toward more coherent and interaction-rich persona-level RPAs. The source code is available at https://github.com/Shiwenlong-source/LSH-RL.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PrivAgentFlow: Agentic Workflow for Automating Privacy Preservation in Web Agents
abstract: Autonomous web agents increasingly operate over sensitive personal data, yet existing privacy-preserving approaches rely on static filtering and globally enforced safeguards misaligned with compositional agent execution. We introduce PrivAgentFlow, a memory-guided agentic workflow framework that formulates privacy preservation as adaptive node-level governance over compositional web-agent workflows. PrivAgentFlow decomposes complex tasks into compositional workflow nodes, where each node operates under a distinct privacy policy conditioned on its execution role and information access requirements, enabling privacy governance to be localized at the execution level rather than globally enforced. Such localized governance is refined through execution memory, where historical task failures and privacy violations serve as corrective signals for improving node-level privacy control without exposing raw user data during planning. We provide theoretical insights showing that compositional web-agent workflows induce subtask-specific privacy–utility trade-offs, formally characterizing the advantage of heterogeneous node-level governance over uniform privacy control. Across 246 web-agent tasks on three platforms, PrivAgentFlow improves task utility by 23.1 percentage points (0.415→0.646), cuts environment-level privacy leakage by 92.3% (0.366→0.028), and reduces API-level leakage from 100% to 3.7% over the strongest prior baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/haorentang/PrivAgentFlow.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: REALM: Reliable Expertise-Aware Language Model Fine-Tuning from Noisy Annotations
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of large language models relies on human-annotated data, yet annotation pipelines routinely involve multiple crowdworkers of heterogeneous expertise. Standard practice aggregates labels via majority vote or simple averaging, discarding annotator identity and causing the model to absorb the errors of unreliable annotators into its parameters. We propose REALM, which jointly learns the model parameters and a scalar expertise value for each annotator, entirely unsupervised and requiring nothing beyond annotator identity. The key idea is to model each observed label as a mixture between the model’s prediction and a uniform random guess, weighted by the annotator’s learned expertise. REALM applies to any task with a fixed label set, and extends to multiple tasks via a learned expertise matrix. On four text-classification datasets with real crowdsourced annotations, REALM is the best method in all 12 configurations of the three heterogeneous-annotator datasets, improving on the strongest applicable baseline, including majority vote and Dawid–Skene aggregation, by +2.9 points on average. On five question answering benchmarks with simulated noisy labels, it outperforms naive noisy fine-tuning in 152 of 162 configurations, by +5.0 points on average, with gains that grow with model capacity. The learned expertise additionally recovers annotator reliability without ever observing it. Our code is available at https://github.com/sajjad-ucsb/REALM.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Data-Driven Red-Teaming: Reusing Adversarial Attacks via Metadata-Aware Retrieval
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world systems, red-teaming has become a critical tool for identifying safety vulnerabilities. However, existing approaches remain largely stateless and inefficient, repeatedly rediscovering similar failure modes for each new model. In this work, we propose a data-driven paradigm for red-teaming that enables the accumulation and reuse of adversarial knowledge across models. We introduce a framework for generating and collecting adversarial attacks enriched with structured metadata, including attack strategies, risk categories, and diagnostic feedback signals. Leveraging this resource, we demonstrate that metadata-aware retrieval significantly improves the efficiency of discovering successful attacks on unseen models, reducing reliance on purely generative search. To support further research, we release a large-scale dataset comprising >188k successful attacks across 8 models, together with rich metadata annotations.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: STAR-Table: Spatial Textual Anchoring and Reconstruction for Hierarchical Table Reasoning via OCR
abstract: Tables are widespread in real-world scenarios. In particular, hierarchical tables encode much richer structural semantics; however, their complex layouts pose severe challenges to Large Language Models (LLMs). The core difficulty lies in precisely aligning complex topological structures with multi-level semantic dependencies, where alignment failures often lead to cross-level aggregation errors and hallucinations. To address this challenge, we propose STAR-Table, a framework that synergizes visual perception with symbolic reasoning. Unlike traditional text-only approaches, STAR-Table leverages OCR models to extract pixel-level spatial coordinates, thereby establishing explicit Spatial-Textual AnchoRs. These anchored spatial priors are formulated as explicit structural hints to guide LLMs in reconstructing the hierarchical topology of tables. Based on the reconstructed topology, complex visual layouts are decomposed into one or more distinct sub-tables, each of which is further mapped into a deterministic flattened database. Finally, we design an adaptive QA module that fuses Vision-Language Model (VLM) semantic summaries with multi-step SQL execution to support robust table-based reasoning. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that STAR-Table achieves superior performance, significantly outperforming specialized fine-tuned models and advanced in-context learning paradigms.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Training-Free Policy Violation Detection via Activation-Space Whitening in LLM
abstract: As organizations increasingly deploy LLMs in sensitive domains such as legal, financial, and medical settings, ensuring alignment with internal organizational policies has become a priority. Existing content moderation frameworks remain largely confined to the safety domain and lack the robustness to capture nuanced organizational policies. LLM-as-a-judge and fine-tuning approaches, though flexible, introduce significant latency and training cost. To address these limitations, we frame policy violation detection as an out-of-distribution (OOD) problem in the model’s activation space. We propose a training-free method that operates directly on the LLM internal representations, leveraging prior evidence that decision-relevant information is encoded within them. Inspired by whitening techniques, we derive policy-violation scores directly from normalized representations of LLM hidden activations. Our method requires only the policy text and a small number of illustrative samples, making it lightweight and easily deployable. We extensively evaluate our method across multiple LLMs and challenging policy benchmarks. It achieves up to 86.0% F1, outperforming both fine-tuned and LLM-as-a-judge baselines while requiring substantially less computation. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/LLM-policy-violation-detection.

title: ASSAY: Reconciling Stability and Validity in Reference-Free Scientific LLM Judges
abstract: LLM judges have emerged as a key approach to evaluating open-ended scientific outputs that resist automated verification, yet their faithfulness in reference-free settings remains underexplored, particularly for fields such as novel materials synthesis where no ground-truth reference exists. Such judges produce false positives that accept scientifically invalid recipes and false negatives that penalize semantically equivalent ones in unfamiliar notation. We introduce ASSAY, a probe suite built on domain-grounded augmentations of ground-truth synthesis recipes, and reveal that these two failure modes form a systematic Stability–Validity trade-off across thirteen judge models. To resolve this trade-off, we train SynthJudge-8B via DPO on contrastive pairs derived from the same augmentations, improving judgment accuracy from 51.4% to 85.1% while maintaining agreement with domain experts. We release our probe suite and trained model to support faithful automated evaluation in scientific fields beyond materials synthesis at https://github.com/SoyeonHH/ASSAY.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Fusian: Multi-LoRA Fusion for Fine-Grained Continuous MBTI Personality Control in Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in simulating diverse human behaviors and personalities. However, existing methods for personality control, which include prompt engineering and standard Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), typically treat personality traits as discrete categories (e.g., "Extroverted" vs. "Introverted"), lacking the ability to precisely control the intensity of a trait on a continuous spectrum. In this paper, we introduce Fusian, a novel framework for fine-grained, continuous personality control in LLMs. Fusian operates in two stages: (1) Trajectory Collection, where we capture the dynamic evolution of personality adoption during SFT by saving a sequence of LoRA adapters, effectively mapping the continuous manifold of a trait; and (2) RL-based Dynamic Fusion, where we train a policy network using Reinforcement Learning to dynamically compute mixing weights for these frozen adapters. By sampling from a Dirichlet distribution parameterized by the policy network, Fusian fuses multiple adapters to align the model’s output with a specific numerical target intensity. Experiments on the Qwen3-14B model demonstrate that Fusian achieves high precision in personality control, significantly outperforming baseline methods in aligning with user-specified trait intensities.

title: PRISM: Multidimensional Safety Risk Detection and Measurement Beyond Superficial Compliance for LLMs
abstract: Existing LLM safety measures operate as black boxes, lacking categorical precision and calibrated severity assessment. We propose **PRISM** (**P**rototypical **R**epresentation for **I**nternal **S**afety **M**apping), a fine-grained two-stage safety auditing framework grounded in internal mechanistic representations. Stage I localizes functional safety zones via spectral analysis and maps internal activations onto concept prototypes for camouflage-resilient categorical risk identification. Stage II decomposes violation severity across orthogonal dimensions through structured CoT reasoning, producing calibrated human-auditable ordinal verdicts. PRISM achieves a new best F1 of 77.60% on the adversarial ToxicChat benchmark and approaches 671B frontier judges within a 2.3% margin on severity calibration, demonstrating that mechanistic grounding and principled task formulation can substitute for scale in fine-grained safety governance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Text Attribution as Continuous Trajectories: Paired AUC Metrics and Mid-Layer Allocation-Effect Decomposition
abstract: Attribution aims to identify which input tokens are responsible for a language model’s predictions, yet its evaluation in NLP remains dominated by discrete Top-k removal tests that poorly reflect global importance and interaction effects. In this work, we reformulate text attribution evaluation as a continuous functional over attribution-induced trajectories and introduce two complementary AUC-based metrics tailored to autoregressive models. Perturbation AUC measures token necessity via progressive embedding-level corruption with a stable logit-based signal, while Recovery AUC evaluates sufficiency by tracking the restoration of internal representations in hidden-state space. Together, these metrics subsume Top- tests and enable principled, ordering-sensitive assessment of attribution quality. Using these diagnostics, we show that most existing attribution methods collapse to near-random rankings under continuous evaluation and fail to capture even first-order interaction effects. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose a mid-layer attribution framework that exploits a layer-wise saturation property of transformer computation to decompose attribution into information allocation and causal effect. Across multiple models and tasks, our method consistently outperforms existing baselines under both Perturbation and Recovery AUC, yielding more faithful and interaction-aware explanations of language model behavior.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: From Detection to Refusal: Safer LLMs via Circuit-Guided Weight Scaling
abstract: Despite extensive alignment efforts, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to generating unsafe content under adversarial prompting, yet the internal mechanisms by which safety behaviors are implemented remain poorly understood. We study LLM safety from a mechanistic interpretability perspective and characterize a multi-stage *safety circuit* that organizes refusal behavior, consisting of (i) \textbf{Harmful Detection Heads} that respond to harmful inputs, (ii) \textbf{Safety Neurons} that mediate and stabilize safety signals in the residual stream, and (iii) \textbf{Refusal Heads} that translate these signals into safe response generation. Using targeted attention-head and neuron-level interventions, we provide causal evidence consistent with this circuit organization, showing that suppressing upstream Harmful Detection Heads disrupts downstream refusal behavior and that safety neurons mediate this interaction. We validate that this decomposition recurs across multiple LLM architectures and adversarial attack settings, and use simple, architecture-preserving weight scaling as a mechanistic probe to test its functional relevance. Across six LLMs, circuit-guided scaling improves safety rates under attacks by 26.5%, while incurring only a 1.7% accuracy drop across four standard benchmarks. Overall, our results support a circuit-level interpretation of LLM safety and suggest that mechanistic abstractions can reveal stable and transferable patterns underlying aligned behavior.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: NDD-R1: Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal LLMs to Understand Communication in Non- and Minimally-Speaking Autistic Individuals
abstract: Over 30% of autistic individuals are non- or minimally-speaking, relying on a complex, idiosyncratic repertoire of multimodal behaviors to communicate. Recognizing these intentional communicative acts in naturalistic environments remains a significant challenge for current multimodal large language models (MLLMs), which often struggle with the inference of subtle nonverbal cues in this domain. We introduce NDD-R1, a multi-stage reasoning framework that adapts a general-purpose MLLM for multi-view communication understanding for this population. Our approach employs a four-stage curriculum alternating between supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning (\text{SFT}_1 \rightarrow \text{GRPO}_1 \rightarrow \text{SFT}_2 \rightarrow \text{GRPO}_2), integrating label-guided distillation, temperature-escalated self-distillation, and difficulty-tiered reward optimization. We evaluate NDD-R1 on an initial dataset collected through the Rapid Online Sample of Communication (ROSCO) protocol, comprising 2,582 caregiver-annotated multi-view videos of 27 non- and minimally-speaking autistic individuals. NDD-R1 outperforms baselines on action and joint classification tasks, achieving competitive function classification performance relative to Gemini, exhibiting strong multi-view scaling and generalization across unseen sessions. Our code is available at https://github.com/SiddhantBikram/NDD-R1.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Preserving General Capability in Personality-Aligned LLMs via Orthogonal Gradient Projection
abstract: Personality alignment tailors Large Language Models (LLMs) for personalized interactions. Most existing studies focus on prompting, post- training, or representation steering to elicit trait expression, but they often compromise the general capabilities like reasoning and truthfulness. In this work, we empirically verified the existence of the Personality Alignment Tax (PAT) that distribution shifts and conflicting objectives during personality updates overwrite pre-trained competencies. To mitigate this tax, we propose a Personality-Orthogonal Gradient Projection (POGP) plug-in that preserves the capability in personality alignment. Specifically, POGP estimates the general-capability subspace from capability reference benchmarks and projects personality gradients onto the orthogonal complement before updating. This isolates and neutralizes conflicting gradients while maintaining the pre-trained reasoning capabilities. Experiments on the BIG5-CHAT dataset with two backbone LLMs demonstrate that POGP achieves a stronger personality plasticity and capability stability trade-off than baselines.

title: EviGen: Predictive Evidence Scaffolding for Verifiable Clinical Rationale Generation
abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) capture years of patient history across notes, codes, labs, and procedures, and contain evidence needed to reason about likely clinical outcomes. However, comprehensive clinician review of these records is impractical, and LLM-based processing is costly and often unreliable, missing some relevant observations while hallucinating others. We therefore propose **EviGen**, a three-layer framework for verifiable clinical rationale generation that addresses these challenges. The **first layer** is a patient-conditioned retriever that uses learnable queries to find evidence predictive of, not just textually relevant to, a clinical outcome and ranks it by prediction attribution scores. The **second layer** is an LLM generator that consumes this ranked evidence as a scaffold to produce a clinical rationale grounded in the retrieved spans. The **third layer** is a process-supervised verifier that checks the generated rationale at the reasoning-step level, flagging unreliable claims. Across three medical prediction datasets, EviGen improves prediction performance and rationale faithfulness over full-context LLM and RAG baselines, and is preferred by clinical reviewers in a usability evaluation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Mirror, Mirror on the Wall: Prompt Echoing in Instruct Language Models
abstract: Prompt echoing is a recognized failure mode of instruct language models, in which a model instead of generating a response, mirrors the provided prompt, even though it did not receive a specific instruction to do so. Is this phenomenon a sign of the model leaking the content of its training dataset, or is it rather caused by a misaligned behavior of the internal induction/copying mechanisms? We investigate prompt echoing small language models from different families (Gemma, Llama, Qwen, SmolLM and OLMo) and show that echoing prompts are likely to have partial overlap with the training dataset but the phenomenon is primarily driven by the model’s induction heads.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Learning to Code by Learning to Verify: Execution-Grounded Co-Evolution of Code Generation and Self-Verification for Reliable Code LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made rapid progress in code generation, yet their ability to verify whether a program is correct has not necessarily improved at the same pace. We identify a generation-verification gap in code LLMs, where scaling substantially improves test-passing code generation, while execution-free correctness reasoning improves much more slowly. This gap challenges existing self-rewarding approaches, which often implicitly assume that a stronger generator also serves as a better judge. To bridge this gap, we propose CoVera, an execution-grounded co-evolution framework that jointly trains a code LLM to generate code and to verify code correctness. In generator mode, the model produces candidate programs and receives execution-based rewards from available tests. In verifier mode, the same model reads a problem-program pair, produces a reasoning trace, and predicts a correctness judgment, which is rewarded according to agreement with execution-derived labels. The calibrated verifier is then used as an auxiliary self-verification signal for generation, while the evolving generator continuously supplies increasingly challenging candidates for verifier training. This co-evolution enables an on-policy curriculum for correctness reasoning and grounds self-verification in execution feedback, without requiring exhaustive test suites or golden reference solutions. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks and model scales show that CoVera improves both code generation and intrinsic correctness verification, outperforming representative baselines from diverse code-learning paradigms.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Cost-efficient Active Learning for Referring Image Segmentation and Grounding
abstract: Collecting natural-language referring expressions along with region annotations, such as masks or boxes, is a major bottleneck in visual grounding (VG), as annotators must write descriptions that distinguish target regions from visually similar ones. We tackle this by formulating active learning (AL) for VG under the realistic setting where only raw images are available without accompanying text. Since ground-truth text is unavailable, sample selection must estimate which images contain ambiguous regions that would require discriminative referring expressions. To address this, we generate auxiliary region-text pairs using foundation models, and introduce Referred Region Ambiguity, a new acquisition function that measures whether the model’s confidence collapses onto a single region or disperses across multiple candidates. It allows our method to prioritize images with strong cross-region competition, which are more informative due to their visual ambiguity. We also design a referring-expression annotation interface that helps annotators quickly focus on writing discriminative language with a few clicks. Experiments on RIS and REC benchmarks show that our AL framework consistently outperforms several AL baselines, while a user study shows up to 1.6\times faster description labeling of ours.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Gaming the Judge: How Unfaithful Chain-of-Thought Can Undermine Agent Evaluation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to evaluate agent performance, particularly in non-verifiable settings where judgments rely on agent trajectories including chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. This paradigm implicitly assumes that the agent’s CoT faithfully reflects both its internal reasoning and the underlying environment state. We show this assumption is brittle: LLM judges are highly susceptible to manipulation of agent reasoning traces. By systematically rewriting agent CoTs while holding actions and observations fixed, we demonstrate that manipulated reasoning alone can increase false positive rates of state-of-the-art vision-language model (VLM) judges by up to 117% relative to the unmanipulated baseline across 800 trajectories spanning diverse web tasks. We study manipulation strategies spanning style-based approaches that alter only the presentation of reasoning and content-based approaches that fabricate signals of task progress, and find that content-based manipulations are consistently more effective. We evaluate mitigation strategies including manipulation-aware prompting and judge-time scaling, which can reduce but do not eliminate the vulnerability. Our findings reveal a fundamental vulnerability in LLM-based evaluation and highlight the need for judging mechanisms that verify reasoning claims against observable evidence.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: From Memory to Skills: Evidence-Grounded Governance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
abstract: Existing memory systems for long-horizon LLM agents often retrieve prior traces as passive context rather than converting them into executable capabilities. In this paper, we propose MSCE, a training-free Memory–Skill Co-Evolution framework that organizes agent experience into grounded step traces, reusable procedural policies, and declarative environmental cognition. MSCE crystallizes evidence-backed L2 policies with positive estimated gain into callable skills that retain evidence links, applicability boundaries, decision guidance, verification rules, and reliability estimates. It further introduces reflection-weighted value backfilling, which propagates sparse terminal feedback through dense local self-reflections to produce evidence-calibrated trace values for governing memory and skill evolution. Experiments on EvoAgentBench and LoCoMo show that MSCE achieves the best aggregate performance among the evaluated skill-augmented and memory-driven baselines, with statistically supported aggregate gains, positive cross-domain transfer, and continual improvement as online experience accumulates. Our code is available at https://github.com/MemTensor/MemOS/tree/main/apps/memos-local-plugin.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Is LoRA Robust to Adversarial Attacks? Expectation-Based Regularization for Parameter-Efficient Adversarial Training
abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is widely used for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet its robustness to textual adversarial perturbations remains understudied. Existing adversarial training methods often improve robustness by solving costly min-max objectives with inner perturbation optimization with suboptimal results. In this research, we propose Expectation-Regularized LoRA (ER-LoRA), a simple expectation-based regularization approach that improves the robustness of LoRA without requiring inner maximization or adversarial example generation. ER-LoRA smooths predictions over a LoRA-aware low-dimensional perturbation distribution and admits a closed-form curvature-aware objective via a local Gaussian approximation. It adds no trainable parameters and keeps the LoRA architecture unchanged. Experiments on adversarial NLP benchmarks and textual attacks show that ER-LoRA improves robustness while preserving clean accuracy and parameter efficiency.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: HINTBench: Horizon-agent Intrinsic Non-attack Trajectory Benchmark
abstract: Existing agent-safety evaluation has focused mainly on externally induced risks. Yet agents may still enter unsafe trajectories under benign conditions. We study this complementary but underexplored setting through the lens of intrinsic risk, where intrinsic failures remain latent, propagate across long-horizon execution, and eventually lead to high-consequence outcomes. To evaluate this setting, we introduce non-attack intrinsic risk auditing, a guard-oriented safety evaluation task, and present HINTBench, a benchmark of 596 agent trajectories, comprising 400 synthetic risky trajectories, 136 synthetic safe trajectories, 30 reconstructed real-world risky trajectories, and 30 reconstructed real-world safe trajectories, with an average length of 24.0 steps. HINTBench supports three tasks: risk detection, risk-step localization, and intrinsic failure-type identification, with annotations organized under a unified five-constraint taxonomy. Experiments reveal a substantial capability gap: strong LLMs perform well on trajectory-level risk detection, but the best model remains below 37 on fine-grained Strict-F1 for risk-step localization. Existing off-the-shelf guard models evaluated under their native prompts transfer poorly to this setting. These findings establish intrinsic risk auditing as an open challenge for agent safety.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CODEPIVOT: Bootstrapping Multilingual Transpilation in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning with Reduced Reliance on Parallel Corpora
abstract: Transpilation, or code translation, aims to convert source code from one programming language (PL) to another. Recent large language model (LLM)-based approaches have demonstrated immense potential for code translation. Training-based methods are important because LLMs currently do not effectively adapt to domain-specific settings that suffer from a lack of knowledge without targeted training. However, existing training-based approaches rely on a pairwise transpilation paradigm, making it impractical to support a diverse range of PLs. Furthermore, these methods shape the reinforcement learning (RL) reward linearly in the test-case pass rate, which underweights the earliest partial progress. To address these limitations, we propose CodePivot, a training framework that leverages Python as an intermediate representation (IR), augmented by a novel RL reward mechanism, Aggressive-Partial-Functional reward, to bootstrap the model’s multilingual transpilation ability with reduced reliance on parallel corpora. Experiments involving 10 PLs show that the resulting 7B model, trained on Python-to-Others tasks, consistently improves performance across both general and low-resource PL-related transpilation tasks. It outperforms substantially larger mainstream models with hundreds of billions more parameters, such as DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, on Python-to-Others tasks and Others-to-All tasks, respectively, and surpasses its counterpart trained directly on Any-to-Any tasks on general transpilation tasks. Code and data: https://github.com/lishangyu-hkust/CodePivot.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MetaGAI: A Large-Scale and High-Quality Benchmark for Generative AI Model and Data Card Generation
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative AI has created a pressing need for rigorous documentation standards that support transparency and governance. Manual creation of Model and Data Cards, however, is difficult to scale, and automated approaches lack the large-scale, high-fidelity benchmarks required for systematic evaluation. We introduce MetaGAI, a benchmark of 2,541 semantically matched document triplets constructed from academic papers, GitHub repositories, and Hugging Face artifacts. Reference cards are produced by a multi-agent pipeline of specialized Retriever, Generator, and Editor agents, and the pipeline is assessed through a four-part validation protocol. We further propose an evaluation framework that combines reference-based automated metrics with a multi-model LLM-as-a-Judge protocol, together with explicit agreement and sensitivity analyses. Among the evaluated baselines, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct achieves the best observed cost–quality trade-off, and the results reveal a recurring tension between faithfulness and completeness. MetaGAI provides a testbed for benchmarking, training, and analyzing automated Model and Data Card generation at scale. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/haoxuan-unt2024/MetaGAI-Benchmark.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Before the Script, Set the Stage: How Worldview Simulation Amplifies Psychologically Grounded Persuasion in Multi-Turn Jailbreaking
abstract: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks demonstrate that harmful intent can be distributed across dialogue, yet existing methods obscure what conversational mechanisms drive vulnerability. We introduce Blueprint, a safety-evaluation framework that separates a factorized social-influence strategy space from WorldviewSim, a cross-turn situational context module. Monte Carlo Tree Search optimizes turn-level combinations of 18 theory-grounded influence factors across a four-turn trajectory. Across six frontier models, Blueprint achieves near-ceiling attack success rates on major open-weight and proprietary models, while requiring the fewest average queries (2.46). The resulting trajectories further reveal model-specific vulnerability among resistant targets: each responds to distinct influence factors and strategy transitions, yet all share a common recovery pathway. Specifically, shifting toward concrete, executable task framing consistently escapes hard-refusal states. Ablations confirm that operational cues matter most: making requests actionable has the largest impact, gain framing is unusually potent, and some legitimacy appeals can backfire. These findings suggest that robust multi-turn safety requires monitoring not only harmful content, but also how dialogue state makes unsafe requests appear concrete and locally executable. The code is open-sourced at: https://github.com/charlottec1583/Blueprint.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Frames2LoRA: Parametric Video Internalization for Vision-Language Models
abstract: Processing video in vision-language models is expensive: each frame occupies hundreds of tokens, and inference cost scales with every frame and every repeated query. We introduce Frames2LoRA, a method for parametric video internalization. A perceiver hypernetwork reads the intermediate representations produced layer-by-layer as a frozen VLM encodes a video, and generates a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter in a single forward pass. Unlike standard LoRA fine-tuning, which requires iterative gradient updates, Frames2LoRA predicts these weights directly from the video. Trained for SmolVLM2 500M and 2.2B on video summarization and captioning, Frames2LoRA enables the same frozen VLM to answer queries from the adapter alone, with zero visual tokens in its context at query time. Frames2LoRA is statistically non-inferior and equivalent to direct video-in-context inference across all five captioning benchmarks at both model scales, and across seven of eight video question answering benchmark-scale pairings. Although trained only on 12 frames at 384px, it remains stable up to 1,024 frames and 1024px, where direct video-in-context inference often degenerates. Across this sweep, it reduces answer-time visual-token load by up to 1,500x and query TTFT by 6-80x, while preserving video-faithful outputs. We also find that independently generated adapters for non-overlapping video segments can compose in rank space, suggesting a path toward chunked long-video internalization.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Should Queries Be Decomposed? A Stage-Aware Study of Query Decomposition for Multi-Condition Retrieval
abstract: Multi-condition retrieval requires systems to identify documents that satisfy multiple distinct constraints, moving beyond mere topical relevance. While query decomposition is widely adopted as an intuitive remedy, its effectiveness across different retrieval pipeline stages remains underexplored. In this paper, we conduct a stage-aware empirical study and uncover a stark, stage-dependent effect: decomposition during initial retrieval frequently harms retrieval performance due to semantic dilution, yet substantially improves reranking by enabling more fine-grained constraint verification. Motivated by these insights, we propose a principled Stage-Aware Decomposition framework that retains the monolithic query during initial retrieval to preserve global semantic context, while employing sub-queries exclusively during reranking for fine-grained constraint matching. Extensive evaluations on the MultiConIR and SSRB benchmarks demonstrate that our framework consistently improves ranking performance for compositional queries across multiple retrieval and reranking models.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Puzzles to Paradigms: A Survey of Human–Agent Collaboration in Scientific Innovation
abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly embedded in scientific workflows, including literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, tool use, writing, and peer review. However, existing surveys and evaluations often emphasize task performance while underexamining how humans and agents coordinate under different epistemic conditions of scientific work. This survey introduces **CSCW**\times**Kuhn**, a coordination-aware framework that connects computer-supported cooperative work dimensions with distinct scientific contexts. Using this framework, we synthesize recent human–agent systems and benchmarks to examine how coordination demands and failure risks may vary across contexts. Our synthesis identifies five recurring failure modes: procedural drift, grounding substitution, evaluative flattening, proxy optimization, and epistemic black-boxing, and argues for evaluations that move beyond task accuracy and toward grounding, provenance, disagreement preservation, and long-horizon scientific reliability. Our corpus and coding artifact are available at https://github.com/jenlia024/CSCWxKuhn-artifact.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TALIM: A Benchmark Dataset for Tajik Academic Language Intelligence Measurement
abstract: We introduce TALIM (Tajik Academic Language Intelligence Measurement), a large-scale academic benchmark for evaluating academic reasoning and language understanding in Tajik. TALIM spans nine subjects and three question formats, multiple-choice, matching, and free-response, sourced natively from the Tajik national curriculum rather than translated from existing benchmarks. We evaluate nine LLMs, both proprietary and open-weight models, finding that proprietary models substantially outperform open-weight models across all subjects and question types. Grammar is the weakest subject across all models, while physics is consistently the strongest. English translation substantially improves open-weight performance while Farsi transliteration yields only marginal gains, indicating that failures stem from data scarcity rather than script unfamiliarity. Chain-of-thought analysis reveals several systematic failure modes: hallucination, reasoning process failures, and grammatical category confusion. We hope TALIM will serve as a resource for assessing Tajik language capabilities of frontier models and motivate similar native benchmark construction efforts for other low-resource languages.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Hybrid PIR: Balancing Token Compression and Structural Invariance via Pāṇinian Role Assignment
abstract: Neural text representations often lack structural guarantees for syntactic variations, relying instead on statistical interpolation to recognize paraphrases. We introduce the Pāṇinian Intermediate Representation (PIR), a deterministic compiler that maps English sentences to role-tagged canonical sequences using Universal Dependency parses. Unlike heuristic methods such as stopword removal, the PIR compiler is deterministic: given a correct dependency parse, syntactically equivalent paraphrases compile to identical strings. On a 200-pair diagnostic suite of templated syntactic alternations spanning active/passive voice, dative shift, and topicalization, the compiler produces identical strings for 196 pairs; all four failures are structurally typed and traced to known parser limitations. Stopword removal produces identical strings for 0 of 200 pairs. To bridge the performance gap in downstream tasks, we propose Hybrid PIR, which selectively restores lexical content through a deduplication mechanism. Hybrid PIR achieves similarity performance comparable to stopword removal (0.8130 vs. 0.8154 average ρ; bootstrap 95% CI on the difference includes zero) at 43.8% token compression, while providing structural guarantees that surface-level methods cannot. On retrieval benchmarks, Hybrid PIR reaches 80% of the English baseline nDCG@10 on BEIR SciFact and 86% of MRR@10 on MS MARCO QA at 39.0% compression. A three-variant representation ablation validates our deduplication design: removing this mechanism degrades retrieval performance by 3.5 points and turns the compression benefit negative (-3.0%). In a QQP-validation duplicate-detection use case (40,430 pairs), Hybrid PIR reaches precision 0.861 with no tuning, matching a tuned embedding threshold and validating the intended deployment as an offline canonicalization tool for deduplication and index construction.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Linearly Readable, Not Robust: How Linear Jailbreak Probes Conflate Benign Register with Adversarial Intent
abstract: A cheap, now-standard safety filter attaches a linear probe to a frozen LLM’s hidden states to flag jailbreak prompts before generation, reaching near-perfect in-distribution accuracy at negligible cost. We show this single-layer probe is not a usable real-time filter, explain why, and give a fix. Across two model families, five attack types, ten languages, and three sets of hard-but-benign prompts, we find: (i) published probes are badly miscalibrated, so the headline 98–100% detection is an artifact of the chosen threshold (expected calibration error 0.20–0.33, and 0.07–0.20 even after a leakage-controlled retraining); (ii) most of the signal is benign writing style—its "register"—since a model-free style classifier reproduces ~0.92 of the probe’s accuracy; (iii) a 5% false-positive guarantee set on in-distribution benign prompts rises to 68–98% on diverse traffic; and (iv) a single 20-token suffix drops recall to near zero. Going beyond correlational "shortcut" diagnoses, we use concept erasure (LEACE) to causally remove a 3-dimensional register subspace: this cuts ~60 points of over-refusal (false flags on benign prompts) while leaving detection essentially intact (AUC drop ≤0.003), and the same subspace recurs across three architectures (verified against a shuffled-source-label null). Our recipe—register erasure plus deployment-time distribution-free calibration—achieves a guaranteed ≤5% false-positive rate on held-out diverse benign prompts at 0.945–0.961 recall, versus 0.18–0.29 for the un-erased probe. Cheap probing is a measurement instrument, deployable as a filter only via this recipe.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EvoCurr: Self-evolving Curriculum with Behavior Code Generation for Complex Decision-making
abstract: Complex decision-making often requires agents to progress through intermediate tasks rather than solve the final target directly. Existing LLM self-refinement methods typically iterate on a fixed target, while curriculum-learning methods often rely on hand-designed schedules, training-time optimization, or domain-specific difficulty metrics. To smooth the learning curve through adaptive curriculum design, we introduce EvoCurr, a general inference-time framework that co-evolves curricula and executable policies. A Designer proposes verifiable intermediate tasks from the latest accepted progress and recent failures, while a Solver generates or trains policies for these tasks.
