Second, to address these defects before they reach the model, we develop SpecValidator, a lightweight LoRA-fine-tuned classifier based on a 1.5B code model, achieving F1 = 0.84 and MCC = 0.79, significantly outperforming few-shot GPT-5-mini (F1 = 0.43) and Claude-Sonnet-4 (F1 = 0.56), and demonstrating that strong code generation ability does not transfer to prompt meta-reasoning. Perhaps more importantly, our analysis indicates that SpecValidator can generalize to unseen issues and detect unknown Under-Specification defects in the original (real) descriptions of the benchmarks used.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Same Tasks, Different Apps: Why Mobile GUI Agents Fail to Generalize?
abstract: Mobile GUI agents deployed in real settings must work across different applications that support the same functionality. Most existing benchmarks test each task in only one app, so a high score can mean the agent understands the task, or only that it knows that particular app. We introduce AnyAppBench, a category-controlled live Android benchmark that evaluates cross-application generalization while keeping the user goal fixed. It spans 10 functional categories, 100 task templates, and 520 task–application pairs over 52 applications. Agents run from raw instructions and with app-independent sub-goals, and a VLM judge labels every failed run under a fixed failure taxonomy whose reliability is measured by human annotation. We find that, across 13 agents, success on the original application does not transfer reliably to new applications with the same goal. Furthermore, providing high-level sub-goal decomposition produces only small, category-dependent changes that do not close the gap, and the mix of failure types changes with the target interface. Based on those insights, we believe the AnyAppBench benchmark provides an important stepping stone toward robust real-world deployment of mobile GUI agents. Our code, data and the leaderboard can be found at the project website https://anyappbench.github.io/.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: More Context, Larger Models, or Moral Knowledge? A Systematic Study of Schwartz Value Detection in Political Texts
abstract: Detecting Schwartz values in political texts is hard: cues are often implicit, and neighboring values differ by fine distinctions. Two remedies are widely assumed to help: more surrounding document text, and explicit moral knowledge. Knowledge-based retrieval has improved benchmarks elsewhere, but whether either transfers here is untested, because published systems vary context, knowledge, and model family at once. We separate these factors under matched conditions on the ValuesML/Touché ValueEval format. The input ranges from the target sentence to a local window to the full document. Retrieval is either absent or drawn from a curated moral knowledge base, injected by early, late, or cross-attention fusion. Supervised DeBERTa-v3 encoders are compared against zero-shot LLMs from 12B to 123B. More context is not uniformly better: full-document input improves the encoders by 2.5-3.8 macro-F1 points but does not consistently help the LLMs. Retrieved knowledge helps more reliably, improving every model family and context under early fusion. A control substituting random knowledge-base entries shows the families gain differently: LLMs from relevance, encoders from exposure to the value ontology. Neither larger encoders nor larger LLMs guarantee gains, and early fusion outperforms both trainable variants. Value-sensitive NLP should evaluate context, knowledge, and model family jointly.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Transfer Accuracy: Mechanism-Guided Controlled Adaptation for Low-Resource Languages
abstract: Existing circuit discovery methods rely on templated tasks with clean counterfactuals, limiting their use on diverse natural text. We adapt Contextual Decomposition for Transformers (CD-T) for unstructured settings via label-balanced activation means and task-directional relevance scoring, enabling counterfactual-free circuit discovery. We leverage the discovered circuits for Circuit-Targeted Supervised Fine-Tuning (CT-SFT), restricting parameter updates to task-relevant heads and LayerNorm. Experiments on NusaX cross-lingual sentiment transfer show that CT-SFT is highly competitive for low-resource adaptation. While non-circuit sparse updates and full fine-tuning sometimes match target accuracy through capacity recruitment, CT-SFT most consistently avoids catastrophic forgetting, preserving source-language and related-task performance. Extensions to XNLI support the source-retention and intervention findings on a harder task and two model families, showing that circuit-targeted adaptation provides a more controlled, intervention-supported alternative to global fine-tuning.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Not All Tokens Are Equal: Syntax-Pattern Weighted Likelihood Difference Joint Detection for Neural-Training-Free AI-Generated Text Detection
abstract: Existing neural-training-free AI-Generated Text (AIGT) detectors usually aggregate token-level probability signals with uniform weights. However, this ignores an important linguistic regularity: human-written and AI-generated texts exhibit different Part-Of-Speech (POS) n-gram patterns, making certain tokens more informative than others. To address the limitations, we propose SWLD-Joint (Syntax-pattern Weighted Log-likelihood Difference Joint Detection), a calibration-based neural-training-free detector without gradient-based optimization or neural classifier fine-tuning. SWLD-Joint first estimates POS n-gram template weights from labeled calibration data and then combines them with a POS-trajectory calibration signal to focus on syntactically informative positions. Experiments on DetectRL, RAID, and HC3_Ext show robust gains under domain shift, generator mismatch, and adversarial perturbations. Ablations, parameter analysis, case studies, score distributions, and ROC curves verify the effectiveness of syntax-pattern weighting. Code and data will be released upon acceptance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: GeoPrune: A Robust and Engine-Friendly Importance Signal Beyond Attention for Vision Token Pruning in VLMs
abstract: Vision token pruning can accelerate vision language model inference by removing redundant visual tokens. However, we observe that ViT attention based pruning drops sharply on Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5. Empirically, we identify the root cause: the last-block MLP of the vision encoder significantly alters the spectral structure of hidden states and induces spectral collapse. Thus, pre-MLP attention rankings no longer reflect downstream token importance. Through further analysis of vision token selection when ViT attention based pruning still succeeds, we find that selected tokens strongly anti-correlate with raw L2 norm in the vision encoder output space S_{out} , while favoring tokens with larger residual energy. Motivated by shared components mask token-specific importance, we propose GeoPrune, a new importance-based pruning method that operates in S_{out} , applies deflation to remove dominant components, and ranks tokens by residual L2 norm. At aggressive pruning rates, GeoPrune is more robust and surpasses ViT attention based pruning by +4.4/+6.3 recovery points on Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5. We further integrate GeoPrune into the production-grade inference engine vLLM, delivering 5.4%-10.5% mean E2E latency reductions with only slight accuracy drops, advancing vision token pruning toward practical deployment.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: LEGO: Synergizing Expert GraphRAG and Expert Chain-of-Thought for Legal Reasoning
abstract: Large language models are increasingly applied to high-risk domains such as law, yet complex legal reasoning remains limited by two structural challenges. First, existing RAG and GraphRAG methods emphasize lexical or semantic similarity while overlooking normative relations among legal provisions. Second, vanilla Chain-of-Thought prompting may generate plausible rationales without enforcing the normative structure of legal reasoning. To deal with the bottleneck of pipelines in the legal reasoning domain, we propose LEGO, a dual-module framework that synergizes Legal Expert GraphRAG and expert Chain-of-thought for complex legal reasoning. ExpertGraphRAG uses an expert-annotated civil code graph encoding these normative relations with a greedy normative-coverage retrieval algorithm to dynamically extract instance-specific provision subgraphs, while ExpertCoT organizes the retrieved provisions and case facts into structured Provision-Fact-Conclusion reasoning. With a Qwen3-8B backbone, LEGO achieves 40.53% exact-match accuracy on LawExamQA_Civil, outperforming the evaluated RAG and CoT baselines and performing comparably to the evaluated larger models, while remaining robust on multi-hop questions. It also achieves the best results among the evaluated baselines on the open-ended benchmarks. Ablation studies confirm the individual and complementary contributions of both modules, demonstrating LEGO’s effectiveness in improving LLMs’ complex legal reasoning ability. Code and dataset can be found in the link: https://github.com/BLK-WHT/LEGO
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: AWM: Answerable Working Memory for Long-Document VQA Agents
abstract: Long-document visual question answering increasingly relies on VLM agents that retrieve candidate pages, inspect page images, write findings to working memory, and synthesize answers. Working memory should carry answer-supporting evidence across page inspections for later grounded answering, yet existing evaluation mainly checks final-answer correctness and evidence-page access. This creates a memory-quality blind spot: an agent may reach the right page and answer correctly while leaving behind memory too generic or incomplete to support answering once page context is removed. We introduce memory-only answerability, a diagnostic that asks whether a reader can answer from the question and terminal working memory alone. Building on this diagnostic, Answerable Working Memory (AWM) treats terminal working memory as an answerable evidence artifact, and AWM-GRPO incorporates this signal into the GRPO reward while preserving final-answer priority. Under GRPO, this reward assigns higher advantages to answer-correct trajectories whose terminal working memory remains answerable. On MMLongBench-Doc, even when gold evidence pages are provided, 42.5% of correct answers still cannot be answered from terminal working memory alone. AWM-GRPO improves final-answer accuracy over the RAG baseline by 8.1 and 11.9 points on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL and reduces the memory-missing-correct rate by 2.7 points over answer-only GRPO.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: What Makes Blood Thicker than Water: Related Word Discrimination in Romance Languages from a Multi-dimensional Perspective
abstract: We provide in this study a multi-faceted analysis of related word detection with automatic methods for Romance languages (including the five main Romance languages: Spanish, French, Romanian, Italian, Portuguese), by combining complementary orthographic, phonetic and semantic features (including both cognates and borrowings in all five languages and a series of classification tasks), with a focus on assessing the impact of the semantic component in specific patterns for Romance related words. We perform quantitative explorations as well as classification experiments for every language pair and different types of etymological relations separately: cognate detection, cognate versus borrowing discrimination and borrowing direction detection.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SafeTutors: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems
abstract: Large language models are rapidly being deployed as AI tutors, yet current evaluation paradigms assess problem-solving accuracy and generic safety in isolation - failing to capture whether a model is simultaneously pedagogically effective and safe across sustained interaction. We argue that tutoring safety is fundamentally different from conventional LLM safety: the primary risk is not toxic content but the quiet erosion of learning through answer over-disclosure, misconception reinforcement, and the abdication of scaffolding. To systematically study this failure mode, we introduce SafeTutors, a benchmark that jointly evaluates safety and pedagogy across mathematics, physics, and chemistry. SafeTutors is organized around a theoretically grounded risk taxonomy comprising 11 harm dimensions and 48 sub-risks drawn from learning-science literature. We uncover that all models show broad harm; scale doesn’t reliably help; and multi-turn dialogue worsens behavior, with pedagogical failures rising from 17.7% to 77.8%. Harms also vary by subject, so mitigations must be discipline-aware, and single-turn “safe/helpful” results can mask systematic tutor failure over extended interaction.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Memory Beyond Recall: A Dual-Process Cognitive Memory System for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
abstract: Long-term memory for an LLM agent requires more than retrieving a relevant passage. Many existing systems address belief revision, causal connections and cross-domain abstraction primarily through storage and retrieval mechanisms, limiting their ability to support implicit personalisation as a user’s preferences evolve. We present DPCM, which organises memory into a capability hierarchy spanning raw inputs, atomic facts, belief trajectories, identity, domain schemas, prospective intentions and cross-domain patterns. A synchronous daytime writer (SYSTEM 1) records revisions as doubly linked supersedes chains; an asynchronous nighttime engine (SYSTEM 2) induces schemas and intentions, then uses cross-domain collisions to derive core schemas. Dual-process theory motivates this separation between online encoding and offline abstraction without implying that agent memory reproduces human cognition. Across single-run evaluations on LongMemEval, PersonaMem and PersonaMem-v2, SYSTEM 2 yields its largest observed gain on implicit cross-session inference (+5.20 on PersonaMem-v2) and its smallest on the recall-oriented LongMemEval aggregate (+0.33). When the inference budget is limited to 8k tokens and the full history no longer fits, DPCMfull exceeds the long-context baseline by 10.5–17.9 points across both backbones.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ToolHACE: A Dataset for Detecting Hallucinations in Tool-Based LLM Responses
abstract: Tool-augmented language models ground their responses in external tool outputs, improving reliability beyond parametric knowledge alone. However, even when the correct tool is called and returns accurate information, models may still contradict such outputs, omit critical details, or generate unsupported claims. Existing hallucination benchmarks for tool-augmented dialogue primarily focus on the tool-calling stage, evaluating whether the correct tool and arguments are selected, while overlooking errors that arise during post-tool response generation. To address this gap, we introduce , a span-level benchmark for hallucination detection in tool-augmented LLM responses, covering five fine-grained hallucination categories. Through extensive experiments with modern hallucination detectors, we show that post-tool-call hallucinations are widespread and remain challenging to detect. Our results further demonstrate that effective detection requires training on specialized tool-augmented corpora, while transfer from tool-agnostic hallucination datasets performs poorly in this setting. These findings highlight the need for dedicated benchmarks and models for reliable hallucination detection in tool-augmented language systems.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Do Prompts Guarantee Safety? Mitigating Toxicity from LLM Generations through Gradient Based Subspace Intervention
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful text generators, yet they can produce toxic or harmful content even when given seemingly harmless prompts. This presents a serious safety challenge and can cause real-world harm. Toxicity is often subtle and context-dependent, making it difficult to detect at the token level or through coarse sentence-level signals. Moreover, efforts to mitigate toxicity often face a trade-off between safety and the coherence, or fluency, of the generated text. In this work, we present a targeted subspace intervention strategy based on gradient signals for identifying and suppressing hidden toxic patterns from underlying model representations, while preserving the overall ability to generate safe, fluent content. On the RealToxicityPrompts, our method achieves strong mitigation performance compared to existing baselines while imposing minimal impact on inference complexity. Across LLMs, our approach reduces the toxicity of state-of-the-art detoxification systems by 8-20%, while maintaining comparable fluency. We further validate cross-benchmark generality on ToxiGen, where the same gains hold under adversarial, implicitly toxic prompts. Through extensive quantitative and qualitative analyses, we show that our approach achieves effective toxicity reduction without impairing generative performance, consistently outperforming existing baselines.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Static Visual Tokens: Structured Sequential Visual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
abstract: Current multimodal LLMs encode images as static visual prefixes and rely on text-based reasoning, lacking goal-driven and adaptive visual access. Inspired by human visual perception—where attention is selectively and sequentially shifted from the most informative regions to secondary cues—we propose Structural Sequential Visual CoT **(SSV-CoT)**. First, a question-relevant saliency map identifies and organizes key visual regions, explicitly modeling the spatial distribution of visual importance. Second, reasoning is performed following this discriminative order, inducing a curriculum-like semantic progression from primary to secondary cues. This method is trained end-to-end, using text cot and answer supervision, without relying on region-level annotations or specialized external tools. Experiments on diverse visual reasoning benchmarks show gains, validating structured and sequential visual cognition.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Understanding Subjectivity Transformation in Academic Meta-Review Generation
abstract: Academic meta-reviews must synthesize several reviewer opinions into a single, consistent judgment, balancing verifiable factual claims against subjective evaluations. Yet how human meta-reviewers transform reviewer subjectivity during summarization and whether large language models (LLMs) reproduce this behavior remains under-explored. To address this, we characterize subjectivity transformation in academic meta-review writing using a sentence-level subjectivity scorer, evaluating four open LLMs across six prompt configurations. Our analysis reveals that meta-review writing performs a regression to the mean of subjectivity: when a meta-review sentence is matched to its source reviewer’s sentence, the change in subjectivity negatively correlates with the source’s original subjectivity. In particular, actual, individual reviewer statements are made more interpretive, while highly subjective language tends to be moderated toward a balanced tone. All four open LLMs reproduce such a transformation closely. Conditioning the prompt on reviewer subjectivity yields only a small calibration gain where the generated meta-review’s overall subjectivity moves slightly closer to the human reference, yet leaves the transformation itself unchanged, implying that there exists a robust latent behavior of LLM summarization rather than a prompt-controllable one.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CePRM: Generative Process Reward Modeling with Calibrated Values and Repair-Aware Supervision
abstract: Generative process reward models (PRMs) improve step-level verification of mathematical reasoning, yet their effectiveness is limited by the quality of process supervision. The dominant Monte Carlo (MC) estimation derives step labels from final-answer accuracy rather than semantic correctness, producing systematic label noise, while standard pipelines discard the implicit tree structure of rollout data that encodes informative failure patterns. We propose CePRM, which addresses both limitations through Step-Cognitive MC Value Scaling, calibrating raw MC scores with step-level semantic signals via multiplicative adjustment, and pivot-step-directed repair mining, which exploits value cliffs in failed trajectories to construct same-prefix contrastive correction pairs via Sibling Advantage filtering. Experiments on ProcessBench and PRMBench show that CePRM, with a 4B backbone, achieves competitive or superior error localization and process verification against 7B-scale baselines, with notably strong error-side recognition.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RULE-EDIT: Benchmarking Rule-Level Knowledge Editing in Large Language Models
abstract: Knowledge editing seeks to update language models without full retraining. While most prior work focuses on isolated factual or instance-level edits, we study a more structured setting: mathematical rules as a controlled stress test for abstract symbolic rule editing. We introduce RULE-EDIT, the first benchmark explicitly designed for editing and evaluating rule-level knowledge in LLMs. Our benchmark investigates two key questions: (1) whether edits to abstract rules propagate to derived instances, and (2) whether edits remain consistent across different representations of the same rule. To evaluate these aspects, we propose two new metrics: Instance Portability and Rule Understanding. Experiments on strong open-source LLMs with representative editing methods show that, although models can often overwrite formula-level knowledge, they struggle to transfer edits to rule-derived instances and to maintain consistency across symbolic and natural-language forms. For example, several methods achieve nearly 100% reliability on direct rule queries, while Instance Portability never exceeds 52% and Rule Understanding remains below 26%. Overall, RULE-EDIT provides a controlled benchmark for studying whether current knowledge editing approaches truly modify abstract symbolic rules in LLMs, rather than merely altering surface outputs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Pancasila-Dilemmas: Evaluating Large Language Models on Indonesian Human Value Dilemmas Grounded in Pancasila
abstract: The value alignment of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for ensuring responses align with human intention and value preferences. However, most evaluations of value alignment focus on Western or universal values, while assessments grounded in the value systems of specific countries remain scarce. In this paper, we introduce Pancasila-Dilemmas, an evaluation dataset of 1,834 questions derived from Indonesian news, classified by 5 values of Pancasila: Religion, Humanity, Unity, Democracy, and Social Justice. This dataset reflects daily life in Indonesia, making it suitable for measuring the value alignment of LLMs deployed for Indonesia. To ensure a more rigorous evaluation, we choose scenarios containing dilemmas. The dataset adopts a multiple-choice format consisting of a scenario, a question, and 4 different options without right/wrong decisions. The dataset is proofread by native speakers and answered by 5 diverse Indonesian citizens. We evaluate 50 closed- and open-source LLMs on our dataset. Results reveal that all evaluated LLMs achieves less than 0.5 Probability Match Score (PMS) and 0.72 Max-Vote Agreement Score (MVAS). Compared by each values, LLMs mostly struggle in Religion and Unity dilemma cases. This highlights a significant gap in capturing Indonesian values. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/Pancasila-Dilemmas.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ViCo: Towards Visual-oriented Coding with Self-Reflection for Chart Replication
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of generating high-quality academic charts that match the visual standards of human-authored papers. While existing AI agents can produce well-structured text and code, their generated visualizations often lack the stylistic and semantic fidelity of human designs. Advanced coding agents that employ self-reflection mechanisms exhibit poor visual reasoning and limited reflection following, resulting in sparse reward signals that severely undermine their reinforcement learning (RL). We propose ViCo, a training framework for visual-oriented coding that employs iterative reflections to align generated chart images progressively with the reference. We first introduce a self-supervised warm-up stage, which augments Monte Carlo Tree Search with consistency-based pruning to synthesize high-quality reflection trajectories, ensuring that each coding step strictly follows the outcomes of prior reflections. A multi-step RL algorithm is then developed on counterfactual baselines to estimate advantage for reflection and action steps within each refinement cycle, thereby addressing the reward sparsity problem. To enable efficient reward in massive training, we propose an automatic, multifaceted evaluation framework that assesses charts’ style, layout, and semantic consistency via a hierarchical heterogeneous layout graph structure. Experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that ViCo, trained on an 8B model, achieves performance close to commercial LLMs with adequate reflection capabilities.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Calibrating Hierarchical Memory Utilization for Long-Term Memory QA
abstract: Long-term memory systems increasingly organize interaction histories into hierarchical contexts, where coarse summaries, mid-level events, and fine-grained evidence provide complementary signals for future queries. Yet after retrieval, these signals are often collapsed into a single generation context and used implicitly. We ask how retrieved hierarchical memory should shape generation after access, framing it as a post-retrieval calibration problem. We propose HiR, a training-free inference-time framework that contrasts full-hierarchy decoding with a coarse-only reference view, preserving the complete hierarchy while tempering over-reliance on broad abstractions. Extensive experiments and analyses show that HiR enables more effective and robust use of hierarchical memory without changing memory construction or retrieval; more broadly, our results suggest that memory research should consider not only what to store or retrieve, but also how retrieved information shapes generation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Token-level Adaptive Weighting via Implicit Rewards for Inference-time Multi-objective Alignment
abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences is challenging due to the inherent heterogeneity and multi-dimensionality of these preferences. Existing inference-time multi-objective alignment methods often rely on fixed weights to combine preference models. However, different tokens contribute unequally to preference objectives during decoding. Ignoring such token-level variation may cause the loss of preference information and lead to objective interference. To alleviate this, we utilize the implicit rewards of preference models to estimate importance differences between tokens, and propose a new training-free and reward-free framework TAW to dynamically balance multiple objectives for inference-time alignment. We design the relative entropy and marginal entropy estimators to quantify the informativeness and uncertainty of preference objectives. TAW with the estimator ensures that more informative or reliable preferences are emphasized, while weak or uncertain signals are suppressed. Experiments on two LLM alignment benchmarks show that TAW outperforms strong baselines without predefined weightings, while also achieves an overall optimal Pareto front when explicit preference weighting is applied.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: T1-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Scenario Agents in Real-World Domains
abstract: Recent advances in reasoning and tool-calling capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have enabled increasingly capable agentic systems. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in task complexity, realism, and domain diversity, and often fail to capture interactions that span multiple domains, limiting their ability to evaluate agents in realistic multi-step settings that require sustained reasoning and coordination. To address these limitations, we introduce T1-Bench, a high-fidelity, comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agentic systems in realistic customer-facing, multi-domain environments, featuring interleaved scenarios that require structured reasoning across multi-turn user-assistant interactions and substantially increasing both compositional complexity and evaluative rigor across 25 domains of varying difficulty. We evaluate T1-Bench using 12 proprietary and open-weight models, providing a reproducible and standardized framework for assessing agent behavior, tool utilization, and conversational quality in complex, multi-step environments. We further complement automatic evaluation with human judgments to strengthen the assessment of qualitative performance. Overall, T1-Bench substantially advances prior benchmarks by increasing task complexity, interaction depth, and domain coverage in simulated multi-domain environments. To facilitate future research on agentic systems, we will publicly release data and evaluation code as open source.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PEFT-Arena: Understanding Parameter-Efficient Finetuning from a Stability-Plasticity Perspective
abstract: Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) has become the standard approach for adapting large language models, yet evaluations largely emphasize downstream accuracy while overlooking the retention of pretrained capabilities. We argue that PEFT should be assessed through the stability-plasticity dilemma: the trade-off between target-task adaptation and resistance to forgetting. We introduce PEFT-Arena, a benchmark that jointly measures downstream performance and general capability retention. Across the studied settings, methods exhibit distinct stability-plasticity profiles, and orthogonal finetuning often lies on a favorable frontier under comparable parameter budgets. We analyze the internal changes associated with these external trade-offs from two complementary geometric perspectives. In weight space, spectral profiles characterize how parameterizations interact with the pretrained singular-value structure. In activation space, representation-similarity diagnostics show a strong association between forgetting and non-isometric distortion on general-evaluation data. Together, these views suggest that preserving pretrained spectral and representational geometry is an important inductive bias for retention, with OFT’s spectrum-preserving updates providing a particularly clear case. Finally, parameterization-aware interpolation shows that final SFT checkpoints can lie beyond a better target-retention operating point. We use post-hoc rewinding as a case study of controlling this trade-off.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Learning from the Best, Differently: A Diversity-Driven Rethinking on Data Selection
abstract: High-quality pre-training data is crucial for large language models (LLMs), yet existing score-based selection approaches often fail to balance quality and diversity. Empirical studies have revealed a non-monotonic relationship between dataset scores and downstream performance: simply selecting the top-scored data often leads to performance degradation due to the collapse of correlated evaluation dimensions, which sacrifices diversity. To address this, we propose **O**rthogonal **Di**versity-Aware **S**election (**ODiS**), a novel framework to preserve both quality and diversity by decomposing correlated evaluation metrics into orthogonal feature dimensions. First, ODiS evaluates data from multiple dimensions, covering language quality, knowledge quality, and comprehension difficulty. The resulting multi-dimensional scores are then decorrelated via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), yielding orthogonal evaluation dimensions. For each dimension, a RoBERTa-based scorer is trained to regress the data onto PCA-projected scores, enabling scalable inference on large corpora. Finally, ODiS constructs the training dataset by selecting the top-scored data from each orthogonal dimension, thereby ensuring both quality and diversity. Empirical results show that ODiS-selected data exhibit less than 2% inter-dimension overlap, confirming the orthogonality between dimensions. More importantly, models trained on ODiS-selected data significantly outperform baselines across multiple downstream benchmarks, underscoring the necessity of orthogonal, diversity-aware data selection for LLMs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Aligning Large Language Models with Pluralistic Values: Case Study in Southeast Asian (SEA) Countries
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed globally, aligning them with pluralistic human values remains a challenge, as current efforts are predominantly Western-focused. To bridge this gap, we introduce SEAPlur, a dataset designed to benchmark and improve LLM alignment with the pluralistic values of four Southeast Asian (SEA) countries: Indonesia, Laos, Myanmar, and Vietnam. SEAPlur consists of independent datasets for each country and is constructed in their respective native, non-English languages. Sourced from local news and structured around the Schwartz’s theory of basic human values, SEAPlur captures local human agreement distributions across complex social dilemmas. In total, the dataset comprises 4,000 curated scenarios. For evaluation, we split 250 scenarios for each country resulting in SEAPlur-Test. The remaining data with "Agree" and "Disagree" annotations is transformed into a SEAPlur-Train 7,460 instruction-response pairs. Our evaluations using SEAPlur-Test reveal that general API LLMs struggle with SEA values, achieving peak overall accuracy (OA) scores of only 0.50. In contrast, region-specific LLMs perform better, reaching OA scores up to 0.58. Furthermore, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using SEAPlur-Train significantly improves alignment. However, this process reveals a critical safety tension: enhancing regional alignment in certain LLMs may trigger unsafe behaviors. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/SEAPlur.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Refinement-Integrated Reasoning Elicits Better Generalization of LLM-Based Code Vulnerability Detection
abstract: Existing code vulnerability detection (CVD) methods face severe challenges in terms of generalization. Most of these methods directly map the source code to a binary vulnerability label or a vulnerability explanation, struggling to capture the deep features within the complex relationship between them. Thus, these works fail to generalize to out-of-distribution data well. To address this issue, we propose a simple yet effective training framework called refinement-integrated reasoning (RIRE), leveraging refinements that indicate the patched code in the CVD task. Firstly, RIRE introduces the refinement as a guiding signal to help LLMs synthesize reasoning chains as explanations, which align with the vulnerability label, and uses these data for supervised fine-tuning. Secondly, refinement is utilized through a hierarchical preference optimization framework to help determine which reasoning-enhanced detection result is of higher quality, further mining essential features for fine-grained distinguishability and detection capability. Experimental results across five benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed RIRE framework achieves superior performance over strong baselines, especially being more generalizable to unseen datasets during training.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: BioPIE: A Biomedical Protocol Information Extraction Dataset for Experiment Understanding
abstract: Understanding biomedical experiments provides a foundation for downstream tasks, e.g., laboratory automation, and facilitates effective cross-disciplinary communication. Two challenges, High Information Density (HID) and Multi-Step Reasoning (MSR), pose unique difficulties for precise automatic experimental understanding. Extracting structured knowledge, e.g., Knowledge Graphs (KGs), is an effective approach to address the HID and MSR. However, existing biomedical datasets for structured knowledge Information Extraction (IE) are limited to a general or coarse-grained level, hindering fine-grained experimental understanding. To address this gap, we introduce Biomedical Protocol Information Extraction Dataset (BioPIE), a dataset providing procedure-centric KGs that captures entities, actions, and relations at a scale sufficient for reasoning across biomedical protocols. We evaluate both supervised and LLM-based IE methods on BioPIE to verify its effectiveness, and implement a biomedical question answering system to provide a quantitative illustration of BioPIE’s effectiveness for downstream understanding tasks. The experimental results demonstrate improved understanding performance on both the HID and MSR question sets.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Majority Vote: Multi-Perspective Adjudication for Medical Hallucination Detection
abstract: Understanding the frequency of factual errors in chatbot-generated text and evaluating systems that detect these errors is critical for determining chatbot safety. Yet factual-error detection is often treated as a single-pass, single-annotator labeling problem. In long-form chatbot responses, factual errors can be subtle and embedded within mostly correct text.We develop a multi-perspective annotation study of medically relevant chatbot responses, combining first-pass annotation, LLM-as-a-Judge candidate discovery, and two forms of adjudication: domain-expert and evidence-based fact-checking. First-pass annotators frequently miss factual errors later validated by adjudicators. LLM-as-a-Judge improves candidate discovery, but is insufficient on its own: it misses factual errors that annotators catch. We also find disagreement among adjudicators, suggesting that adjudication over multiple candidate sources can improve benchmark completeness, but does not eliminate the need to apply judgment and expertise. Applied to an existing benchmark, this technique reveals a similar pattern of missed errors.Together, these results suggest that single-pass hallucination benchmarks achieve scale, but likely undercount errors. Multi-pass adjudication improves coverage, but benchmark results will still need to be interpreted in light of the judgment, expertise, and evidence used when deciding if an error is present.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: K-Humor: Dynamic Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Generation of Culturally Grounded Korean Jokes
abstract: Humor generation is a challenging task in natural language generation that requires fluency, surprise, and cultural grounding. Although large language models (LLMs) show promise in English, little work addresses low-resource and culturally specific humor, such as in Korean. We propose **K-Humor**, a *dynamic multi-agent framework* for generating Korean jokes. Unlike static one-shot models, K-Humor integrates specialized agents for cultural awareness, audience simulation, editing, and punchline creation, which are coordinated through a dynamic iterative refinement loop. A human-data-grounded mechanism further guides the punchlines using authentic Korean jokes. Evaluation with automatic metrics, agent-internal diagnostics, LLM-as-a-judge, and human ratings shows that K-Humor consistently outperforms a single-prompt baseline and ablations in criteria such as fluency and cultural appropriateness. Although human-written jokes remain stronger overall, particularly on core creative dimensions, K-Humor demonstrates that dynamic, culturally grounded multi-agent systems can improve humor generation over standard LLM baselines in low-resource settings. Code is available at https://github.com/dxlabskku/k-humor.

title: SWE-World: Building Software Engineering Agents in Docker-Free Environments
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled software engineering agents to solve complex code modification tasks. However, most existing approaches rely on execution feedback from Docker-based environments, which require dependency-complete setup, program execution, and test validation, making agent training costly and difficult to scale. We propose SWE-World, a Docker-free framework that replaces containerized execution during downstream agent optimization with a learned surrogate environment. Trained on real agent-environment interaction traces, SWE-World predicts both step-level execution feedback and final test outcomes, preserving the standard agent-environment loop without repeatedly constructing or running Docker environments. This surrogate also enables test-time scaling (TTS) by scoring multiple candidate trajectories through simulated evaluation. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified show that SWE-World improves Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct from 6.2% to 52.0% with Docker-free SFT, 55.0% with Docker-free RL, and 68.2% with TTS. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SWE-World-2D1E.

title: One-Token Rollout: Guiding Supervised Fine-Tuning of LLMs with Policy Gradient
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the predominant method for adapting large language models (LLMs), yet it often struggles with generalization compared to reinforcement learning (RL). In this work, we posit that this performance disparity stems not just from the loss function, but from a more fundamental difference: SFT learns from a fixed, pre-collected dataset, whereas RL utilizes on-policy data sampled from the current policy. Building on this hypothesis, we introduce one-token rollout (OTR), a novel fine-tuning algorithm that guides SFT with the policy gradient method. OTR reframes the autoregressive learning process by treating each token generation as a single-step reinforcement learning trajectory. At each step, it performs a Monte Carlo ”rollout” by sampling multiple candidate tokens from the current policy’s distribution. The ground-truth token from the supervised data is then used to provide a reward signal to these samples. Guided by policy gradient, our algorithm repurposes static, off-policy supervised data into a dynamic, on-policy signal at the token level, capturing the generalization benefits of on-policy learning while bypassing the costly overhead of full sentence generation. Through extensive experiments on a diverse suite of challenging benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general domain reasoning, we demonstrate that OTR consistently outperforms standard SFT. Our findings establish OTR as a powerful and practical alternative for fine-tuning LLMs and provide compelling evidence that the on-policy nature of data is a critical driver of generalization, offering a promising new direction for fine-tuning LLMs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Towards Contextual Sensitive Data Detection
abstract: The emergence of open data portals necessitates more attention to protecting sensitive data before datasets get published and used. To do so effectively, we observe the need to refine and broaden our definitions of sensitive data. We argue that the sensitivity of data depends on its context, and that this context should be considered in methods for assessing data sensitivity. To this end, we introduce a framework, termed ConSenser, for contextual sensitive data detection based on two aspects: 1) type contextualization, which considers the type of data values within the overall context of the dataset or document to assess their true sensitivity, and 2) domain contextualization, which assesses the sensitivity of data values informed by domain-specific information external to the dataset, such as geographic origin of a dataset. Experiments instrumented with language models confirm that type-contextualization significantly reduces the number of false positives for type-based sensitive data detection and reaches a recall of 94% compared to 63% with commonly used tools. Moreover, domain-contextualization through retrieval of sensitivity rules effectively grounds sensitive data detection in relevant context in non-standard data domains. A case study with humanitarian data experts also illustrates that context-grounded explanations provide useful guidance in manual data auditing processes. We open-source the code and annotated datasets at https://github.com/trl-lab/sensitive-data-detection.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RING: Retrieval-Internalized Generation for Continual Large-Scale Knowledge Injection
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality but adds latency and engineering overhead at serving time. We propose RING (Retrieval-Internalized Generation), a holistic paradigm spanning both architecture and training that injects large-scale external knowledge into a Mixture-of-Memory Experts and learns parametric search over this internal memory via reinforcement learning, removing the external retriever entirely. Training proceeds in three stages: continued pre-training injects new corpora into a Knowledge Expert via our novel Dual Causal Attention; supervised fine-tuning teaches a “search-then-answer” pattern; and reinforcement learning with hierarchical rewards optimizes the routing-and-search policy over the parametric memory. Unlike prior parametric injection methods that pair internal memory with a fixed or rule-based retriever, RING learns its retrieval policy directly from task signals. We further frame RING theoretically as a search-free approximation to the classical RAG objective. To evaluate large-scale injection of genuinely new knowledge without test-time leakage, we further construct News-2025, a benchmark built from news strictly post-dating the base LLM’s pretraining cutoff. RING matches or surpasses both search-based RAG and parametric injection baselines in accuracy and efficiency.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Exemplar Choice Matters for Morphological Reasoning: Model Confidence Vs Exemplar Similarity
abstract: LLMs have shown impressive linguistic competencies in a wide range of NLP tasks, yet morphological generalization remains challenging. Models can benefit from in-context learning, where the choice of few-shot examples significantly influences the outcome. We probe LLMs’ morphological capabilities by assessing how two targeted in-context exemplar selection strategies, Iterative Confidence-Based Exemplar Selection (i-CES) and Similarity-Based Exemplar Selection (SES), influence the model’s ability for inflectional and derivational modeling across multiple languages. Our experiments with LLaMA 3.3-70B-instruct and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct models indicate that SES is more effective for accessing latent linguistic knowledge, showing a substantial performance advantage over i-CES in both derivational and inflectional tasks. In contrast, i-CES offers no clear advantage over random sampling.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: LLM generation novelty through the lens of semantic similarity
abstract: Generation novelty is a key indicator of an LLM’s ability to generalize, yet measuring it against full pretraining corpora is computationally challenging. Existing evaluations often rely on lexical overlap, failing to detect paraphrased text, or do not consider the full pretraining corpus. We frame novelty as a semantic retrieval problem. This framing enables us to address novelty with modern embedding and indexing pipelines, allowing for efficient analysis at pre-training scale. Specifically, we propose a three-stage framework that retrieves semantically similar samples, reranks them at varying subsequence lengths, and calibrates scores using a human novelty reference for interpretability. We apply this framework to the SmolLM model family and report three key findings: (1) models draw on pretraining data across much longer sequences than previously reported; (2) some task domains systematically promote or suppress generation novelty; and (3) instruction tuning not only alters style but also increases novelty. These results highlight the value of semantic novelty analysis for studying generalization. To support reproducibility and further research, we release \sim 20 TB of corpus chunks and index artifacts upon acceptance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Transferring Math Reasoning Abilities from LLMs to MLLMs via Causal-Aware Model Merging
abstract: To build a math MLLM, current research efforts predominantly rely on elaborate training schemes or high-quality multi-modal math reasoning data. On the other hand, model merging has attracted much attention recently due to its low-cost and tune-free property, which has shown great potential for constructing math MLLM. However, most recent attempts either assume all parameters are task-relevant or adopt a less interpretable parameter selection strategy, thus merging parameters on a coarse granularity, leading to limited or even degrading performance. In this paper, we propose a causal-analysis–guided parameter merging framework, which identifies the math reasoning-related parameters in a finer granularity and interpretable manner, then merges the math LLMs with MLLM. Specifically, we first construct targeted arithmetic and logical tasks, generate reference and counterfactual samples, and then apply intervention-based causal attribution to localize parameters that are causally responsible for math reasoning. Once we identify the crucial reasoning parameters in the math LLM that exhibit higher causal effects, we can more precisely align and merge only the corresponding parameters from the math LLM into the base MLLM. The procedure is tuning-free and enhances both math reasoning and general reasoning abilities. Experimental results of three model families on four math reasoning benchmarks and two general reasoning benchmarks validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Sparse Long Memory and Transition Bottlenecks Shape Positional Recall in Mamba Language Models
abstract: Mamba language models process sequences recurrently, but recurrent processing does not imply that all tokens are retained equally. We study this gap using structured recall tasks that expose primacy, recency, and lost-in-the-middle behavior. Our results suggest that Mamba uses two functional memory regimes: a short-lived state that supports recency, and a sparse long-lived channel subspace that preserves selected early inputs. Targeted interventions on this long-memory subspace selectively degrade early recall and transfer to long-context QA and summarization, indicating that the same channels support real long-context use. We then ask why middle items are forgotten despite being processed sequentially. We find that the central failure is a short-to-long memory transition bottleneck: middle items are no longer recent enough for short memory, but are often not promoted into the sparse long-lived subspace. Repeated input structure strengthens this bottleneck by changing the input-dependent discretization dynamics. These findings provide a mechanistic account of Mamba’s U-shaped recall curve as the interaction between long memory, short memory, and a fragile transition between them.

title: TCHV: Type-Conditioned Hypothesis Verification for Multimodal Named Entity Recognition
abstract: Multimodal Named Entity Recognition (MNER) uses supplementary images to resolve ambiguity in entity mentions in noisy, short-form social-media text. Prevailing approaches typically fuse text with visually aligned features, but such cues often lack sufficient discriminative power and may support conflicting entity-type hypotheses. To address this issue, we propose TCHV, a lightweight framework grounded in a type-conditioned hypothesis-verification perspective. By formulating each span-type pair as a distinct hypothesis during inference, TCHV predicts the latent feature evidence expected under each hypothesis and validates it against observed multimodal representations through bidirectional text-image matching, using a visual relevance gate to suppress unin- formative images. Verification scores serve as surrogate evidence statistics; TCHV improves over established non-VLLM multimodal baselines on Twitter-2015/2017, and TCHV† leads the compared VLLM-based methods on Twitter-2017. Extensions demonstrate applicability to grounded and fine-grained settings. Code: https://github.com/ hanfeiyu703/ImaginE.git.

title: Toward Cultural Alignment: Human-Centered Evaluation of Multimodal AI Stories Across Five African Communities
abstract: In this paper, we examine how well AI-generated multimodal stories align with the lived practices, relationships, language, values, and visual expectations of the communities they represent. We conduct a community-grounded mixed-methods evaluation with 19 culture representatives across five African communities, combining quantitative annotations with qualitative focus group discussions. We find that cultural alignment depends not simply on recognizable cultural markers, but on how those markers fit social, linguistic, procedural, and visual context. From these evaluations, we develop a taxonomy of cultural alignment comprising five broader cultural marker categories and eight recurring mechanisms of misalignment. We additionally evaluate five multimodal LLM judges to examine whether automated evaluation can approximate community-grounded judgments at scale. Judge reliability and score calibration vary substantially across communities, with no single judge performing consistently across all five settings. These findings motivate community-calibrated evaluation pipelines in which automated judges are validated against community judgments to determine where they can be trusted and where human review remains necessary.

title: Pivot Gradient Scaling: Reducing Dwell Time to Stabilize Extreme Low-Bit Quantization-aware Training
abstract: Extreme low-bit quantization-aware training (QAT) is often unstable due to synchronized bin transitions, which can trigger catastrophic loss spikes. While prior works rely on scale-side controls to mitigate this fragility, we demonstrate that restricting pivot movement alone is insufficient. Instead, we identify a critical weight-side state governing low-bit QAT stability: pivot-proximal residence, where latent weights persistently linger near quantization pivots. We formalize this duration as dwell time and show that long dwell times accumulate a large, vulnerable population of weights prone to synchronized mass flips. To resolve this vulnerability, we propose Pivot Gradient Scaling (PGS) as a principled modification to the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) that leaves the forward pass intact and selectively amplifies latent-weight gradients within a localized pivot band. Crucially, we provide a mathematical guarantee proving that this sign-preserving amplification increases pivot-proximal mobility and systematically shortens expected dwell time under both SGD and Adam. Exhaustive empirical evaluations across Llama 3.2 and Qwen3 model families under full-training regimes up to 30 billion tokens demonstrate that PGS structurally stabilizes optimization, attenuates transition bursts, and delivers substantial downstream accuracy gains.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Emergence of Relevance Through Axiomatic Attention Patterns During LoRA Fine-Tuning
abstract: LoRA fine-tuning is standard for adapting LLMs to reranking, but it remains unclear where in the network task-specific relevance behavior is learned and what attention-level changes accompany that learning. Through ablation and attention experiments, we identify where LoRA attention updates to RankLLaMA improve performance and whether those gains coincide with interpretable relevance-oriented attention patterns such as lexical matching, rarity sensitivity, and query-document interaction. We find that given LoRA fine-tuned MLPs throughout the network, restricting LoRA attention updates to a compact mid-network region is sufficient for recovering over half of the performance gained by applying LoRA to all attention layers, and that omitting attention fine-tuning in this region hurts performance more than elsewhere in the network. Additionally, we show that regions where applying LoRA affects performance the most overlap with regions where fine-tuning increased attention to axiomatic IR features. Rarity sensitivity, document-query interaction, and several compositional features are highly correlated with gains in ranking performance. Our results support an interpretable, correlational account of how relevance-oriented behavior emerges during LoRA fine-tuning and point toward improved strategies for adapting rerankers.

title: Probe and Steer: Localizing and Mitigating Position Bias in Pairwise LLM-as-a-Judge
abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has emerged as a scalable alternative to costly human evaluation. However, LLM judges suffer from position bias in pairwise evaluation: the judge systematically favors the first or second candidate regardless of content, forcing practitioners to perform bidirectional evaluation at twice the inference cost. We propose Probe-and-Steer (PaS), a probe-localized, single-layer steering method for mitigating position bias. PaS localizes the bias-critical layer via a layer-wise logit-difference probe and trains a single residual-stream steering vector at that layer under a multi-objective loss, requiring minimal labeled data while keeping the LLM fully frozen. Through layer-wise probing across multiple model families, we uncover three qualitatively distinct bias-distribution patterns and delineate a clear applicability boundary for residual-stream steering. Experiments on an XSum-based dataset with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show that PaS delivers the largest gains among all compared methods, improving consistency by 22.9 pp and accuracy by 16.4 pp while shrinking positional asymmetry by 33\times (from 0.471 to 0.014), adding the lowest inference overhead at 4%.

title: PaveDSL: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Plan Specification and Verification for Multi-Agent Code Generation
abstract: Recent multi-agent code generation frameworks often verify natural-language plans by simulating their behavior on test cases before code generation. However, such verification remains unreliable because model hallucination may cause flawed plans to be incorrectly accepted. Inspired by neuro-symbolic reasoning, we propose PaveDSL, which transforms natural-language plans into structured designs expressed in a domain-specific language. Based on this structured representation, PaveDSL combines symbolic checks with neural inference to examine plans before code generation. Specifically, PaveDSL applies two complementary verifiers in parallel. The deterministic symbolic verifier checks structural constraints without invoking an LLM, while the agent verifier performs graph-guided semantic reasoning over the structured design. If verification fails, a repair agent localizes errors and revises the design before code generation. Experiments on multiple benchmarks with different LLMs show that PaveDSL consistently improves the performance of baseline code generation methods.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: LLMTrace: A Corpus for Classification and Fine-Grained Localization of AI-Written Text
abstract: The widespread use of human-like text from Large Language Models (LLMs) necessitates the development of robust detection systems. However, progress is limited by a critical lack of suitable training data; existing datasets are often generated with outdated models, are predominantly in English, and fail to address the increasingly common scenario of mixed human-AI authorship. Crucially, while some datasets address mixed authorship, none provide the character-level annotations required for the precise localization of AI-generated segments within a text. To address these gaps, we introduce LLMTrace, a new large-scale, bilingual (English and Russian) corpus for AI-generated text detection. Constructed using a diverse range of modern proprietary and open-source LLMs, our dataset is designed to support two key tasks: traditional full-text binary classification (human vs. AI) and AI-generated interval detection, facilitated by character-level annotations. We believe LLMTrace will serve as a vital resource for training and evaluating the next generation of more nuanced and practical AI detection models.

title: GATE: General Arabic Text Embedding for Enhanced Semantic Textual Similarity with Matryoshka Representation Learning and Hybrid Loss Training
abstract: Semantic textual similarity (STS) is central to retrieval, clustering, and semantic understanding, yet Arabic remains underserved by high-quality sentence-embedding models and evaluation resources. We introduce GATE, a compact family of Arabic sentence embedding models and a controlled study of Arabic-specific backbones, contrastive Matryoshka Representation Learning, dimensional truncation, and hybrid STS-NLI supervision. We evaluate the resulting models across Arabic semantic similarity, NLI, pair classification, sentence classification, clustering, retrieval, reranking, and dialectal semantic relatedness, against strong multilingual baselines including BGE-M3, Arctic-Embed-v2, and Qwen3-Embedding. Despite their 135M-parameter scale, GATE-family models are competitive with substantially larger multilingual encoders and achieve strong results on several native-Arabic semantic tasks. A three-annotator audit further finds high Arabic surface adequacy and 84.2% majority relation preservation for the translated supervision. The released checkpoints, data resources, and experimental artifacts support reproducible Arabic embedding research.

title: Kwai Summary Attention
abstract: Long-context capability has become increasingly critical for next-generation Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the quadratic time complexity of standard softmax attention introduces substantial computation and memory overhead as sequence length grows, limiting the scalability of LLMs in long-context scenarios. Beyond existing approaches such as linear recurrent architectures and KV-cache compression methods, we propose Kwai Summary Attention (KSA), a novel attention mechanism that reduces sequence modeling cost by compressing historical contexts into learnable summary tokens. Specifically, summary tokens are periodically inserted into the input sequence and interleaved with text tokens, partitioning the sequence into distinct chunks while enabling text tokens and summary tokens to operate under different attention scopes. This design preserves dense local expressiveness through full attention among neighboring text tokens, while modeling long-range dependencies efficiently via summary tokens. Empirical results demonstrate that hybrid-KSA consistently outperforms existing hybrid attention variants in long-context modeling. Moreover, KSA is fully orthogonal to GQA and MLA during inference, and combining KSA with these methods achieves up to 8x KV-cache compression while preserving model performance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SaToMe: Salience-Driven Token Merging for Omni-Capable Diffusion MLLMs
abstract: Omni-capable Diffusion multimodal large language models (Diffusion MLLMs) unify text-to-image (T2I) generation and image-to-text (I2T) understanding within one backbone, but at substantial cost on both fronts: visual tokens far outnumber surrounding text, and for T2I this per-step cost compounds across many denoising steps. Token merging has been studied separately in adjacent fields, yet training-free acceleration spanning T2I+I2T in one omni-capable Diffusion MLLM remains limited. We present SaToMe, a training-free token-merging method built around a local-deviation operator that we interpret as measuring local representational uniqueness. The denoising trajectory exposes two natural inputs to this operator: the state h and the update direction Δh. Their spreads behave very differently along the trajectory: state-salience spread is dynamic and identifies the active merging window, while update-salience masks are window-stable and serve as a single-step protection signal for cell-level structural content. T2I uses both signals; I2T, with no temporal axis, instantiates the same uniqueness criterion on the state alone, producing a single-pass additive merge. The same I2T form transfers directly to a separate I2T-only Diffusion MLLM with a different visual representation, supporting its applicability across these visual representations. SaToMe attains +20.14% T2I wall-clock speedup on LLaDA-o at 68% visual-token retention while largely preserving reported generation quality, +35.5% I2T wall-clock speedup on LLaDA-o, and +27.5% I2T speedup on LaViDa.

title: Skill Retrieval Augmentation for Agentic AI
abstract: Agentic AI systems powered by large language models are increasingly expected to solve capability-intensive tasks by using reusable external skills, which package instructions, tool-use procedures, executable code, and auxiliary resources. However, mainstream skill-based systems typically assume that available skills can be directly placed in the prompt. As skill libraries grow, this assumption becomes impractical: large corpora cannot be fully exposed to the model, while excessive candidate exposure can distract the agent and degrade skill selection. Therefore, scalable skill augmentation requires retrieving a small set of task-relevant skills from a large corpus before incorporating them into the agent’s context. We formulate this paradigm as Skill Retrieval Augmentation (SRA), where agents dynamically retrieve, incorporate, and apply reusable skills from large external corpora on demand. To systematically study SRA, we introduce SRA-Bench, which enables decomposed evaluation across three stages: skill retrieval, skill incorporation, and skill application. SRA-Bench contains 5,400 capability-intensive instances from six domains, 636 manually constructed gold skills, and a corpus of 26,262 skills. Experiments across multiple LLM and skill-use strategies show that SRA can consistently improve agent performance, but current agents struggle to realize this promise in practical pipelines. Specifically, they remain sensitive to distractor skills, lack need-aware skill loading, and often fail to translate relevant skills into correct task execution. Together, these results establish SRA as a distinct research problem and provide a foundation for developing scalable skill-augmented agents.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Ranking: Role-Specific Signals for Token-Budgeted SFT Data Selection
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a core stage in post-training general-purpose language models, but modern SFT training corpora are often large, heterogeneous mixtures, making data selection important under fixed token budgets. Simple ranking approaches can be informative yet insufficient: ranking alone does not determine how to allocate a fixed token budget across examples. We study the role-specific use of likelihood-derived signals for token-budgeted subset construction. An external instruction-tuned reference model computes response-side negative log-likelihood scores to rank training examples. We then combine this ranking with base model likelihood filtering to restrict the candidate region and response-side cosine filtering to reduce redundancy in the selected subset. In the OLMo fine-tuning setting studied here, ranking examples only by reference-model likelihood underperforms the random baseline, whereas the same ranking becomes more effective when combined with base model likelihood filtering and cosine-based redundancy control. Our results support viewing token-budgeted SFT data selection as a budget-allocation problem rather than only as an example-ranking problem.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Influence Guided Sampling for Domain Adaptation of Text Retrievers
abstract: General-purpose open-domain dense retrieval systems are usually trained with a large, eclectic mix of corpora and search tasks. How should these diverse corpora and tasks be sampled for training? Conventional approaches sample them uniformly, proportional to their instance population sizes, or depend on human-level expert supervision. It is well known that the training data sampling strategy can greatly impact model performance. However, how to find the optimal strategy has not been adequately studied in the context of embedding models. We propose **Inf-DDS**, a novel reinforcement learning–driven sampling framework that adaptively reweighs training datasets guided by influence-based reward signals and is much more lightweight w.r.t. GPU consumption. Our technique iteratively refines the sampling policy, prioritizing datasets that maximize model performance on a target development set. We evaluate the efficacy of our sampling strategy on a wide range of text retrieval tasks, demonstrating strong improvements in retrieval performance and better adaptation compared to existing gradient-based sampling methods, while also being 1.5\text{—}4\times cheaper in GPU compute. Our sampling strategy achieves a \mathbf{5.03} absolute NDCG@10 improvement while training the multilingual bge-m3 model and an absolute NDCG@10 improvement of \mathbf{0.94} while training all-MiniLM-L6-v2, even when starting from expert-assigned weights on a large pool of training datasets.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond the Explicit: A Bilingual Dataset for Dehumanization Detection in Social Media
abstract: Digital dehumanization, although a critical issue, remains largely overlooked within the field of computational linguistics and Natural Language Processing (NLP). To our best knowledge, this work presents the most comprehensive annotated bi-lingual dataset on dehumanization, with almost 16.000 instances (44% dehumanizing) that exists today and can serve as both a training resource for machine learning models and a benchmark for evaluating future dehumanization detection techniques. Our comparison of 15 methods shows that traditional hate speech detection approaches perform poorly on dehumanization detection, particularly for implicit forms. By leveraging our dataset in few-shot and fine-tuning settings, LLMs achieve comparable performance on implicit and explicit dehumanization and substantially outperform zero-shot baselines, with average gains of 39% and 65%, respectively. However, detection accuracy remains slightly lower for mechanistic than for animalistic dehumanization, the latter being the dominant focus of prior work.

title: Efficient Agentic Reinforcement Learning with On-Policy Intrinsic Knowledge Boundary Enhancement
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has proven effective for training LLM-based agents with external tool-use capabilities. However, we identify that agentic RL training induces increasing redundant tool calls and blurs the model’s intrinsic knowledge boundary, where the model fails to distinguish when tools are needed versus when parametric knowledge suffices. Existing solutions based on reward shaping create coarse-grained optimization targets that tend to incentivize indiscriminate tool-call suppression, leading to reward hacking. In this paper, we propose **AKBE** (**A**gentic **K**nowledge **B**oundary **E**nhancement), an on-policy method that dynamically probes the model’s intrinsic knowledge boundary through dual-path (with-tool and no-tool) rollouts during training. We define the knowledge boundary as the per-instance determination of whether tools are required and the minimum tool calls necessary. By comparing correctness across paths, AKBE categorizes trajectories and constructs targeted supervisory signals that guide efficient tool-use patterns for each question. These signals are integrated seamlessly into the agentic RL training loop. Experiments on seven QA benchmarks demonstrate that AKBE improves task accuracy by on average +1.85 and reduces tool calls by 18% over standard agentic RL, yielding 25% higher tool productivity without any accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Further analysis suggests its plug-and-play compatibility across different RL algorithms and the mechanism of each signal category.

title: Values Are Not Enough: Situational Modifiers Shape Moral Decisions in LLMs and Humans
abstract: Personal values alone cannot fully explain moral decisions. They are often treated as the main driver of moral choice, yet situational pressures can still shift actions when values are fixed. To study this effect, we introduce VISDA (Value-Informed Scenario-Driven Actions), a dataset of 80 binary moral scenarios across various themes. Keeping value profiles constant, we evaluate three open-weight LLMs (Gemma 4 31B, Qwen 2.5 32B, LLaMA 3.1 8B), a utility-based mathematical baseline over 95 Schwartz profiles, and humans for their decisions under modifiers. Each scenario is augmented with eight situational modifier axes designed to capture contextual pressures on decision-making. LLMs reverse decisions (flips) less frequently (2.03%-8.92%), with larger models showing greater sensitivity. In LLMs, authority and self-preservation modifiers drive most flips and remain statistically significant. Humans showed a pooled shift (12.36%) in their decisions. Humans prioritized stakes and affective modifiers, while LLMs overweight personal-cost modifiers. This work reveals axis-level misalignment between human and LLM sensitivity to situational moral factors.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: DisasterLex: An Expert Concept-to-Schema Knowledge Graph for Geospatial Reasoning in Disaster Analytics
abstract: Disasters are inevitable and increasingly costly, and effective response depends on querying structured tabular data: precise, information-dense records of hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and lifeline infrastructure that underpin disaster management. Current text-to-SQL methods enable natural-language access to such tables but transfer poorly to the disaster domain, where queries span heterogeneous geospatial schemas and require reasoning over causal relations. We introduce DisasterLex, a knowledge-graph-mediated framework that inserts an Expert Knowledge Graph (EKG) of curated concepts and typed causal edges between the user query and the database, bridged to schema by concept-to-table links. The orchestration runs four stages (identifying query entities, routing to the operational domain, planning over causal edges, and grounding the SQL), restricting the schema passed to the model at each step. We instantiate it on a disaster-analytics database (36 geospatial tables, 150 columns) with an EKG of 107 concepts, 117 causal edges, and 52 concept-to-schema links, evaluated on a 75-query test set. On all seven base models spanning proprietary and open-weight families, DisasterLex beats four state-of-the-art baselines (LightRAG, HippoRAG 2, ReFoRCE, CHESS) by 1.4\times to 2.75\times, with absolute scores of 1.65 to 3.56 (of 5.0). Error analysis shows baseline failures cluster in routing and multi-table SQL composition, the operations our orchestration explicitly addresses. Code, data, and the EKG artifact are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DisasterLex-3D64.

title: Mitigating New-Tail Collapse in Long-Tailed Class-Incremental Learning with CLIP
abstract: Pre-trained vision–language models such as CLIP provide strong priors for class-incremental learning (CIL), yet they degrade sharply under long-tailed class streams. We show that this degradation is not merely a byproduct of forgetting: in frozen-CLIP long-tailed CIL, newly introduced tail classes are disproportionately absorbed into previously learned old classes, a boundary-level failure we call new-tail collapse. We diagnose this failure with an old-new margin and analyze it through a boundary-risk view, where CLIP semantic overlap, sparse tail supervision, and old-class expansion jointly increase old-dominant violations. Motivated by this view, we propose Smooth Boundary-Risk Loss (SBRL), which estimates effective old rivals from CLIP’s vision-language geometry and suppresses their smooth old-side pressure against new-tail samples. MC-SMERG further consolidates task-wise adapters into a single efficient model. Across ImageNetSubset-LT, CIFAR100-LT, and Food101-LT, our method consistently outperforms strong CLIP-based CIL baselines and substantially reduces boundary violations in high-similarity, low-shot regimes.
