title: Where Do Apparent LLM Clinical Triage Failures Arise? Localizing the Multiple-Choice Format Effect
abstract: LLM evaluations using clinician-authored triage vignettes have reported substantial under-triage under constrained multiple-choice testing. Yet model performance on the same clinical cases can change when responses are generated in free text. We test whether this format effect appears while the case is processed or when clinical information is mapped to the final answer. Using sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features in Gemma 3 4B/12B IT and Qwen3-8B, we find that medical features fire on the shared clinical narrative under both formats but are inactive at the multiple-choice decision token. Emergency-tier information is linearly decodable from vignette representations with ROC-AUC 0.95–1.00 under both formats, with no significant format difference, but is attenuated at the decision token. Natural-language autoencoder verbalization and top-feature characterization associate that token with the multiple-choice scaffold. In a direct linear projection, the identified medical features contribute zero, whereas scaffold-peaking features account for over 91% of unsigned attribution in both Gemma models. Behaviorally, whether multiple choice improves or worsens performance depends on the model. Option-order shuffles rule out simple positional bias, and cases that differ between formats are usually one severity tier apart. Together, these findings place the strongest correlates of the format effect at answer selection while leaving open whether unmeasured clinical representations also differ.

title: Beyond Binary: Turning Partial Success into Dense Verifiable Rewards for Reinforcement Learning in Code Generation
abstract: Effective reward design is a central challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL) for code generation. Mainstream test-suite-level outcome rewards enforce functional correctness but induce sparsity, while external Reward Models (RMs) provide dense supervision at the cost of misalignment and additional overhead. Since code evaluation naturally yields multiple test-case-level outcomes, partial success—passing a subset of test cases—offers an intrinsic, verifiable source of dense supervision. In this paper, we propose VeRPO (Verifiable Dense Reward Policy Optimization), an RL framework that systematically turns verifiable partial success into reliable dense rewards. We analyze partial-success rewards using a weighted sum formulation, theoretically identifying a critical cardinality bias that causes policy updates to disproportionately favor gains from easy-test successes over progress on frontier tests. Based on this, VeRPO introduces a dynamic, density-calibrated local reward that explicitly corrects this bias and provides robust dense supervision from partial success. To enhance alignment with end-to-end functional correctness, VeRPO further integrates the local dense reward with global execution outcomes. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and settings demonstrate that VeRPO outperforms outcome-driven and RM-based baselines, achieving up to +8.83 pass@1 gain with negligible time cost (< 0.02%) and zero GPU memory overhead.

title: Binned Relative Policy Optimization towards Efficient Thinking of VLMs
abstract: Recent VLMs improve multimodal reasoning by generating explicit chains of thought, but often overthink with redundant reasoning. Although conventional length penalties mitigate this redundancy, they rely on coarse global rewards that fail to discern intermediate process quality or adapt to task complexity. To address this dilemma, we propose Binned Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO), a training-efficient framework that enables non-trivial process-level evaluation without introducing costly process reward models. Specifically, BRPO leverages high entropy lexical markers to segment reasoning trajectories into discrete intermediate prefixes, evaluating their problem-solving potential through forced answer completions. Building on this, we introduce Bin Normalization along with a length-aware adjustment to map prefixes into process bins, dynamically calibrating rewards and regulating length constraints based on reasoning stages and visual complexity. Experiments on six multimodal math benchmarks show that our method improves both accuracy and efficiency: on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it raises average accuracy from 47.8% to 53.6% while reducing the average response length by 39.0%.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: S2J: Bridging the Gap Between Solving and Judging Ability in Generative Reward Models
abstract: With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), generative reward models (GRMs) have been widely adopted for reward modeling and evaluation. Previous studies have primarily focused on training specialized GRMs by optimizing them on preference datasets with the judgment correctness as supervision. While it’s widely accepted that GRMs with stronger problem-solving capabilities typically exhibit superior judgment abilities, we first identify a significant solve-to-judge gap when examining individual queries. Specifically, the solve-to-judge gap refers to the phenomenon where GRMs struggle to make correct judgments on some queries (14%-37%), despite being fully capable of solving them. In this paper, we propose the Solve-to-Judge (S2J) approach to address this problem. Specifically, S2J simultaneously leverages both the solving and judging capabilities on a single GRM’s output for supervision, explicitly linking the GRM’s problem-solving and evaluation abilities during model optimization, thereby narrowing the gap. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that S2J effectively reduces the solve-to-judge gap by 16.2%, thereby enhancing the model’s judgment performance by 5.8%. Notably, S2J achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance among GRMs built on the same base model while utilizing a significantly smaller training dataset.

title: Progressive Behavioral Drift through Compression Valleys in Large Language Models
abstract: We show that attention sinks and compression valleys create a vulnerable region in decoder-only Transformers, where small activation perturbations can be amplified through the autoregressive trajectory. Based on this, we propose Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a progressive activation-space attack that anchors perturbations at the beginning-of-sequence token and adaptively reinforces them at sensitive layers and tokens. Instead of forcing an abrupt behavioral change, SSS induces a staged drift, making outputs gradually shift toward the target behavior while remaining fluent and benign-looking in early generations. Across multiple open-weight models and four behavioral axes, SSS achieves high attack success, preserves coherence, and causes negligible degradation to general capabilities. These results show that attention sinks and compression valleys are not merely mechanistic features; rather, they expose exploitable amplification mechanisms that can be treated as hidden-state weaknesses for activation-space attacks in white-box and supply-chain LLM deployments.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Towards Faithful and Controllable Personalization via Critique-Post-Edit Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning has driven the largest post-training gains on tasks with verifiable rewards, such as code and math. Extending this success to subjective tasks remains difficult: good responses must satisfy multiple soft criteria simultaneously, and no scalar reward can indicate which aspect of a response should improve. Personalization is a clear instance of this. A personalized response must balance helpfulness, user-specific relevance, and naturalness, yet standard verifiers cannot localize which specific dimension needs improvement. In this regime, supervised fine-tuning quickly saturates, and PPO with Bradley-Terry reward models is prone to reward hacking, especially via length bias, producing verbose or superficially personalized responses. We propose Critique-Post-Edit, an RL framework that combines (1) a personalized Generative Reward Model (GRM) producing multi-dimensional scores and natural-language critiques, and (2) a critique-guided editing step that turns feedback into nearby alternative responses for policy learning. The reward signal stays scalar; our contribution is to use personalized critiques to construct more informative local alternatives (responses close to the on-policy rollout in edit distance) during training. Under length-controlled evaluation, Critique-Post-Edit improves over PPO by 11.0 and 11.6 win-rate points on Qwen2.5-7B and 14B models, respectively. Notably, the 14B model matches or outperforms GPT-4.1 on the evaluated benchmarks. A static mechanism study further shows that critique-guided edits stay more local than extra rollouts and shift scores more favorably than generic rewrites. All of our experiments are on personalization; systematic evaluation on other subjective tasks is left to future work.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TopoCurate: Modeling Interaction Topology for Tool-Use Agent Training
abstract: Training tool-use agents typically relies on outcome-based filtering: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on successful trajectories and Reinforcement Learning (RL) on pass-rate-selected tasks. However, this paradigm ignores interaction dynamics—successful trajectories may lack error recovery or exhibit redundancy, while pass rates fail to distinguish structurally informative tasks from trivial ones. To bridge this gap, we propose TopoCurate, an interaction-aware framework that shifts the paradigm from linear outcome filtering to topological interaction modeling. By projecting multi-trial rollouts into a unified semantic quotient topology within the same task, we construct a structured manifold that explicitly captures the divergence between success and failure pathways across tool invocations and environmental responses. Leveraging this representation, we introduce a dual-selection mechanism: for SFT, we prioritize trajectories demonstrating reflective recovery, semantic efficiency, and strategic diversity to mitigate covariate shift and mode collapse; for RL, we select tasks with high error branch ratios and strategic heterogeneity, maximizing gradient Signal-to-Noise Ratio to address vanishing signals in sparse-reward settings. Evaluations on BFCLv3 and Tau2 Bench show that TopoCurate achieves consistent gains of 4.2% (SFT) and 6.9% (RL) over state-of-the-art baselines.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Selective Knowledge Edit Reversal via Gated Singular Vector Shrinkage
abstract: Knowledge editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in large language models. However, malicious edits may introduce safety risks, making it necessary to reverse undesirable editing effects. Existing reversal methods for parameter-modifying edits mainly focus on global removal, which may also erase beneficial edits that should be preserved. In this paper, we study selective reversal of edited knowledge, where the goal is to reverse targeted edited facts while preserving the remaining edited facts. Based on the hypothesis that each edit is sparsely encoded within the dominant subspace of the edited matrix, we propose a spectral-based reversal framework that locates edit-sensitive components within the dominant singular subspace of edited weights. Experiments across multiple settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in reversing selected edits while preserving unrelated edited facts. These results suggest that different edits are sparsely encoded within dominant singular components and can be separable when the number of edits is moderate, making selective spectral reversal a promising direction for locating edit-specific components and repairing edited language models.

title: Text-to-SQL Benchmarks Toward Enterprise Realities: Under Massive Scopes, Complex Schemas and Scattered Knowledge
abstract: Existing Text-to-SQL benchmarks remain idealized compared with enterprise scenarios, which require massive query scopes, complex schemas, and scattered external knowledge. We present BIRD-Ent and Spider-Ent, two enterprise-oriented benchmarks constructed via a refinement framework, together with Dual-Retrieval-Augmented-Generation (DRAG) Text-to-SQL, which formalizes table-schema and knowledge retrieval before SQL generation. The benchmarks feature over 4,000 columns per query and, for BIRD-Ent, documents totaling 1.5M tokens. Evaluation on state-of-the-art models shows sharp drops, with only 39.1% EX on BIRD-Ent and 60.5% EX on Spider-Ent. These results establish the Ent-series as a discriminative testbed for structurally robust and retrieval-aware Text-to-SQL.

title: Full-Distribution Self-Distillation for Optimizing Soft Latent Reasoning
abstract: Soft latent reasoning extends chain-of-thought reasoning beyond discrete token sequences by using continuous concept tokens. However, effectively training models in this space remains challenging: conventional reinforcement learning methods mainly optimize sampled rollout-action likelihoods and therefore underuse the full distributions produced during soft rollouts. We propose **Full-Distribution Self-Distillation (FDSD)**, an off-policy training framework that treats stochastic soft rollout distributions as dense pseudo-labels. FDSD aligns the current model distribution with advantage-weighted rollout targets via KL minimization and importance correction, enabling the model to learn from the full rollout distribution rather than only from sampled-action likelihoods. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH-500, OlympiadBench, and out-of-domain benchmarks show that FDSD achieves consistent average improvements in mathematical reasoning across model scales while preserving OOD generalization, with only modest computational overhead. These results suggest that full-distribution alignment is a promising training direction for soft latent reasoning.

title: Anom3W: A Unified Benchmark for Video Anomaly Grounding and Understanding
abstract: Understanding anomalies in real-world videos requires reasoning about when events occur, where they happen, and what actions unfold. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ignore one or more of these dimensions, making it difficult to evaluate whether multimodal large models (MLLMs) truly understand abnormal events beyond simple detection. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{Anom3W}, a benchmark designed to evaluate MLLMs across \textbf{temporal, spatial, and semantic dimensions}. Our semi-automatic pipeline consolidates heterogeneous anomaly resources into verified spatio-temporal annotations, enabling rigorous, reasoning-oriented evaluation. By treating spatial boxes and tubes as evidence cues, Anom3W challenges models to reason about entities, locations, and behaviors, rather than merely flag anomalies. Experiments demonstrate that even state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle, highlighting the critical importance of spatial grounding and semantic understanding. Anom3W establishes a new standard for interpretable, context-aware video anomaly reasoning.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Factorized Soft Prompts with Inference-Time Latent Control for LLM Personalization
abstract: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) requires reflecting stable user preferences while adapting their expression to each target context. Soft-prompt personalization has become a practical route to this goal, but existing methods produce soft prompts in which stable preferences, target-induced content, and context-dependent expression are bundled into an entangled conditioning signal without separately addressable components, leaving inference with no principled space to intervene on individual aspects of personalization. We propose Factorized soft prompts with Latent Control (FaLCon), an LLM personalization framework built on two coupled stages. First, factorized soft prompts replace this entangled conditioning with a set of separately addressable preference factors, forming a structured control interface. Second, inference-time latent control treats the resulting factor weights as a continuous action space and adapts them per instance from teacher-forced likelihood feedback, keeping the LLM frozen and updating only a low-dimensional factor-weight posterior without back-propagating through the LLM. Experiments on multiple personalized generation tasks reveal that FaLCon consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating the individual necessity and joint effectiveness of the structured interface and the inference-time controller.

title: Refinement Provenance Inference: Detecting LLM-Refined Training Prompts from Model Behavior
abstract: Instruction tuning increasingly relies on LLM-based prompt refinement, where prompts in the training corpus are selectively rewritten by an external refiner to improve clarity and instruction alignment. This motivates an instance-level audit problem: for a fine-tuned model and a training prompt–response pair, can we infer whether the model was trained on the original prompt or its LLM-refined version within a mixed corpus? This matters for dataset governance and dispute resolution when training data are contested. However, it is non-trivial in practice: refined and raw instances are interleaved in the training corpus with unknown, source-dependent mixture ratios, making it harder to develop provenance methods that generalize across models and training setups. In this paper, we formalize this audit task as Refinement Provenance Inference (RPI) and show that prompt refinement yields stable, detectable shifts in teacher-forced token distributions, even when semantic differences are not obvious. Building on this phenomenon, we propose RePro, a logit-based provenance framework that fuses teacher-forced likelihood features with logit-ranking signals. During training, RePro learns a transferable representation via shadow fine-tuning, and uses a lightweight linear head to infer provenance on unseen victims without training-data access. Empirically, RePro consistently attains strong performance and transfers well across refiners, suggesting that it exploits refiner-agnostic distribution shifts rather than rewrite-style artifacts.

title: Surveying Representation Collapse in Pretrained Models of American Sign Language
abstract: The American Sign Language (ASL) lexicon contains heterogeneous sign types, including established signed words, neologisms, ad-hoc depictions of real-world phenomena, and fingerspelled words. Productions within each type exhibit unique phonotactics and substantial variability, potentially confounding models pretrained on downstream ASL tasks. To survey the capacity for representation collapse, we isolate and annotate 14 types of ASL productions as they appear in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) educational content. We then probe seven pretrained models’ latent representations of the annotated clips, reporting collapse metrics with respect to domain, sign type, and meaning. Our findings show that out-of-distribution signs are more frequent in STEM content, and that pretrained models lose information about their visual and semantic contents in varing ways. Among the tested models, those which encoded the phonological properties of signs generalized to STEM data more effectively, while English- and gesture-based models can exhibit more brittleness. Future work can design interventions to mitigate the kinds of collapse documented here or extend this survey by evaluating additional models and datasets.

title: EYELIGNR: Aligning Gaze and Text via Contrastive Learning for Improved Reading Scanpath Prediction
abstract: Modeling the interaction between gaze dynamics and linguistic structure remains a central challenge in scanpath prediction. Existing approaches either incorporate linguistic information in ways that do not fully respect the temporal progression of reading, or ignore linguistic structure altogether. Their effectiveness is further limited by the scarcity and heterogeneity of available eye-tracking data. To address these issues, we introduce EYELIGNR, a framework for spatiotemporal scanpath prediction that integrates linguistic information at the representation level. EYELIGNR conditions language representations on fixation order and aligns gaze and text within a shared embedding space through contrastive learning. Experiments on five reading corpora show that EYELIGNR generalizes effectively across reading conditions, improving over prior state of the art on multiple scanpath metrics (e.g., up to NLD ~57%, NLL ~27%, and FLA ~59%).
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: HiDet: Hierarchical AI Text Detection via Coarse Filtering and Multi-Grained Contrastive Learning
abstract: Humanizing methods of AI-generated texts are emerging, which leads to severe performance degradation of current AI text detectors. Most existing detectors are struggling to ensure consistent performance in the huge span from detecting simple AI texts to detecting AI texts humanized in various ways. Targetedly, we propose HiDet, which contains coarse module and subdivision module to give AI texts a double check. We decouple the complete detection process into simple sample detection and difficult sample detection, the coarse module of HiDet filters out simple samples, while hard-to-detect samples like humanized AI texts will be carefully discriminated through the subdivision module which applies a multi-grained contrastive learning strategy. This hierarchical framework makes up for the loophole that humanized AI texts can successfully escape the traditional detector after a single detection, and shows excellent robustness in the task of detecting humanized AI texts. Meanwhile, our framework is flexiable, the subdivision module can be deployed separately on the existing detector as a plug-and-play patch to tremendously improve their performance when facing large-scale humanized AI texts. We hope our work can inspire new sparks in the field of AI-generated text detection.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Mind the Motions: Benchmarking Theory-of-Mind in Everyday Body Language
abstract: Our ability to interpret others’ mental states through nonverbal cues (NVCs) is fundamental to our survival and social cohesion. While existing Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmarks have primarily focused on false-belief tasks and reasoning with asymmetric information, they overlook other mental states beyond belief and the rich tapestry of human nonverbal communication. We present Motion2Mind a framework for evaluating the ToM capabilities of machines in interpreting NVCs. Leveraging an expert-curated body-language reference as a knowledge base, we build Motion2Mind, a carefully curated video dataset with fine-grained nonverbal cue annotations paired with manually verified psychological interpretations. It encompasses 222 types of nonverbal cues and 397 mind states. Our evaluation reveals that current AI systems struggle significantly with NVC interpretation, exhibiting not only a substantial performance gap in Detection, as well as patterns of over-interpretation in Explanation compared to human annotators.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: FAIR-Eval: Reliable and Efficient Adaptive Benchmarking for Large Language Models
abstract: Evaluating large language models typically requires thousands of benchmark items, making the process expensive and increasingly impractical. Existing protocols rely on average accuracy over fixed item sets, treating all items as equally informative—yet many items are too easy or too hard to distinguish between models, making evaluation both wasteful and imprecise. Item Response Theory (IRT) with Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) offers a principled alternative—separately estimating model ability and item difficulty, then adaptively selecting the most informative items. However, practical deployment is bottlenecked by costly item calibration, and standard greedy selection causes severe over-exposure of frequently picked items while leaving the rest of the bank under-utilized, which risks data contamination over time. We propose FAIR-Eval with two components: Feature-Driven Calibration (FDC), which jointly learns item parameters from text features and sparse responses, enabling low-cost bank expansion requiring only minimal model responses; and Maximum Fisher Information Plus (MFI+), which counteracts greedy selection by incorporating exposure control, while simultaneously enforcing difficulty coverage and domain diversity to systematically activate under-utilized items. On a 6,796-item bank (193 calibration models, 50 held-out), FAIR-Eval achieves Pearson r = 0.9882 and Spearman \rho = 0.9828 against full evaluation using around 3% of items. Crucially, it broadens difficulty coverage from 60.0% to 68.7%, achieving a more comprehensive and robust assessment of model capabilities with minimal test length.

title: RubricReviewer: From Direct Critique to Rubric-Driven Review via Agentic Evidence Synthesis and Human-Aligned Generation
abstract: Peer review at major venues is under unprecedented submission pressure, motivating the use of large language models (LLMs) as review assistants. Existing LLM-based reviewers, however, face two structural limitations. First, they map manuscripts directly to reviews, leaving the underlying rubric implicit and entangling its derivation with the judgement. Second, the prevailing paradigms each capture only half of a good review: training-free agents gather broad evidence but produce undirected critiques, while training-based reviewers inherit human discriminative judgement together with its noise and uneven coverage. We introduce RubricReviewer, a fully rubric-driven framework that addresses both limitations. It makes rubric generation an explicit intermediate step, so that both review generation and the final assessment are conditioned on paper-adaptive rubrics. It further combines a training-free agent Scout that gathers external evidence with a human-aligned trained model Aligner that consumes this evidence, fusing the strengths of both supervision sources. Experiments on real-world submissions show that RubricReviewer produces reviews that are markedly more comprehensive and more discriminative than prior systems, and exhibits the strongest robustness against adversarial prompt-injection attacks. Ablation studies further confirm the necessity of each component.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PersuaRL: Reinforcement Learning-Driven Multi-Expert Selection for Persuasive Dialogue Generation in Insurance
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are revolutionizing digital communication by powering conversational agents deployed across domains such as customer service, digital sales, and insurance. These agents, built on LLMs, can understand user input, retrieve relevant information, and generate coherent responses. However, while they excel at factual communication, they often lack the ability to engage in truly persuasive, context-sensitive dialogue, especially in domains like insurance, where trust and clarity are critical. Building on this need within the insurance domain, our work focuses on improving the persuasiveness of digital agents, aka LLMs. To support this, we introduce InsureDial, a Persuasive Insurance Dialogue dataset, designed to capture the nuances of persuasive communication specific to motor insurance interactions. We introduce PersuaRL, a reinforcement learning–based framework that equips LLM-driven dialogue agents with the ability to adaptively explore, select, and coordinate strategies across multiple expert modules, guided by the evolving dialogue context, to achieve more effective persuasion. We conduct extensive automatic human and qualitative evaluations on two benchmark persuasion dialogue datasets, including our InsureDial. Our evaluations consistently demonstrate that PersuaRL outperforms baseline, generating contextually appropriate and highly persuasive responses.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Filter by Quality, Stop by Difficulty: Confidence-Aware Self-Consistency with Adaptive Early Stopping
abstract: Self-consistency improves LLM reasoning by majority voting over multiple sampled solutions, but always exhausts the sampling budget and trusts every solution equally. Early-stopping methods cut token cost substantially via convergence monitoring. However, deciding when to stop cannot change what is voted on, so they save tokens without meaningfully improving accuracy. We introduce CASE (Confidence-Aware Self-consistency with Adaptive Early stopping), which improves both accuracy and efficiency by leveraging token-level confidence normalized at two scales: within-problem to filter low-quality solutions and weight survivors, and cross-problem to adapt the stopping threshold to problem difficulty. Across 5 models and 6 benchmarks, CASE simultaneously saves 85% of tokens and improves accuracy by +2.24pp over majority voting, outperforming every early-stopping baseline on both accuracy and efficiency. Component and role-swap analyses confirm that filtering and weighting are complementary and the two normalization scales are non-interchangeable.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Routing Before Looking: Query-Adaptive Evidence Acquisition for Long-form Video Understanding
abstract: Long-form video understanding remains challenging for video agents due to the mismatch between query demands and evidence acquisition strategies. Although recent planning-before-perception methods outperform query-agnostic pipelines, they often rely on a single dominant strategy, either generation-based strategy or retrieval-based strategy, limiting their ability to handle diverse query demands. We propose **Route2Look**, a lightweight and model-agnostic framework for query-adaptive evidence acquisition in long-form video understanding. Route2Look operates in a Route-Look-Memorize loop with three tools: Global Browse for holistic context, Temporal Ground for explicit temporal cues, and Semantic Retrieve for semantic search. The core component is a routing policy that dynamically selects evidence acquisition tools based on the query. To build this policy, Route2Look adopts a two-stage design: first distilling the routing skill from differential contrastive analysis between generation-based and retrieval-based trajectories, and then applying the distilled skill with hard routing rules and continue-or-stop criteria during inference. Experiments on challenging long-video benchmarks show that Route2Look achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining strong frame efficiency across datasets and query types. Oracle routing analysis further reveals the potential of query-adaptive evidence acquisition for future long-form video understanding.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Skill-CDPO: Evolving Agent Tool-Use via Critical Step Preference Optimization
abstract: Compact open-source language models lag behind their larger counterparts in agentic tool-use reliability, yet standard remedies face fundamental obstacles: supervised fine-tuning suffers from exposure bias, while reinforcement learning is hampered by sparse credit assignment over long tool-interaction trajectories. We introduce Skill-CDPO, a progressive framework that first acquires tool-use skills at inference time through static tool analysis and dynamic strategy refinement, then distills the resulting error-correction signals into parameter updates via Critical Step DPO (CDPO). CDPO identifies the specific trajectory steps where model capability is the bottleneck—through rollout divergence between a local policy and an expert model—and constructs distributional preference pairs from all cross-group rollouts at those steps, weighted by both step-level criticality and pair-level score gaps. This provides dense, fine-grained supervision without requiring a process reward model. We evaluate Skill-CDPO on three medical agent benchmarks—PubMed Search (a new PubMed-based deep research benchmark we contribute), CureBench, and MedBrowseComp—using an 8B-parameter deep research model. Skill-CDPO substantially outperforms SFT and trajectory-level DPO baselines and achieves competitive or superior performance compared to GPT-5.2 on retrieval-intensive tasks. Our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Skill-CDPO-BF51.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Learning When to Think in Latent Visual Space: Reasoning Mode Adaptive Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Latent Visual Reasoning (LVR) unfolds reasoning in a continuous visual embedding space, markedly improving Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on vision-intensive tasks. However, our experiments reveal a hidden cost: LVR inevitably undermines VLMs’ strong textual reasoning ability, causing substantial degradation on logic-intensive tasks. This motivates us to unify both reasoning modes within a single VLM that adaptively selects the appropriate one. We propose MoLaT (Mixture of Latent and Textual Reasoning), a novel method that trains VLMs via reinforcement learning (RL) to select LVR and text-only reasoning adaptively. MoLaT is trained in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning endows the VLM with a dual-mode capability using mixed CoT data. Then, MoLaT introduces two complementary designs: 1) The mode-adaptive advantage decouples the mode-selection signal from per-rollout correctness reward at the token level: mode-selection tokens receive dedicated cross-mode gradients, while content tokens retain the group-relative advantage. 2) The entropy-modulated advantage weight uses sequence-level entropy as a difficulty proxy, modulating signal strength to prevent premature mode commitment. Experiments confirm that MoLaT improves both vision-intensive and logic-intensive abilities, validating adaptive mode selection as key to general-purpose reasoning VLMs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MMLDSum-LLM: Multimodal Long-Document Summarization with Visual-Alignment and Keyword-Aware
abstract: Multimodal long documents are core carriers of professional knowledge, where critical evidence is sparsely distributed across paragraphs and modalities. This easily causes key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in summarization by multimodal LLMs. These issues stem from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment. To address this, we introduce MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. We further propose MMLDSum-LLM, a reproducible two-stage training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by GRPO with a multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control). Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol — including LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE — demonstrate that our approach significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Relational Over-Regularization: Graph-Based AI-Generated Text Detection via Sentence Transition Deviation
abstract: Detecting AI-generated text (AIGT) remains challenging because existing approaches rely on token-level statistical signals or independent stylometric features, causing them to overfit to specific generators and fail under distribution shift. We identify a structural signal at the sentence-pair level: LLMs produce inter-sentence transition variance that deviates from human writing through inflated variance driven by recurring similarity bursts at paragraph boundaries and templated transitions. We formalize this as Relational Over-Regularization (ROR) and validate it across four benchmarks (p < 0.001). To exploit this signal, we propose the Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG), a graph-based framework that encodes positional, sequential, semantic, and transition deviation signals as learnable GNN edge features. We emphasize that the core contribution is this relational problem formulation itself, not the GNN architecture - CSFG is one concrete instantiation for operationalizing ROR. The per-edge signed deviation \delta_{ij} operationalizes ROR without hand-crafted thresholds and acts as a false-positive calibrator. CSFG achieves 97.14% accuracy under binary detection, outperforming the strongest graph-based baseline by 11.14 pp, with a false-positive rate of 1.57% and robust generalization to unseen LLMs in the inflated-variance regime; detection degrades for generators whose transition variance falls at or below the human baseline.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Directional Drift in Arithmetic Reasoning: How Comparative Cues Steer LLM Predictions
abstract: Arithmetic tasks are widely used to evaluate LLM reasoning because they provide objective truth. Yet accuracy alone cannot distinguish whether prompt sensitivity reflects random prediction instability or systematic semantic bias. We study this question in comparative arithmetic, where semantically equivalent framings can cue directional outcomes such as more, less, or equal. We introduce MathComp, a balanced benchmark of 10,800 controlled comparison problems spanning multiple framing conditions and answer formats. Across ten LLMs, semantically equivalent comparative cues systematically bias predictions toward cued outcomes even when it is numerically incorrect. Notably, this effect persists even when cue words are removed from the answer options, suggesting that framing bias reflects broader semantic steering rather than simple label copying. Chain-of-thought reasoning mitigates the effect substantially, but residual directional drift remains. These findings suggest that prompt sensitivity in arithmetic reasoning can exhibit structured semantic bias toward linguistically cued outcomes, with implications for robustness evaluation and benchmark design.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation
abstract: Evaluating multi-turn conversational systems remains a fundamental challenge. Conventional pipelines rely on manual rubrics and fixed context, a static approach that limits coverage and fails to capture emergent dialogue behaviors. To address this, we introduce CoReflect (A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation), which unifies dialogue simulation and evaluation into an adaptive, iterative process. CoReflect employs a conversation planner that generates structured templates to guide a user simulator through diverse, goal-directed dialogues. Subsequently, a reflective analyzer processes these dialogues to identify systematic behavioral patterns and automatically refine the evaluation rubrics. Crucially, the insights from the conversation analysis are fed back into the planner to update conversation templates for subsequent iterations. This co-evolution loop ensures that the complexity of test cases and the diagnostic precision of rubrics improve in tandem. By minimizing human intervention, CoReflect provides a scalable and self-refining methodology that allows evaluation protocols to adapt alongside the rapidly advancing capabilities of dialogue models.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Active Adaptation, Not Static Defense: Temporal Dynamics of Preventative Steering in Adversarial Fine-Tuning
abstract: Large language models remain fragile against malicious fine-tuning, motivating training-time defenses against harmful persona drift. Preventative Steering injects undesirable-trait persona vectors during fine-tuning and removes them at evaluation time, yet the mechanism behind its lasting protection remains unclear. Analyzing its temporal optimization dynamics, we find that the defense emerges from an early compensatory adaptation phase followed by a steady-state phase where the corrective signal decays; in parameter space, attention output projections emerge as the dominant residual-write route for defensive updates. Through Intervention Delta Preservation (IDP) and IDP Continuation experiments, we further show that preserving or reinjecting the weight offset fails to maintain protection, indicating that preventative steering relies on active adaptation rather than a static defense. Motivated by this finding, we propose Progressive Intensity Scheduling (PIS), which starts with a moderate injection strength and increases it after static-strength alignment begins to decay. Across the evaluated Qwen2.5 and Gemma-3 models, PIS improves safety robustness over static-strength steering while reducing harmful trait expression.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Benchmark Is Not the Construct: Toward Distribution-Based Evaluation in NLP
abstract: Current NLP evaluation often treats a scalar score on a fixed benchmark dataset as if it directly measured the construct the benchmark is intended to represent. This Measurement-as-Instance paradigm is appropriate for a fixed evaluation configuration, but can suppress uncertainty, variance, and robustness when a single result is used to support broader capability or generalisation claims. In this position paper, we argue for extending static evaluation with Measurement-as-Distribution: a structured evaluation procedure involving principled data generation, validated perturbations, repeated evaluation, and distributional reporting. The framework is configurable: the amount of distributional evidence required should scale with the strength and breadth of the claims being made. We synthesise existing robustness, dynamic-evaluation, prompt-sensitivity, and uncertainty-reporting practices into a general measurement-theoretic framework for distribution-based NLP evaluation and provide a call to action for more rigorous reporting. Using the protocol \mathcal{P} = (\mathcal{C}, G, \Phi, E, R), we identify three risks of relying exclusively on fixed scalar evaluation and derive implications for peer review, benchmark publication, leaderboard reporting, and computational cost. Two case studies demonstrate feasibility: a SQuAD evaluation of 14 models reveals modest but axis-specific performance changes and stable overall rankings with uncertainty-aware comparisons, while a verifier-backed Knights-and-Knaves study illustrates how perturbations of rigid logical tasks can be generated and validated formally.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Charts Deceive Web Agents: A Paired Benchmark for Misleading Visualization-Grounded Tasks
abstract: Web agents increasingly browse, interpret, and act on web content on behalf of users. In many realistic workflows, however, the visual evidence they consume is not neutral: charts and dashboards can be misleading, shaping judgments without issuing any explicit malicious instruction. Unlike chart question answering, Web Agents treat charts as intermediate evidence whose misinterpretation can propagate into concrete downstream actions — a reliability risk that remains underexplored. We introduce MisVisAgentBench, the first paired executable benchmark for evaluating how misleading visualizations affect Web Agent execution. It comprises 280 task instances in matched clean–misleading pairs that differ only in chart evidence. We further provide a diagnostic framework that isolates misleading-induced failures from baseline task difficulty and captures execution-level effects such as extra browsing steps and decision hesitation. Across eleven vision-language Web Agents, replacing clean charts with misleading counterparts nearly halves the average task success rate, an absolute drop exceeding 34 percentage points. Moreover, these failures predominantly follow the targeted misleading action branch, suggesting that deceptive charts systematically redirect rather than randomly disrupt agent decisions. These results reveal that visualization robustness is a critical yet understudied dimension of Web Agent safety and reliability.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Moral Safety in LLMs: Exposing Performative Compliance with Puzzled Cues
abstract: As large language models take on morally consequential roles in healthcare, legal, and hiring contexts, verifying that their ethical behavior is genuine rather than superficial becomes essential. We show that current fairness evaluations substantially overestimate moral safety. Models judged fair when demographic identity is explicitly labeled become measurably less fair when the same identity must be inferred — a pattern we term performative compliance: safety behavior contingent on surface-level evaluation signals rather than internalized fairness principles. We introduce a cue-variation methodology that holds moral content fixed while varying only whether demographic identity is stated or must be inferred, and apply it to 14 models across 100 everyday dilemmas spanning 3 genders and 5 races. Hiding the label leaves decisions that benefit the described individual unchanged (+0.9pp) while raising decisions that harm them by +4.4pp. This asymmetry persists even when models correctly infer the demographic, ruling out attribution error. We propose the Direct vs Puzzled gap as a model-agnostic robustness metric that requires no new annotation, changes model safety rankings, and can be adopted by any existing fairness evaluation to separate genuine from performative moral safety. We argue that fairness evaluations that omit cue-variation measure surface compliance, not moral robustness, and should not ground deployment decisions in high-stakes settings.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Reliability-Calibrated Guidance for Few-Step Categorical Flow-Map Text Generation
abstract: Few-step flow-map guidance provides an efficient way to steer generation without retraining, but its updates are defined in a continuous or relaxed state space. In categorical text generation, however, the final output is determined by simplex-constrained token distributions and hard decoding. Under low NFE, where each update induces a relatively large finite displacement, this continuous-to-discrete mismatch can make terminal reward guidance unreliable, causing overshoot, reward–quality conflict, saturation, or poor transfer from relaxed reward gains to decoded tokens.We present Reliability-Calibrated Flow Guidance (RCFG), a sampling-time reliability-calibration framework for terminal reward pullback in few-step categorical flow maps. Rather than replacing the underlying guidance primitive, RCFG calibrates its magnitude and direction according to transition scale, reward saturation, local reward–quality conflict, and categorical endpoint structure. Experiments on LM1B and Text8 show more favorable aggregate control–likelihood operating points after calibration: on LM1B, RCFG maintains or improves verifier Reward and Target while reducing NLL and PPL relative to terminal reward-pullback guidance, while Text8 shows a modest aggregate improvement in lexical-control balance. Code and reproduction instructions are available at: https://github.com/ZionLau/RCFG
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: APEX-EM: Non-Parametric Online Learning for Autonomous Agents via Structured Procedural-Episodic Experience Replay
abstract: LLM agents rerun full reasoning for every task, even one they solved moments earlier. We introduce APEX-EM, a non-parametric experience memory that stores complete procedural-episodic traces in a typed Procedural Knowledge Graph (PKG) and retrieves them through three channels: semantic search, structural-signature matching over abstract operation sequences, and graph traversal. A Plan-Retrieve-Generate-Iterate-Ingest (PRGII) workflow produces, quality-gates, and commits experiences, indexing both successes and failures so the agent learns what to reuse and what to avoid. No weights change during deployment. We evaluate on five benchmarks: BigCodeBench, KGQAGen-10k, HLE, Lifelong Agent Bench, and ALFWorld. Because prior work uses different backbones, we base our claims on same-backbone comparisons that hold model capability fixed. On held-out BigCodeBench transfer with a shared GPT-4o backbone, APEX-EM gains +7.6pp over the no-memory baseline, which is 3.3x MemRL’s +2.3pp under the identical setup. On Lifelong Agent Bench with a shared GPT-4o-mini backbone, APEX-EM gains +1.4pp (OS) and +1.0pp (DB) cumulative success. On KGQAGen-10k, frozen memory transfers to a blind 1,079-question test split at 73.7% versus 42.0% with no memory, approaching an oracle that is handed the ground-truth subgraph (84.9%). Across three Opus scales the memory gain stays at  +27pp to +32pp, so it adds to model capability rather than substituting for it. Component analysis shows no single mechanism dominates: teacher feedback is negligible for code but adds +10.3pp on structured queries, structural signatures give 3.3 times the transfer of semantic-only retrieval, and within-epoch iteration recovers most of the gain when rich feedback is unavailable. These results argue for modular memory composed per domain.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: DisGAR: Machine Generated Text Detection via Disentangled Generative Artifact Representation
abstract: The widespread misuse of large language models (LLMs) has made machine-generated text detection (MGTD) a critical task. Existing detection methods are often vulnerable to stylistic noise, which limits their generalization in real-world scenarios and robustness on short texts. Furthermore, many methods generate multiple auxiliary texts through LLM-based rewriting or similar strategies, substantially increasing detection latency and limiting their practicality. To address these challenges, we propose the **DisGAR** detection framework, which strips stylistic noise from the input text to mitigate its impact on detection performance, thereby improving cross-domain and cross-model robustness. Specifically, we first fine-tune the attention layers of the proxy model to capture generation-specific patterns. Then we further introduce a global artifact aggregation mechanism and a contrastive learning strategy based on rewritten texts, enabling the separation of stylistic artifacts from the underlying generation patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that DisGAR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in unseen-model and unseen-domain detection. Moreover, DisGAR achieves detection efficiency comparable to Fast-DetectGPT, successfully balancing detection performance and efficiency. Source code is available at https://github.com/m-Clown/DisGAR.git
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Guardrails without Shackles: Mitigating Over-Defense in Inference-Time Detection of Fixed-Target Backdoors for LLMs
abstract: Fixed-target backdoor attacks can silently hijack the outputs of large language models by driving models to generate attacker-specified sequences upon trigger activation, motivating lightweight inference-time detection. Recent defenses like ConfGuard, which we term Local-window Confidence Detectors, leverage sliding windows to identify local spans where the top-1 probability, referred to as token confidence, exceeds 0.99 as indicators of backdoor activation. However, benign deterministic tasks such as math reasoning can exhibit similar sustained high-confidence patterns, causing confidence conflation. On the GSM8K dataset, ConfGuard’s default settings yield a 72.89% false positive rate, causing substantial over-defense. Our empirical analysis reveals that benign deterministic generation exhibits sparse confidence "dips", whereas backdoor-triggered generation forms a sustained high-confidence "plateau". Building on this, we propose RatioGuard, which utilizes a global high-confidence token ratio computed over the generated prefix to address confidence conflation. Across models and datasets, RatioGuard reduces false positives by up to 71.57 percentage points over ConfGuard while maintaining over 99% true positive rate with 1.005\times runtime latency.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Anchored by an Afterthought: Cross-Modal Numerical Anchoring in VLMs
abstract: When a vision-language model (VLM) is shown an irrelevant image containing a digit (the anchor image) alongside a numeric question, the model’s numeric answer shifts toward that digit. This matters because multi-image inputs (retrieval-augmented QA, multi-screenshot analysis, VLM-as-judge) routinely contain irrelevant numeric content. We call this phenomenon cross-modal numerical anchoring: across six VLMs and five numeric VQA datasets, the per-model mean SDF (signed direction-follow rate) ranges from 3% to 24%, with the effect growing stronger as the model’s confidence in the base answer decreases. Masking only the digit pixels of the anchor image, leaving the rest of the image intact, recovers the non-anchored answer, isolating the digit pixels as the causal channel, with the effect concentrated at low confidence. We propose a mitigation that uses this anchored-masked contrast as a calibration signal: at a single per-model integration site, we estimate a low-rank subspace spanning the anchoring directions and remove it via a projection at inference time. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, the projection reduces anchoring (\Delta\mathrm{SDF}_a=-1.64 pp, rel% -30.0\%) without degrading accuracy on non-anchored inputs or average performance on six capability benchmarks (within \pm1 pp).
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Not All LoRA Parameters Are Essential: Insights on Inference Necessity
abstract: Current research on LoRA primarily focuses on minimizing the number of fine-tuned parameters or optimizing its architecture. However, the necessity of all fine-tuned LoRA layers during inference remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate the contribution of each LoRA layer to the model’s ability to predict the ground truth and hypothesize that lower-layer LoRA modules play a more critical role in model reasoning and understanding. To address this, we propose a simple yet effective method to enhance the performance of large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA. Specifically, we identify a “boundary layer” that distinguishes essential LoRA layers by analyzing a small set of validation samples. During inference, we drop all LoRA layers beyond this boundary. We evaluate our approach on three strong baselines across four widely-used text generation datasets. Our analysis and experimental results show that selectively retaining critical LoRA layers during inference is effective across tasks of different types.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Known Event Types: Open-Domain Event Detection via Ontology-Guided Grounding–Discovery Resolution
abstract: Open-domain event detection aims to identify known event types while discovering previously unseen ones from unstructured documents. In practice, event detection systems often operate with an evolving event set rather than a complete type inventory. Under this setting, existing zero-shot event detection methods can fail in two ways when the event type is absent from the predefined set: the model may either miss the event or assign it to a plausible but wrong known type, hiding the need for discovery. To address this problem, we propose OGED, an \underline{\textbf{O}}ntology-\underline{\textbf{G}}uided open-domain \underline{\textbf{E}}vent \underline{\textbf{D}}etection framework for grounding–discovery resolution, i.e., deciding whether an event mention should be assigned to an existing type or should induce a new type. OGED organizes the available event types into a hierarchical search structure, uses cluster-level scheduler and adaptive planning to keep known-type assignment and new-type discovery jointly active, and applies retrieval-gated verification together with conflict selection to resolve competing assignments before output. Experiments on a unified benchmark with 564 event types show that OGED outperforms strong baselines on both known-type detection and unknown-type discovery. Code is available at https://github.com/chenzhouli/OGED.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Energy-Aware Benchmarking of Generative Information Extraction
abstract: Using Large Language Models (LLMs) for Information Extraction (IE) inherently involves transforming diverse textual inputs into strictly formatted outputs. Guaranteeing this structural validity introduces a hidden energy tax driven by constrained decoding mechanisms, serialisation formats, and underlying serving configurations. Consequently, standard token-level metrics fail to capture the true energy cost of generative IE, which also cannot be predicted by model size alone. To address this, we introduce the first dedicated benchmark evaluating the energy-accuracy trade-offs of generative IE. Our framework establishes task-aligned energy metrics, including Energy per True Positive (J/TP) and the F1-Energy Ratio (F_1/\mathrm{kJ}). Through comprehensive ablation across architectures, decoding regimes, and serving-layer limits, we demonstrate that efficiency is governed by complex parameter interactions. We translate these findings into actionable configuration guidelines, equipping practitioners to maximise predictive accuracy, optimise energy yield, or achieve a sustainable Pareto balance.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: A Hyperbolicity Atlas of Large Language Model Hidden States
abstract: Hidden states of large language models (LLMs) are typically analyzed as flat Euclidean vectors through probing, anisotropy, and intrinsic-dimension lenses. Yet much of what these models process (taxonomies, program structure, multi-step derivations) is hierarchical, and whether hidden-state distances reflect such hierarchy remains untested. We present the first systematic study of Gromov hyperbolicity (GH), a distance-based measure of tree-likeness, in prompt-token hidden states of open-weight LLMs. Across model families, scales, layer depths, and domains spanning math, code, commonsense, and truthfulness benchmarks, we construct a hyperbolicity atlas charting the normalized statistic \delta_{\mathrm{rel}} along each axis. Four findings emerge: (i) depth dominates, with middle layers forming a high-\delta_{\mathrm{rel}} plateau and final layers dropping toward tree-like structure; (ii) scale is weak and non-monotonic; (iii) matched-scale families occupy distinct regimes, with specialization gaps exceeding scale effects; and (iv) domains interact with specialization, e.g., HumanEval shifts from the highest- to the lowest-\delta_{\mathrm{rel}} domain between base and coder checkpoints. GH thus serves as a lightweight diagnostic that localizes where hierarchical distance structure emerges and which comparisons warrant deeper analysis.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Leak-Resistant Unlearning: A New Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Hop Reasoning Consistency and Recovery Robustness
abstract: Benchmarking machine unlearning methods is critical to understand whether sensitive knowledge is removed from large language models (LLMs) or not. Current unlearning benchmarks include mainly single-hop questions and a narrow set of multi-hop questions. Although effective, they still face two challenges. (1) Knowledge is not isolated, whereby diverse multi-hop reasoning paths can potentially induce knowledge leakage than normal queries. (2) Unlearning may be fragile: unlearned knowledge can be partially recovered through recovery attacks such as lightweight post-unlearning adaptation, making static evaluation insufficient. Therefore, in this paper, we introduce Leak-resistant Unlearning as a novel benchmark to understand robust LLM knowledge removal across diverse reasoning paths and recovery attacks. We experiment with this benchmark on 3 models, 6 unlearning methods, and 2 carefully curated datasets. Results show that existing methods are vulnerable to multi-hop reasoning paths and recovery attacks. We further explore the trade-off among forget quality, robustness, and model utility for LLM unlearning.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MetaGen: Self-Evolving Roles and Topologies for Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems, where specialized roles communicate and collaborate through structured interactions to solve complex tasks that often exceed the capacity of a single agent. However, most existing systems still rely on a fixed role library and an execution-frozen interaction topology, a rigid design choice that frequently leads to task mismatch, prevents timely adaptation when new evidence emerges during reasoning, and further inflates inference cost. We introduce MetaGen, a framework that adapts both the role space and the collaboration topology at inference time, without updating base model weights. MetaGen generates and rewrites query-conditioned role specifications to maintain a controllable dynamic role pool, then instantiates a constrained execution graph around a minimal backbone. During execution, it iteratively updates role prompts and adjusts structural decisions using lightweight feedback signals. Experiments on code generation and multi-step reasoning benchmarks show that MetaGen improves the accuracy and cost tradeoff over strong multi-agent baselines.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Stratified Topographic Similarity
abstract: Topographic Similarity (TopSim) is the most widely used metric for compositionality in emergent communication research. However, when evaluated on a class of languages where compositional structure is fully known (simple natural-language word concatenations), TopSim, along with other well-known metrics, under-reports compositionality. We investigate and trace TopSim’s failure to a distributional imbalance in pairwise object distances that grows with the input space size, and propose stratified-TopSim, a minimal fix that remains stable across settings and reliably evaluates languages of varying compositional structure, on both controlled benchmarks and emergent languages.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Padamitra: Grounded Glossary Generation for Classical Sanskrit
abstract: We introduce grounded glossary generation, a structured task requiring models to recover semantically meaningful Sanskrit phrases and produce translation-grounded meanings from a śloka-translation pair, formalizing the traditional pāṭha-commentary practice as an evaluable NLP objective. We construct a benchmark of 31,316 śloka-translation-glossary triples from the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa and Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, paired with two metrics: Jaccard for phrase recovery and Meaning Faithfulness for semantic consistency. Across zero-shot, few-shot, and instruction fine-tuned variants of Gemma-3n-E4B, Gemma-3-12B, Phi-4, and Qwen3.5-9B, instruction fine-tuning substantially outperforms prompting, while explicit segmentation yields gains. Error analysis identifies over-segmentation of sandhi and samāsa compounds as the dominant failure mode, pointing to morphological modeling as the key bottleneck for faithful Sanskrit lexical decomposition.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Routed Graph Handoff: Adaptive Format Selection for Multi-Agent LLM Delegation
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems coordinate through natural-language messages that consume 40–60% of their token budget. Replacing these with structured graphs reduces cost but fails on tasks requiring adaptive reasoning. We propose Routed Graph Handoff, where a lightweight LLM router (155 tokens, 0.15% overhead) selects between a typed dependency graph and natural language for each delegation. On four benchmarks (1,050+ trajectories), the routed system matches or exceeds NL-only on every task: +12.7,pp on Tau-retail at 3.2 X compression (p<0.01), +8.7,pp on BrowseComp at 2.2 compression (p<0.05), and parity on BFCL and AppWorld. Without the router, graph-only delegation regresses 14.6,pp on AppWorld—the router eliminates this at near-zero cost. A graph-aware executor prompt is load-bearing: the same schema without interpretation guidance yields no gain. An oracle analysis reveals 8.6,pp of additional headroom, motivating execution-time adaptive routing as future work.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: HiSVR: Hierarchical Semantic Visual Reconstruction for Unified Multimodal Models
abstract: Unified multimodal models use a shared Transformer backbone for visual understanding and image generation. Existing post-training signals primarily constrain final outputs, output-side representations, or task-level behavior, providing limited supervision for how visual semantics are organized across intermediate layers. We propose HiSVR, a hierarchical semantic visual reconstruction method for post-training unified multimodal models. A frozen semantic visual tokenizer extracts residual semantic codes from each training image, which supervise image-associated hidden states at different Transformer depths. Shallow layers predict shorter semantic-code prefixes, while deeper layers reconstruct longer prefixes, yielding coarse-to-fine supervision over intermediate representations. To balance the differing optimization difficulty across depths and prefix lengths, we introduce an uncertainty-weighted progressive reconstruction loss. HiSVR is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving the original architecture and inference cost. Experiments on unified multimodal backbones show that HiSVR improves visual understanding while maintaining image generation quality. These results indicate that hierarchical semantic reconstruction effectively regularizes intermediate representations in unified multimodal models.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: STAR: Detecting Inference-time Backdoors in LLM Reasoning via Prior-Posterior Amplification
abstract: Recent LLMs increasingly rely on explicit reasoning mechanisms such as Chain-of-Thought, but these reasoning traces also create a new attack surface for inference-time backdoors that steer the model toward malicious reasoning paths without modifying its parameters. Such attacks can remain linguistically coherent, making them difficult to detect with surface-, consistency-, or confidence-based signals. We propose \textbf{STAR}, a lightweight detection framework that compares input-conditioned token probabilities with prior-only reasoning probabilities. STAR measures token-level prior-posterior amplification and applies CUSUM to identify persistent anomalies in the generated reasoning process. Experiments across four LLMs (8B-70B), five reasoning benchmarks, and three inference-time backdoor attacks show that STAR achieves strong detection performance, with an average AUROC of 0.980, and substantially lower TFLOPs than high-overhead baselines such as Onion. STAR also remains effective under top-k logit access and the evaluated burn-in-aware adaptive attacks, while exposing a trade-off between evasion attempts and attack success.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Sample Learning State Guided Dynamic SFT–RL Integration Post-training
abstract: Integrating supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models. Existing methods typically rely on sequential SFT–RL pipelines or static loss weights, overlooking sample-level heterogeneity and evolving learning states. We propose Sample Learning State (SLS), a rollout-based characterization of each training sample using two complementary signals: sample mastery and exploration-trajectory dispersion. These signals estimate whether reward-driven updates are reliable for the core task and whether current rollouts provide informative contrast for RL optimization, respectively. Based on SLS, we design a state-aware coefficient that dynamically balances SFT and RL losses, increasing the RL weight only when the model demonstrates sufficient core-task competence and the sampled trajectories provide useful reward contrast. Experiments on Qwen2.5-Math models show that SLS achieves state-of-the-art results on four in-distribution and two out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks. In multi-reward settings, SLS preserves core reasoning performance while mitigating reward hacking induced by auxiliary rewards.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: FrameBench: A Language Understanding Benchmark Based on Frame Semantics
abstract: In frame semantics, sentence comprehension is assumed to proceed by relating lexical meaning to background knowledge called semantic frames, thereby enabling readers to implicitly enrich the text with unstated information. Recent large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of downstream tasks; however, it remains unclear whether they can reproduce the kinds of implicit enrichment that humans naturally make during comprehension. To address this question, we introduce FrameBench, a benchmark grounded in frame semantics. FrameBench consists of multiple-choice questions that test whether models distinguish the frames evoked by the same verb across contexts. We construct the benchmark for English and Japanese using FrameNet-style resources and a generation-and-verification pipeline with native-speaker judgments. Our experiments on a diverse set of models reveal challenges for small models, while several large models surpass the human reference scores. We release the constructed FrameBench dataset and the code for dataset construction and evaluation at https://github.com/SasanoLab/FrameBench
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Case-based Statute Retrieval for Multi-turn Legal Consultation with Fact-level and Rationale-level Mixed Evidence Graphs
abstract: Statute retrieval in multi-turn legal consultation is challenging because users often describe evolving facts in colloquial language, while statutes formulate legal conditions in abstract terms. This mismatch makes direct query–statute matching insufficient to capture the intermediate evidence needed to determine statutory applicability. Legal cases can bridge this gap by documenting how concrete facts and legal rationales support applicable statutes. However, case retrieval is noisy: factually similar cases may concern different legal issues, whereas cases with dissimilar surface facts may share the same applicability rationale. We propose FR-MEG, a Fact-level and Rationale-level Mixed Evidence Graph for turn-level statute retrieval. FR-MEG organizes case-derived evidence into two complementary views that model case–statute relationships through factual descriptions and legal rationales. The two views are calibrated and fused with full-corpus LegalDense retrieval, enabling case evidence to improve statute ranking without limiting candidates to graph-covered statutes. Experiments on LexRAG show that FR-MEG improves Recall@10 from 38.83% to 43.81% and NDCG@10 from 25.64% to 28.23% over the LegalDense backbone.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MEDitor: A Plug-and-Play Medical Multi-Agent Routing Protocol
abstract: Reliable medical reasoning with large language models (LLMs) is hindered by a practical trade-off between accuracy and deployment cost: larger models often perform strongly but are expensive to host, while compact open-source medical LLMs can fail on difficult cases. We propose MEDitor, a training-free, plug-and-play multi-agent routing protocol that improves accuracy and traceability by selectively escalating disagreement cases. MEDitor first queries two lightweight medical experts and terminates early upon agreement. For disagreements, it escalates to an evidence-grounded coordinator that constructs option-aligned evidence, followed by a candidate-constrained judge that selects between the competing candidates or abstains. A deterministic fallback guarantees reproducibility. Across five English-language medical multiple-choice QA (MCQA) benchmarks, MEDitor achieves 65.94% average accuracy, competitive with representative \sim70B open-source models on the same evaluation suite. These results show that lightweight expert orchestration can provide a parameter-efficient and auditable route to competitive medical MCQA accuracy by reserving evidence-grounded arbitration for contested cases.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Tacit Coordination of Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings that require coordination without communication, from human–AI interaction to safety-critical scenarios. Humans often overcome the absence of communication through focal points: salient solutions that naturally stand out to all participants. We present the first large-scale evaluation of how, when, and why focal points emerge in LLMs, comparing their behaviour with humans across cooperative and competitive games, including realistic search rescue scenarios, demonstrating when focal points enable effective coordination. Across more than 20 open- and closed-source models, we find that LLMs exhibit a remarkable ability to coordinate without communication, often matching or outperforming humans. However, the same models consistently fail in tasks requiring numerical common sense or culturally nuanced notions of salience. We additionally evaluate simple learning-free strategies that substantially improve coordination both among LLMs and between humans and LLMs. Our results reveal striking coordination capabilities, as well as social limitations in modern LLMs, and offer new insight into the latent notions of salience encoded within them. Our findings caution against assuming that LLMs share humans’ cultural and perceptual substrate when deployed in coordination settings.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Personalized News Headline Generation via Multi-Agent User Simulation
abstract: Personalized news headline generation has emerged as a promising avenue for optimizing user engagement and satisfaction in online news consumption. However, prevailing methods predominantly adopt an indirect modeling paradigm, inferring user preferences from related tasks rather than capturing their direct headline preferences. Direct modeling remains underexplored due to two primary challenges: (1) the scarcity of large-scale personalized headline datasets and (2) the risk of factual inaccuracies when models overly cater to subjective user preferences. To address these challenges, we propose USG, a novel multi-agent user simulator headline generation framework. USG introduces three specialized agents: the User provides subjective feedback to guide headline personalization; the Editor enforces editorial standards (i.e., factual consistency and no clickbait); and the Writer iteratively refines candidates via a Critique-and-Refine algorithm guided by feedback from the User and Editor agents. The multi-agent interactions yield optimal personalized headlines and reasoning chains distilled from the interaction trajectories, forming a high-quality dataset. This dataset directly supervises the fine-tuning of a standalone generator. Extensive experiments demonstrate that USG outperforms the strongest baseline by nearly 6% on personalization, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both personalization and factual consistency, while enabling efficient end-to-end inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/Leah-HKBU/USG.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: DialPO: Dialectical Prompt Optimisation
abstract: Existing textual-gradient prompt optimisers rely on a single Large Language Model (LLM) to diagnose failures, propose edits, and judge the results, conflating critique and refinement into one model’s judgement. We introduce DialPO (Dialectical Prompt Optimisation), a multi-agent framework that replaces the single- model feedback loop with a structured de- bate: an Advocate defends what the prompt does well, a Critic attacks failures, cross- examination filters their arguments adversar- ially, a data-isolated Synthesis model drafts the revised prompt from surviving arguments alone, and a regression gate rejects edits that degrade batch accuracy. We provide a theo- retical framework identifying three precondi- tions under which multi-agent debate improves the feedback-reasoning bottleneck of textual- gradient methods, and show that DialPO in- stantiates them by construction. Across 12 benchmarks spanning classification, reasoning, summarisation, and question answering, Di- alPO achieves the highest scores across various Target models, winning or tying a majority of datasets in head-to-head comparisons against each baseline while using 8–18× fewer LLM calls than beam-search optimisers. Compo- nent ablations across five Target models reveal that DialPO’s advantage scales inversely with Target-model strength, clarifying when dialec- tical debate helps prompt optimisation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Chain-of-Thought Fails, the Solution Hides in the Hidden States
abstract: Whether intermediate reasoning is computationally useful or merely explanatory depends on whether chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens contain task-solving information.
