To investigate this behavior, we introduce SSM-Interpret, a frequency-domain framework that shows a “spectral shift" toward short-range dependencies during fine-tuning. Guided by these findings, we propose architectural modifications that significantly improve the performance of SSM-based code model by upto +6 MRR on NLCodeSearch. This demonstrates that our analysis not only explains model behavior but also leads directly to better designs.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: A Systematic Survey of Large Language Model Routing
abstract: Available LLMs differ substantially in cost, latency, and capability. Their strengths vary across queries, so the natural question becomes: which model for which query? This is the LLM routing problem. Routing is already used in production, and the academic literature has grown across cascading, bandit, generative, and benchmark threads, each with its own vocabulary, each largely ignoring the others. We argue the field is best read along a single axis: the algorithmic operation the router performs. We organise the recurring operations under four labels. Predictive routers score candidates before their answers are generated. Adaptive routers try a model, observe the outcome, and adjust. Generative routers let an LLM itself reason about the decision. Infrastructure work studies routing rather than performs it, via benchmarks and adversarial analysis. This survey formalises the routing decision under this four-paradigm lens, traces the methodological development of the field, compares assumptions and tradeoffs across paradigms, and identifies open research directions revealed by the taxonomy. A continuously updated reading list lives at https://github.com/wuxingyu-ai/LLM-Routing.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: AgSynth: A Multi-Agent Reverse Synthesis Framework for Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning Data Generation
abstract: Multimodal large language models show significant potential in mathematical reasoning, yet they remain constrained by a scarcity of high-quality training data for visually grounded problems. Existing approaches commonly suffer from narrow coverage, image-text inconsistency, and heavy imitation of seed problems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes AgSynth, a multi-agent collaborative reverse synthesis framework. It first constructs solution logic programmatically and renders the corresponding images, then generates problem statements backward from the visual facts, thereby embedding answer correctness and image-text consistency directly into the generation pipeline. Meanwhile, AgSynth distills the core competencies tested in seed problems and performs divergent reconstruction, enabling synthesized problems to be substantially novel in both structure and visual presentation. Based on this framework, we construct the AgSynth-10K dataset, comprising 10{,}477 multimodal mathematical reasoning problems that have undergone two-tier quality control, spanning four major domains: geometry, algebra, combinatorics, and number theory. Experiments demonstrate that reinforcement learning training on AgSynth-10K significantly improves model performance on reasoning-intensive benchmarks (WeMath +7.42, LogicVista+9.15), validating the effectiveness of this traceable synthesis paradigm. The framework is publicly available at https://github.com/Yaxuan7690/AgSynth.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Lusopol: How do LLMs Handle Politically Charged Questions? The Use Case of Portugal
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted worldwide, evaluating their alignment across diverse cultural contexts is essential, especially when handling sensitive, politically charged requests. Yet what counts as “sensitive” is shaped by social, historical, and cultural factors, leaving model robustness across cultures poorly understood. We investigate this in the context of Portugal, a country whose layered history surfaces many culturally sensitive topics absent from existing benchmarks. We introduce Lusopol, a benchmark of 1{,}400 English and Portuguese prompts spanning seven thematic categories—from colonial history and the Estado Novo dictatorship to contemporary political issues—designed to stress-test models under deliberately controversial framings. Testing 16 state-of-the-art LLMs on Lusopol, we find substantial performance variance: frontier closed models and leading open-weight families set the pace, while European-focused open models lag behind. To close this gap, we synthesize a preference corpus of more than 7.5K samples. Targeted alignment training on this resource significantly reduces skewed responses and makes European open models competitive, demonstrating that culturally situated preference data is a practical path toward closing the alignment gap for underrepresented societies.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: UniFinEval: Towards Unified Evaluation of Financial Multimodal Models across Text, Images and Videos
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown increasing potential for applications in the financial domain. However, the challenges posed by real-world financial scenarios, including high-information-density, strong noise interference, and cross-modal multi-hop reasoning, go beyond the evaluation scope of existing financial multimodal benchmarks. To this end, we propose UniFinEval, the first unified multimodal financial evaluation benchmark designed for high-density financial information environments, covering three modalities: text, image, and video. UniFinEval abstracts three progressive core scenarios from perception to reasoning and decision-making, and further refines them into six task categories. It contains 5,567 high-quality Chinese and English question–answer (QA) pairs constructed by financial experts. We systematically evaluate 10 mainstream MLLMs under zero-shot and chain-of-thought (CoT) settings. Experimental results show that Gemini-3-Pro achieves the best overall performance, but still exhibits a significant gap compared with financial experts. Further error analysis reveals the capability deficiencies of MLLMs in financial scenarios. UniFinEval aims to systematically evaluate the capabilities of MLLMs in real financial scenarios, thereby promoting the application of MLLMs in the financial domain. The related code and data are available at https://github.com/aifinlab/UniFinEval.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Memes-as-Replies: Can Models Select Humorous Manga Panel Responses?
abstract: Memes are widely used not only as static artifacts but also as interactive replies in online conversations. While computational research has focused on analyzing intrinsic properties of memes, the dynamic and contextual use of memes to create humor remains largely unaddressed. We introduce the Meme Reply Selection task and present MaMe-Re, a benchmark of 100,000 human-annotated context–meme pairs built from openly licensed Japanese manga panels. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) large language models show modest advantages over embedding methods by capturing social cues such as irony and exaggeration beyond surface-level semantic matching; (2) visual information does not improve performance, revealing a gap between understanding visual content and effectively using it for contextual humor; (3) while models can match human judgments when the humorous option is clearly distinguishable, they struggle to distinguish subtle differences in wit among semantically similar candidates. These findings establish contextually humorous reply selection as an open challenge for current models.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TRIPPULSE: Multi-Agent Travel Planning with Review-Grounded Reasoning
abstract: Travel itinerary generation requires balancing strict spatio-temporal constraints with human preferences. Existing LLM-based planners mainly rely on structured attributes and predefined traveler personas, but real travel decisions are often shaped by reviews that reveal experiential factors such as comfort, safety, service quality, ambiance, crowding, and hidden risks absent from structured databases. Incorporating such review information is therefore critical to realistic, user-centric itinerary generation. We propose TRIPPULSE (Captures experiential signals from reviews beyond rigid hard constraints), a multi-agent framework for review-grounded travel planning. Instead of relying on a monolithic planner (and face context and reasoning bottlenecks), TRIPPULSE decomposes itinerary generation into specialized agents (each operating over localized contexts) for accommodations, transportation, meals, attractions, and events, coordinated through a global orchestrator with scheduling mechanisms that enforce temporal and budget feasibility. We augment TripCraft with 100K+ real-world reviews and introduce Review-Grounded Persona Alignment (RGPA), an LLM-as-a-Judge metric for evaluating alignment with human-centric travel experiences. Experiments across multiple trip durations and diverse proprietary and open-source models show that TRIPPULSE maintains strong constraint satisfaction while generating more personalized and experientially grounded itineraries.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When Disagreement Meets Noise: Noise Robust Annotator Embeddings for Subjective NLP
abstract: Subjective NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis and hate speech classification often involve inherent annotator disagreement, reflecting diverse perspectives shaped by annotators’ lived experiences. Although conventional approaches resolve disagreement through majority voting or aggregation, these methods risk erasing valuable nuances and minority viewpoints. Recent embedding-based and multitask models have advanced the modeling of annotator-specific judgments, yet their robustness to annotation noise remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate how state-of-the-art multi-annotator learning models perform in the presence of noisy labels, and find that embedding-based approaches are more robust than aggregation and multitask baselines on datasets with many sparse annotators. Furthermore, we propose a new methodology, Noise-Robust Annotator Embedding (NRA-Embed), which integrates Robust InfoNCE (RINCE) contrastive loss to enhance models’ robustness under noisy annotation conditions. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that NRA-Embed effectively captures subjective disagreement while maintaining robustness to noise, achieving performance that is comparable to state-of-the-art in clean settings while providing numerically greater robustness under noise.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CPSD: Counterfactual Patches Self-Distillation in RLVR
abstract: Self-distillation in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) uses successful in-group rollouts to teach the failed ones, with no external teacher needed. Whether it actually helps turns on three closely related design questions that the canonical method does not handle carefully: how to construct an appropriate teacher context for a given loser, where in the response the distillation loss should act, and what kind of signal it should carry. The canonical Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) instantiation answers all three by default: a random in-group winner, a global distillation loss on the whole response, and a Jensen–Shannon divergence on the full top-K distribution. These three defaults compound into a catastrophic late-training failure that short-horizon evaluation hides. We propose CPSD (Counterfactual Patches Self-Distillation), which replaces each default in turn: pick the teacher by minimum embedding-weighted edit distance, localise distillation to an adaptive-stop counterfactual patch beginning at the first divergent token, and replace JS with a Plackett–Luce listwise loss that preserves only the teacher’s ranking. Across six reasoning benchmarks at a fixed 150-step budget, CPSD eliminates the SDPO cliff and lifts average accuracy by +5.7 pp over GRPO on Qwen3-8B and +4.2 pp on Qwen3-4B.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SMUGRI-COPA: Evaluating Commonsense Reasoning for Low-Resource Finnic Languages
abstract: We introduce SMUGRI-COPA, a commonsense reasoning benchmark for two heavily under-resourced Finnic languages: Võro and Livonian. Existing evaluation resources for these languages rely on a translated subset of FLORES sentences, limiting linguistic diversity and the evaluation of broader language understanding. To address this gap, we human-translate the COPA (Choice of Plausible Alternatives) benchmark into Võro and Livonian, creating, to our knowledge, the largest discriminative benchmark currently available for these languages. We evaluate a wide range of proprietary and open-weight language models on SMUGRI-COPA and compare the results with Estonian XCOPA. Our results reveal a substantial performance gap between Estonian and the lower-resource languages, with most models failing to significantly outperform random guessing on Livonian. We further find that enabling reasoning for GPT-5 substantially improves accuracy for Võro and Livonian, while its reasoning summaries show frequent reliance on explicit translation of the tasks. Our work highlights the challenges of evaluating endangered language understanding and provides a new resource for multilingual evaluation research.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SinoGlyphBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Chinese Glyph-Level Obfuscation in Language-Model Moderation
abstract: Glyph-level obfuscation can leave harmful Chinese content readable to humans while degrading automated moderation. We introduce SinoGlyphBench, a diagnostic benchmark that identifies label-critical semantic anchors and creates matched original and glyph-obfuscated inputs in text and image modalities. By perturbing anchors, background context, or both, this design distinguishes corruption of moderation-relevant evidence from general surface variation. Across 176,916 paired evaluations of 12 LLMs and MLLMs, obfuscation increases harmful false-negative and false-positive rates by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively, and reduces four-way accuracy by 5.0 points. Models retain 75.7% of the decisions that were correct on the matched original inputs. Full-scope perturbations cause the largest degradation, anchor-only perturbations are more damaging than background-only perturbations, and cross-script substitution is particularly difficult in the text modality. Analysis of structured outputs identifies observable mismatches in visible-form reading, intended-message recovery, and final safety judgment. The evaluated models, therefore, remain brittle to Chinese content written with non-canonical glyphs. Resources are available at https://github.com/fengshun124/SinoGlyphBench.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MemesOverTime: A Decade-Scale Study of Meme Dynamics
abstract: Internet memes evolve as they are repurposed across online communities, yet studying how their usage and language shift requires corpora that follow the same templates over many years, which existing resources rarely provide. To address this gap, we collect a decade of posts from Reddit meme subreddits (2016–2025) and introduce MemesOverTime, a semi-automatically curated dataset of 6.6M memes annotated with 6,584 unique templates. We use it to conduct an empirical study of meme template dynamics. We find that templates differ markedly in their temporal activity patterns: most reach peak usage within the first third of their active period, with short-lived templates peaking especially early. For long-lived templates, lexical drift is generally modest, with templates with more instances showing greater stability. Case studies reveal that creators spontaneously develop conventionalized expressions for some templates, while topical references shift over time.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Contextual Observer Grounding: Evaluating Situated Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Reasoning over language instructions in embodied tasks such as robotics often requires understanding spatial relations from a speaker’s situated perspective. Humans infer such perspectives from shared environmental knowledge, activity context, and commonsense. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) appear capable of spatial reasoning, but their ability to infer a speaker’s viewpoint from contextual cues and interpret situated spatial relations from that viewpoint remains unclear. We call this capability contextual observer grounding. To study this capability, we construct the Point-of-View Benchmark (POVBench), a dataset of 3D scenes and queries that disentangles Inferred, Stated, and Given forms of observer grounding in natural embodied communication. Given multi-view observations and a natural-language sentence, models must localize unseen or underspecified targets from situated spatial and contextual cues. Across state-of-the-art VLMs, localizing targets from directional language remains challenging, even when observer grounding is made explicit. We find that explicit breakdowns of observer-relative spatial reasoning improve target localization. Our project page is available at https://mimo-owl.github.io/POVBench/.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TEVI: Text-Conditioned Editing of Visual Representations via Sparse Autoencoders for Improved Vision-Language Alignment
abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP are highly useful for diverse tasks due to their shared image-text embedding space. Despite this, the image and text embeddings are often poorly aligned, affecting downstream performance. Recent work has hypothesized that this can be attributed to an information imbalance: images contain more information than their captions describe. In this work, we propose TEVI, a framework that uses captions as a signal for what to retain from image embeddings. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders to disentangle image embeddings and train a masking module to selectively reconstruct the embedding based on a given caption. In a controlled setup with synthetic captions, we show that TEVI is effective at preserving caption-described attributes while discarding others. We find that this extends to CLIP models trained on natural images, where TEVI learns to mask meaningfully and allows retrieval based on conditioning. Finally, we use TEVI to achieve improved retrieval performance across coarse-grained and fine-grained benchmarks. Code available at https://github.com/neuroexplicit-saar/TEVI.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Do LLMs Use Cultural Knowledge Without Being Told? A Multilingual Evaluation of Implicit Pragmatic Adaptation
abstract: Many benchmarks show that large language models can answer direct questions about culture. We study a different question: do they also change how they speak when culture is only implied by the situation? We introduce a triad-diagnostic framework; applying it to four deployed endpoints to evaluate 60 culturally grounded conversational scenarios. We examine responses across five languages in three conditions: a neutral baseline (Prompt A), an explicit cultural instruction (Prompt B), and implicit situational cueing (Prompt C). We use an LLM-judge ensemble with explicit rubrics to score responses on 12 pragmatic features covering deference to authority, individual-versus-group framing, and uncertainty management. We define Pragmatic Context Sensitivity (PCS) as the fraction of the judge-scored Prompt A\rightarrowB feature shift that reappears under Prompt A\rightarrowC. Across four deployed LLM endpoints and five languages (English, German, Hindi, Nepali, and Urdu), the primary stable-only PCS mean is 0.196 (SD = 0.113), indicating that the tested models recover only about one-fifth of the explicitly prompted rubric-aligned shift. Transfer is strongest for authority-related cues (0.299) and weakest for individual-versus-group framing (0.120). We argue that multilingual cultural pragmatics is an explicit-versus-implicit deployment problem, not only a factual knowledge problem.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Entropy Is Not Enough: Unlocking Effective Reinforcement Learning for Visual Reasoning via Vision-Anchored Token Selection
abstract: While token-level entropy is commonly recognized as effective for credit assignment in text-only reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), it remains unclear whether this mechanism still holds in visual reasoning. Our controlled study shows that this mechanism collapses in visual reasoning due to the omission of vision-sensitive tokens with naturally low entropy. Although existing multimodal RL methods increasingly acknowledge the importance of visual perception, they struggle to satisfy the inherent demand for interleaving precise perceptual grounding with semantic reasoning, either lacking systematic visual measurements or overlooking that token entropy primarily drives semantic exploration. To address this, we introduce VEPO (Vision-Entropy token-selection for Policy Optimization), an effective RL framework explicitly integrating visual sensitivity with token entropy via a principled multiplicative coupling, where VEPO redirects gradient credit toward tokens which are simultaneously visually grounded and highly informative. Extensive experiments demonstrate VEPO’s leading performance, consistently outperforming the strongest RL baseline at 7B-scale and 3B-scale. Ablations further substantiate the soundness of our method.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Riemannian Large Language Modeling
abstract: Current large language models perform next-token prediction under the implicit assumption that all tokens lie in a shared Euclidean embedding space, which treats every token uniformly. However, natural language contains rich structural relationships, including hierarchical, compositional, and cyclic patterns, which the flat geometry of Euclidean space cannot model well. To address this limitation, we propose rLLM (Riemannian Large Language Modeling), which introduces a token-adaptive positive-definite diagonal metric tensor into the LM head. This metric dynamically adjusts the local quadratic score for each hidden state and its context, allowing the model to better capture the relationships among tokens and prompts, with less than 0.01% additional parameters. We train rLLM from scratch across three different scales (2.8B to 5.0B parameters), covering the full pretraining, SFT, and RL pipeline. Extensive experiments show that rLLM improves Base CORE, a composite of 22 in-context learning tasks, by up to +2.5pp at the two smaller GPT scales and obtains higher ChatCORE at all three scales, with gains up to +3.0pp after RL. These results suggest that revisiting the geometric assumptions underlying token representations is a promising direction for building more expressive and capable language models. Code is available at https://github.com/digailab/riemannianllm.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Privacy-Hallucination Tradeoff in Differentially Private Language Models
abstract: Both privacy and factual accuracy are paramount in high-stakes domains like healthcare. Concerningly, we uncover and investigate a _privacy-hallucination tradeoff_ in differentially private (DP) language models. First, we empirically show that models pre-trained or fine-tuned with DP tend to produce more hallucinations than non-DP counterparts, with increased severity as the privacy budget grows stricter. Second, we investigate model properties driving this tradeoff, demonstrating that DP mechanisms flatten output distributions, potentially redistributing probability mass toward factually incorrect alternatives. Third, through experiments where we control fact frequency in training data, we characterize how information frequency can reduce hallucination risks in DP models. Overall, our findings underscore the need for more nuanced privacy-preserving interventions that offer rigorous privacy guarantees without compromising factual accuracy.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Fooling: Model Manipulation Under Explanation-aware Training
abstract: Feature-level explanations are commonly used to interpret transformer-based NLP models. Still, little is known about how explanation-aware objectives influence model behaviour during training. While prior work has demonstrated training-time manipulation of explanations in vision models, its implications for transformers and token-level explainability remain unexplored. We study training-time manipulation of token-level explanations in transformer-based NLP classifiers and introduce sequence-aware objectives suited to text input. We show that explanation-aware training systematically alters token relevance patterns while largely preserving task accuracy. Importantly, masking and cross-method evaluations reveal that these attribution changes can coincide with shifts in functional model reliance rather than isolated failures of specific explanation methods. Our results suggest that apparent vulnerabilities of feature-level explanations can reflect deeper model adaptations, underscoring the need to consider learning dynamics when interpreting explanation robustness.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Intervention-Certified Amplification: A Validity Gate for \sigma-Weighted Post-Training
abstract: Post-training methods use training-side signals to decide which supervision to emphasize, but those signals need not identify behavior that is capability-bearing in the target environment. We probe this with DIAA (Dual-Implicit Adversarial Amplification), a per-sample σ = sigmoid(-βΔ) SFT/RL hybrid: after every literal Python code fence is deleted from the anchor data, the model still emits unexecuted Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) form on 29% of MATH-500 prompts, three times vanilla GRPO, and suppressing the form recovers accuracy. A paired within-prompt intervention decomposes the removable drag along GRPO → SFT → DIAA as +2.2 → +8.5 → +10.6 pp, identifying SFT imitation and σ-amplification as comparable sources; a teacher RFT with 0% TIR likewise trains a student emitting TIR at 45.8%. We propose Intervention-Certified Amplification (ICA), which gates the per-sample weight by a certificate derived from paired rollouts, σ_eff(x) = σ(x)·c(x; θ_c). Frozen and online instantiations cut TIR to 13.8% and 11.2%, more than halve residual drag while improving accuracy, and carry the joint improvement to held-out GSM8K without retuning the certificate.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Don’t Forget Your Embeddings: Robust Knowledge Erasure via Precise Editing of Embeddings
abstract: As language models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the ability to erase specific knowledge from them becomes critical for safety and compliance. Prominent methods seek persistent removal by updating the model’s parameters, yet the target knowledge often can be recovered through adversarial prompting or relearning. In this work, we hypothesize this limitation stems in part from existing methods overlooking the embedding layer. To address this, we introduce EMBedding ERasure (EMBER), a plug-n-play erasure module that leverages Sparse Matrix Factorization for precise erasure of concept-related features from token embeddings. Through comprehensive evaluations across diverse concepts on Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we find that augmenting existing methods with EMBER consistently improves erasure efficacy and specificity across task formats, with minimal coherence loss. Moreover, EMBER dramatically improves robustness to relearning, reducing regained accuracy by up to 50%, limiting it to 35% on Llama compared to 70%–76% for prior methods. Further analysis shows that the coherence cost is localized, affecting only a small set of concept-exclusive tokens. Our work establishes that precise embedding-level intervention is necessary for robust concept erasure, and demonstrates that existing methods can benefit from such augmentation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Understanding Why Language Models Hallucinate: Testing Reasoning Against Priors
abstract: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers that violate prompt-level constraints. A key diagnostic question is whether these failures reflect missing knowledge, or whether the model has the relevant information but follows the wrong inference path. We study this phenomenon as *inference misalignment*: a mismatch between the answer supported by the prompt and the answer favored by statistically salient latent associations. We formalize this view with a latent key–task model, in which pretraining-frequency imbalance can cause a shortcut path to dominate the constraint-sensitive path and induce positive inference loss. The framework predicts two failure modes: task-retrieval bias in entity disambiguation and key-selection bias in action choice. We introduce *TrapQA*, a controlled diagnostic testbed with two components. *ScientistQA* tests disambiguation among similar scientists with supplementary factual probes, while *Real-Life Constrained QA* tests everyday constraint following under salient shortcuts. Our results show that hallucination can arise from biased latent inference rather than absent knowledge alone.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions
abstract: The alignment of large language models (LLMs) with human values increasingly relies on using other LLMs as automated judges, or "autoraters". However, their reliability is limited by a foundational issue: they are trained on discrete preference labels, forcing a single ground truth onto tasks that are often subjective, ambiguous, or nuanced. We argue that a reliable autorater must learn to model the full distribution of preferences defined by a target population. In this paper, we propose a general framework for calibrating probabilistic autoraters to any given preference distribution. We formalize the problem and present two learning methods tailored to different data conditions: 1) a direct supervised fine-tuning for dense, probabilistic labels, and 2) a reinforcement learning approach for sparse, binary labels. Our empirical results show that finetuning autoraters with a distribution-matching objective leads to verbalized probability predictions that are better aligned with the target preference distribution, with improved calibration and significantly lower positional bias, all while preserving performance on objective tasks.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Asclepius: An Adaptive Harness for Long-Horizon Clinical Agents
abstract: LLM agents are predominantly benchmarked on short, single-task trajectories, yet real deployments run for hours under contention, surfacing a different class of failures. We use the Clinical Environment Simulator (CES), in which an agent manages an entire emergency-department shift under continuous time and resource pressure, as a testbed: long-horizon execution failures manifest measurably in a single rollout under structured, multi-dimensional grading. On CES, current agents reach the correct diagnosis in most cases yet fail to deliver complete and timely critical actions, revealing an execution gap. We attribute this gap to three long-horizon failure modes, each operationalized as a per-trace counter: instruction-adherence drift, treatment incompleteness, and a severity-equity gap in timeliness. We then introduce Asclepius, an adaptive agent scaffolding with a self-evolving harness that rewrites the operating manual between shifts from trace-level feedback, an externalized clinical skills library for high-stakes regimen knowledge, and three isolated subagents that partition per-turn decisions across the patient queue. On held-out batches never observed during harness evolution, Asclepius improves critical-action correctness by 22% (p = 0.024) over a strong baseline agent framework while preserving diagnostic accuracy, with consistent gains across five LLM judges from three model families; on the full ten-batch set, improvements reach 25% on critical actions and 13% on timeliness. The three failure modes form a coupled bottleneck: decisive reductions appear only when all three components act together.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Asymmetric Multimodal Learning with Residual Decomposition for Multimodal Intent Recognition
abstract: Multimodal intent recognition predicts a speaker’s intent from text, audio, and video, enabling conversational AI and human–computer interaction. However, existing methods share two limitations: (I) the three modalities are assigned equivalent roles even though text alone carries most of the predictive signal; (II) nonverbal cues that complement text are mixed with cues that merely repeat it. We propose Asymmetric Multimodal Learning with Residual Decomposition (AML), in which text produces the primary prediction and nonverbal signals enter only as a correction. The correction splits into Hierarchical Modality Calibration (HMC), which removes cues already present in text, and Asymmetric Multimodal Disentanglement (AMD), which carries cues that add new information. Extensive experiments on MIntRec2.0 and IEMOCAP-DA show that AML consistently surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods across all reported metrics, and additional analyses confirm the structural advantages of the asymmetric design.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Reinforcement Learning Elicits Contextual Learning of Unseen Language Translation
abstract: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) can translate unseen or low-resource languages by undergoing continued training or even by encoding a grammar book in their context. However, both methods typically treat specific languages, with limited zero-shot transfer at test time. To translate extremely low-resource languages at scale, we argue that a model should be able to use in-context linguistic knowledge regardless of language, rather than memorize specific training languages. In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to unseen language translation given rich linguistic context, using a surface-level translation metric as the reward. Empirically, despite the lightweight reward, our RL-trained models effectively extract and apply relevant linguistic information from the provided context, leading to better translations on completely unseen languages than in-context learning or supervised fine-tuning. Our analyses suggest that outcome-based RL can extend beyond conventional reasoning tasks like math and coding to serve as a recipe for low-resource translation from linguistic context.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: A Recipe for Long-Context Reasoning in Large Language Models via On-Policy Optimization and Distillation
abstract: Existing approaches to post-train models for long-context tasks face complementary limitations: (i) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides stable supervision but suffers from exposure bias; (ii) reinforcement learning methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) train on model-generated trajectories but struggle with long-horizon credit assignment and sparse rewards; and (iii) on-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level guidance but does not directly optimize task rewards. We study these complementary strategies for long-context alignment and derive a recipe that combines GRPO with OPD-style teacher guidance: the student learns from its own rollouts using outcome-level rewards, while a stronger teacher provides dense token-level regularization in place of the standard reference policy. This is especially useful when process-level supervision is difficult to obtain. To support this study, we introduce LongBlocks, a synthetic multilingual dataset spanning multi-hop reasoning, contextual grounding, and long-form generation. Through controlled ablations, we isolate the roles of cold-start initialization, teacher anchoring, and data mixing, showing that our recipe yields a more stable and effective path to long-context reasoning than GRPO or OPD while preserving short-context capabilities.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Judge Can Debias Itself: Awareness and Self-Debiasing for Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge
abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge systems are increasingly employed for automated evaluation, yet remain susceptible to systematic biases that undermine their reliability. We demonstrate that the judge can effectively debias itself without additional training. We propose two lightweight strategies: bias-aware prompting, which explicitly alerts the judge to potential target biases prior to evaluation, and self-debiasing, in which the judge critiques the initial judgment for bias influence. To broaden the evaluation scope, we introduce three novel benchmarks—authority bias (fabricated citations), confidence bias (assertive phrasing), and formatting bias (structured presentation)—and evaluate across seven bias types in total. Across three frontier models, self-debiasing improves performance in 20 out of 21 model–bias combinations with gains up to 15 percentage points, while bias-aware prompting also yields consistent improvements. The recent fine-tuned external critic, however, does not generalize as reliably to the newly-introduced bias types (degradation observed in 5 out of 9 cases). Our findings demonstrate that prompting a judge to reason about bias, either preemptively or retrospectively, is a robust and generalizable approach for enhancing evaluation integrity.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PercepLog-0: LLM-Augmented Backward Chaining for Legal Reasoning
abstract: In-depth logical reasoning in domains such as legal analysis remains challenging for large language models (LLMs), exhibiting brittle and inconsistent performance on tasks requiring multi-step deductive inference. This limitation is expected, as LLMs primarily rely on learned distributional associations rather than performing explicit step-by-step logical inference through formal rule application. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework, called PercepLog, that incorporates a classical deductive reasoning algorithm, backward chaining, within an outer control loop, while utilizing LLMs for primitive operations such as substitution and unification. By following the backward chaining algorithm, the framework benefits from the interpretability and explainability of symbolic reasoning procedures while retaining the flexibility of LLM perception for processing natural-language legal text. We evaluate the proposed method on statutory reasoning tasks across a range of legal domains as well general logical reasoning. The results demonstrate that our approach enables more robust, explainable, and principled reasoning over unstructured legal text, where exhaustive formalization is often brittle and prone to hallucination. Our method yields average relative performance improvements of 58% over direct LLM reasoning and 16% over formal LLM-based translation and Prolog inference pipelines.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Retrieval: Learning Compact User Representations for Scalable LLM Personalization
abstract: Personalizing large language models requires adapting model behavior to individual users while preserving robustness and deployment-scale efficiency. Existing approaches typically personalize LLMs either at the input level, by retrieving user histories or constructing profile prompts, or at the parameter level, by maintaining user-specific parameter-efficient modules. The former makes personalization sensitive to retrieval quality and prompt design, whereas the latter incurs storage and maintenance costs that grow with the user population. To address these limitations, we propose TAP-PER (Temporal Attentive Prefix for PERsonalization), a prefix-based framework that encodes user preferences as learnable representations, avoiding the serialization of user histories into prompts and replacing heavy per-user adapters with lightweight user-state prefix embeddings. Inspired by personalized recommendation systems, TAP-PER decomposes user modeling into user-state and query-conditioned components, and incorporates temporal signals to capture the evolving nature of user interests. Experiments on six LaMP tasks show that TAP-PER consistently outperforms prompt-based and model-based baselines across classification, rating, and generation settings. Moreover, TAP-PER uses 130× fewer per-user parameters than OPPU and roughly half the total parameter footprint of PER-PCS at the 1,000-user scale, demonstrating scalable personalization without prompt-serialized histories or heavy per-user adapters.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: DSL-LLaDA: Scaling Continuous Denoising to 8B Masked Diffusion LMs
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative parallel decoding, but at low step budgets, committing many tokens independently can produce premature termination or repetitive outputs. Continuous embedding-space denoising can mitigate this failure mode by maintaining soft states for all positions, yet training such models from scratch at scale remains challenging. We show that a pretrained masked DLM can instead be efficiently adapted to support continuous denoising. Starting from LLaDA-8B-Instruct, we perform only 1,000 steps of continued pretraining with Discrete Stochastic Localization (DSL), replacing binary masking with continuous per-token Gaussian noise mapped to soft embedding mixtures. The adapted model supports SDE-based inference that evolves all positions jointly and defers hard token commitment to the final step. At \leq16 denoising evaluations, DSL-LLaDA substantially mitigates the premature-termination and repetition tradeoff in open-ended generation and achieves the best ROUGE-1 among the evaluated diffusion baselines on all four zero-shot summarization benchmarks. The same adaptation also enables selective correction of corrupted tokens while preserving more than 98% of clean tokens. Same-compute controls indicate that these behaviors arise from continuous-noise exposure rather than additional training alone.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: An Algorithmic Account of Few-Shot Concept Induction in Language Models
abstract: Both models and minds not only encode features that describe an entity, but can specifically represent which features of that entity are relevant for a given context. This core capability underlies in-context learning in language models and a variety of cognitive phenomena in minds, yet it is unclear how intelligent systems identify and promote relevant features. In this work, we propose Amortized Direction Accentuation (ADA), an algorithmic hypothesis that provides an explanation for how relevance is determined in the context of few-shot concept induction—the ability to infer a latent concept from a small number of positive examples. Under ADA, concept induction proceeds by forming a summary representation of the examples in a feature space that is shaped by amortized knowledge about which features tend to be useful for finding commonalities between items. We investigate and validate ADA in language models using a few-shot concept induction task. This work provides a novel perspective on the mechanisms supporting contextualization in language models and a promising hypothesis for a core aspect of cognition.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Localizing Prompt Ambiguity in Large Language Models with Probe-Targeted Attribution
abstract: Prompt ambiguity is a common source of failure in large language models, but is difficult to localize because it is a latent property of the prompt, while existing attribution methods are designed to explain observable outputs such as logits or generated tokens. We introduce PRIG, a gradient attribution method that uses a probe logit to attribute latent properties to token positions. Specifically, PRIG trains a linear probe to distinguish clear prompts from ambiguous prompts and attributes the probe score to earlier token representations in the residual stream. To enable token-level evaluation, we construct synthetic ambiguity datasets across coding, math, and writing by rewriting one task-critical sentence per prompt, and complement them with a human-written gold benchmark. In this setting, PRIG localizes ambiguous spans substantially better than gradient attribution baselines, achieving 0.840 AUROC on the combined synthetic benchmark. It also outperforms GPT-5.4 on sentence-level ambiguity identification and retains useful signal out-of-domain. More broadly, these results show that latent prompt properties can be localized through intermediate representations, rather than through output-level attribution.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ERASE: Precise Machine Unlearning via Geometry-Aware Gradient Shaping and Adaptive Loss Control
abstract: Large language models frequently memorize specific factual associations from their training data, necessitating post-hoc removal of targeted knowledge. However, standard gradient-based unlearning techniques treat all parameter directions uniformly, often leading to catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities. We introduce **ERASE** (**E**igenspace-**R**egulated **A**daptive **S**elective **E**rasure), a geometry-aware unlearning framework that combines three complementary mechanisms: (1) a *spectral filter* that attenuates gradient updates along principal directions of retained model knowledge, confining forgetting pressure to low-interference subspaces; (2) *selective error-signal construction*, which restricts gradients to semantically meaningful token positions, avoiding diffuse collateral damage; and (3) an *adaptive Cross-Entropy Target (CET) loss with dynamic per-sample stopping*, which drives each forget example toward a target cross-entropy and halts on convergence, preventing both under- and over-forgetting. Our method requires no reference model, no retain-set loss, and no auxiliary task supervision during training. On TOFU within the OpenUnlearning evaluation framework, ERASE achieves the highest aggregate score across four model families and two forget splits, attaining the best privacy and near-original utility among all compared baselines; on the document-level MUSE-News benchmark, with forget spans recovered automatically via named entity recognition, it simultaneously attains the strongest forgetting and retention with the privacy score closest to the retrain oracle. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ItzikWaizman/ERASE.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: From Distribution to Decision: A Diagnostic for Composable PTQ Primitives
abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are typically architecture-specific. Yet two distributional pathologies they target, dense cores with sparse outliers and input-conditioned activation clusters, recur across model families. We argue that for these pathologies the unit of selection should be the tensor distribution, not the architecture. We propose two composable primitives, dispatched from one calibration pass by a two-statistic diagnostic: Dual-Band Affine Folding (DBAF) where a per-tensor outlier gate fires, and Prompt-Conditioned Scale Anchoring (PCSA) where a per-prompt compactness ratio does. The diagnostic is a selection heuristic, not a calibrated predictor. Four prediction-then-outcome checks are consistent with the dispatch: a rotation cliff on a six-host LLaMA-3-8B W4A4 matrix, cross-family transfer to Qwen-2.5-7B, per-site gating on the KV-cache and SAM-B (+5pp NIAH at 8k, +4.8 mAP), and a negative SwinIR-×3 prediction at training-free W4A16. Both primitives are training-free and calibrate in seconds. The gate’s boundary is learnable, not merely hand-set: a logistic dispatcher trained with each model family held out reproduces it at mean AUC 0.962. Calibrated once on LLaMA-3-8B, the same thresholds dispatch across seven model families in six domains; off distribution the gate errs toward skipping.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MoraLink: Bridging Morals and Narrative Fables for Retrieval
abstract: A fable is a short narrative whose purpose is to convey a moral lesson. While semantically related, morals and fables differ fundamentally in form: morals are abstract and propositional, while fables express the same idea through characters and plot. In this work, we ask how well this conceptual relationship is captured in the latent representations of embedding models. To study this, we introduce MoraLink, a benchmark for moral-to-fable retrieval in which models must retrieve the correct fable for a given moral. We find that off-the-shelf embedding models struggle with this task, and that augmenting fable documents with LLM-generated moral-style summaries substantially improves retrieval, identifying document representation as the primary bottleneck. Contrastive fine-tuning further improves performance, and we release MoraLink as a challenging testbed for probing how well embedding models capture the abstraction gap between a moral principle and the narrative that embodies it.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Inference-Time Scaling in Diffusion Models: A Beam Search Approach to Visual Sequences Generation
abstract: While diffusion models produce high-quality images, they often lack consistency in sequences, especially for non-linear visual sequences. To solve this, we introduce an inference-time scaling beam search strategy for latent space exploration, enabling the conditional generation of coherent image sequences through beam search diffusion. In contrast to earlier methods that rely on fixed latent priors, our method dynamically samples past latents to search for an optimal sequence of latent representations, ensuring coherent visual transitions. As the latent denoising space is explored, the beam search graph is pruned with a cross-attention mechanism that efficiently scores search paths, prioritizing alignment with both textual prompts and visual context. Human and automatic evaluations confirm that BeamDiffusion outperforms other baseline methods, producing full sequences with superior coherence, visual continuity, and textual alignment.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PragReST: Self-Reinforcing Counterfactual Reasoning for Pragmatic Language Understanding
abstract: Natural language understanding often depends on meanings that are implied rather than explicitly stated, requiring pragmatic reasoning. Despite strong performance on math and logical reasoning, large language models (LLMs) still trail humans on pragmatic inference, often defaulting to literal interpretations. To improve LLM pragmatic reasoning, we introduce PragReST, a self-supervised framework that constructs pragmatic QA data, generates counterfactual reasoning traces, and trains models to internalize them through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, without human-labeled training data or distillation from a stronger teacher. Across four pragmatic benchmarks (PRAGMEGA, LUDWIG, METOQA, and ALTPRAG) and multiple model families, including Qwen3, Gemma, and GPT-OSS, PragReST consistently improves over backbone models, task-specific pragmatic tuning baselines, and non-counterfactual variants of the same pipeline. On accuracy-based benchmarks, PragReST improves over the instruct backbone by 5.37% and 5.50% (absolute) for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, respectively. Our error analysis and ablations underscore the importance of counterfactual reasoning: PragReST primarily reduces errors caused by failures to contrast observed utterances with plausible alternatives, and removing counterfactual reasoning substantially reduces performance. Moreover, our training preserves out-of-domain performance on general-knowledge and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: VeriSim: A Configurable Framework for Stress-Testing Medical AI Under Patient Communication Noise
abstract: Medical large language models are typically evaluated on idealized patient cases that do not reflect how real patients communicate. We introduce VeriSim, a patient simulation framework that injects controllable noise along six clinically grounded communication dimensions while substantially preserving each patient’s medical record. Truth adherence is supported by a verifier that extracts atomic claims from each candidate utterance and judges them against a UMLS-grounded vector index built with BioLORD embeddings, using the retrieved atoms’ structured clinical metadata (e.g., drug class, anatomical site, treats-condition relations) rather than surface-text similarity alone. Across seven open-weight LLMs, realistic noise reduces diagnostic accuracy by 15-25 percentage points and increases conversation length by 34-55%; the 7-8B models degrade 1.4x more than 70B+ models. A board-certified physician and a licensed nurse rate VeriSim’s conversations highly on truth, realism, clinical utility, and noise fidelity (inter-annotator agreement >=0.80 across all dimensions), and an LLM-as-judge closely tracks their ratings, enabling scalable evaluation.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Right Frame, Wrong Rule: Cultural Cues Expose the Financial Knowledge Gap They Were Meant to Close
abstract: When multiple normative frameworks yield equally valid answers, which framework should a language model select, and can it answer correctly within it? We formalize this as normative pluralism and study it in Islamic finance with a four-choice taxonomy that decomposes framework selection from within-framework correctness. The decomposition exposes a failure mode invisible to two-choice instruments, the stereotype trap: a model leans toward the culturally appropriate framework but produces factually wrong answers within it. Across twelve models, two languages, and fifty demographic signals, cultural cues redirect framework selection at severe cost: redirection and correctness are inversely coupled (r=−0.89 Arabic, r=−0.81 English). Under the strongest signal, large open-weight models reach 97% Islamic-frame selection, a result two-choice instruments would report as near-perfect alignment, yet 57-66% of those responses misquote the Islamic rule. We argue that cultural default bias is competence-conditioned routing: models default to the framework where they are most accurate, and the cues prescribed as mitigation expose the competence gap they were meant to correct.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: AREAs-Lab: An Interactive Environment for AI-driven Requirement Elicitation for AI Systems
abstract: Building effective AI systems increasingly depends on writing high-quality task requirements, yet users often struggle to articulate the constraints, preferences, and edge cases that determine success. This problem is especially acute in AI development, where behavior is shaped not only by human expectations but also by data characteristics. We present AREAs-Lab, an interactive environment for AI-driven Requirement Elicitation for AI systems. In AREAs-Lab, an assistant iteratively refines an initially incomplete requirement by analyzing the underlying dataset and asking targeted clarification questions to uncover the user’s latent intent. To study this setting systematically, we construct a synthetic benchmark grounded in 16 public datasets spanning diverse domains and task types. Each benchmark instance includes a user profile, a complete reference requirement, and an intentionally underspecified version that serves as the assistant’s starting point. We further introduce an automated evaluation pipeline based on an AI-simulated user that reveals hidden information only when appropriately prompted, enabling scalable and reproducible assessment of interactive elicitation quality. AREAs-Lab provides a controlled testbed for studying how AI assistants can transform vague user goals into actionable requirements for AI systems.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Counterexample Generation via Per-Theorem Symbolic Verifiers: When Imitation Hurts and Reinforcement Repairs
abstract: Large language models often solve a theorem forward yet fail to disprove a closely related false one: a falsification gap that supervised fine-tuning does not close and can actively worsen. We frame counterexample generation as constrained witness emission against a deterministic per-theorem Python verifier, and release SymCE, a corpus of 4,707 false undergraduate-algebra and real-analysis conjectures, each paired with executable verifiers. The verifier also serves as the reward function, making SymCE a training environment. Training Qwen3-4B with SFT followed by GRPO under this oracle reveals an imitation trap: counterexample-only SFT collapses true-theorem recognition from 0.27 to 0.00, while RLVR with a sparse outcome-only reward repairs this and exceeds the base, to 0.66. The collapse replicates across four seeds and on Gemma-3-4B. Sparse and dense rewards yield statistically indistinguishable in-domain success yet diverge by 33 points on a held-out calibration probe, a dissociation we trace to the partial-credit term. Our 4B model outperforms every evaluated 7B open-weights math specialist, remains competitive with six frontier commercial APIs, and transfers under unchanged prompting to GSM8K, MATH-500 and MMLU-college-math. A human audit of 177 verifier decisions finds 97.7% accuracy. Code, data, verifier modules and annotations: https://github.com/ce-rlvr/SymCE.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ERGA: An Explorer–Refiner Game with Backdoor-Adjusted Verdict Aggregation for LLM-based Claim Verification
abstract: LLM-based fact-checking verifies complex claims through decomposition, retrieval, and reasoning aggregation. Existing methods expand verification inputs to cover more factual conditions, but added fragments can be redundant or misleading, compete with decisive evidence, and bias predictions toward surface relevance. Debiasing methods mitigate this bias by estimating shortcut effects from claim-side cues or biased signals in constructed inputs. However, because they calibrate verifier predictions after input construction, they are not designed to repair missing or noisy verification states. Thus, complex fact-checking should balance factual coverage and noise control during verification-state construction. We propose ERGA, an Explorer–Refiner Game with Backdoor-Adjusted Verdict Aggregation. ERGA formulates verification as editable state construction, initializing the state from decomposed verification units, retrieved evidence, and local analyses. It then runs an adversarial Explorer–Refiner game over this state: the Explorer strengthens under-covered factual signals, while the Refiner merges redundancy and separates weak or misleading fragments. Through this game interaction, ERGA obtains a refined state with a better coverage–noise balance and a removed fragment record. For verdict aggregation, ERGA uses the removed-fragment record to condition verifier predictions and aggregates them in a backdoor-adjusted form to reduce residual shortcut effects. Experiments on HoVer and FEVEROUS-S show that ERGA outperforms strong baselines.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Identifying Crucial Attention Heads for Multilingual Language Models: Retrieval and Retrieval-Transition Heads
abstract: Retrieval heads, a subset of attention heads in Transformers, were studied in English, showing its crucial role in retrieving information from the context. We expand the study of retrieval heads to multilingual context and find that while nearly half of all retrieval heads are often shared across multiple languages, language-specific retrieval heads also emerge. We further design a cross-lingual needle-in-the-haystack task, to identify \textit{Retrieval Transition Heads (RTH)} that retrieve key information and further map it to target-language output. Our experiments reveal that RTHs do not always overlap with RH, and can be more vital for Chain-of-Thought reasoning in multilingual LLMs. Across four multilingual benchmarks (MMLU-ProX, MGSM, MLQA, and XQuAD) and two model families (Qwen2.5-7B Instruct and Llama3.1-8B Instruct), we demonstrate that masking RTH induces bigger performance drop than masking Retrieval Heads (RH). Specifically, for Llama3.1-8B Instruct, masking the top-25 RTHs results in an average 37.3-point drop (against 19.5-point drop from RH masking) in reasoning accuracy (MMLU-ProX, MGSM) and 9.0 F1-score reduction (against 5.1 drop for RH) in extractive QA (MLQA, XQuAD). Our work advances the understanding of multilingual LMs by isolating the attention heads responsible for mapping to target languages. Code available at https://github.com/NerdyVisky/multilingual-retrieval-transition-heads

title: Separating Syntax from Language: A Mechanistic Account of Translation in Multilingual LLMs
abstract: Multilingual large language models (mLLMs) achieve strong performance in machine translation, yet our understanding of the mechanisms by which they transform representations from one language to another remains incomplete. Prior work suggests that translation decomposes into separable processes within an mLLM, where conceptual content is first represented independently, followed by a production into language-specific form.In this work, we show that translation is even more modular than previously assumed and that the output language production in translation processes is actually further separable into a syntax and a surface language process. We construct controlled multilingual datasets that isolate cross-linguistic differences in word order and use causal interventions and probing to track how representations are transformed during translation. We find that models first construct target-side word order before realizing the target language surface form. We identify individual attention heads that are selectively sensitive to syntactic transformations while remaining largely invariant to language identity. These results establish the commitment to a syntactic structure as an independent stage in translation, extending prior decompositions and showing how translation is implemented by functionally different components within mLLMs.

title: Structural Collapse of Safety-Critical Weight Protection Scorers Under Group-Wise Post-Training Quantization
abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) of instruction-tuned LLMs to 3 bits often destroys safety alignment, motivating safety-protection methods that keep a small budget of "safety-critical" weight blocks in full precision. We give a theoretical account of the many scoring rules proposed to choose those blocks. We prove that under symmetric group-wise PTQ the Taylor (SSMP) scorer concentrates to the gradient magnitude times a per-group constant; the gradient-times-weight (SNIP) scorer is empirically near-identical, so the entire compound family \alpha|g\cdot w|+\beta|g\cdot\delta w| collapses to a single block ranking (worst-case Spearman 0.9971), and only pure magnitude or pure Fisher selects different blocks. We further show that recovered refusal behavior under small budgets is decoupled from the underlying safety mechanism: refusal can be restored while capability, adversarial robustness, and over-refusal balance stay at the unprotected level; at 3 bits heuristic attack metrics conflate incoherence with harm; and on weakly-aligned models protection raises classifier-judged attack success above the unprotected floor. Experiments on five open-weight 8–9B models across 110 conditions, including classifier-judged GCG and PAIR attacks and activation-level analysis, confirm every prediction; a four-category classification predictable from one baseline metric explains the cross-model variation. Code and configurations: https://github.com/jc-su/Safepress.

title: A Multi-Agent Approach for Claim Verification from Tabular Data Documents
abstract: We present a novel approach for claim verification from tabular data documents. Recent LLM-based approaches either employ complex pretraining/fine-tuning or decompose verification into subtasks, often lacking comprehensive explanations and generalizability. To address these limitations, we propose a Multi-Agentic framework for Claim vErification (MACE) consisting of three specialized agents: Planner, Executor, and Verifier. Instead of elaborate fine-tuning, each agent employs a zero-shot Chain-of-Thought setup to perform its tasks. MACE produces interpretable verification traces, with the Planner generating explicit reasoning strategies, the Executor providing detailed computation steps, and the Verifier validating the logic. Experiments demonstrate that MACE achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on two datasets and performs on par with the best models on two others, while achieving 80–100% of best performance with substantially smaller models: 27–92B parameters versus 235B. This combination of competitive performance, memory efficiency, and transparent reasoning highlights our framework’s effectiveness.

title: Morphological Analysis and Disambiguation of Agglutinative Assamese through Rule-Based Synthesis and Neural Candidate Ranking
abstract: Assamese is a highly agglutinative language that uses suffix sequences to convey various kinds of information. A single morpheme may exhibit multiple syntactic or semantic functions depending on its position in a word and the preceding morpheme. Such ambiguities and the inadequacy of supervised data make morphological analysis difficult for Assamese. Our approach is based on the observation that a word has a limited set of valid morphological analyses, among which one is contextually the most appropriate. We curate a morphological lexicon, a bigram transition rule set, and several derivational rules, which our rule-based analyzer uses to generate valid analyses of a word by segmenting its surface form. The rule-based analyzer facilitates context-based annotation of over 11.8K tokens across more than 1K sentences. We construct morphological feature vectors from each analysis of a word and train a neural model to discriminate between correct and incorrect sequences of morphological vectors. The trained model is evaluated on the task of assigning the highest score to the correct sequence of morphological vectors among all the candidate sequences. The model achieves a word-level disambiguation accuracy of 80.76% by resolving 1045 out of 1294 ambiguities on the test set without using lexical semantics. The results indicate regularity in sentence-level morphological patterns. The annotated dataset and other resources are available at https://github.com/Pragyanur/morphological-analysis-assamese.

title: When Chatbots Accommodate: Auditing the Response Policies of AI Companions in Vulnerable Conversations
abstract: Millions turn to AI companion chatbots during loneliness, grief, and personal crises. How these companion platforms respond in such moments can shape the trajectory of a user’s vulnerable state. Yet existing model audits evaluate reactions to pre-defined crisis prompts and miss the response policy that governs sustained real-world interaction. We address these gaps with two key contributions. First, we introduce the AI Companion Vulnerability-Response Taxonomy, a grounded, paired taxonomy of user vulnerability and chatbot response designed for analyzing extended companion chatbot interactions. Second, we apply Maximum Causal Entropy Inverse Reinforcement Learning to ~47k turns of real-world user conversations with GPT-4.1, Character.AI, and Replika to infer each platform’s short-horizon response policy: the probability of each response category given the user’s current vulnerability state. Our findings reveal distinct response profiles of AI companions in conversations with vulnerable users: GPT-4.1 reaches for advice, Character.AI spreads its response across different strategies, and Replika consistently asks questions and stays present. Over four weeks of repeated interaction, GPT-4.1 asks progressively fewer follow-up questions when users are distressed and increasingly sets boundaries or refers users out rather than pushing back. Within each platform, exploratory comparisons across user groups suggest that response policies also differ with users’ pre-existing psychological risks and their bonds with the companion. Estimated model response policies are invisible to shallow behavioral audits, providing a new lens for auditing chatbots in the wild and enabling more realistic safety evaluation.

title: Balanced Aggregation: Understanding and Fixing Aggregation Bias in GRPO
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a central paradigm for improving reasoning and code generation in large language models, and GRPO-style training is widely adopted for its simplicity and effectiveness. However, an important design choice remains underexplored: how token-level policy gradient terms are aggregated within each sampled group. Standard GRPO uses sequence aggregation, while recent work has advocated token aggregation as a better alternative. We show that these two rules induce different optimization biases: token aggregation introduces sign-length coupling, while sequence aggregation implicitly downweights longer responses through sequence-level equal weighting. To address this tension, we propose Balanced Aggregation (BA), a simple drop-in replacement that computes token-level means separately within the positive and negative subsets and then combines them with sequence-count-based weights. Experiments with Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Qwen3-1.7B on DAPO-17k and Polaris, evaluated on six reasoning and coding benchmarks, show that BA consistently improves training stability and final performance over standard token and sequence aggregation. Our analysis further shows that the relative effectiveness of token and sequence aggregation is largely governed by response-length variation and the positive-negative length gap, highlighting aggregation as a critical design dimension in GRPO-style RLVR.

title: PACEShop: Evaluating Personalized, Actionable, Compositional, and Evidence-grounded Shopping Assistants
abstract: Shopping assistants are shifting from ranked product lists toward structured decision support, where systems must synthesize shopper context, product evidence, and next-step guidance into a coherent recommendation experience. This changes the unit of evaluation: a fluent response can still fail by ignoring shopper context, contradicting itself across components, or leaving defects too vague to localize. Existing personalization, grounding, and LLM-as-a-judge benchmarks cover pieces of this problem, but they do not define a joint evaluation target for structured shopping-assistant responses. We formulate this missing evaluation target as PACE: Personalized, Actionable, Compositional, and Evidence-grounded evaluation. We instantiate PACE with two artifacts: PACEShop, a benchmark dataset that makes the target measurable through 22,625 controlled records with structured personas, auditable evidence pools, GOOD/BAD labels, and gold defect family and location annotations; and PACEJudge, a training-free judging protocol that makes the target reportable through a structured output contract. Our experiments show that generic judges can recognize broad quality but fail to recover the diagnostic fields required for PACE; PACEShop makes these failures verifiable, and PACEJudge improves persona-source, cross-component, grounding, and family/location closure without retraining, showing that realistic shopping-assistant evaluation requires a task-matched output contract rather than only a stronger backbone or scalar prompt.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TRIS: A Tri-Layer Retrieval Integrity Sieve Against Knowledge Poisoning
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external corpora, but implicit trust in retrieved documents creates a critical attack surface: PoisonedRAG shows that a handful of crafted passages can dominate dense retrieval and steer generation toward attacker-chosen answers. We present the Tri-Layer Sieve, a middleware defense that sanitizes retrieved evidence through cross-embedding-space clustering with an independent judge model, structural filtering of trigger–payload artifacts, and LLM consistency verification. The design exploits a key weakness of retrieval-stage poisoning: a single document must satisfy one embedding geometry, one internal Trigger–Payload structure, and one generation objective — rarely all three simultaneously, a fragility that persists even against an adaptive attacker who paraphrases around it. On Natural Questions, HotpotQA, and MS-MARCO with Contriever retrieval (k=50), the Sieve reduces black-box Attack Success Rate from 67.0/87.0/64.0% to 3.0/14.0/4.0%, mitigates white-box HotFlip attacks from \sim74% to 27.8% on NQ with Layer 3 enabled, and drives poisoned-document MRR to 0.000, while restoring clean accuracy from 13–33% under attack to 58–76%. Under an architecture-aware adversary who paraphrases triggers to evade the structural filter, enabling the consistency layer halves adaptive ASR (32.0% \to 15.0% on NQ) while raising clean accuracy by 18 points, at an added latency of \sim\!16–19 s/query under live retrieval.

title: PPE-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating MLLM Unlearning under Private-Public Entanglement
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong capabilities, but they may memorize private information from web data, raising privacy concerns. Machine unlearning offers a way to remove such private knowledge without retraining from scratch. However, existing MLLM unlearning benchmarks have two major limitations. First, they rely on simplified images that contain only the single target individual, failing to reflect the visual complexity of real-world photos. Second, they typically assume that the forget set and retain set are fully separated, ignoring the fact that private information is often visually entangled with benign public information. For example, a private individual may appear with a public figure or in front of a well-known landmark, where unlearning the private target should not damage the public context. To address these limitations, we propose PPE-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating MLLM unlearning under private-public entanglement. Each image contains a target individual to be forgotten and public information to be preserved, including public figure and landmark. We further introduce two simple but effective methods to better preserve public information during unlearning. Through experiments, we find that existing unlearning methods can reduce private information leakage, but often substantially harm adjacent public information.
booktitle: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TRACER: Trace-Regularized Training Against Indirect Prompt Injection
abstract: Indirect prompt injection exploits a core tension in LLM systems: models must use retrieved documents, tool outputs, and agent messages that are useful but untrusted. Existing defenses are often trained and evaluated within a single presentation wrapper, implicitly assuming that robustness transfers across framings. We show that this assumption is unsafe: for a model trained to resist malicious follow-up messages, the same injected instruction succeeds only 18% of the time as a follow-up message, but 53% of the time when embedded in retrieved context. Thus, robustness is not payload-only; it is channel-conditioned. We address this with TRACER (Trace-Regularized Adversarial Channel Exposure with Reward-shaping), a channel-aware adversarial training algorithm that treats the wrapper as part of the optimization problem. TRACER combines channel-sampled adversarial exposure with two training components: an answer-anchored, evidence-gated composite reward for post-attack behavior, and ATRC, a trace-regularization loss that aligns attacked reasoning with clean anchor spans when injected evidence is invalid. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, TRACER reduces RAG-framed ASR from 65.5% to 6.1%, while preserving 78–82% clean accuracy. Cross-framing experiments reveal a depth–breadth trade-off: RAG-specialized training gives the strongest native defense, tool-output training transfers most uniformly, and joint RAG+tool training achieves the best 3B average ASR of 13.9%. At 7B scale, a single epoch reaches 9.4% average ASR. TRACER substantially narrows the framing gap, highlighting the need to train and evaluate defenses across deployment channels.
